The Chapter on Impermanence (Aniccavagga) The Discourse on Internal Impermanence (Ajjhattāniccasutta) At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, whatever is impermanent is suffering; whatever is suffering is non-self; whatever is non-self should be seen with right wisdom as it really is: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self. When this was said, a certain bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, what now is impermanent? What is suffering? What is non-self? “Bhikkhu, the eye is impermanent; that which is impermanent is suffering; that which is suffering is non-self; that which is non-self should be seen with right wisdom as it really is: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self. “The ear is impermanent... The nose is impermanent... The tongue is impermanent... The body is impermanent... The mind is impermanent; that which is impermanent is suffering; that which is suffering is non-self; that which is non-self should be seen with right wisdom as it really is: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self. “Venerable sir, it is wonderful, it is marvelous! How well this has been stated by the Blessed One: ‘Whatever is impermanent is suffering; whatever is suffering is non-self; whatever is non-self should be seen with right wisdom as it really is: “This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self. “Bhikkhu, if one were to say: ‘I shall show you the way leading to the cessation of form,’ that would be a mere word. If one were to say: ‘I shall show you the way leading to the cessation of feeling... perception... volitional formations... consciousness,’ that would be a mere word. But when it is said: ‘I shall show you the way leading to the cessation of ignorance,’ that is not a mere word. For, bhikkhu, through the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance comes the cessation of volitional formations; through the cessation of volitional formations comes the cessation of consciousness; through the cessation of consciousness comes the cessation of name-and-form; through the cessation of name-and-form comes the cessation of the six sense bases; through the cessation of the six sense bases comes the cessation of contact; through the cessation of contact comes the cessation of feeling; through the cessation of feeling comes the cessation of craving; through the cessation of craving comes the cessation of clinging; through the cessation of clinging comes the cessation of existence; through the cessation of existence comes the cessation of birth; through the cessation of birth, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair cease. Such is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering. Thus, bhikkhu, the way leading to the cessation of suffering has been shown by me. When this was said, that bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it is wonderful, it is marvelous! How well this has been stated by the Blessed One: ‘Whatever is impermanent is suffering; whatever is suffering is non-self; whatever is non-self should be seen with right wisdom as it really is: “This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self. “Bhikkhu, if one were to say: ‘I shall show you the way leading to the cessation of form,’ that would be a mere word. If one were to say: ‘I shall show you the way leading to the cessation of feeling... perception... volitional formations... consciousness,’ that would be a mere word. But when it is said: ‘I shall show you the way leading to the cessation of ignorance,’ that is not a mere word. For, bhikkhu, through the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance comes the cessation of volitional formations; through the cessation of volitional formations comes the cessation of consciousness; through the cessation of consciousness comes the cessation of name-and-form; through the cessation of name-and-form comes the cessation of the six sense bases; through the cessation of the six sense bases comes the cessation of contact; through the cessation of contact comes the cessation of feeling; through the cessation of feeling comes the cessation of craving; through the cessation of craving comes the cessation of clinging; through the cessation of clinging comes the cessation of existence; through the cessation of existence comes the cessation of birth; through the cessation of birth, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair cease. Such is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering. Thus, bhikkhu, the way leading to the cessation of suffering has been shown by me. Thus have I heard.
At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
“Monks,” [the Blessed One said]. “Venerable sir,” those monks replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One spoke as follows:
“Bhikkhus, the eye is impermanent.
What is impermanent is suffering;
what is suffering is non-self.”
That which is not-self should be seen as it really is with correct wisdom thus: “This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.
The ear is impermanent.
That which is impermanent... [and so on].
The nose is impermanent.
Whatever is impermanent … [as before] … the tongue is impermanent.
What is impermanent is suffering;
what is suffering is non-self.
What is non-self should be seen as it really is with correct wisdom thus: “This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.”
The body is impermanent.
That which is impermanent ... [and so on] ... the mind is impermanent.
What is impermanent is suffering;
what is suffering is non-self.
What is non-self should be seen as it really is with correct wisdom thus: "This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self."

Seeing thus, monks, the well-taught noble disciple becomes disenchanted with the eye, disenchanted with the ear, disenchanted with the nose, disenchanted with the tongue, disenchanted with the body, and disenchanted with the mind. Through disenchantment, he becomes dispassionate;
through dispassion, he is liberated. In liberation, the knowledge arises: "It is liberated."
‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.
This is the first [discourse]. *Saṃyutta Nikāya* 35.2 (SN 35.2, PTS SN iv 2).
1. The Chapter on Impermanence:
The Discourse on Internal Suffering “Bhikkhus, the eye is suffering.”
That which is suffering is non-self;
that which is non-self should be seen as it really is with correct wisdom thus: "This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.
The ear is suffering … [and so on] …
The nose is suffering; ...
the tongue is suffering; ...
the body is suffering; ...
The mind is suffering.
That which is suffering is non-self;
that which is non-self should be seen as it really is with correct wisdom thus: “This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.”
"Seeing thus...
he understands: 'There is nothing further beyond this state.
This is the second [sutta].

Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.3 (SN 35.3, PTS SN iv 2) 1. The Chapter on Impermanence The Discourse on the Non-Self of the Internal At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, the eye is non-self. Whatever is non-self is not mine; that is not my self; that is not what I am. Thus, as it actually is with right wisdom, it should be seen as it is: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self. “The ear is non-self... The nose is non-self... The tongue is non-self... The body is non-self... The mind is non-self. Whatever is non-self is not mine; that is not my self; that is not what I am. Thus, as it actually is with right wisdom, it should be seen as it is: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self. “Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the instructed noble disciple experiences revulsion toward the eye, revulsion toward the ear, revulsion toward the nose, revulsion toward the tongue, revulsion toward the body, revulsion toward the mind. Experiencing revulsion, he becomes dispassionate. Through dispassion [his mind] is liberated. When it is liberated there comes the knowledge: ‘It is liberated.’”
“Bhikkhus, the eye is not-self.
That which is not-self should be seen as it really is with correct wisdom thus: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.
The ear is not-self … [and so on for the other sense bases].”
The nose is not-self;
… the tongue is not-self;
… the body is not-self; …
The mind is non-self.
That which is non-self should be seen as it really is with correct wisdom thus: "This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.
Seeing thus... [as before]...
“He understands: ‘There is nothing further beyond this state of being.
Thus [ends] the third [discourse]. *Saṃyutta Nikāya* 35.4 (SN 35.4, PTS SN iv 2).
1. The Chapter on Impermanence: The Discourse on External Impermanence “Bhikkhus, forms are impermanent.”
What is impermanent is suffering;
what is suffering is non-self.
What is non-self should be seen as it really is with correct wisdom thus: "This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self."
Sounds … odors … tastes …
Tangible objects … mental phenomena are impermanent.
What is impermanent is suffering;
Whatever is suffering is non-self.
Whatever is non-self should be seen with right wisdom, exactly as it is, thus: "This is not mine; this I am not; this is not my self.

Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the well-taught noble disciple becomes disenchanted with forms, disenchanted with sounds, disenchanted with odors, disenchanted with tastes, disenchanted with tangibles, and disenchanted with mental phenomena.
“Becoming disenchanted, one becomes dispassionate; through dispassion, one is liberated. In liberation, the knowledge arises: ‘It is liberated. One understands:
‘Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.
This is the fourth.

Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.5 (SN 35.5, PTS SN iv 3) 1. Aniccavagga Bāhiradukkhasutta (The Discourse on External Suffering) “Monks, I shall teach you about external suffering and the origin of external suffering. Listen to that, and pay close attention; I will speak. “Yes, venerable sir,” those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: “And what, monks, is external suffering? It is the eye, the ear, the nose, the tongue, the body, and the mind. This, monks, is called external suffering. “And what, monks, is the origin of external suffering? It is craving, which brings renewal of being, is accompanied by delight and lust, and delights in this and that; namely, craving for sensual pleasure, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence. This, monks, is called the origin of external suffering. “This, monks, is external suffering, and this is the origin of external suffering.”
“Bhikkhus, forms are suffering.
What is suffering is non-self;
what is non-self should be seen as it really is with correct wisdom thus: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’”
Sounds … odors … tastes …
Tangible objects...
mental phenomena are suffering.
That which is suffering is non-self.
“Whatever is not-self should be seen as it really is with correct wisdom thus: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.
Seeing thus... one understands:
‘There is nothing further beyond this state of being.’”
The Fifth.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 35.6 (SN 35.6, PTS SN iv 3) 1.
The Chapter on Impermanence (Aniccavagga)
The Discourse on the External Non-Self:
“Bhikkhus, forms are non-self.
That which is non-self should be seen as it really is with correct wisdom thus: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’”
Sounds … smells … tastes …
Tangible objects ...
mental phenomena are not-self.
That which is not-self should be seen as it really is with correct wisdom thus: "This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self."
"Seeing thus...
he understands: ‘...there is nothing further beyond this state of being.
The sixth.

Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.7 Chapter 1: The Section on Impermanence (Aniccavagga) The Discourse on Internal Impermanence in the Past and Future “Bhikkhus, whatever is impermanent, whether past or future, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near—all that is impermanent. Seeing thus, bhikkhus, as it really is with correct wisdom, one grows weary of the eye, weary of forms, weary of eye-consciousness, weary of eye-contact, and weary of whatever feeling arises—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that arises dependent on eye-contact. One grows weary of the ear... of the nose... of the tongue... of the body... of the mind, weary of mental phenomena, weary of mind-consciousness, weary of mind-contact, and weary of whatever feeling arises—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that arises dependent on mind-contact. Being weary of it, one becomes dispassionate; through dispassion, one is liberated; through liberation, one knows and sees: ‘Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.’”
“Bhikkhus, the eye is impermanent— both past and future,
let alone the present.
Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the well-taught noble disciple is indifferent toward the past eye.”
He does not delight in future eye;
he practices for the sake of disenchantment with, for the fading away of lust for, and for the cessation of the present eye.
The ear is impermanent…
The nose is impermanent...
The tongue is impermanent, both past and future,
let alone the present.
Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the well-taught noble disciple is indifferent toward the past tongue;
he does not delight in the future tongue;
and he is practicing for the sake of disenchantment with, the fading away of lust for, and the cessation of the present tongue.
The body is impermanent...
[and so on] ...the mind is impermanent, both past and future;
what need is there to mention the present?
"Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the well-taught noble disciple is indifferent toward past mind;
he does not delight in future mind;
and he is practicing for the sake of disenchantment with, for the fading away of lust for, and for the cessation of present mind."
The Seventh.
Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.8 (SN 35.8, PTS SN iv 4) 1.
The Chapter on Impermanence (Aniccavagga)
The Discourse on Internal Suffering Past and Future:
“Bhikkhus, the eye is suffering in the past and in the future;
what need is there to speak of the present?
Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the well-taught noble disciple is indifferent toward the eye that has passed away;
he does not delight in the eye yet to come;
and he practices for the sake of disenchantment with, for the fading away of lust for, and for the cessation of the present eye.
The ear is suffering … the nose is suffering … the tongue is suffering, both past and future;
What need is there to speak of the present?
Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the well-taught noble disciple is indifferent toward the past tongue;
he does not delight in the future tongue.
He practices for the sake of disenchantment with, for the fading away of lust for, and for the cessation of the present tongue.
The body is suffering...
[and so on] ...the mind is suffering, both past and future.
What need is there to speak of the present?
Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the learned noble disciple is indifferent toward past mind;
he does not delight in future mind.
“He is practicing for disenchantment with, for the fading away of lust for, and for the cessation of the present mind.
The eighth.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 35.9 (SN 35.9, PTS SN iv 4).
1. The Chapter on Impermanence:
The Discourse on the Internal Non-Self in the Past and Future “Bhikkhus, the eye, whether past or future, is non-self;”
What need is there to speak of the present?
Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the learned noble disciple is indifferent toward the past eye;
he does not delight in the future eye.
He practices for the sake of disenchantment with, for the fading away of lust for, and for the cessation of the present eye.
The ear is non-self … [and so on] … the nose is non-self … [and so on] …
The tongue is non-self, both past and future;
what need is there to speak of the present?
Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the well-taught noble disciple is indifferent toward the past tongue.
He does not delight in the future tongue;
he practices for the sake of disenchantment with, for the fading away of lust for, and for the cessation of the present tongue.
The body is non-self …pe…
The mind is not-self, both past and future;
what need is there to speak of the present?
Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the well-taught noble disciple is indifferent toward the past mind.
One does not delight in future mind;
one practices for the sake of disenchantment with, dispassion toward, and the cessation of present mind. Thus ends the ninth [sutta].

Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.10 (SN 35.10, PTS SN iv 5) 1. Aniccavagga Bāhirāniccātītānāgatasutta The Discourse on the External Impermanence of the Past and Future At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, form is impermanent, both in the past and in the future. Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the instructed noble disciple experiences revulsion towards form; experiencing revulsion, he becomes dispassionate; through dispassion, he is liberated; through liberation, there is the knowledge: ‘It is liberated. “Feeling is impermanent, both in the past and in the future... Perception is impermanent, both in the past and in the future... Volitional formations are impermanent, both in the past and in the future... Consciousness is impermanent, both in the past and in the future. Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the instructed noble disciple experiences revulsion towards consciousness; experiencing revulsion, he becomes dispassionate; through dispassion, he is liberated; through liberation, there is the knowledge: ‘It is liberated.’”
“Bhikkhus, forms of the past and future are impermanent;
what need is there to speak of those of the present?
Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the well-taught noble disciple is indifferent toward forms of the past.”
He does not delight in future forms;
he practices for the sake of revulsion toward, the fading away of lust for, and the cessation of present forms.
[The same applies to] sounds...
Odors … tastes … tangibles …
Phenomena are impermanent, both past and future;
what need is there to speak of those of the present?
Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the well-taught noble disciple is indifferent toward past phenomena.
He does not delight in future phenomena;
he practices for the sake of disenchantment with, for the fading away of lust for, and for the cessation of present phenomena.
The tenth.

Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.11 Chapter 1: The Section on Impermanence (Aniccavagga) Sutta 11: External Suffering—Past and Future “Bhikkhus, whatever is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change, that is not mine, that I am not, that is not my self. This is the way it should be seen with right wisdom as it really is: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self. “Bhikkhus, what is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change? The eye is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change. Forms are impermanent, suffering, and subject to change. Eye-consciousness is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change. Eye-contact is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change. Whatever feeling arises with eye-contact as its condition—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change. “The ear... The nose... The tongue... The body... The mind is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change. Mental phenomena are impermanent, suffering, and subject to change. Mind-consciousness is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change. Mind-contact is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change. Whatever feeling arises with mind-contact as its condition—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change. “Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the instructed noble disciple experiences revulsion toward the eye, revulsion toward forms, revulsion toward eye-consciousness, revulsion toward eye-contact, and revulsion toward whatever feeling arises with eye-contact as its condition. He experiences revulsion toward the ear... the nose... the tongue... the body... the mind, revulsion toward mental phenomena, revulsion toward mind-consciousness, revulsion toward mind-contact, and revulsion toward whatever feeling arises with mind-contact as its condition. “Experiencing revulsion, he becomes dispassionate. Through dispassion, he is liberated. When liberated, there comes the knowledge: ‘It is liberated. He understands: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being.’”
“Bhikkhus, forms—past and future—are suffering;
what need is there to speak of those in the present?
Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the well-taught noble disciple is indifferent toward past forms.”
“He does not delight in future forms; he practices for the sake of revulsion toward, for the fading away of lust for, and for the cessation of present forms.
…pe… The eleventh.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 35.12 (SN 35.12, PTS SN iv 6)
1. The Chapter on Impermanence:
The Discourse on External Non-Self in the Past and Future “Bhikkhus, forms—whether past or future—are non-self.”
What need is there to speak of those of the present?
Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the well-taught noble disciple is indifferent toward past forms;
he does not delight in future forms.
He practices for the sake of revulsion toward, the fading away of lust for, and the cessation of present forms.
[The same applies to] sounds … odors … [tastes … tangibles … mental phenomena].
Tastes … tangibles … mental phenomena are non-self, whether past or future.
What need is there to speak of those of the present?
Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the well-taught noble disciple is indifferent toward past phenomena and does not delight in future phenomena.
“He is practicing for the sake of disenchantment with, for the fading away of lust for, and for the cessation of presently arisen phenomena.
The twelfth.
The first chapter on impermanence is finished.
Its summary verse:
Impermanent, suffering, and non-self;
threefold, internal and external.
Those three that were spoken of as impermanent are each both internal and external.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 35.13 (SN 35.13, PTS SN iv 6)
2. Yamaka Chapter:
The First Discourse on Formerly Before Awakening.
Setting at Sāvatthī.
“Bhikkhus, before my enlightenment, while I was still an unenlightened bodhisatta, this occurred to me:
‘What now is the gratification in the eye, what is the danger, and what is the escape? What is the gratification in the ear... [and so on].”
Who is there for the nose?
Who is there for the tongue?
Who is there for the body?
“What is the gratification, what is the danger, and what is the escape in regard to the mind?
Then, monks, this occurred to me:
“The pleasure and joy that arise dependent upon the eye—this is the gratification of the eye.”
That the eye is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—this is the danger in the eye.

That the removal of desire and lust for the eye, the abandoning of desire and lust for the eye—this is the escape from the eye. That the ear is [impermanent, suffering, and subject to change] …pe… [and so on for the remaining sense bases].
Whatever pleasure and gladness arise in dependence on the nose... [and so on] ...whatever pleasure and gladness arise in dependence on the tongue, this is the gratification in the tongue.
That the tongue is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—this is the danger in the tongue.
The removal of desire and lust for the tongue, the abandoning of desire and lust for the tongue— this is the escape from the tongue.
That pleasure and joy which arise in dependence on the body … [and so on] … that pleasure and joy which arise in dependence on the mind— this is the gratification of the mind.
‘That the mind is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—this is the danger in the mind.
The removal of desire and lust for the mind, the abandoning of desire and lust for the mind—this is the escape from the mind.
As long as I, monks, [did not directly know] in this way the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding these six internal sense bases...
As long as I did not understand, as they really are, the gratification in terms of gratification, the danger in terms of danger, and the escape in terms of escape, I did not, monks,
claim to have awakened to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment in this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, in this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans.
But when, monks, I had thus directly known, as they really are, the gratification in these six internal sense-bases as gratification,
the danger as danger, and the escape as escape, then, monks,
in this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, among this generation with its ascetics and brahmins...
“Among gods and humans, I claimed to have fully awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.
And knowledge and vision arose in me:
‘My liberation is unshakable; this is my last birth; now there is no further existence.’”
First.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 35.14 (SN 35.14, PTS SN iv 8) 2.
Yamakavagga (The Book of Pairs)
The Second Discourse on Formerly Unawakened:
“Monks, before my awakening, while I was still unawakened and a bodhisatta, this occurred to me:
‘What now is the gratification in forms, what the danger, and what the escape?’”
Who [owns] sounds?
… Who [owns] odors?
… Who [owns] tastes? …
‘What is the gratification, what is the danger, and what is the escape in the case of tangibles… what is the gratification, what is the danger,
and what is the escape in the case of mental phenomena? Then, monks, this occurred to me:
‘Whatever pleasure and joy arise in dependence on forms: this is the gratification in forms.
That forms are impermanent, suffering, and subject to change: this is the danger in forms.
The removal of desire and lust for forms, the abandoning of desire and lust for forms: this is the escape from forms.’
Whatever [is felt] in regard to sound … odor … taste …
In tangible objects...
whatever pleasure and joy arise in dependence on mental phenomena: this is the gratification in mental phenomena.
That mental phenomena are impermanent, suffering, and subject to change: this is the danger in mental phenomena.
‘The removal of desire and lust for phenomena, the abandoning of desire and lust for phenomena— this is the escape from phenomena. Monks,
as long as I did not directly know these six external sense bases as they really are— in terms of their gratification as gratification,
their danger as danger, and the escape from them as escape— I did not, for that long, [claim to have awakened].”
“Monks, in this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, among this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans,
I claimed to have awakened to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.
And from the time, monks, that I had thus seen the gratification in these six external sense bases as gratification...”
When I had fully understood, as they really are, the danger in what is dangerous and the escape from what provides escape,
then, monks, in this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, among this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans,
I claimed to have awakened to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.
"And the knowledge and vision arose in me:
‘My liberation is unshakable; this is my last birth; now there is no further becoming. This is the second [sutta].

Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.15 (SN 35.15, PTS SN iv 8) 2. Yamaka-vagga First Discourse on the Search for Gratification Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus! “Venerable sir,” they replied. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, when a noble disciple has truly seen as it really is with correct wisdom how things have come to be, he does not seek gratification in the eye; he does not seek gratification in the ear; he does not seek gratification in the nose; he does not seek gratification in the tongue; he does not seek gratification in the body; he does not seek gratification in the mind. Why is that? Because, bhikkhus, the gratification in these things has been well seen by him as it really is with correct wisdom, and their danger has been well seen, and the escape from them has been well seen. [The Buddha then spoke in detail regarding each sense-faculty: “Bhikkhus, when a noble disciple has truly seen as it really is with correct wisdom how things have come to be, he does not seek gratification in forms cognizable by the eye... in sounds cognizable by the ear... in odors cognizable by the nose... in tastes cognizable by the tongue... in tangibles cognizable by the body... in mental phenomena cognizable by the mind; he does not seek gratification in the consciousness associated with those mental phenomena. Why is that? Because, bhikkhus, the gratification in these things has been well seen by him as it really is with correct wisdom, and their danger has been well seen, and the escape from them has been well seen. When this was said, a certain bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “But, venerable sir, what is the gratification in the eye? What is the danger in the eye? What is the escape from the eye? “The gratification in the eye, bhikkhu, is its pleasure and joy. The danger in the eye is its impermanence, suffering, and changeability. The escape from the eye is its complete dispassion, its fading away, and its cessation. [The same structure is repeated for each sense-faculty and its respective objects. “When, bhikkhus, a noble disciple has thus abandoned the five lower fetters, he is due to reappear spontaneously [in the Pure Abodes] and there attain final Nibbāna, without ever returning from that world. This is called a noble disciple who is a stream-enterer, no longer subject to perdition, bound for enlightenment, assured, destined for Nibbāna. This is what the Blessed One said. Elated, those bhikkhus delighted in the Blessed One’s words. *End of Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.15: The First Discourse on the Search for Gratification.*
“Bhikkhus, I set out in search of the gratification in the eye.
I discovered whatever gratification there was in the eye;
I have clearly seen with wisdom to the full extent of the gratification in the eye.
“Bhikkhus, I set out in search of the danger in the eye.
Whatever danger there is in the eye, that I discovered.
To whatever extent there is danger in the eye, that has been clearly seen by me with wisdom.”
“Bhikkhus, I set out seeking the escape from the eye.
I attained that which is the escape from the eye;
to the full extent of the escape from the eye, it was well-seen by me through wisdom.”
“Bhikkhus, in regard to the ear… in regard to the nose… in regard to the tongue,
I set out on a search for its gratification.”
Whatever gratification there is in the tongue, that I have discovered.
To whatever extent there is gratification in the tongue, that has been clearly seen by me through wisdom.
Monks, I pursued the search for the danger in the tongue.
Whatever danger there is in the tongue, that I have understood.
To whatever extent there is danger in the tongue, that has been clearly seen by me through wisdom.
Monks, I pursued the search for escape from the tongue.
I attained that which is the escape from the tongue.
To whatever extent there is an escape from the tongue, that has been well-seen by me through wisdom...
Monks, I pursued the search for the gratification of the mind.
Whatever gratification there is in the mind, that I have attained.
To whatever extent there is gratification in the mind, that has been clearly seen by me through wisdom.
Monks, I pursued the search for the danger in the mind.
Whatever danger there is in the mind, that I have attained.
To whatever extent there is danger in the mind, that has been clearly seen by me through wisdom.
Monks, I pursued the search for escape from the mind.
I attained that which is the escape from the mind.
To whatever extent there is an escape from the mind, that has been clearly seen by me through wisdom.

Monks, as long as I did not understand, as they really are, the gratification in these six internal sense bases as gratification, the danger as danger, and the escape as escape … [as before] … I did not claim to have awakened to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment in this world with its devas, Māra, and Brahmā, in this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans. But when I had understood, as they really are, the gratification in these six internal sense bases as gratification, the danger as danger, and the escape as escape, then it was, monks, that I claimed to have awakened to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment in this world with its devas, Māra, and Brahmā, in this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans. And this knowledge and vision of mine arose: ‘Unshakable is my liberation of mind; this is my last birth; now there is no more renewed existence.’”
I acknowledged it.
And knowledge and vision arose in me:
‘My liberation is unshakable; this is my last birth; now there is no more renewed existence.’”
Third.
Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.16 (SN 35.16, PTS SN iv 9) 2.
Yamaka-vagga (The Book of Pairs)
The Second Discourse on the Search for Gratification:
“Bhikkhus, I set out in search of the gratification in forms.
Whatever gratification there is in forms, that I discovered.”
"To the extent that there is gratification in forms, that has been well seen by me through wisdom.
Monks, I pursued the search for the danger in forms,
and I discovered whatever danger there was in forms."
To whatever extent there is danger in forms, that has been clearly seen by me through wisdom.
Monks, I pursued the search for escape from forms,
and I attained that which is the escape from forms.
To whatever extent there is an escape from forms, that has been well seen by me through wisdom.
As for sounds, monks... as for odors, monks...
"Bhikkhus, I pursued the search for gratification in tastes... in tangibles... in mental phenomena, bhikkhus."
Whatever gratification there is in phenomena, that I have attained.
To whatever extent there is gratification in phenomena, that has been clearly seen by me through wisdom.
Monks, I undertook a search for the danger in phenomena.
Whatever danger there is in phenomena, that I have fully understood.
To the full extent of the danger in phenomena, it has been clearly seen by me through wisdom.
Monks, I set out in search of the escape from phenomena.
I attained that which is the escape from phenomena. To whatever extent there is an escape from phenomena, that has been clearly seen by me through wisdom.

Monks, as long as I did not understand, as they really are, the gratification in these six external sense bases as gratification, the danger as danger, and the escape as escape... [as before] ...I did not claim to have fully awakened to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment in this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, in this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans. But when I had understood, as they really are, the gratification in these six external sense bases as gratification, the danger as danger, and the escape as escape... [as before] ...I claimed to have fully awakened to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment in this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, in this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans. It is in this way that I am Tathāgata, Arahant, and Perfectly Enlightened One.”
And knowledge and vision arose in me:
“Unshakable is my liberation; this is my last birth; now there is no more renewed existence. Thus it was for the fourth time.

Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.17 Yamakavagga Paṭhamanoceassādasutta “Bhikkhus, if one were to say: ‘There is no pleasure in the world that is not accompanied by suffering,’ this would be an improper statement. For what reason? Because there is indeed pleasure in the world that is not accompanied by suffering. If one were to say: ‘There is no suffering in the world that is not accompanied by pleasure,’ this would be an improper statement. For what reason? Because there is indeed suffering in the world that is not accompanied by pleasure. If one were to say: ‘There is no pleasure in the world that is not accompanied by happiness,’ this would be an improper statement. For what reason? Because there is indeed pleasure in the world that is not accompanied by happiness. If one were to say: ‘There is no happiness in the world that is not accompanied by pleasure,’ this would be an improper statement. For what reason? Because there is indeed happiness in the world that is not accompanied by pleasure.”
“Bhikkhus, if there were no gratification in the eye, beings would not become infatuated with the eye. But because there is gratification in the eye, beings become infatuated with it.
If there were no danger in the eye, beings would not become disenchanted with the eye.”
But because, monks, there is a danger in the eye, beings become disenchanted with the eye.
If, monks, there were no escape from the eye, beings would not escape from the eye.
But because, monks, there is an escape from the eye, beings do escape from the eye.
If, monks, there were no gratification in the ear...
if, monks, there were no gratification in the nose...
if, monks, there were no gratification in the tongue, beings would not become infatuated with the tongue.
But because, monks, there is gratification in the tongue, beings are infatuated with the tongue.
If, monks, there were no danger in the tongue, beings would not become disenchanted with the tongue.
But because, monks, there is danger in the tongue, beings become disenchanted with the tongue.
If, monks, there were no escape from the tongue, beings would not escape from the tongue.
But because, monks, there is an escape from the tongue, beings escape from the tongue.
If, monks, there were no gratification in the body...
If, monks, there were no gratification in the mind, beings would not become infatuated with the mind.
But because there is gratification in the mind, monks, beings become infatuated with the mind.
If, monks, there were no danger in the mind, beings would not become disenchanted with the mind.
But because, monks, there is a danger in the mind, beings become disenchanted with the mind.
If, monks, there were no escape from the mind, beings would not escape from the mind.
But because, monks, there is an escape from the mind, beings escape from the mind.
“Bhikkhus, as long as beings have not directly known, as they really are, the gratification as gratification, the danger as danger, and the escape as escape regarding these six internal sense bases,
so long, bhikkhus, will beings not be freed from this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, from this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans.”
They dwelt with a mind that had escaped, was detached, and was completely liberated, having made an end of the boundaries [of the round].

But when, monks, beings have directly known, as it really is, the gratification in terms of gratification, the danger in terms of danger, and the escape in terms of escape regarding these six internal sense bases, then, monks—
“Beings— this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans— dwell having escaped from it,
detached from it, completely liberated, with a mind that has transcended all boundaries.
Thus ends the fifth [discourse].

Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.18 (SN 35.18, PTS SN iv 12) 2. Yamakavagga The Second Discourse on If There Were No Gratification (Noceassādasutta) “Bhikkhus, if there were no gratification in the eye, the world would not be ensnared by the eye; they would not find delight in the eye, and this world would not be held in bondage by the eye. But because there is gratification in the eye, the world is ensnared by the eye; they find delight in the eye, and this world is held in bondage by the eye. “If there were no gratification in the ear... in the nose... in the tongue... in the body... in the mind, the world would not be ensnared by the mind; they would not find delight in the mind, and this world would not be held in bondage by the mind. But because there is gratification in the mind, the world is ensnared by the mind; they find delight in the mind, and this world is held in bondage by the mind. “If there were no danger in the eye, the world would not be repelled by the eye; they would not seek escape from the eye, and this world would not be held in bondage by the eye. But because there is danger in the eye, the world is repelled by the eye; they seek escape from the eye, and this world is held in bondage by the eye. “If there were no danger in the ear... in the nose... in the tongue... in the body... in the mind, the world would not be repelled by the mind; they would not seek escape from the mind, and this world would not be held in bondage by the mind. But because there is danger in the mind, the world is repelled by the mind; they seek escape from the mind, and this world is held in bondage by the mind. “If there were no escape from the eye, the world would not be released from the eye; they would not find liberation in the eye, and this world would not be held in bondage by the eye. But because there is an escape from the eye, the world is released from the eye; they find liberation in the eye, and this world is held in bondage by the eye. “If there were no escape from the ear... in the nose... in the tongue... in the body... in the mind, the world would not be released from the mind; they would not find liberation in the mind, and this world would not be held in bondage by the mind. But because there is an escape from the mind, the world is released from the mind; they find liberation in the mind, and this world is held in bondage by the mind.”
“Bhikkhus, if there were no gratification in forms, beings would not become infatuated with forms. But because there is gratification in forms, beings become infatuated with them.
Bhikkhus, if there were no danger in forms, beings would not experience revulsion toward forms.”
But because, monks, there is a danger in forms, beings grow weary of forms.
If, monks, there were no escape from forms, beings would not escape from forms.
But because, monks, there is an escape from forms, beings escape from forms.
Do not give way, monks, to sounds...
to odors...
to tastes...
If there were no gratification in tangibles ... or in mental phenomena, beings would not become infatuated with mental phenomena.
But because there is gratification in mental phenomena, monks, beings become infatuated with them.
If, monks, there were no danger in phenomena, beings would not become disenchanted with phenomena.
But because there is danger in phenomena, monks, beings become disenchanted with them.
If, monks, there were no escape from phenomena, beings would not escape from phenomena.
But because, monks, there is an escape from phenomena, therefore beings escape from phenomena. And as long as, monks,
beings have not understood, as they really are, the gratification as gratification, the danger as danger, and the escape as escape regarding these six external sense bases, for that long—
“Monks, beings in this world— with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, and among this generation with its ascetics and brahmins,
its devas and humans— had escaped, were detached, and were utterly liberated, dwelling with a mind that had transcended all boundaries. But when, monks,
beings [perceived] the gratification in these six external sense-bases as gratification...”
When they have directly known, as it really is, the danger as danger and the escape as escape, then, monks, beings—
along with the world of devas, Māras, and Brahmās, and this generation with its ascetics and brahmins,
its devas and humans— become escaped, detached, and utterly liberated, dwelling with a mind for which the boundaries of the realm of Māra are no more.”
Sixth. Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.19 (SN 35.19, PTS SN iv 13) 2.
Yamaka Vagga (The Book of Pairs)
The First Discourse on Delighting:
“Monks, whoever delights in the eye delights in suffering.
Whoever delights in suffering, I say, is not liberated from suffering.”
Whoever delights in the ear … whoever delights in the nose … whoever delights in the tongue, he delights in suffering.
"Whoever delights in suffering, I say, is not liberated from suffering.
Whoever delights in the body...
[and so on] ... whoever delights in the mind, that person delights in suffering."
“Whoever delights in suffering, I say, is not liberated from suffering.
“But whoever, monks, does not delight in the eye, he does not delight in suffering.
Whoever does not delight in suffering, I say, is liberated from suffering.”
Whoever does not delight in the ear …pe… whoever does not delight in the nose …pe… whoever does not delight in the tongue, he does not delight in suffering.
Whoever does not delight in suffering, I say that person is liberated from suffering.
Whoever does not delight in the body...
[and so on] ... whoever does not delight in the mind, such a person does not delight in suffering.
“Whoever does not delight in suffering, he is liberated from suffering,” I say.
Seventh.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 35.20 (SN 35.20, PTS SN iv 13).
2. Yamaka Chapter:

The Second Discourse on Delighting “Bhikkhus, whoever delights in form delights in suffering. Whoever delights in feeling... whoever delights in perception... whoever delights in volitional formations... whoever delights in consciousness delights in suffering.”

Whoever delights in suffering, I say that person is not liberated from suffering. Whoever [delights] in sounds... in odors... [in tastes... in tangibles... in mental phenomena... whoever delights in suffering, I say that person is not liberated from suffering.
One who delights in tastes … in tangibles … in mental phenomena delights in suffering.
“Whoever delights in suffering, I say, is not liberated from suffering.
But whoever, monks, does not delight in form, he does not delight in suffering.
Whoever does not delight in suffering, I say, is liberated from suffering.”
Whoever [is attached] to sounds … smells … tastes … [or tangibles].
One does not delight in tangible objects... nor in mental phenomena; one does not delight in suffering.
I say that whoever does not delight in suffering is liberated from suffering.
Eighth. Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.21 (SN 35.21, PTS SN iv 14) 2.
Yamaka Vagga (The Book of Pairs)
The First Discourse on the Arising of Suffering:

“Bhikkhus, whatever is the arising, the persistence, the manifestation, and the appearance of the eye—that is the arising of suffering, the persistence of diseases, and the manifestation of aging and death. Whatever is the [arising, persistence, manifestation, and appearance] of the ear... [and so forth].”
Whatever [clinging] there is to the nose… whatever [clinging] there is to the tongue… whatever [clinging] there is to the body…
Whatever is the arising, the persistence, the generation, and the manifestation of the mind—that is the arising of suffering, the persistence of diseases, and the manifestation of aging and death.
And whatever, monks, is the cessation, the subsiding, and the passing away of the eye—that is the cessation of suffering, the subsiding of diseases, and the passing away of aging and death.
Whatever [is the cessation of] the ear...
Whatever [clinging] there is to the nose... whatever [clinging] there is to the tongue... whatever [clinging] there is to the body...
“The cessation, subsiding, and passing away of the mind: this is the cessation of suffering, the subsiding of diseases, and the passing away of aging and death.
The ninth [sutta].
Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.22 (SN 35.22, PTS SN iv 14).
2. The Chapter on Pairs:

The Second Discourse on the Arising of Suffering “Monks, whatever is the arising, the persistence, the manifestation, and the appearance of forms—that is the arising of suffering, the persistence of diseases, and the appearance of aging and death.”
That which [is the craving] for sounds … for odors … for tastes … [and so forth].

Whatever is the arising, the persistence, the production, and the manifestation of tactile objects... whatever is the arising, the persistence, the production, and the manifestation of mental phenomena (*dhammā*), this is the arising of suffering, the persistence of diseases, and the manifestation of aging and death.
But, monks, whatever is the cessation, the subsiding, and the passing away of forms, this is the cessation of suffering, the subsiding of diseases, and the passing away of aging and death.
That which [is the craving] for sounds … for odors … for tastes … [and so forth].

That which is the cessation, the subsiding, and the passing away of tactile objects... that which is the cessation, the subsiding, and the passing away of mental phenomena—this is the cessation of suffering, the subsiding of diseases, and the passing away of aging and death.
The Tenth.
The second chapter is the Yamaka-vagga.
Its summary verse (uddāna) is:
Two [verses] were spoken by means of Sambodha.
Two others are taught by way of gratification (*assāda*);
two by way of non-attachment (*no cetana*);
and two others by way of delight (*abhinanda*).
"Two [types of suffering] are spoken of by way of arising;
therefore, this is called a 'chapter' (*vagga*).
— *Saṃyutta Nikāya* 35.23 (SN 35.23, PTS SN iv 15)
3. The Chapter on All (Sabbavagga). The Discourse on All (Sabbasutta).
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
“Bhikkhus, I will teach you ‘the all.
Listen to that.
And what, bhikkhus, is the all?
The eye and forms, the ear and sounds, the nose and odors, the tongue and tastes, the body and tangibles, and the mind and mental phenomena—
this, monks, is called "all. Monks,
if anyone were to say this:
‘Having renounced all this, I shall prescribe something else entirely’—his words would be groundless;
when questioned, he would not be able to provide an answer, and he would fall into further distress. Why is that?
“Just as that would be, monks, outside one’s own domain.
First.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 35.24 (SN 35.24, PTS SN iv 15)
3. The Chapter on All:
The Discourse on Abandoning “Monks, I shall teach you the Dhamma for the abandoning of all things.”
Listen to that.
And what, bhikkhus, is the Dhamma for the abandoning of everything?
The eye, bhikkhus, is to be abandoned; forms are to be abandoned; eye-consciousness is to be abandoned; eye-contact is to be abandoned.
That which arises conditioned by eye-contact— whether it be pleasant, painful,
or neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling— that too must be abandoned.
…pe… The tongue must be abandoned, tastes must be abandoned, tongue-consciousness must be abandoned, and tongue-contact must be abandoned.
Whatever feeling arises conditioned by tongue-contact— whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—
that too must be abandoned.
The body must be abandoned...
The mind is to be abandoned; mental phenomena are to be abandoned; mind-consciousness is to be abandoned; mind-contact is to be abandoned;
and whatever feeling arises conditioned by mind-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too is to be abandoned.
“This, monks, is the teaching for the total abandoning of everything.
The second [discourse]. *Saṃyutta Nikāya* 35.25. (SN 35.25, PTS SN iv 16)
3. Sabbavagga:
Abhiññāpariññāpahānasutta “Bhikkhus, I will teach you the Dhamma for the sake of direct knowledge, full understanding, and abandoning of all.”
Listen to that.
And what, monks, is the Dhamma for the direct knowledge, full understanding, and abandoning of everything?
The eye, monks, is to be directly known, fully understood, and abandoned; forms are to be directly known, fully understood, and abandoned; eye-consciousness is...
Direct knowledge and full understanding are to be abandoned; eye-contact is to be abandoned through direct knowledge and full understanding;
and whatever feeling arises conditioned by eye-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too is to be abandoned through direct knowledge and full understanding.

…pe… The tongue is to be abandoned through direct knowledge and full understanding; tastes are to be abandoned through direct knowledge and full understanding; tongue-consciousness is to be abandoned through direct knowledge and full understanding.
Full understanding is to be abandoned; tongue-contact is to be abandoned through direct knowledge and full understanding;
and whatever feeling arises conditioned by tongue-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too is to be abandoned through direct knowledge and full understanding.
The body is to be abandoned through direct knowledge and full understanding...
The mind is to be abandoned through direct knowledge and full understanding; mental phenomena are to be abandoned through direct knowledge and full understanding;
mind-consciousness is to be abandoned through direct knowledge and full understanding; mind-contact is to be abandoned through direct knowledge and full understanding;
and whatever feeling arises conditioned by mind-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too is to be abandoned through direct knowledge and full understanding.
“This, monks, is the Dhamma for the full understanding through direct knowledge and for the abandoning of everything. Thus it was said.
The third [discourse]. Saṁyutta Nikāya 35.26. (SN 35.26, PTS SN iv 17)
3. The Chapter on All.
First Discourse on Non-Understanding:
“Bhikkhus, without directly knowing all, without fully understanding all, without becoming dispassionate toward all, and without abandoning all, one is incapable of the destruction of suffering.”
And what, monks, is it that one who does not directly know, does not fully understand, does not become dispassionate toward, and does not abandon, is incapable of the destruction of suffering?
The eye, monks, one who does not directly know, does not fully understand, does not become dispassionate toward, and does not abandon, is incapable of the destruction of suffering.
Visible forms, one who does not directly know, does not fully understand, does not become dispassionate toward, and does not abandon, is incapable of the destruction of suffering.
Without directly knowing, fully understanding, becoming dispassionate toward, and abandoning eye-consciousness, one is incapable of the destruction of suffering.
Without directly knowing, fully understanding, becoming dispassionate toward, and abandoning eye-contact, one is incapable of the destruction of suffering.

Whatever feeling arises conditioned by eye-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—without directly knowing, fully understanding, becoming dispassionate toward, and abandoning that as well, one is incapable of the destruction of suffering... [and so on].
Without directly knowing the tongue, without fully understanding it, without becoming dispassionate toward it, and without abandoning it, one is incapable of the destruction of suffering.
[The same applies to] tastes … tongue-consciousness … [and so forth].

Tongue-contact …pe… whatever feeling arises conditioned by tongue-contact— whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant— that too, by not fully knowing it, not fully understanding it, not becoming dispassionate toward it, and not abandoning it, one is incapable of the destruction of suffering. Body …pe…
Without directly knowing the mind, without fully understanding it, without dispassion toward it, and without abandoning it, one is incapable of the destruction of suffering.
[The same applies to] phenomena … mental consciousness … [and so forth].
Mind-contact...

and whatever feeling arises conditioned by mind-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—one who does not directly know it, does not fully understand it, does not become dispassionate toward it, and does not abandon it, is incapable of the destruction of suffering.
Indeed, monks, one who does not directly know all this, does not fully understand it, does not become dispassionate toward it, and does not abandon it, is incapable of the destruction of suffering.
"Monks, by directly knowing and fully understanding everything, by dispassion toward it and abandoning it, one is capable of the destruction of suffering.
And what, monks, is that 'everything' which, by directly knowing and fully understanding, by dispassion toward and abandoning it, one is capable of the destruction of suffering?
The eye, monks, by directly knowing and fully understanding, by dispassion toward and abandoning it, one is capable of the destruction of suffering."
By directly knowing and fully understanding form, by making it fade away and abandoning it, one is capable of the destruction of suffering.
By directly knowing and fully understanding eye-consciousness, by making it fade away and abandoning it, one is capable of the destruction of suffering.
By directly knowing and fully understanding eye-contact, by making it fade away and abandoning it, one is capable of the destruction of suffering.

Whatever feeling arises conditioned by eye-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—one who directly knows it, fully understands it, fades away from passion for it, and abandons it, is capable of the destruction of suffering.

… [and so on] … one who directly knows the tongue, fully understands it, fades away from passion for it, and abandons it, is capable of the destruction of suffering. [Regarding] tastes … [and so on] …
Tongue-consciousness …pe… tongue-contact …pe… and whatever feeling arises conditioned by tongue-contact—

whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant— one who fully understands this, fully comprehends it, fades away from passion for it, and abandons it, is capable of the destruction of suffering.

By directly knowing and fully understanding the body … [and so on] … the mind, by removing lust for it and abandoning it, one is capable of the destruction of suffering. By directly knowing and fully understanding phenomena … [and so on] … one is capable of the destruction of suffering.
Mental consciousness...
mental contact...

and whatever feeling—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—arises conditioned by mental contact: by directly knowing that, fully understanding it, fading away from it, and abandoning it, one is capable of the destruction of suffering.
“Monks, it is by directly knowing and fully understanding all this, by dispassion toward it and abandoning it, that one is capable of the destruction of suffering.
Thus was the fourth [discourse]. *Saṃyutta Nikāya* 35.27.
3. The Chapter on All (Sabbavagga) The Second Discourse on Non-Comprehension (Dutiya-aparijānana-sutta):
“Bhikkhus, without directly knowing, without fully comprehending, without becoming dispassionate toward, and without abandoning all, one is incapable of the destruction of suffering.”

And what, monks, is that all which, if one has not directly known it, has not fully understood it, has not become dispassionate toward it, and has not abandoned it, makes one incapable of the destruction of suffering?
It is the eye, monks, and forms, and eye-consciousness, and the phenomena cognizable by eye-consciousness...
[and so on] ...the tongue, and tastes, and tongue-consciousness, and the phenomena cognizable by tongue-consciousness.
Whatever body, whatever tangible objects, whatever body-consciousness, and whatever phenomena cognizable by body-consciousness;
whatever mind, whatever mental phenomena, whatever mind-consciousness, and whatever phenomena cognizable by mind-consciousness—this, monks, is called "all.
Without directly knowing, without fully understanding, without becoming dispassionate toward, and without abandoning this all, one is incapable of the destruction of suffering.
“Monks, by directly knowing, fully understanding, detaching from, and abandoning everything, one is capable of the destruction of suffering.
And what, monks, is that ‘everything’ which, by directly knowing, fully understanding, detaching from, and abandoning, one is capable of the destruction of suffering?
It is the eye, monks, and forms, and eye-consciousness, and those phenomena cognizable by eye-consciousness; ... [and so on for the other sense bases] ...”
The tongue and tastes, and tongue-consciousness, and the mental phenomena cognizable by tongue-consciousness;
the body and tangibles, and body-consciousness, and the mental phenomena cognizable by body-consciousness;
the mind and mental phenomena, and mind-consciousness, and the mental phenomena cognizable by mind-consciousness.
“Monks, by directly knowing and fully understanding all this, by detaching from it and abandoning it, one is capable of the destruction of suffering.
The fifth.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 35.28 (SN 35.28, PTS SN iv 19)
3. The Chapter on All Things: The Discourse on the Burning.
At one time the Blessed One was staying at Gayā on Gayāsīsa together with a thousand bhikkhus.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
“Bhikkhus, everything is burning.
And what, bhikkhus, is that ‘everything’ which is burning?”
“Bhikkhus, the eye is on fire; forms are on fire; eye-consciousness is on fire; eye-contact is on fire.
And whatever feeling arises conditioned by eye-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too is on fire.”
“By what is it ablaze?
“It is ablaze with the fire of lust, the fire of hatred, and the fire of delusion; it is ablaze with birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair,” I say.

… “The tongue is ablaze, tastes are ablaze, tongue-consciousness is ablaze, tongue-contact is ablaze. Whatever feeling arises conditioned by that tongue-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too is ablaze.”
“By what is it ablaze?
“It is ablaze with the fire of lust, the fire of hatred, and the fire of delusion; it is ablaze with birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair,” I say.

… The mind is ablaze, mental phenomena are ablaze, mind-consciousness is ablaze, and mind-contact is ablaze. Whatever feeling arises conditioned by that mind-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too is ablaze.
"By what is it ablaze?
"It is ablaze with the fire of lust, the fire of hatred, and the fire of delusion; it is ablaze with birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair—so I say.
Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the well-taught noble disciple becomes disenchanted with the eye and becomes disenchanted with forms."
He becomes disenchanted with eye-consciousness; he becomes disenchanted with eye-contact;
and he becomes disenchanted with whatever feeling arises conditioned by eye-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant.
…pe… He becomes disenchanted with whatever feeling arises conditioned by mind-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant.
“Through disenchantment, one becomes dispassionate; through dispassion, one is liberated. In liberation, the knowledge arises: ‘It is liberated. One understands:
‘Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
The bhikkhus were uplifted and rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words.
And while this exposition was being spoken, the minds of those one thousand bhikkhus were liberated from the taints through non-clinging.
Thus ends the sixth [discourse].

Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.29 (SN 35.29, PTS SN iv 20) 3. Sabbavagga Addhabhūtasutta The Discourse on Being Overwhelmed “Bhikkhus, when one is overwhelmed by form, one does not understand form as it really is; when one is overwhelmed by feeling, one does not understand feeling as it really is; when one is overwhelmed by perception, one does not understand perception as it really is; when one is overwhelmed by volitional formations, one does not understand volitional formations as they really are; when one is overwhelmed by consciousness, one does not understand consciousness as it really is. When one is overwhelmed by form, one does not understand form as it really is; when one is overwhelmed by feeling, one does not understand feeling as it really is; when one is overwhelmed by perception, one does not understand perception as it really is; when one is overwhelmed by volitional formations, one does not understand volitional formations as they really are; when one is overwhelmed by consciousness, one does not understand consciousness as it really is. Bhikkhus, when one is overwhelmed by form, one does not understand form as it really is; when one is overwhelmed by feeling, one does not understand feeling as it really is; when one is overwhelmed by perception, one does not understand perception as it really is; when one is overwhelmed by volitional formations, one does not understand volitional formations as they really are; when one is overwhelmed by consciousness, one does not understand consciousness as it really is. Therefore, bhikkhus, you should train yourselves thus: ‘We will not be overwhelmed by form; we will understand form as it really is. We will not be overwhelmed by feeling; we will understand feeling as it really is. We will not be overwhelmed by perception; we will understand perception as it really is. We will not be overwhelmed by volitional formations; we will understand volitional formations as they really are. We will not be overwhelmed by consciousness; we will understand consciousness as it really is. Thus, bhikkhus, should you train yourselves.”
Thus have I heard:
at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
“Everything, monks, has been overcome.
And what, monks, is that ‘everything’ which has been overcome?
The eye, monks, has been overcome; forms have been overcome; eye-consciousness has been overcome; eye-contact [has been overcome].”
It has been burnt up; and whatever feeling arises conditioned by eye-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too has been burnt up.
By what has it been burnt up?
“I say that it is overwhelmed by birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief,
and despair… the tongue is overwhelmed, tastes are overwhelmed, tongue-consciousness is overwhelmed, tongue-contact is overwhelmed,
and whatever feeling arises conditioned by tongue-contact— whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant— that too is overwhelmed.”
Or even that which has been overwhelmed.
By what has it been overwhelmed?
"It has been overwhelmed by birth, by aging, by death, by sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair," I say.
The body is broken apart... [and so on] ...the mind is broken apart, mental phenomena are broken apart, mind-consciousness is broken apart, mind-contact is broken apart,
and whatever feeling arises conditioned by mind-contact— whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant— that too is broken apart.
Or even that which has been overwhelmed.
By what has it been overwhelmed?
"It has been overwhelmed by birth, by aging, by death, by sorrows, lamentations, pains, griefs, and despairs," I say.
Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the well-taught noble disciple becomes disenchanted with the eye, disenchanted with forms, disenchanted with eye-consciousness, and disenchanted with eye-contact...
[and so on] ...he becomes disenchanted with whatever feeling—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—arises conditioned by mind-contact.
Through disenchantment, he becomes dispassionate; through dispassion, he is liberated. When liberated, the knowledge arises: "It is liberated."
“He understands: ‘Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.
This is the seventh [discourse]. *Saṃyutta Nikāya* 35.30. (SN 35.30, PTS SN iv 21)
3. The Chapter on All:
The Discourse on What is Conducive to the Uprooting of All Conceivings “Monks, I will teach you the practice that is conducive to the uprooting of all conceivings.”
"Listen to that, and pay close attention; I shall speak.
And what, monks, is that practice suitable for the uprooting of all conceiving?
Here, monks, a monk does not conceive the eye, he does not conceive in the eye, he does not conceive from the eye, he does not conceive "the eye is mine."
He does not conceive of form, he does not conceive in forms, he does not conceive from form, he does not conceive "form is mine.
He does not conceive of eye-consciousness, he does not conceive in eye-consciousness, he does not conceive from eye-consciousness, he does not conceive "eye-consciousness is mine.
He does not conceive of eye-contact, he does not conceive in eye-contact, he does not conceive from eye-contact, he does not conceive "eye-contact is mine."

Whatever feeling arises conditioned by eye-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—one does not conceive that, one does not conceive in that, one does not conceive from that, one does not conceive "that is mine. ... [And so on] ...
one does not conceive the tongue, one does not conceive in the tongue, one does not conceive from the tongue, one does not conceive "the tongue is mine.
One does not conceive tastes, one does not conceive in tastes, one does not conceive from tastes, one does not conceive "tastes are mine."
One does not conceive of tongue-consciousness; one does not conceive in tongue-consciousness; one does not conceive from tongue-consciousness; one does not conceive, "Tongue-consciousness is mine.
One does not conceive of tongue-contact; one does not conceive in tongue-contact; one does not conceive from tongue-contact; one does not conceive, "Tongue-contact is mine."

Whatever feeling arises conditioned by tongue-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—one does not conceive it, one does not conceive in it, one does not conceive from it, and one does not conceive "this is mine. ... [and so on] ...
One does not conceive the mind, one does not conceive in the mind, one does not conceive from the mind, and one does not conceive "the mind is mine.
One does not conceive mental phenomena, one does not conceive in mental phenomena, one does not conceive from mental phenomena, and one does not conceive "mental phenomena are mine."
One does not conceive of mind-consciousness; one does not conceive in mind-consciousness; one does not conceive from mind-consciousness; one does not conceive, "Mind-consciousness is mine.
One does not conceive of mind-contact; one does not conceive in mind-contact; one does not conceive from mind-contact; one does not conceive, "Mind-contact is mine.

Whatever feeling arises conditioned by mind-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—one does not conceive that; one does not conceive in it; one does not conceive from it; one does not conceive, "That is mine."
He does not conceive anything as "all," he does not conceive in anything as "all," he does not conceive from anything as "all," and he does not conceive "all is mine.
Not conceiving thus, he does not cling to anything in the world.
Not clinging, he is not agitated. Being unagitated, he personally attains final Nibbāna.
‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.
This, monks, is the practice conducive to the uprooting of all conceiving.
The eighth.

Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.31 (SN 35.31, PTS SN iv 23) 3. Sabbavagga First Discourse on What is Conducive to Uprooting “Bhikkhus, there are these three kinds of craving. What three? Craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence. These, bhikkhus, are the three kinds of craving. “Now, bhikkhus, what is conducive to the uprooting of these three kinds of craving? It is the Noble Eightfold Path. That is, right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. This, bhikkhus, is what is conducive to the uprooting of these three kinds of craving.”
“Monks, I will teach you the practice conducive to the uprooting of all conceivings.
Listen to that.
And what, monks, is the practice conducive to the uprooting of all conceivings?”
Here, monks, a bhikkhu does not conceive of the eye; he does not conceive in the eye; he does not conceive from the eye; he does not conceive, "The eye is mine.
He does not conceive of forms … [and so on] … he does not conceive of eye-consciousness; he does not conceive of eye-contact; nor that which arises conditioned by eye-contact.
Whatever feeling arises— whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant— one does not conceive it, one does not conceive in it,
one does not conceive from it, and one does not conceive,
"This is mine. For, monks, whatever one conceives, in whatever one conceives, from whatever one conceives, and that which one conceives as "mine"— from that, it becomes otherwise.
Subject to change and attached to existence, the world delights only in existence … [as before] … one does not conceive the tongue,
one does not conceive by means of the tongue, one does not conceive from the tongue, one does not conceive "the tongue is mine.
One does not conceive tastes … [as before].
One does not conceive of tongue-consciousness; one does not conceive of tongue-contact.

Whatever feeling arises conditioned by tongue-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—one does not conceive of that; one does not conceive in that; one does not conceive from that;
one does not conceive, "This is mine. For, monks, whatever one conceives, in whatever one conceives, from whatever one conceives, and whatever one conceives as "mine"—from that, it becomes otherwise.
The world, subject to change and attached to existence, delights only in existence … [as before] … one does not conceive of the mind,
one does not conceive in the mind, one does not conceive from the mind, one does not conceive "the mind is mine.
One does not conceive of phenomena … [as before] …
One does not conceive of mind-consciousness; one does not conceive of mind-contact.

Whatever feeling arises conditioned by mind-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—one does not conceive that, one does not conceive in that, one does not conceive from that, and one does not conceive "this is mine.
For whatever one conceives, bhikkhus, in whatever one conceives, from whatever one conceives, and that which one conceives as "mine"—from all that, it becomes otherwise.
The world, subject to change and attached to existence, delights only in existence.

To whatever extent there are aggregates, elements, and sense-bases, monks, one does not conceive them, one does not conceive in them, one does not conceive from them, and one does not conceive "this is mine.
Not conceiving thus, one does not cling to anything in the world.
Not grasping, one does not tremble. Not trembling, one attains nibbāna right here and now.
One understands: "Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.
This, monks, is the practice conducive to the uprooting of all conceiving.
The Ninth.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 35.32 (SN 35.32, PTS SN iv 24) 3.
The Chapter on All (Sabbavagga)
The Discourse on What is Conducive to the Second Uprooting “Monks,
I will teach you the practice that is conducive to the uprooting of all conceiving.
Listen to it.”
"And what, monks, is that practice conducive to the uprooting of all conceiving?
What do you think, monks,
is the eye permanent or impermanent?"
“Impermanent, venerable sir.
“But what is impermanent, is that suffering or happiness?
“Suffering, venerable sir.”
“But that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—is it fitting to regard it thus:
‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?
“Certainly not, Bhante.”
“Are forms … eye-consciousness … eye-contact permanent or impermanent?”
“Impermanent, Bhante.
… [as before] … “And this feeling that arises conditioned by eye-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—is that permanent or impermanent?
“Impermanent, Bhante.”
“But what is impermanent, is that suffering or happiness?”—
“Suffering, Bhante.”—
“But what is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change— is it fitting to regard it thus:”
‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?
— “Certainly not, Bhante.
… “Is the tongue permanent or impermanent?”
“Impermanent, venerable sir.
… [and so on] … “Tastes … tongue-consciousness …”
“Is tongue-contact …pe… and whatever feeling arises conditioned by tongue-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—is that permanent or impermanent?
“It is impermanent, venerable sir. …pe…
“Are mental phenomena … mind-consciousness … and mind-contact permanent or impermanent?”
“Impermanent, venerable sir.
“And that feeling which arises conditioned by mind-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—is that permanent or impermanent?
“Impermanent, venerable sir.”
“But what is impermanent, is that suffering or happiness?”—
“Suffering, Bhante.”—
“But what is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change— is it fitting to regard it thus:”
‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?”— “Certainly not, Bhante. “Seeing thus, bhikkhus,
the well-taught noble disciple becomes disenchanted with the eye, disenchanted with forms, disenchanted with eye-consciousness, and disenchanted with eye-contact.”

One becomes disenchanted with whatever feeling—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—arises conditioned by eye-contact; ... [and so on] ... one becomes disenchanted with the ear, with sounds, ... [and so on] ... one becomes disenchanted with whatever feeling—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—arises conditioned by ear-contact; ... [and so on] ... one becomes disenchanted with the nose, with odors, ... [and so on] ...

one becomes disenchanted with whatever feeling—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—arises conditioned by nose-contact; ... [and so on] ... one becomes disenchanted with the tongue, with tastes, ... [and so on] ... one becomes disenchanted with whatever feeling—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—arises conditioned by tongue-contact; ... [and so on] ... one becomes disenchanted with the body, with tangibles, ... [and so on] ... one becomes disenchanted with whatever feeling—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—arises conditioned by body-contact; ... [and so on] ...
one becomes disenchanted with the mind, one becomes disenchanted with mental phenomena, one becomes disenchanted with mind-consciousness, and one becomes disenchanted with mind-contact.
Whatever feeling arises conditioned by mind-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—one becomes disenchanted with that as well.
Through disenchantment, one becomes dispassionate; through dispassion, one is liberated. In liberation, the knowledge arises: "It is liberated. One understands:
"Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being."
“This, monks, is the practice conducive to the uprooting of all conceiving.
Tenth. The Third Chapter on All.
Its summary verse:
All [the truths], both abandonments,
two thorough knowledges, and another two.
