"Blazing and aflame," "the two suitable ones," and "the beneficial"—
therefore this chapter is called by that name.

Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.33–42 (SN 35.33, PTS SN iv 26) 4. Jātidhammavagga The Ten Suttas on Being Subject to Birth, etc. (Jātidhammādisuttadasaka) 33. Jātidhammasutta – Subject to Birth “Bhikkhus, the body is subject to birth. Whatever is subject to birth is, by nature, suffering. 34. Jarādhammasutta – Subject to Aging “Bhikkhus, the body is subject to aging. Whatever is subject to aging is, by nature, suffering. 35. Byādhidhammasutta – Subject to Illness “Bhikkhus, the body is subject to illness. Whatever is subject to illness is, by nature, suffering. 36. Maraṇadhammasutta – Subject to Death “Bhikkhus, the body is subject to death. Whatever is subject to death is, by nature, suffering. 37. Sokadhammasutta – Subject to Sorrow “Bhikkhus, the body is subject to sorrow. Whatever is subject to sorrow is, by nature, suffering. 38. Saṅkilesikadhammasutta – Subject to Defilement “Bhikkhus, the body is subject to defilement. Whatever is subject to defilement is, by nature, suffering. 39. Assāsikadhammasutta – Not to Be Relied Upon “Bhikkhus, the body is not to be relied upon. Whatever is not to be relied upon is, by nature, suffering. 40. Vipariṇāmadhammasutta – Subject to Change “Bhikkhus, the body is subject to change. Whatever is subject to change is, by nature, suffering. 41. Dukkhadhammasutta – Subject to Suffering “Bhikkhus, the body is subject to suffering. Whatever is subject to suffering is, by nature, suffering. 42. Anattadhammasutta – Subject to Non-Self “Bhikkhus, the body is subject to non-self. Whatever is subject to non-self is, by nature, suffering.”
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
There, the Blessed One said:
“Bhikkhus, all things are subject to birth.”
And what, bhikkhus, is everything subject to birth?
The eye, bhikkhus, is subject to birth;
visible forms...
Eye-consciousness...
eye-contact is subject to birth.
Whatever feeling arises conditioned by eye-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too is subject to birth... [and so on].
The tongue … tastes … tongue-consciousness …
Tongue-contact...
and whatever feeling arises conditioned by tongue-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too is subject to birth.
Body... [and so on]...
The mind is subject to birth; mental phenomena are subject to birth; mind-consciousness is subject to birth; mind-contact is subject to birth.
Whatever feeling arises conditioned by mind-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too is subject to birth.
Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the well-taught noble disciple becomes disenchanted with the eye, with forms, with eye-consciousness, and with eye-contact... [and so on].
“He understands: ‘There is nothing further beyond this state of being.
The first.
“Bhikkhus, all is subject to aging …”
[The rest is] abbreviated.
Second.
“Bhikkhus, everything is subject to illness…”
[This is] abbreviated.
The third [sutta].
“Monks, everything is subject to death …”
[This is] abbreviated.
The fourth [sutta].
“Bhikkhus, everything is subject to sorrow …”
[This is] abbreviated.
The fifth.
“Monks, all things that are subject to defilement….”
[The rest is] abbreviated. The sixth.
“Bhikkhus, everything is subject to destruction….”
[The rest is] abbreviated.
The seventh [sutta].
“Bhikkhus, everything is subject to decay …”
[This is] abbreviated.
The eighth.
“Bhikkhus, everything is subject to arising….”
[The rest is] abbreviated. Ninth.
“Bhikkhus, everything is subject to cessation. ...
Abbreviated.
The tenth [sutta].
The fourth chapter on the nature of birth.
Its summary verse:
Birth, aging, sickness, and death,
sorrow, and that which is subject to defilement.
“Arising and passing away,
with cessation as their nature— these ten things for you.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 35.43–51 (SN 35.43, PTS SN iv 28)
5. The Chapter on All is Impermanent.
The Set of Nine Discourses on Impermanence, etc.
Setting at Savatthī.
There, [the Blessed One] said this: “…pe… ‘Bhikkhus, all is impermanent.
And what, bhikkhus, is all that is impermanent?’”
“Bhikkhus, the eye is impermanent, forms are impermanent, eye-consciousness is impermanent, eye-contact is impermanent.

And whatever feeling arises conditioned by eye-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too is impermanent. … [The same applies to] the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. … The tongue is impermanent, tastes are impermanent, tongue-consciousness is impermanent, tongue-contact is impermanent. And whatever feeling arises conditioned by tongue-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too is impermanent.”
Whatever feeling arises conditioned by tongue-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too is impermanent.
The body is impermanent...
[and so on] ...the mind is impermanent; mental phenomena are impermanent; mind-consciousness is impermanent; mind-contact is impermanent.
Whatever feeling arises conditioned by mind-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too is impermanent.
Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the well-taught noble disciple becomes disenchanted with the eye, disenchanted with forms, disenchanted with eye-consciousness, and disenchanted with eye-contact.
Whatever feeling arises conditioned by eye-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—he becomes disenchanted with that as well... [and so on].

One becomes disenchanted with the mind, one becomes disenchanted with mental phenomena, one becomes disenchanted with mind-consciousness, one becomes disenchanted with mind-contact, and one becomes disenchanted with whatever feeling—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—arises conditioned by mind-contact.
Through disenchantment, passion fades away; through the fading of passion, one is liberated. In liberation, the knowledge arises: "It is liberated."
‘Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being,’ he understands.
The first.
“Bhikkhus, all is suffering … [as before] …”
The second [discourse].
“All, monks, is non-self” … [as before] … The third [discourse].
“Bhikkhus, everything is to be directly known ... [as before] ...
Fourth.
“Bhikkhus, everything is to be fully understood ... [as before] ...”
Fifth. “Bhikkhus,
everything is to be abandoned … [as before] … Sixth.”
“Bhikkhus, all is to be realized … [as before] … Seventh. “Bhikkhus,
all is to be fully understood through direct knowledge … [as before] …”
The eighth:
"Everything, bhikkhus, is afflicted... [as before] ...The ninth.

Saṁyutta Nikāya 35.52 (SN 35.52, PTS SN iv 29) 5. The Chapter on All is Impermanent Upassaṭṭha Sutta: Oppressed by Suffering At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, form is impermanent. What is impermanent is suffering. What is suffering is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self. Feeling is impermanent... Perception is impermanent... Volitional formations are impermanent... Consciousness is impermanent. What is impermanent is suffering. What is suffering is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self. Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the instructed noble disciple experiences revulsion towards form, revulsion towards feeling, revulsion towards perception, revulsion towards volitional formations, revulsion towards consciousness. Experiencing revulsion, he becomes dispassionate. Through dispassion [his mind] is liberated. When it is liberated there comes the knowledge: ‘It is liberated. If, bhikkhus, one is oppressed by form, one will seek delight in the cessation of form. If one is oppressed by feeling, one will seek delight in the cessation of feeling. If one is oppressed by perception, one will seek delight in the cessation of perception. If one is oppressed by volitional formations, one will seek delight in the cessation of volitional formations. If one is oppressed by consciousness, one will seek delight in the cessation of consciousness. If, bhikkhus, one seeks delight in the cessation of form, one will attain Nibbāna. If one seeks delight in the cessation of feeling, one will attain Nibbāna. If one seeks delight in the cessation of perception, one will attain Nibbāna. If one seeks delight in the cessation of volitional formations, one will attain Nibbāna. If one seeks delight in the cessation of consciousness, one will attain Nibbāna.”
“Everything, bhikkhus, is afflicted.
And what, bhikkhus, is everything that is afflicted?

Whatever feeling—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—arises conditioned by eye-contact, that too is afflicted...

Whatever feeling—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—arises conditioned by tongue-contact, that too is afflicted.
The body is afflicted;
the mind is afflicted; mental phenomena are afflicted; mind-consciousness is afflicted; mind-contact is afflicted.
Whatever feeling arises conditioned by that mind-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too is afflicted.
Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the well-taught noble disciple becomes disenchanted with the eye, disenchanted with forms, disenchanted with eye-consciousness, and disenchanted with eye-contact.

Through disenchantment, one becomes dispassionate; through dispassion, one is liberated. In liberation, the knowledge arises: "It is liberated. One understands:

The fifth chapter, "All Impermanent.
Its summary verse:
Impermanent, suffering, and non-self;
it is to be directly known, to be fully understood;
it is to be abandoned, and to be realized.
That which is to be directly known and fully understood;
that which is afflicted and oppressed—

the Aniccavagga and the Yamaka.

Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.63 (SN 35.63, PTS SN iv 35) 7. Migajālavagga Paṭhamamigajālasutta (The First Discourse to Migajāla) At Sāvatthī. Then the Venerable Migajāla approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said to the Blessed One: "Venerable sir, it would be good if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief, so that, having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, I might dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute. "Migajāla, when one does not understand as they really are the gratification, the danger, and the escape in the case of the six bases for contact, one does not understand suffering as it really is; one does not understand the origin of suffering as it really is; one does not understand the cessation of suffering as it really is; one does not understand the way leading to the cessation of suffering as it really is. "But, venerable sir, how does one not understand as they really are the gratification, the danger, and the escape in the case of the six bases for contact? "In the case of the eye-base, Migajāla, whatever pleasure and joy arise in dependence on it—this is the gratification in the eye-base. That the eye-base is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—this is the danger in the eye-base. The removal and abandonment of desire and lust for the eye-base—this is the escape from the eye-base. In the case of the ear-base... In the case of the nose-base... In the case of the tongue-base... In the case of the body-base... In the case of the mind-base, Migajāla, whatever pleasure and joy arise in dependence on it—this is the gratification in the mind-base. That the mind-base is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—this is the danger in the mind-base. The removal and abandonment of desire and lust for the mind-base—this is the escape from the mind-base. When one does not understand as they really are the gratification, the danger, and the escape in the case of these six bases for contact, one does not understand suffering as it really is; one does not understand the origin of suffering as it really is; one does not understand the cessation of suffering as it really is; one does not understand the way leading to the cessation of suffering as it really is. But when one understands as they really are the gratification, the danger, and the escape in the case of these six bases for contact, one understands suffering as it really is; one understands the origin of suffering as it really is; one understands the cessation of suffering as it really is; one understands the way leading to the cessation of suffering as it really is. Then the Venerable Migajāla, having delighted and rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him on his right, departed. Then, dwelling alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute, the Venerable Migajāla, by realizing it for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life entered and dwelt in that unsurpassed goal of the holy life for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness. He directly knew: "Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being. And the Venerable Migajāla became one of the arahants. Then, when the night was well advanced, the Venerable Migajāla rose from meditation and went to the Blessed One. Having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One, sat down to one side, and said to the Blessed One: "Venerable sir, I have attained arahantship. "I hope, Migajāla, that you have attained arahantship. "Yes, venerable sir, I have attained arahantship. "By what training, Migajāla, did you attain arahantship? "Venerable sir, I understood as they really are the gratification, the danger, and the escape in the case of the six bases for contact. It was by this training, venerable sir, that I attained arahantship. "It is wonderful, Migajāla! It is marvelous, Migajāla! How well this has been expressed by you, Migajāla. For, Migajāla, this Dhamma has been well expounded by me, made plain, disclosed, revealed, stripped of patchwork, and made clear. Here, Migajāla, a disciple of the noble ones, reflecting wisely, feels revulsion towards the eye; feeling revulsion, he becomes dispassionate. Through dispassion [his mind] is liberated. When it is liberated, there comes the knowledge: ‘It is liberated. He understands: ‘Destroyed is birth, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being. And so too for the ear... the nose... the tongue... the body... the mind. It was by this training, venerable sir, that I attained arahantship. "It is wonderful, Migajāla! It is marvelous, Migajāla! How well this has been expressed by you, Migajāla. For, Migajāla, this Dhamma has been well expounded by me, made plain, disclosed, revealed, stripped of patchwork, and made clear.

"There are, Migajāla, tastes cognizable by the tongue that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual pleasure,
and provocative of lust. If a bhikkhu delights in them, welcomes them, and remains attached to them,
delight arises in him as he delights in them, welcomes them, and remains attached to them."
When there is delight, there is lust;
when there is lust, there is bondage.
Migajāla, a bhikkhu who is bound by the fetter of delight is said to be one who dwells with a companion.

And although, Migajala, a bhikkhu dwelling in such a way resorts to remote lodgings in forest thickets and jungle groves— places of little sound, little noise, secluded from people, hidden from the crowd, and suitable for retreat—
he is nevertheless said to be one who dwells with a companion.
For what reason?
Craving is indeed his companion, and it has not been abandoned by him.
Therefore, he is called "one who dwells with a companion.
Furthermore, Migajala, there are forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, lovely, pleasing, dear, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust.
If a bhikkhu does not delight in that, does not welcome it, and does not remain clinging to it,
then for him who does not delight in it, does not welcome it, and does not remain clinging to it, delight ceases. When there is no delight, there is no lust.
When passion for the essential is absent,
there is no fetter. Migajāla, a bhikkhu who is detached from the fetter of delight is said to be one who dwells alone … There are,
Migajāla, tastes cognizable by the tongue … [as before] …
Furthermore, Migajāla, there are mental phenomena cognizable by the mind that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, endearing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust.
If a bhikkhu does not delight in them, does not welcome them, and does not remain clinging to them,
then for him who does not delight, welcome, or remain clinging to them, delight ceases.
When there is no delight, there is no lust;
when there is no lust, there is no fetter.
Migajāla, a bhikkhu who is dissociated from the fetter of delight is said to be one who dwells alone.

And, Migajāla, even if a bhikkhu who dwells in such a way lives in a village, surrounded by bhikkhus, bhikkhunīs, male lay followers, female lay followers, kings, royal ministers, members of other sects, and their disciples,
he is nevertheless said to be one who dwells alone. For what reason?
“Craving is indeed his second; that has been abandoned by him.
Therefore he is called ‘one who dwells alone. Thus was the first [discourse].

Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.64 (SN 35.64, PTS SN iv 37) 7. Migajālavagga The Second Discourse to Migajāla At Sāvatthī. There, the Blessed One said this: “Migajāla, form is impermanent; whatever is impermanent is suffering; whatever is suffering is not-self; whatever is not-self should be seen with right wisdom as it really is: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self. “Feeling is impermanent... Perception is impermanent... Volitional formations are impermanent... Consciousness is impermanent; whatever is impermanent is suffering; whatever is suffering is not-self; whatever is not-self should be seen with right wisdom as it really is: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self. “When one sees this thus with right wisdom as it really is, Migajāla, one becomes disenchanted with form, disenchanted with feeling, disenchanted with perception, disenchanted with volitional formations, disenchanted with consciousness. Being disenchanted, one becomes dispassionate. Through dispassion, [the mind] is liberated. When it is liberated, there comes the knowledge: ‘It is liberated. One understands: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Having said this, the Sublime One rose from his seat and entered his dwelling. Then, not long after the Blessed One had left, the Venerable Migajāla approached the Venerable Ānanda and said to him: “Friend Ānanda, just now the Blessed One spoke these words: ‘Migajāla, form is impermanent... [as above] ...there is no more for this state of being,’ and having said this, he rose from his seat and entered his dwelling. “Friend Migajāla, when the Blessed One spoke these words, what was the underlying intention? “Friend Ānanda, regarding form: form is impermanent; whatever is impermanent is suffering; whatever is suffering is not-self; whatever is not-self should be seen with right wisdom as it really is: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self. “Regarding feeling: feeling is impermanent... Regarding perception: perception is impermanent... Regarding volitional formations: volitional formations are impermanent... Regarding consciousness: consciousness is impermanent; whatever is impermanent is suffering; whatever is suffering is not-self; whatever is not-self should be seen with right wisdom as it really is: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self. “When one sees this thus with right wisdom as it really is, friend Ānanda, one becomes disenchanted with form, disenchanted with feeling, disenchanted with perception, disenchanted with volitional formations, disenchanted with consciousness. Being disenchanted, one becomes dispassionate. Through dispassion, [the mind] is liberated. When it is liberated, there comes the knowledge: ‘It is liberated. One understands: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being. “It is wonderful, friend Migajāla! It is marvelous, friend Migajāla! How well this has been stated by you, friend. For indeed, friend, when the Blessed One spoke these words, this was his underlying intention. Then the Venerable Migajāla, having delighted and rejoiced in the Venerable Ānanda’s words, rose from his seat and departed. Not long after the Venerable Migajāla had left, the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and reported everything that had occurred, adding: “Then, venerable sir, the Venerable Migajāla, having delighted and rejoiced in my words, rose from his seat and departed. Not long after he had left, I approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and reported everything that had occurred, saying: ‘Venerable sir, when the Blessed One spoke these words, what was the underlying intention? “Ānanda, when I spoke these words to the Venerable Migajāla, this was my underlying intention: ‘Form is impermanent; whatever is impermanent is suffering; whatever is suffering is not-self; whatever is not-self should be seen with right wisdom as it really is: “This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self. “‘Feeling is impermanent... Perception is impermanent... Volitional formations are impermanent... Consciousness is impermanent; whatever is impermanent is suffering; whatever is suffering is not-self; whatever is not-self should be seen with right wisdom as it really is: “This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self. “When one sees this thus with right wisdom as it really is, Ānanda, one becomes disenchanted with form, disenchanted with feeling, disenchanted with perception, disenchanted with volitional formations, disenchanted with consciousness. Being disenchanted, one becomes dispassionate. Through dispassion, [the mind] is liberated. When it is liberated, there comes the knowledge: ‘It is liberated. One understands: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being. “It is wonderful, venerable sir! It is marvelous, venerable sir! How well this has been stated by the Blessed One, both in brief and in detail. This is what the Venerable Ānanda said.

Elated, the Venerable Migajāla delighted in the Venerable Ānanda’s words. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus! “Venerable sir! those bhikkhus replied. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, if anyone should say: ‘Without directly knowing form as it really is, without fully understanding it, without becoming disenchanted with it, without becoming dispassionate toward it, without making it cease, one can realize the supreme security from bondage, Nibbāna’—this, bhikkhus, is impossible. “If anyone should say: ‘Without directly knowing feeling as it really is... perception as it really is... volitional formations as they really are... consciousness as it really is, without fully understanding it, without becoming disenchanted with it, without becoming dispassionate toward it, without making it cease, one can realize the supreme security from bondage, Nibbāna’—this, bhikkhus, is impossible. “But, bhikkhus, if anyone should say: ‘Directly knowing form as it really is, fully understanding it, becoming disenchanted with it, becoming dispassionate toward it, making it cease, one can realize the supreme security from bondage, Nibbāna’—this, bhikkhus, is possible. “If anyone should say: ‘Directly knowing feeling as it really is... perception as it really is... volitional formations as they really are... consciousness as it really is, fully understanding it, becoming disenchanted with it, becoming dispassionate toward it, making it cease, one can realize the supreme security from bondage, Nibbāna’—this, bhikkhus, is possible. This is what the Blessed One said. Having said this, the Sublime One rose from his seat and entered his dwelling. Then, not long after the Blessed One had left, the Venerable Migajāla approached the Venerable Ānanda and said to him: “Friend Ānanda, just now the Blessed One spoke these words: ‘Bhikkhus, if anyone should say: “Without directly knowing form as it really is... [as above] ...this, bhikkhus, is possible,’ and having said this, he rose from his seat and entered his dwelling. [The rest of the discourse follows the same structure as above. “This is wonderful, friend Ānanda! This is marvelous, friend Ānanda! How well this has been stated by the Blessed One, both in brief and in detail. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus! “Venerable sir! those bhikkhus replied. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, if anyone should say: ‘Without directly knowing form as it really is, without fully understanding it, without becoming disenchanted with it, without becoming dispassionate toward it, without making it cease, one can realize the destruction of craving, the removal of desire, the cessation, and the relinquishment of craving’—this, bhikkhus, is impossible. “If anyone should say: ‘Without directly knowing feeling as it really is... perception as it really is... volitional formations as they really are... consciousness as it really is, without fully understanding
Then the Venerable Migajāla approached the Blessed One...
[as before] ...and sat down to one side. Sitting there, the Venerable Migajāla said this to the Blessed One:

“It would be well, Bhante, if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief, so that having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, I might dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute.”
“Migajāla, there are indeed forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust.
If a bhikkhu delights in them, welcomes them, and remains attached to them,
then delight arises in him as he delights in them, welcomes them, and remains attached to them.”
“With the arising of delight, Migajāla, there is the arising of suffering; so I say...
There are, Migajāla, tastes cognizable by the tongue...
There are, Migajāla, mental phenomena cognizable by the mind that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual pleasure, and provocative of lust.”
If a bhikkhu delights in that, welcomes it, and remains clinging to it, then delight arises in him as he delights in it, welcomes it, and remains clinging to it.
From the arising of delight comes the arising of suffering, Migajāla; so I say.
Moreover, Migajāla, there are forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, lovely, pleasing, dear, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust.

If a bhikkhu does not delight in them, does not welcome them, and does not remain clinging to them, then for him who does not delight in them, does not welcome them, and does not remain clinging to them, delight ceases.
With the cessation of delight, there is the cessation of suffering; so I say, Migajāla. …pe…
Furthermore, Migajāla, there are tastes cognizable by the tongue that are desirable, lovely... [as before] ...
Furthermore, Migajāla, there are mental phenomena cognizable by the mind that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, endearing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust.
If a bhikkhu does not delight in them, does not welcome them, and does not remain attached to them, then for him who does not delight, welcome, or remain attached to them, delight ceases.
“With the cessation of delight comes the cessation of suffering; so I say, Migajāla.
Then the Venerable Migajāla, having rejoiced and delighted in the Blessed One’s words, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him to his right, departed.
Then, dwelling alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute, it was not long before the Venerable Migajāla—[attained that goal] for the sake of which...
These sons of noble family went forth from the household life into homelessness in the right way;
and having realized for himself with direct knowledge, he entered and dwelt in that supreme goal of the holy life, even in this very life.
He directly knew: "Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being."
And the venerable Migajāla became one of the arahants.
Thus ends the second [discourse]. *Saṃyutta Nikāya* 35.65 (SN 35.65, PTS SN iv 38).
7. The Migajāla Chapter.
The First Discourse on the Question of Māra Samiddhi.
At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.
Then the Venerable Samiddhi approached the Blessed One...
[as before] ...and said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable sir, it is said, 'Māra, Māra.'"
“To what extent, venerable sir, would there be Māra or the designation of Māra?
“Wherever, Samiddhi, there is the eye, there are forms, there is eye-consciousness, and there are phenomena cognizable by eye-consciousness—there is Māra or the designation of Māra.
Wherever there is the ear, there are sounds, there is ear-consciousness, and there are phenomena cognizable by ear-consciousness—there is Māra or the designation of Māra.”
There is the nose, there are odors, there is nose-consciousness, there are phenomena cognizable by nose-consciousness; therein exists either Māra or the designation of Māra.
There is the tongue, there are tastes, there is tongue-consciousness, there are phenomena cognizable by tongue-consciousness; therein exists either Māra or the designation of Māra.
There is the body, there are tangibles, there is body-consciousness, there are phenomena cognizable by body-consciousness; therein exists either Māra or the designation of Māra.
There is the mind, there are mental phenomena, there is mind-consciousness, and there are mental phenomena cognizable by mind-consciousness; therein exists Māra or the designation of Māra.
But where, Samiddhi, there is no eye, no forms, no eye-consciousness, and no mental phenomena cognizable by eye-consciousness—therein exists neither Māra nor the designation of Māra.
There is no ear... [and so on].
There is no nose... [and so on] ...
there is no tongue, no tastes, no tongue-consciousness, no mental phenomena cognizable by tongue-consciousness; therein there is neither Māra nor the designation of Māra.
There is no body... [and so on].

“There is no mind, there are no mental phenomena, there is no mind-consciousness, there are no mental phenomena cognizable by mind-consciousness; therein there is no Māra, nor any designation of Māra.
The third.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 35.66 (SN 35.66, PTS SN iv 39)
7. Migajālavagga:
The Discourse on the Question of a Being by Samiddhi “Venerable sir, it is said: ‘a being, a being.’”
“To what extent, venerable sir, would there be a being or the designation of a being?
…pe… The fourth.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 35.67 (SN 35.67, PTS SN iv 39)
7. Migajālavagga:
The Discourse on the Question on Suffering by Samiddhi “Venerable sir, it is said: ‘Suffering, suffering.’”
“To what extent, venerable sir, might there be suffering, or the designation of suffering?
…pe… The fifth.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 35.68 (SN 35.68, PTS SN iv 39)
7. The Migajāla Chapter:
The Discourse on Samiddhi’s Questions about the World “Venerable sir, it is said: ‘the world, the world.’”
“To what extent, venerable sir, might there be the world, or the designation of a world?

“Wherever, Samiddhi, there is the eye, there are forms, there is eye-consciousness, and there are phenomena cognizable by eye-consciousness—there, to that extent, there is the world or the designation of a world.
… [Similarly for] the ear … the nose … the tongue …”

There is the mind, there are mental phenomena, there is mind-consciousness, and there are mental phenomena cognizable by mind-consciousness; therein exists either the world or the designation of the world.
But where, Samiddhi, there is no eye, no forms, no eye-consciousness, and no mental phenomena cognizable by eye-consciousness—therein exists neither the world nor the designation of the world...
[and so on] ...there is no tongue... [and so on].

“There is no mind, there are no mental phenomena, there is no mind-consciousness, there are no mental phenomena cognizable by mind-consciousness; therein there is neither world nor designation of a world.
The sixth.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 35.69 (SN 35.69, PTS SN iv 40).
7. The Migajāla Chapter:
The Discourse on Upasena and the Venomous Snake On one occasion, the Venerable Sāriputta and the Venerable Upasena were staying at Rājagaha in the Cool Grove, at the Sappasoṇḍika Cave.
Now at that time, a venomous snake had fallen upon the body of the Venerable Upasena.
Then the Venerable Upasena addressed the bhikkhus:
"Come, friends, lift this body of mine onto a couch and carry it outside."
"Before long, this body will fall apart right here,
just like a handful of chaff.
When this was said, the Venerable Sāriputta said this to the Venerable Upasena:
“Yet we do not perceive any alteration in the body of the Venerable Upasena, nor any change in his faculties.
And yet the Venerable Upasena says this:
‘Come, friends, lift this body of mine onto a bed and carry it outside.’”
“Formerly this body was scattered right here,
just like a handful of chaff.
“Surely, friend Sāriputta, it would be for one who thinks thus:”
‘I am the eye,’ or ‘the eye is mine’ … pe … ‘I am the tongue,’ or ‘the tongue is mine’ … ‘I am the mind,’ or ‘the mind is mine.’
"Friend Sāriputta, there might be a change in his body or a transformation of his faculties.
But as for me, friend Sāriputta, it does not occur to me:
'I am the eye,' or 'The eye is mine' ... [and so on]."
‘I am the tongue’ or ‘the tongue is mine’ …pe… ‘I am the mind’ or ‘the mind is mine. Yet,
friend Sāriputta, what change could there be in my body, or what transformation of the faculties?”
For indeed, in the Venerable Upasena, the underlying tendencies of the conceits of "I-making," "mine-making," and "I-conceit" have long been thoroughly eradicated.
Therefore, it does not occur to the Venerable Upasena:
"I am the eye," or "the eye is mine," and so forth...
“‘I am the tongue’ or ‘the tongue is mine’ …pe… ‘I am the mind’ or ‘the mind is mine.
Then those bhikkhus placed Venerable Upasena’s body on a bier and carried it outside.
Then the body of the Venerable Upasena was scattered right there,
just like a handful of chaff.
This is the seventh [sutta].

Saṁyutta Nikāya 35.70 (SN 35.70, PTS SN iv 41) 7. Migajālavagga Upavāṇasandiṭṭhikasutta Then the Venerable Upavāṇa approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it would be good if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief, so that, having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, I might dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute. “Upavāṇa, when one sees what truly is, one sees this world as it really is; when one sees this world as it really is, one sees what truly is. When one feels what truly is, one feels this world as it really is; when one feels this world as it really is, one feels what truly is. When one perceives what truly is, one perceives this world as it really is; when one perceives this world as it really is, one perceives what truly is. When one volitions what truly is, one volitions this world as it really is; when one volitions this world as it really is, one volitions what truly is. “But, venerable sir, how does one see what truly is, how does one feel what truly is, how does one perceive what truly is, how does one volition what truly is, so that one sees this world as it really is, feels this world as it really is, perceives this world as it really is, and volitions this world as it really is? “Upavāṇa, when one sees form as it truly is with correct wisdom, one sees this world as it really is; when one feels feeling as it truly is with correct wisdom, one feels this world as it really is; when one perceives perception as it truly is with correct wisdom, one perceives this world as it really is; when one volitions volitional formations as they truly are with correct wisdom, one volitions this world as it really is. When one sees form as it truly is with correct wisdom, one sees this world as it really is; when one feels feeling as it truly is with correct wisdom, one feels this world as it really is;

when one perceives perception as it truly is with correct wisdom, one perceives this world as it really is; when one volitions volitional formations as they truly are with correct wisdom, one volitions this world as it really is. When one sees form as it truly is with correct wisdom, one feels this world as it really is; when one feels feeling as it truly is with correct wisdom, one feels this world as it really is; when one perceives perception as it truly is with correct wisdom, one feels this world as it really is; when one volitions volitional formations as they truly are with correct wisdom, one feels this world as it really is. When one sees form as it truly is with correct wisdom, one perceives this world as it really is; when one feels feeling as it truly is with correct wisdom, one perceives this world as it really is; when one perceives perception as it truly is with correct wisdom, one perceives this world as it really is; when one volitions volitional formations as they truly are with correct wisdom, one perceives this world as it really is. When one sees form as it truly is with correct wisdom, one volitions this world as it really is; when one feels feeling as it truly is with correct wisdom, one volitions this world as it really is; when one perceives perception as it truly is with correct wisdom, one volitions this world as it really is; when one volitions volitional formations as they truly are with correct wisdom, one volitions this world as it really is. Thus, Upavāṇa, seeing form as it truly is with correct wisdom, feeling feeling as it truly is with correct wisdom, perceiving perception as it truly is with correct wisdom, and volitioning volitional formations as they truly are with correct wisdom, one sees this world as it really is, feels this world as it really is, perceives this world as it really is, and volitions this world as it really is. When this was said, the Venerable Upavāṇa said to the Blessed One: “Magnificent, venerable sir! Magnificent, venerable sir!... From today let the Blessed One remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life.”
Then the Venerable Upavāṇa approached the Blessed One ... [as before] ...
and sat down to one side. Sitting there, the Venerable Upavāṇa said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable sir, it is said: ‘The Dhamma is directly visible, the Dhamma is directly visible.’"
"To what extent, venerable sir, is the Dhamma directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, leading onward, and to be personally realized by the wise?
"In this case, Upavāṇa, a bhikkhu, having seen a form with the eye, experiences the form and also experiences passion for the form.
And when there is passion for forms within him, he understands: 'There is passion for forms within me.'"

“Upavaṇa, when a bhikkhu, having seen a form with the eye, experiences the form and also experiences lust for the form, and if there is lust for forms within him, he understands: ‘There is lust for forms within me.
In this way too, Upavaṇa, there is a Dhamma visible here and now, timeless, inviting inspection, leading onward, to be realized by the wise for themselves….”
Furthermore, Upavāṇa, having tasted a flavor with the tongue, a bhikkhu is both a perceiver of the flavor and a perceiver of lust for the flavor.
And when there is lust for flavors within him, he understands: ‘There is lust for flavors within me.
That, Upavāṇa, is how a bhikkhu, having tasted a flavor with the tongue, is both a perceiver of the flavor and a perceiver of lust for the flavor.
When there is lust for flavors within himself, he understands: ‘There is lust for flavors within me.
In this way too, Upavaṇa, this Dhamma is directly visible, timeless, inviting one to come and see, leading onward, and to be personally realized by the wise.
… Furthermore, Upavaṇa, when a bhikkhu has cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, he experiences the phenomenon and experiences passion for the phenomenon.
When there is lust for mental phenomena within himself, he understands: "There is lust for mental phenomena within me.

Upavaṇa, when a bhikkhu, having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, is sensitive to the phenomenon and sensitive to the lust for the phenomenon, and when there is lust for mental phenomena within himself, he understands: "There is lust for mental phenomena within me."
In this way too, Upavāṇa, the Dhamma is directly visible... to be personally realized by the wise...
Here, Upavāṇa, a bhikkhu, having seen a form with the eye, experiences the form but does not experience passion for the form.
And since there is no passion within him regarding forms, he understands: "There is no passion in me regarding forms."
“Upavāṇa, when a bhikkhu, having seen a form with the eye, experiences the form but does not experience passion for the form, and since there is no passion within him regarding forms, he understands:
‘There is no passion in me regarding forms’—even this, Upavāṇa, is a Dhamma visible here and now, timeless, inviting one to come and see, leading onward, to be personally realized by the wise. …pe…
Furthermore, Upavāṇa, a bhikkhu, having tasted a flavor with the tongue, experiences the flavor but does not experience craving for the flavor.
And since there is no craving within him regarding flavors, he understands:
‘There is no craving in me regarding flavors. …pe…
Furthermore, Upavaṇa, when a bhikkhu has cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, he experiences the phenomenon itself but does not experience passion for the phenomenon.
And since passion for phenomena is absent within him, he understands: ‘There is no passion in me regarding phenomena.
That, Upavaṇa, is how a bhikkhu, having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, experiences the phenomenon itself but does not experience passion for the phenomenon.
And when there is no lust for phenomena within oneself, one understands: ‘There is no lust in me for phenomena within.
In this way too, Upavāṇa, is there a Dhamma visible here and now, timeless, inviting one to come and see, leading onward, to be personally realized by the wise.
This is the eighth [discourse].
Saṁyutta Nikāya 35.71 (SN 35.71, PTS SN iv 43) 7. Migajālavagga First Discourse on the Six Bases of Contact “Bhikkhus, there are these six bases of contact.

What six? The eye as a base of contact, the ear as a base of contact, the nose as a base of contact, the tongue as a base of contact, the body as a base of contact, and the mind as a base of contact. These, bhikkhus, are the six bases of contact.”

“Bhikkhus, whatever bhikkhu does not understand, as they really are, the origin and the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding the six bases of contact—he has not lived the holy life;
he is far from this Dhamma and Vinaya.
When this was said, a certain bhikkhu said this to the Blessed One:
“In this matter, Bhante, I have found no consolation.
For I, Bhante, do not understand as they really are the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding the six bases of contact.
“What do you think, bhikkhu?”
"Do you regard the eye as 'this is mine, this I am, this is my self'?
"Certainly not, Bhante.
"Good, bhikkhu. And herein, bhikkhu, the eye will be well-seen by you with right wisdom, exactly as it is, thus: 'This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.'"
“This is the end of suffering … [as before] … Do you regard the tongue thus: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?
“Certainly not, venerable sir.”
“Good, bhikkhu! And in this case, bhikkhu, will your tongue be well-seen by you with right wisdom as it really is: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self’?
This indeed is the end of suffering...
[as before] ... Do you regard the mind thus: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?”
“No, venerable sir.
“Good, bhikkhu. And in this matter, bhikkhu, you will have clearly seen with correct wisdom, as it really is, that the mind is ‘not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.
This is the end of suffering.”
The Ninth.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 35.72 (SN 35.72, PTS SN iv 44) 7.
Migajālavagga
The Second Discourse on the Six Bases for Contact:

“Bhikkhus, whatever bhikkhu does not understand, as they really are, the arising and the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding the six bases for contact—for him the holy life has not been lived;
he is far removed from this Dhamma and Vinaya.”
When this was said, a certain bhikkhu said to the Blessed One:
“In this matter, Bhante, I am lost and utterly bewildered.
For I do not understand, as they really are, the arising, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding the six bases of contact.”
“What do you think, bhikkhu,
do you regard the eye as ‘this is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self’?
“Yes, venerable sir.”
“Excellent, bhikkhu! And herein, bhikkhu, you will have clearly seen with right wisdom, as it really is, that the eye is ‘this is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.
In this way, this first base of contact will be abandoned by you for the sake of no further existence in the future… [and so on] … Do you regard the tongue thus:
‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self’?”
“Yes, venerable sir.

“Good, bhikkhu. And herein, bhikkhu, you will have clearly seen with correct wisdom, as it actually is, this tongue thus: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self. In this way, this fourth base for contact [will be understood] by you.”
“It will be abandoned for the sake of no further becoming in the future...
[and so on]. “Do you regard the mind thus: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self’?
“Yes, venerable sir.”
“Excellent, bhikkhu! And herein, bhikkhu, you will have clearly seen this with right wisdom as it really is: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.
In this way, this sixth base of contact will be abandoned by you for the sake of no further existence in the future.
The tenth.

Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.73 (SN 35.73, PTS SN iv 44) 7. Migajālavagga Tatiyachaphassāyatanasutta (The Third Discourse on the Six Bases of Contact) “Bhikkhus, there are these six bases of contact. What six? The eye as a base of contact, the ear as a base of contact, the nose as a base of contact, the tongue as a base of contact, the body as a base of contact, and the mind as a base of contact.
These, bhikkhus, are the six bases of contact.”

“Bhikkhus, whatever bhikkhu does not understand, as they really are, the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding the six bases of contact—that bhikkhu has not lived the holy life;
he is far from this Dhamma and Vinaya.
When this was said, a certain bhikkhu said this to the Blessed One:
“In this matter, Bhante, I have found no support and have lost my way.
For I do not understand, as it really is, the arising, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding the six bases of contact.
“What do you think, bhikkhu?”
“Is the eye permanent or impermanent?
“Impermanent, venerable sir.
“But that which is impermanent, is it suffering or happiness?”
“It is suffering, venerable sir.
“But that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—is it fitting to regard it thus:
‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?”
“No, venerable sir.
“The ear… the nose…”
“Is the tongue… the body… the mind permanent or impermanent?”
“Impermanent, venerable sir.
“But what is impermanent, is that suffering or happiness?
“Suffering, venerable sir.”
“But that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—is it fitting to regard it thus:
‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?
“Certainly not, Bhante.”

“Seeing thus, bhikkhu, the well-taught noble disciple becomes disenchanted with the eye, disenchanted with the ear, disenchanted with the nose, disenchanted with the tongue, disenchanted with the body, and disenchanted with the mind. Through disenchantment, he becomes dispassionate;
through dispassion, he is liberated. When liberated, there comes the knowledge: ‘It is liberated.’”
‘Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being,’ he understands.
Thus ends the eleventh [sutta].
The second chapter, the Migajāla Chapter.
Its summary verse:
Two were spoken by Migajāla,
and four by Samiddhi.
Upasena, Upavāṇa,
and the three on the six bases of contact.
(Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.74)

First Discourse on the Sick.
Setting at Sāvatthī.
Then a certain bhikkhu approached the Blessed One... [as before] ...and sitting to one side, that bhikkhu said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, in such-and-such a monastery there is a certain bhikkhu who is new, unknown, afflicted, suffering, and gravely ill.
It would be well, venerable sir, if the Blessed One would approach that bhikkhu out of compassion.”
Then the Blessed One, having heard both the report concerning the new [monk] and the report concerning the sick one, and perceiving,
"The monk is unknown," approached that monk. Seeing the Blessed One coming from afar,
that monk sat up on his bed.
Then the Blessed One said this to that bhikkhu:
“Enough, bhikkhu; do not lie down on the couch.
These seats have been prepared; there I shall sit.”
The Blessed One sat down on the prepared seat.

“Venerable sir, I do not understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One for the sake of purification of virtue.
“If, bhikkhu, you do not understand the Dhamma taught by me for the sake of purification of virtue, then for what purpose, bhikkhu, do you understand the Dhamma taught by me?
“Venerable sir, I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One for the sake of the fading away of lust.”
“Excellent, excellent, bhikkhu!
It is excellent that you, bhikkhu, understand the Dhamma taught by me for the purpose of the fading away of lust.
For the Dhamma, bhikkhu, has been taught by me for the purpose of the fading away of lust.”
“What do you think, bhikkhu,
is the eye permanent or impermanent?
“Impermanent, Bhante.”
The ear ...
the nose ...”
“Is the tongue … the body … the mind permanent or impermanent?”
“Impermanent, Bhante.
“But what is impermanent, is that suffering or happiness?
“Suffering, Bhante.”
“But that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—is it fitting to regard it thus:
‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?
“Certainly not, venerable sir.”
“Seeing thus, bhikkhu, the well-taught noble disciple becomes disenchanted with the eye, disenchanted with the ear … [and so on] … disenchanted with the mind.
Through disenchantment, he becomes dispassionate; through dispassion, he is liberated. When liberated, there comes the knowledge:

8. Gilānavagga:
The Second Discourse on the Sick Then a certain bhikkhu ... [approached] the Blessed One and said this to him:
“Venerable sir, in such-and-such a monastery there is a certain bhikkhu who is new, unknown, afflicted, suffering, and gravely ill.
It would be well, venerable sir, if the Blessed One would approach that bhikkhu out of compassion.
Then the Blessed One, having heard the report concerning the newcomer and the report concerning the illness, and perceiving, “This bhikkhu is unknown,” approached that bhikkhu.
That bhikkhu saw the Blessed One coming from afar.

“… [as before] … The ear …”
The nose … the tongue … the body …
The mind … mental consciousness … mind-contact …
“And as for this feeling that arises conditioned by mind-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—is that permanent or impermanent?
“Impermanent, Bhante.
“And what is impermanent, is it suffering or happiness?”

“But that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—would it be fitting to regard it thus:
‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?”

“Seeing thus, bhikkhu, the well-taught noble disciple becomes disenchanted with the eye … [and so on] … with the mind.”
He becomes disenchanted with mind-consciousness as well, and with mind-contact as well.
He becomes disenchanted with whatever feeling arises conditioned by mind-contact— whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant.
“Through disenchantment, one becomes dispassionate; through dispassion, one is liberated. In liberation, the knowledge arises: ‘It is liberated. One understands:

Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.76 (SN 35.76, PTS SN iv 48) 8. Gilānavagga Rādha-anicca-sutta (The Discourse to Rādha on Impermanence) At Sāvatthī. Then the Venerable Rādha approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it would be good if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief, so that, having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, I might dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute. “Rādha, whatever is impermanent is suffering; whatever is suffering is non-self; whatever is non-self should be seen with right wisdom as it really is: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self. “Venerable sir, I understand the detailed exposition of the Blessed One’s brief statement thus: ‘Whatever is impermanent is suffering; whatever is suffering is non-self; whatever is non-self should be seen with right wisdom as it really is: “This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self. “If, Rādha, you understand the detailed exposition of my brief statement thus, then, Rādha, you have indeed understood the detailed exposition of my brief statement. When this was said, the Venerable Rādha said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it is wonderful, it is marvelous! How well this has been stated by the Blessed One: ‘Whatever is impermanent is suffering; whatever is suffering is non-self; whatever is non-self should be seen with right wisdom as it really is: “This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self. Venerable sir, when I had previously heard this Dhamma taught in brief by the Blessed One, I did not understand it; but now, having heard it explained in detail by the Blessed One, I understand it. Just as one might turn upright what had been overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who was lost, or bring an oil lamp into a dark place so that those with eyes might see forms, even so has the Blessed One made the Dhamma clear in many ways.

Venerable sir, I go for refuge to the Blessed One, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. May I receive the going forth under the Blessed One, may I receive the full admission. “Rādha, whoever has previously belonged to another sect and desires the going forth and the full admission in this Dhamma and Discipline must wait four months; at the end of four months, being satisfied in character, they are to be granted the going forth and the full admission as bhikkhus. But there is an exception in the case of one possessed of special qualities. “Venerable sir, if whoever has previously belonged to another sect and desires the going forth and the full admission in this Dhamma and Discipline must wait four months... and there is an exception in the case of one possessed of special qualities, then I will wait four months. At the end of four months, being satisfied in character, may I receive the going forth and the full admission as a bhikkhu. Then the Venerable Rādha waited four months. At the end of four months, being satisfied in character, he approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, if whoever has previously belonged to another sect and desires the going forth and the full admission in this Dhamma and Discipline must wait four months... and there is an exception in the case of one possessed of special qualities, then I have waited four months. At the end of four months, being satisfied in character, may I receive the going forth and the full admission as a bhikkhu. Then the Venerable Rādha received the going forth under the Blessed One, and he received the full admission. Not long after his full admission, dwelling alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute, the Venerable Rādha, by realizing it for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life entered and dwelt in that unsurpassed goal of the holy life for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness. He directly knew: “Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being. And the Venerable Rādha became one of the arahants.

Mind-consciousness...

and whatever feeling—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—arises conditioned by mind-contact, that too is impermanent. In regard to that, you should abandon desire.

Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.79 (SN 35.79, PTS SN iv 49) 8. Gilānavagga First Discourse on the Abandoning of Ignorance At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, when ignorance is abandoned by a bhikkhu, and true knowledge has arisen, he understands as it really is: ‘This is suffering. He understands as it really is: ‘This is the origin of suffering. He understands as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of suffering. He understands as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. When ignorance is abandoned by a bhikkhu, and true knowledge has arisen, he understands as it really is: ‘These are the taints’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the origin of the taints’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of the taints’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of the taints. When ignorance is abandoned by a bhikkhu, and true knowledge has arisen, he understands as it really is: ‘This is the noble truth of suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the noble truth of the origin of suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering. When ignorance is abandoned by a bhikkhu, and true knowledge has arisen, he understands as it really is: ‘This noble truth of suffering has been fully understood’; he understands as it really is: ‘This noble truth of the origin of suffering has been abandoned’; he understands as it really is: ‘This noble truth of the cessation of suffering has been realized’; he understands as it really is: ‘This noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering has been developed. When ignorance is abandoned by a bhikkhu, and true knowledge has arisen, he understands as it really is: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being.’”
Then a certain bhikkhu approached the Blessed One...
and, sitting to one side, that bhikkhu said this to the Blessed One:
"Is there, venerable sir, a single dharma, by the abandoning of which ignorance is abandoned in a bhikkhu and true knowledge arises?"
“There is, bhikkhu, one thing by the abandoning of which ignorance is abandoned in a bhikkhu and true knowledge arises.
“But what, Bhante, is that one thing by the abandoning of which ignorance is abandoned in a bhikkhu and true knowledge arises?
“Ignorance itself, bhikkhu, is that one thing by the abandoning of which ignorance is abandoned in a bhikkhu and true knowledge arises.”
“But how, venerable sir, for a bhikkhu who knows what and sees what is ignorance abandoned and true knowledge arisen?
“Bhikkhu, for one who knows and sees the eye as impermanent, ignorance is abandoned and true knowledge arises.

For one who knows and sees forms … eye-consciousness … eye-contact … and whatever feeling arises conditioned by eye-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—as impermanent, ignorance is abandoned and true knowledge arises. … [as above] …
For a bhikkhu who knows and sees the mind as impermanent, ignorance is abandoned and true knowledge arises. [The same applies to] mental phenomena... mental consciousness... mental contact...

and whatever feeling—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—arises conditioned by mental contact, for a bhikkhu who knows and sees that too as impermanent, ignorance is abandoned and true knowledge arises.
It is in this way, bhikkhu, that for a bhikkhu who knows thus and sees thus, ignorance is abandoned and true knowledge arises.”

Eye-consciousness … eye-contact … and whatever feeling arises conditioned by eye-contact— whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant— that too he sees as something other … pe …

Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.81 (SN 35.81, PTS SN iv 50) 8. Gilānavagga Sambahulabhikkhusutta Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus! “Venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu is sick, there are these five things that he should attend to. What five? (1) He should attend to the perception of unattractiveness. (2) He should attend to the perception of death. (3) He should attend to the perception of the repulsiveness of food. (4) He should attend to the perception of non-delight in the entire world. (5) He should attend to the perception of impermanence. When a bhikkhu is sick, these are the five things that he should attend to. This is what the Blessed One said. Having said this, the Fortunate One, the Teacher, further said this: “When a bhikkhu is afflicted by illness, These five things should be attended to: The perception of unattractiveness, And the perception of death; The perception of the repulsiveness of food, And non-delight in the entire world; And the perception of impermanence— For one who attends to these, The affliction of illness will fade away, And he will soon attain Nibbāna.”
Then a number of bhikkhus approached the Blessed One... and having sat down to one side, those bhikkhus said this to the Blessed One:
"Here, Bhante, wanderers of other sects ask us:
'For what purpose, friends, is the holy life lived under the ascetic Gotama?'"
“Venerable sir, when we are asked this by those wanderers of other sects, we answer them thus:
‘Friends, the holy life is lived under the Blessed One for the sake of the full understanding of suffering.
Venerable sir, when we are asked this and answer in this way, do we state what has been said by the Blessed One, and do we not misrepresent him with an untruth?”
"And we do not misrepresent the Blessed One with what is false; we explain in accordance with the Dhamma, and no legitimate point of criticism can be found against us.
"Truly, monks, when questioned thus, by answering in this way you have spoken as I would say."
And you have not misrepresented me with what is untrue; you have explained in accordance with the Dhamma, and no legitimate point of criticism or reproach arises against you.
For, monks, the holy life is lived under me for the sake of the full understanding of suffering.
"But if, monks, wanderers of other sects should ask you thus:
'But what, friends, is that suffering for the full understanding of which the holy life is lived under the ascetic Gotama?'—
being asked thus, monks, you should answer those wanderers of other sects as follows:"
“Friend, the eye is suffering; for the full understanding of it, the holy life is lived under the Blessed One.
Visible forms...
[and so on] ...whatever feeling arises conditioned by eye-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too is suffering.”
The holy life is lived under the Blessed One for the sake of full understanding of that: ... [and so on] ...
the mind is suffering; ...
and whatever feeling arises conditioned by mind-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too is suffering.
“The holy life is lived under the Blessed One for the sake of fully understanding that.
This, friends, is suffering; the holy life is lived under the Blessed One for the sake of its full understanding.
Thus, monks, being asked by those wanderers of other sects, you should answer them in this way.
The Eighth.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 35.82 (SN 35.82, PTS SN iv 52) 8.

The Discourse on the Question of the World.
Then a certain bhikkhu approached the Blessed One... [as before] ...and sitting to one side, that bhikkhu said this to the Blessed One:
