“To what extent, venerable sir, is it said that there is a ‘world’? “It is called a ‘world,’ bhikkhu, because it breaks up.

And what is it that breaks up? The eye breaks up; forms break up; eye-consciousness breaks up; eye-contact breaks up; and whatever feeling arises in dependence on eye-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neutral—that too breaks up. The ear breaks up; sounds break up... The nose breaks up; odors break up... The tongue breaks up; tastes break up... The body breaks up; tangibles break up... The mind breaks up; mental phenomena break up; mind-consciousness breaks up; mind-contact breaks up; and whatever feeling arises in dependence on mind-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neutral—that too breaks up. It is because it breaks up that it is called a ‘world.’”
The eye, bhikkhu, breaks up; forms break up;
eye-consciousness breaks up; eye-contact breaks up; and whatever feeling arises conditioned by eye-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too breaks up.
…pe… The tongue breaks up. …pe…

“The mind disintegrates, mental phenomena disintegrate, mind-consciousness disintegrates, mind-contact disintegrates, and whatever feeling arises conditioned by mind-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too disintegrates.
It is because it disintegrates (*lujjati*), bhikkhu, that it is called ‘the world’ (*loka*).
This was the ninth [sutta].

Saṁyutta Nikāya 35.83 (SN 35.83, PTS SN iv 52) 8. Gilānavagga Phaggunapañhāsutta: The Question of Phagguna At Sāvatthī. Then the Venerable Phagguna approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it would be good if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief, so that, having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, I might dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute. “Phagguna, when one does not understand as they really are the gratification, the danger, and the escape in the case of the six bases for contact, one does not understand suffering, the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the way leading to the cessation of suffering. “But, Phagguna, when one understands as they really are the gratification, the danger, and the escape in the case of the six bases for contact, one understands suffering, the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the way leading to the cessation of suffering. When this was said, the Venerable Phagguna said to the Blessed One: “It is wonderful, venerable sir! It is amazing, venerable sir! How well this has been stated by the Blessed One: ‘Phagguna, when one does not understand as they really are the gratification, the danger, and the escape in the case of the six bases for contact... Then the Venerable Phagguna, having delighted and rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him on his right, departed. Not long after the Venerable Phagguna had left, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus, suppose there were a blind man who could not see any objects at all, whether things that were beneficial or harmful. Would he know: ‘This is beneficial for me; this is harmful for me’? “No, venerable sir. “Bhikkhus, suppose there were a man with eyes who could see objects that were beneficial and harmful. Would he know: ‘This is beneficial for me; this is harmful for me’? “Yes, venerable sir. “In the same way, bhikkhus, when one does not understand as they really are the gratification, the danger, and the escape in the case of the six bases for contact, one does not understand suffering, the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the way leading to the cessation of suffering. But when one understands these things as they really are, one understands suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the way leading to its cessation. When this was said, the Venerable Phagguna said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it is wonderful how well this has been stated by the Blessed One! Venerable sir, I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One thus: ‘When one does not understand as they really are the gratification, the danger, and the escape in the case of the six bases for contact, one does not understand suffering, the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the way leading to the cessation of suffering. Venerable sir, I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One thus: ‘When one understands as they really are the gratification, the danger, and the escape in the case of the six bases for contact, one understands suffering, the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the way leading to the cessation of suffering. “Good, good, Phagguna! It is good that you understand the Dhamma taught by me thus. When one does not understand as they really are the gratification, the danger, and the escape in the case of the six bases for contact, one does not understand suffering, the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the way leading to the cessation of suffering. But when one understands these things as they really are, one understands suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the way leading to its cessation. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Elated, the Venerable Phagguna delighted in the Blessed One’s words.
Then the Venerable Phagguna … [as before] … sat down to one side and said this to the Blessed One:

“Is there, venerable sir, such an eye by means of which one, describing those Buddhas of the past who have attained final Nibbāna—whose conceptual proliferation is cut off, whose cycle is ended, whose round is finished, and who have transcended all suffering—could describe them? … [as before] …

“Venerable sir, is there such a tongue by which one, when describing, could describe those past Buddhas who have attained final Nibbāna, for whom the proliferations are cut off, the rounds are broken, the cycle is ended, and who have transcended all suffering?

… Is there such a mind, venerable sir, by which one, when describing, could describe those past Buddhas who have attained final Nibbāna, for whom the proliferations are cut off, the rounds are broken, the cycle is ended, and who have transcended all suffering?”

“Phagguna, there is no eye by which one describing the Buddhas of the past—who have attained final Nibbāna, cut off proliferation, cut off the cycle, exhausted the round, and transcended all suffering—could describe them...

Phagguna, there is no tongue by which one describing the Buddhas of the past—who have attained final Nibbāna, cut off proliferation, cut off the cycle, exhausted the round, and transcended all suffering—could describe them...”

“Phagguna, there is no mind by means of which one, describing those Buddhas of the past who have attained final Nibbāna, for whom the proliferation of becoming has been cut off, the cycle of rebirth has been severed, the round has been exhausted, and who have transcended all suffering, could describe them.
Tenth. The Third Chapter on the Sick.
Its summary verse:
Two are spoken of regarding the sick,
and another three regarding Rādha.
“And two [topics] have been spoken of regarding ignorance: ‘The world, O Bhikkhu,
and Phagguna,’” as stated in Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.84 (SN 35.84, PTS SN iv 53).
9. Channa Chapter: Palokadhammasutta (The Discourse on the Nature of Disintegration).
Setting at Sāvatthī.
Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One... [as before] ...and sitting to one side, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable sir, it is said, 'the world, the world.
In what way, venerable sir, is it called 'the world'?"
“Ānanda, that which is subject to disintegration is called ‘the world’ in the discipline of the Noble One.
And what, Ānanda, is subject to disintegration?

The eye, Ānanda, is subject to disintegration; forms are subject to disintegration; eye-consciousness is subject to disintegration; eye-contact is subject to disintegration; and whatever feeling arises conditioned by eye-contact—that too is subject to disintegration... [and so on for the other sense bases].”

The tongue is subject to disintegration; tastes are subject to disintegration; tongue-consciousness is subject to disintegration; tongue-contact is subject to disintegration; and whatever feeling arises conditioned by tongue-contact—whether pleasant or painful—that too is subject to disintegration.
… The mind is subject to disintegration; mental phenomena are subject to disintegration; mind-consciousness is subject to disintegration; mind-contact is subject to disintegration;
and whatever feeling arises conditioned by mind-contact—whether pleasant or painful—that too is subject to disintegration.
or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too is subject to disintegration.
Whatever, Ānanda, is subject to disintegration is called ‘the world’ (loka) in the discipline of the Noble One. Thus was the first [discourse].

Saṁyutta Nikāya 35.85 (SN 35.85, PTS SN iv 54) 9. Channavagga Suññatalokasutta The Discourse on the World as Empty “Bhikkhus, this world is empty of a self or of what belongs to a self. And by what is this world empty? It is empty of a self or of what belongs to a self. “Bhikkhus, it is because one sees with right wisdom according to reality that ‘this world is empty of a self or of what belongs to a self’ that one is called a person of right view, one who holds correct views, one whose view is straight, one who has arrived at the true Dhamma, one who stands upon the true Dhamma, one who has entered the stream of the Dhamma.”
Then the Venerable Ānanda … [approached] the Blessed One and said this to him:
“‘Empty is the world, empty is the world,’ it is said, Bhante.
To what extent, Bhante, is it said that ‘the world is empty’?”
“But because, Ānanda, it is empty of a self or of what belongs to a self, therefore the world is said to be ‘empty.
And of what, Ānanda, is it empty of a self or of what belongs to a self?
The eye, Ānanda, is empty of a self or of what belongs to a self.”
“Forms are empty of self or of what belongs to self; eye-consciousness is empty of self or of what belongs to self; eye-contact is empty of self or of what belongs to self...pe...
Whatever feeling arises conditioned by mind-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too is empty of self or of what belongs to self.
And because, Ānanda, it is empty of self or of what belongs to self, therefore it is called ‘the world is empty.’”
The Second.
Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.86 (SN 35.86, PTS SN iv 54) 9.
Channa-vagga
The Discourse on the Dharma in Brief.
Seated to one side, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:

“It would be well, Bhante, if the Blessed One would teach me the Dharma in brief, so that having heard the Dharma from the Blessed One, I might dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute.”
“What do you think, Ānanda,
is the eye permanent or impermanent?
“Impermanent, Bhante.”
“But what is impermanent, is that suffering or happiness?
“Suffering, venerable sir.
“But what is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—is it fitting to regard it thus:”
‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?”—
“Certainly not, Bhante.”—
“Are forms permanent or impermanent?”
“Impermanent, Bhante.
… [as before] … “Is eye-consciousness … and whatever feeling arises conditioned by eye-contact— whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant— that too permanent or impermanent?”
“Impermanent, venerable sir.
“But what is impermanent, is that suffering or happiness?
“Suffering, venerable sir.”
“But that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—would it be fitting to regard it thus:
‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?
“Certainly not, venerable sir. …pe…
“Is the tongue permanent or impermanent?
“Impermanent, venerable sir.
… [and so on] … “Tongue-consciousness …”
“Is tongue-contact …pe… and whatever feeling arises conditioned by mind-contact— whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant— that too permanent or impermanent?
“Impermanent, venerable sir.”
“But that which is impermanent, is it suffering or happiness?”—
“Suffering, venerable sir.”—
“But that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change— is it fitting to regard it thus:”
‘This is mine, this am I, this is my self’?”—
“Certainly not, Bhante. “Seeing thus,
Ānanda, the well-taught noble disciple becomes disenchanted with the eye … and becomes disenchanted with eye-contact …”
Whatever feeling arises conditioned by mind-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—one becomes disenchanted with that as well.
Through disenchantment, passion fades away; through the fading of passion, one is liberated. In liberation, the knowledge arises: "It is liberated. One understands:
"Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being."
Third.
Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.87 (SN 35.87, PTS SN iv 55) 9.
Channa-vagga (The Chapter on Channa)
The Channa Sutta.
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.
Now at that time the Venerable Sāriputta, the Venerable Mahācunda, and the Venerable Channa were dwelling on Gijjhakūṭa Mountain.
Now at that time, the Venerable Channa was afflicted, suffering, and gravely ill.
Then, in the evening, the Venerable Sāriputta emerged from seclusion and approached the Venerable Mahācunda. Having approached, he said this to the Venerable Mahācunda:
"Come, friend Cunda, let us go to the Venerable Channa to inquire after his illness."
“Yes, friend,” the Venerable Mahācunda replied to the Venerable Sāriputta.
Then the Venerable Sāriputta and the Venerable Mahācunda approached the Venerable Channa;
having approached, they sat down on the prepared seats. Once seated, the Venerable Sāriputta said this to the Venerable Channa:
“I hope it is bearable for you, friend Channa; I hope you are getting by. I hope that the painful feelings are subsiding and not increasing, and that their subsiding is apparent, not their increase?
“Friend Sāriputta, it is not bearable for me, nor am I getting by. The painful feelings are severe; they are increasing and not subsiding, and their increase is apparent, not their subsiding.”
"Friend, it is just as if a strong man were to strike one on the head with a sharp spear; even so, friend, violent winds are piercing my head.
Friend, it is not endurable for me, nor can I maintain myself... there is no improvement.
Friend, it is just as if a strong man were to wrap a tight leather strap around one's head as a headband; even so, friend, there is an intense pain in my head."
"Friends, it is not endurable for me, it is not sustainable... there is no improvement.
Just as if, friends, a skilled butcher or a butcher’s apprentice were to cut open a cow's belly with a sharp carving knife, even so, excessive winds cut through my belly.
Friends, it is not endurable for me, it is not sustainable... there is no improvement."

"Friend, it is just as if two strong men were to seize a weaker man by both arms and roast him over a pit of glowing embers, thoroughly scorching him. Even so, friend, there is an intense burning in my body.
It is not endurable for me, friend; it is not sustainable. My sharp painful feelings are increasing and do not subside; their increase is apparent, not their subsiding.
Friend Sāriputta, I shall take up the knife; I have no desire to live."
“Venerable Channa, do not take up the blade.
May the venerable Channa live on; we wish for the venerable Channa to live.
If the venerable Channa lacks suitable food, I shall seek out suitable food for the venerable Channa.”
If the Venerable Channa has no suitable medicines, I will seek suitable medicines for the Venerable Channa.
If the Venerable Channa has no suitable attendants, I will attend upon the Venerable Channa.
Let the Venerable Channa not take up a blade.
“Venerable Channa, live on! We wish for the venerable Channa to live on.
“Friends, it is not that I lack suitable food; I have suitable food.”
It is not that I lack suitable medicines; I have suitable medicines.
It is not that I lack suitable attendants.
"I have suitable attendants.
Moreover, friends, for a long time I have served my Teacher with what is pleasing, not with what is displeasing.
For this is fitting for a disciple, friends: that he should serve the Teacher with what is pleasing, not with what is displeasing."
“‘The bhikkhu Channa will take up the knife without blame’—thus, friend Sāriputta, you should remember this.
“We would ask the venerable Channa about a certain point, if the venerable Channa would grant us the opportunity to answer the question.
“Ask, friend Sāriputta; having heard it, we shall know.”
“Friend Channa, do you regard the eye, eye-consciousness, and the phenomena cognizable by eye-consciousness as ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?...
[and so on] ...do you regard the tongue, tongue-consciousness, and the phenomena cognizable by tongue-consciousness as ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?...
[and so on] ...do you regard the mind, mind-consciousness, and the phenomena cognizable by mind-consciousness as ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?”
“Friend Sāriputta, regarding the eye, eye-consciousness, and the phenomena cognizable by eye-consciousness, I regard them thus: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.
… [and so on] … Regarding the tongue, tongue-consciousness, and the phenomena cognizable by tongue-consciousness, I regard them thus: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.
… [and so on] … Regarding the mind, mind-consciousness, and the phenomena cognizable by mind-consciousness, I regard them thus: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’”
“Friend Channa, having seen what in the eye, in eye-consciousness, and in things cognizable by eye-consciousness,
and having directly known what, do you regard the eye, eye-consciousness, and things cognizable by eye-consciousness thus:
‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self’?”
“Friend Channa, having seen what, having directly known what regarding the tongue, tongue-consciousness,
and the phenomena cognizable by tongue-consciousness, do you regard the tongue, tongue-consciousness, and the phenomena cognizable by tongue-consciousness thus:
‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self’?”
“Friend Channa, having seen what, having directly known what in regard to the mind, mind-consciousness, and the phenomena cognizable by mind-consciousness,
do you regard the mind, mind-consciousness, and the phenomena cognizable by mind-consciousness thus:
‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self’?”

“Friend Sāriputta, having seen cessation in the eye, in eye-consciousness, and in the phenomena cognizable by eye-consciousness, and having directly known that cessation, I regard the eye, eye-consciousness, and the phenomena cognizable by eye-consciousness thus:
‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self. … [and so on for the other sense bases] …”

"Friend Sāriputta, having seen cessation in the tongue, in tongue-consciousness, and in the phenomena cognizable by tongue-consciousness, and having directly known that cessation, I regard the tongue, tongue-consciousness, and the phenomena cognizable by tongue-consciousness thus: ‘This is not mine;
this I am not; this is not my self. … [as before] …"

"Friend Sāriputta, having seen cessation in the mind, in mind-consciousness, and in the phenomena cognizable by mind-consciousness, and having directly known that cessation, I regard the mind, mind-consciousness, and the phenomena cognizable by mind-consciousness thus:
'This is not mine; this I am not; this is not my self.'"
When this was said, the Venerable Mahācunda said this to the Venerable Channa:
“Therefore, friend Channa, this teaching of the Blessed One should be carefully attended to at all times:
‘For one who is dependent there is wavering; for one who is independent there is no wavering.’”
When equanimity exists, tranquility arises.
When tranquility exists, there is no inclination.
When there is no inclination, there is no coming and going.
"When there is no coming and going, there is no passing away and being reborn.
When there is no passing away and being reborn, there is neither this world nor the world beyond, nor anything in between these two.
This, indeed, is the end of suffering."
Then the Venerable Sāriputta and the Venerable Mahācunda, having exhorted the Venerable Channa with this instruction, rose from their seats and departed.
Not long after those venerable ones had left, the Venerable Channa drew a sword.

Then the Venerable Sāriputta approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Venerable Sāriputta said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, the Venerable Channa has taken up a blade.
What is his destination, what is his future state?
“Sāriputta, did not the bhikkhu Channa declare his own blamelessness right before your very eyes?”
“There is, venerable sir, a Vajjian village called Pubbavijjhana.
There, the venerable Channa has families who are his friends, families who are his close associates, and families who are his relatives.
“Indeed, Sāriputta, the bhikkhu Channa does have such families who are his friends, families who are his close associates, and families who are his relatives.”
But I do not say, Sāriputta, that one is blameworthy merely to this extent.
Whoever, Sāriputta, lays down this body and takes up another body—that person I call blameworthy.
That does not apply to the bhikkhu Channa.
‘A monk who is secluded may draw the sword without fault’—
thus, Sāriputta, you should remember this.
The fourth [sutta].

Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.88 (SN 35.88, PTS SN iv 60) 9. Channavagga Puṇṇasutta At Sāvatthī. “Puṇṇa, if anyone should say: ‘Without directly knowing and fully understanding the eye, without developing disenchantment toward it, without making it utterly exhausted, one will here and now make an end of suffering’—this is impossible. “If anyone should say: ‘Without directly knowing and fully understanding forms, without developing disenchantment toward them, without making them utterly exhausted, one will here and now make an end of suffering’—this is impossible. “If anyone should say: ‘Without directly knowing and fully understanding eye-consciousness... eye-contact... whatever feeling arises with eye-contact as condition—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—without directly knowing and fully understanding that feeling, without developing disenchantment toward it, without making it utterly exhausted, one will here and now make an end of suffering’—this is impossible. “If anyone should say: ‘Without directly knowing and fully understanding the ear... the nose... the tongue... the body... the mind... whatever feeling arises with mind-contact as condition—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—without directly knowing and fully understanding that feeling, without developing disenchantment toward it, without making it utterly exhausted, one will here and now make an end of suffering’—this is impossible. “But, Puṇṇa, if anyone should say: ‘Having directly known and fully understood the eye, having developed disenchantment toward it, having made it utterly exhausted, one will here and now make an end of suffering’—this is possible. “[And so on for each sense base. ... Having directly known and fully understood whatever feeling arises with mind-contact as condition—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—having developed disenchantment toward it, having made it utterly exhausted, one will here and now make an end of suffering’—this is possible.”
Then the Venerable Puṇṇa approached the Blessed One. Having approached, ... [he sat down to one side] and said to the Blessed One:
“It would be well, Bhante, if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief, so that having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, I might dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute.
“There are, Puṇṇa, forms cognizable by the eye—desirable, lovely, pleasing, endearing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust.
If a bhikkhu delights in that, welcomes it, and remains clinging to it, delight arises in him as he delights in it, welcomes it, and remains clinging to it.
"With the arising of delight comes the arising of suffering," Puṇṇa, I say... [and so on].
"There are, Puṇṇa, tastes cognizable by the tongue...
There are, Puṇṇa, mental phenomena cognizable by the mind that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual pleasure, and provocative of lust.
If a bhikkhu delights in them, welcomes them, and remains clinging to them..."
For one who delights in that, welcomes it, and remains attached to it, delight arises.
"From the arising of delight comes the arising of suffering," Puṇṇa, I say.
There are, Puṇṇa, forms cognizable by the eye—desirable, lovely, pleasing, endearing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust.

If a bhikkhu does not delight in that, does not welcome it, and does not remain clinging to it, then for him, by not delighting in it, not welcoming it, and not remaining clinging to it, delight ceases.
“With the cessation of delight comes the cessation of suffering,” Puṇṇa, I say. ...
There are, Puṇṇa, mental phenomena cognizable by the mind that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust.

“If a bhikkhu does not delight in that, does not welcome it, and does not remain clinging to it, then for him who does not delight in it, does not welcome it, and does not remain clinging to it, delight ceases.
‘With the cessation of delight comes the cessation of suffering,’ Puṇṇa, I say.
Having been exhorted by me with this brief exhortation, Puṇṇa, in which country will you dwell?”
“There is, venerable sir, a country named Sunāparanta; there I shall dwell.
“The people of Sunāparanta, Puṇṇa, are fierce;
the people of Sunāparanta, Puṇṇa, are harsh.”
“If, Puṇṇa, the people of Sunāparanta abuse and revile you, what will you think about that?
“If, Bhante, the people of Sunāparanta abuse and revile me, I will think:
‘These people of Sunāparanta are indeed excellent; these people of Sunāparanta are truly very kind, in that they do not strike me with their hands.’”
“It will be so here, Blessed One; it will be so here, Sugata.
“But if the people of Sunāparanta, Puṇṇa, should give you a blow with their hand, what would you think about that, Puṇṇa?”
“If, venerable sir, the people of Sunāparanta give me a blow with their hand, it will occur to me:
‘These people of Sunāparanta are indeed excellent, these people of Sunāparanta are indeed very excellent, in that they do not give me a blow with a clod.
Thus it will be there, Blessed One.”
“In this way, Sugata, it shall be here.
“But if, Puṇṇa, the people of Sunāparanta should strike you with clods of earth, what will you think then, Puṇṇa?
“If, Bhante, the people of Sunāparanta should strike me with clods of earth, then I will think thus:”
“‘How fortunate indeed are these people of Sunāparanta! How truly blessed are these people of Sunāparanta, in that they do not strike me with a staff!
Thus it shall be here, Blessed One;
thus it shall be here, Sugata.”
“But if, Puṇṇa, the people of Sunāparanta give you a blow with a staff, what will you think of that, Puṇṇa?
“If, Bhante, the people of Sunāparanta give me a blow with a staff, I will think:
‘These people of Sunāparanta are indeed good; these people of Sunāparanta are truly excellent, in that they do not strike me with a weapon.’”
“It will be so here, Blessed One; it will be so here, Sugata.
“But if, Puṇṇa, the people of Sunāparanta give you a blow with a weapon, what will you think then, Puṇṇa?”
“Venerable sir, if the people of Sunāparanta should give me a blow with a weapon, it would occur to me:
‘These people of Sunāparanta are indeed good; these people of Sunāparanta are indeed very good, in that they do not deprive me of life with a sharp weapon.
It will be thus in this matter, Blessed One.”
“In this way, Sugata, it will be so here.
“But if, Puṇṇa, the people of Sunāparanta should deprive you of life with a sharp sword, what will you think then, Puṇṇa?
“If, Bhante, the people of Sunāparanta should deprive me of life with a sharp sword, then I will think thus:”

“There are indeed disciples of that Blessed One who, distressed, ashamed, and disgusted by both body and life, seek an assassin. This assassin, whom I did not even have to seek out, has been found by me.
“So it shall be here, Blessed One; so it shall be here, Sugata,” he said.
“Excellent, excellent, Puṇṇa!
Endowed with this self-taming and tranquility, you will be able to dwell in the Sunāparanta country.
Now, Puṇṇa, do as you think it is time to do.”
Then the Venerable Puṇṇa, having rejoiced and delighted in the Blessed One’s words, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One,
and keeping him to his right, put his lodging in order, took his bowl and robe,
and set out on a wandering tour toward the Sunāparanta country.
Wandering on his journey by stages, he arrived at the country of Sunāparanta.
There, indeed, the Venerable Puṇṇa dwelt in the country of Sunāparanta.
Then, during that very rainy season retreat, the Venerable Puṇṇa instructed about five hundred lay followers.
Within that same interval of a year, he announced himself as five hundred female lay disciples;
within that same interval of a year, he realized the threefold knowledge;
and within that same interval of a year, he attained final nibbāna.
Then a number of bhikkhus approached the Blessed One... Sitting to one side, those bhikkhus said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable sir, that clansman named Puṇṇa, who was instructed by the Blessed One with a brief exhortation, has passed away.
What is his destination? What is his future state?"
“Monks, the clansman Puṇṇa was wise; he practiced in accordance with the Dhamma and did not trouble me on account of the Dhamma.
Monks, the clansman Puṇṇa has attained final Nibbāna.
This is the fifth [sutta].

Saṁyutta Nikāya 35.89 (SN 35.89, PTS SN iv 63) 9. Channavagga Bāhiyasutta At Sāvatthī. “Bāhiya, you should train yourself thus: ‘In the seen there shall be just the seen; in the heard there shall be just the heard; in the sensed there shall be just the sensed; in the cognized there shall be just the cognized. When this was said, the Venerable Bāhiya said to the Blessed One: “It is wonderful, venerable sir! It is amazing, venerable sir! How well this has been stated by the Blessed One: ‘Bāhiya, you should train yourself thus: “In the seen there shall be just the seen; in the heard there shall be just the heard; in the sensed there shall be just the sensed; in the cognized there shall be just the cognized. But how, venerable sir, is the meaning of this statement by the Blessed One to be understood? “Bāhiya, when it was said by me: ‘Bāhiya, you should train yourself thus: “In the seen there shall be just the seen; in the heard there shall be just the heard; in the sensed there shall be just the sensed; in the cognized there shall be just the cognized,” it was with reference to this that this was said by me. For, Bāhiya, as long as in regard to the seen there will be for you the state of ‘the seen,’ and in regard to the heard there will be for you the state of ‘the heard,’ and in regard to the sensed there will be for you the state of ‘the sensed,’ and in regard to the cognized there will be for you the state of ‘the cognized,’ so long will you not transcend death; you will remain within the domain of Death. But when, Bāhiya, in regard to the seen there will be for you no more the state of ‘the seen,’ and in regard to the heard there will be for you no more the state of ‘the heard,’ and in regard to the sensed there will be for you no more the state of ‘the sensed,’ and in regard to the cognized there will be for you no more the state of ‘the cognized,’ then, Bāhiya, you will not be [subject to] death; you will transcend the domain of Death. Therefore, Bāhiya, you should train yourself thus: ‘In the seen there shall be just the seen; in the heard there shall be just the heard; in the sensed there shall be just the sensed; in the cognized there shall be just the cognized. When this was said, the Venerable Bāhiya said to the Blessed One: “Magnificent, venerable sir! Magnificent, venerable sir!... From today let the Blessed One remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life. Then the Venerable Bāhiya, having delighted and rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him on his right, departed. Not long after he had left, while the Venerable Bāhiya was alone in seclusion, the thought arose in him: “I have not yet fulfilled the training in the Teacher’s Dispensation, yet I am about to die. Then, with the divine ear, which is purified and surpasses the human, the Blessed One heard the Venerable Bāhiya’s reflection. Then the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda: “Ānanda, let us go to the Gabled Hall in the Great Forest. “Yes, venerable sir,” the Venerable Ānanda replied. Then the Blessed One went with a large assembly of bhikkhus to the Gabled Hall in the Great Forest. At that time, the Venerable Bāhiya was sitting not far from the Blessed One, with his legs crossed, holding his body erect, having set up mindfulness before him. The Blessed One saw the Venerable Bāhiya sitting not far away... and said to him: “Bāhiya, is it true that, while you were alone in seclusion, the thought arose in you: ‘I have not yet fulfilled the training in the Teacher’s Dispensation, yet I am about to die’? “Yes, venerable sir. “Bāhiya, you should train yourself thus: ‘In the seen there shall be just the seen; in the heard there shall be just the heard; in the sensed there shall be just the sensed; in the cognized there shall be just the cognized. “Venerable sir, it is wonderful! Venerable sir, it is amazing! How well this has been stated by the Blessed One: ‘Bāhiya, you should train yourself thus: “In the seen there shall be just the seen;

in the heard there shall be just the heard; in the sensed there shall be just the sensed; in the cognized there shall be just the cognized. But how, venerable sir, is the meaning of this statement by the Blessed One to be understood? “Bāhiya, when it was said by me: ‘Bāhiya, you should train yourself thus: “In the seen there shall be just the seen; in the heard there shall be just the heard; in the sensed there shall be just the sensed; in the cognized there shall be just the cognized,” it was with reference to this that this was said by me. For, Bāhiya, as long as in regard to the seen there will be for you the state of ‘the seen,’ and in regard to the heard there will be for you the state of ‘the heard,’ and in regard to the sensed there will be for you the state of ‘the sensed,’ and in regard to the cognized there will be for you the state of ‘the cognized,’ so long will you not transcend death; you will remain within the domain of Death. But when, Bāhiya, in regard to the seen there will be for you no more the state of ‘the seen,’ and in regard to the heard there will be for you no more the state of ‘the heard,’ and in regard to the sensed there will be for you no more the state of ‘the sensed,’ and in regard to the cognized there will be for you no more the state of ‘the cognized,’ then, Bāhiya, you will not be [subject to] death; you will transcend the domain of Death. Therefore, Bāhiya, you should train yourself thus: ‘In the seen there shall be just the seen; in the heard there shall be just the heard; in the sensed there shall be just the sensed; in the cognized there shall be just the cognized. “Venerable sir, it is wonderful! Venerable sir, it is amazing! How well this has been stated by the Blessed One: ‘Bāhiya, you should train yourself thus: “In the seen there shall be just the seen; in the heard there shall be just the heard; in the sensed there shall be just the sensed; in the cognized there shall be just the cognized. And this is how the meaning of this statement by the Blessed One is to be understood. When this was said, the Blessed One said to the Venerable Bāhiya: “Well said, Bāhiya! Well said, Bāhiya! For this is how the meaning of this statement by me is to be understood. Then the Venerable Bāhiya, having delighted and rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him on his right, departed. And not long after the Venerable Bāhiya had left, he attained final Nibbāna. Then the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus, even if a bhikkhu attains final Nibbāna right here, he should still be honored, respected, revered, and venerated, and a shrine should be made for him. This is because it is a gain for his relatives, a great gain for his relatives, that a clansman who has gone forth from the household life into homelessness out of faith in the Tathāgata attains final Nibbāna. Just as one might honor, respect, revere, and venerate a royal khattiya who has just ascended the throne, and a shrine should be made for him, because it is a gain for his relatives, a great gain for his relatives, that a khattiya youth who has gone forth from the household life into homelessness attains the position of a king—so too, bhikkhus, even if a bhikkhu attains final Nibbāna right here, he should still be honored, respected, revered, and venerated, and a shrine should be made for him. This is because it is a gain for his relatives, a great gain for his relatives, that a clansman who has gone forth from the household life into homelessness out of faith in the Tathāgata attains final Nibbāna. Thus the Blessed One spoke. Having said this, the Sublime One rose from his seat and entered his dwelling. Then, not long after the Blessed One had gone, the bhikkhus considered: “Friends, the Blessed One has spoken in brief and then risen from his seat and entered his dwelling.
Then the Venerable Bāhiya approached the Blessed One... [as before] ...and sat down to one side. Sitting there, the Venerable Bāhiya said this to the Blessed One:
“It would be well, Bhante, if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief, so that having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, I might dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute.
“What do you think, Bāhiya?”
“Is the eye permanent or impermanent?”—
“Impermanent, venerable sir.”—
“But that which is impermanent, is it suffering or happiness?”
“It is suffering, venerable sir.
“But that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—is it fitting to regard it thus:
‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?”
“No, venerable sir.
“Are forms permanent or impermanent?
“Impermanent, venerable sir. … [as before] …
“Is eye-consciousness … [and so on] … eye-contact … [and so on] … even that feeling—
whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant— that arises conditioned by mind-contact, is that permanent or impermanent?”
“Impermanent, venerable sir.
“But what is impermanent, is that suffering or happiness?
“Suffering, venerable sir.”
“But that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—is it fitting to regard it thus:
‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?
“Certainly not, Bhante.”
“Seeing thus, Bāhiya, the well-taught noble disciple becomes disenchanted with the eye, disenchanted with forms, disenchanted with eye-consciousness, and disenchanted with eye-contact...
[and so on] ...he becomes disenchanted with whatever feeling arises conditioned by mind-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant.
Through disenchantment, he becomes dispassionate; through dispassion, he is liberated. In liberation, there is the knowledge: ‘It is liberated.’”
‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.
Then the Venerable Bāhiya, having rejoiced and delighted in the Blessed One’s words, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him to his right, departed.
Then, dwelling alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute, the Venerable Bāhiya—in no long time—[attained that goal] for the sake of which...
Those sons of noble family went forth from the home life into homelessness in the right way;
and having realized for himself with direct knowledge, he attained and dwelt in that unsurpassed culmination of the holy life, even in this very life.
He directly knew: "Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being."
And the venerable Bāhiya became one of the arahants.
Thus ends the sixth [discourse]. Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.90 (SN 35.90, PTS SN iv 64).
9. The Chapter on Concealment (Channavagga) First Discourse on Agitation (Paṭhama-ejāsutta) “Monks, agitation is a disease; agitation is a tumor; agitation is a dart.”
"Therefore, monks, the Tathāgata dwells unshaken, with the arrow removed.
Therefore, monks, if a monk should wish, 'May I dwell unshaken, with the arrow removed,' he should not conceive of the eye,
he should not conceive in the eye, he should not conceive from the eye, and he should not conceive, 'The eye is mine';"
One should not conceive of form, one should not conceive in forms, one should not conceive from form, one should not conceive "form is mine.
One should not conceive of eye-consciousness, one should not conceive in eye-consciousness, one should not conceive from eye-consciousness, one should not conceive "eye-consciousness is mine.
One should not conceive of eye-contact, one should not conceive in eye-contact, one should not conceive from eye-contact, one should not conceive "eye-contact is mine."

Whatever feeling arises conditioned by eye-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—one should not conceive it, one should not conceive in it, one should not conceive from it, and one should not conceive, "This is mine.
One should not conceive the ear...
[and so on] ...one should not conceive the nose... [and so on].
One should not conceive of the tongue; one should not conceive by means of the tongue; one should not conceive from the tongue; one should not conceive, "The tongue is mine.
One should not conceive of tastes … [and so on] … one should not conceive of tongue-consciousness … [and so on].

One should not conceive of tongue-contact … and so on … one should not conceive of that feeling—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that arises conditioned by tongue-contact; one should not conceive of it, one should not conceive in it, one should not conceive from it, nor should one conceive, "This is mine.
One should not conceive of the body … and so on …
One should not conceive of the mind, one should not conceive in the mind, one should not conceive from the mind, one should not conceive "the mind is mine";
one should not conceive of mental phenomena …pe… [one should not conceive] of mind-consciousness …pe…
Mental contact...

[and so on] ...whatever feeling arises conditioned by mental contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—one should not conceive it, one should not conceive in it, one should not conceive from it, one should not conceive "this is mine.
One should not conceive anything at all, one should not conceive in anything, one should not conceive from anything, one should not conceive "this is everything of mine."
Thus, not conceiving in this way, one does not cling to anything in the world.
Not clinging, one is not agitated. Being unagitated, one personally attains Nibbāna.
One understands: “Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.”
Seventh.

Channa-vagga
The Second Discourse on Agitation:
“Agitation, bhikkhus, is a disease; agitation is a tumor; agitation is a dart.
Therefore, bhikkhus, the Tathāgata dwells unagitated, with the dart removed.”
Therefore, monks, if a monk should wish, "May I dwell unshaken, with the dart removed," he should not conceive of the eye,
he should not conceive in the eye, he should not conceive from the eye, he should not conceive, "The eye is mine";
he should not conceive of forms...

One should not conceive of eye-consciousness… one should not conceive of eye-contact… nor should one conceive of whatever feeling— whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant— that arises conditioned by eye-contact; one should not conceive of that, one should not conceive in that, one should not conceive from that, and one should not conceive "that is mine."
For whatever one conceives, whatever one conceives in, from whatever one conceives, and whatever one conceives as "mine"—that becomes otherwise.
The world, subject to change and attached to existence, delights only in existence...
[as before] ...One should not conceive the tongue; one should not conceive in the tongue; one should not conceive from the tongue; one should not conceive, "The tongue is mine."
One should not conceive of taste … tongue-consciousness … tongue-contact …

Whatever feeling arises conditioned by tongue-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—one should not conceive it, one should not conceive in it, one should not conceive from it, and one should not conceive "this is mine.

For whatever one conceives, monks, in whatever one conceives, from whatever one conceives, and that which one conceives as "mine"—from that, it becomes otherwise. The world, being subject to change and attached to existence, delights only in existence... [as before].
One should not conceive in regard to the mind; one should not conceive in the mind; one should not conceive from the mind; one should not conceive, "The mind is mine"...
[regarding] mind-consciousness... mind-contact...

Whatever feeling arises conditioned by mind-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—one should not conceive it, one should not conceive in it, one should not conceive from it, and one should not conceive, "This is mine.
For, monks, whatever one conceives, in whatever one conceives, from whatever one conceives, and that which one conceives as "mine"—from all that, it becomes otherwise.
The world, being subject to change and attached to existence, delights only in existence.

“Monks, to whatever extent there are aggregates, elements, and sense-bases, one should not conceive them, one should not conceive in them, one should not conceive from them, and one should not conceive ‘this is mine.
Not conceiving thus, one does not cling to anything in the world.
Not clinging, one is not agitated. Being unagitated, one personally attains final Nibbāna.”
‘Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.
This is the eighth [discourse]. *Saṃyutta Nikāya* 35.92.

9. Channa Chapter:
Second Discourse on the Pair “Bhikkhus, consciousness arises dependent upon a pair.”
And how, monks, does consciousness arise in dependence on a dyad?
Dependent upon the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises.
The eye is impermanent, subject to change, and subject to alteration.
Forms are impermanent, subject to change, and subject to becoming otherwise.
Thus, this dyad is both unstable and wavering; it is impermanent, subject to change, and subject to becoming otherwise.
Eye-consciousness is impermanent, subject to change, and subject to becoming otherwise.
Whatever cause and whatever condition there is for the arising of eye-consciousness, that cause and that condition is also impermanent, subject to change, and liable to become otherwise.
But, monks, how could eye-consciousness—which has arisen in dependence upon a condition that is impermanent—be permanent?
Monks, the meeting, the coming together, and the conjunction of these three things is called eye-contact.
Eye-contact, too, is impermanent, subject to change, and bound to become otherwise.
Whatever cause and whatever condition there may be for the arising of eye-contact, that cause and that condition are also impermanent, subject to change, and bound to become otherwise.
Now, monks, how could eye-contact, which has arisen in dependence upon a condition that is impermanent, be permanent?
"Monks, touched one feels; touched one intends; touched one perceives.
Thus these phenomena are indeed unstable, wavering, impermanent, subject to change, and liable to become otherwise... [etc.
...Dependent on the tongue and tastes, tongue-consciousness arises."
The tongue is impermanent, subject to change, and subject to alteration.
Tastes are impermanent, subject to change, and subject to alteration.
Thus, this dyad is both unstable and precarious; it is impermanent, subject to change, and subject to alteration.
Tongue-consciousness is impermanent, subject to change, and subject to alteration.
Whatever cause and whatever condition there is for the arising of tongue-consciousness, that cause and that condition are also impermanent, subject to change, and subject to alteration.
But, monks, how could tongue-consciousness that has arisen in dependence upon a condition that is itself impermanent be permanent?
Monks, the meeting, the conjunction, the coming together of these three things is called tongue-contact.
Tongue-contact, too, is impermanent, subject to change, and subject to alteration.
Whatever cause and whatever condition there is for the arising of tongue-contact, that cause and that condition are also impermanent, subject to change, and subject to alteration.
“Monks, since tongue-contact arises dependent on a condition that is indeed impermanent, how could it be permanent?
Monks, one feels when touched; one intends when touched; one perceives when touched.
Thus, these states are also shifting and unstable, impermanent, subject to change, and liable to become otherwise. …pe…
Dependent upon the mind and mental phenomena, mind-consciousness arises.
The mind is impermanent, subject to change, and subject to alteration.
Mental phenomena are impermanent, subject to change, and subject to alteration.
Thus this dyad is both unstable and wavering; it is impermanent, subject to change, and liable to become otherwise.
Mental consciousness is impermanent, subject to change, and liable to become otherwise.
Whatever cause and whatever condition there may be for the arising of mental consciousness, that cause and that condition are also impermanent, subject to change, and liable to become otherwise.
“Bhikkhus, since mental consciousness has arisen dependent on a condition that is impermanent, how could it be permanent?
Bhikkhus, the meeting, the coming together, the coincidence of these three things is called mind-contact.
Mind-contact, too, is impermanent, subject to change, and subject to alteration.”
Whatever cause and whatever condition there is for the arising of mind-contact, that cause and that condition is impermanent, subject to change, and liable to become otherwise.
But, monks, how could mind-contact, having arisen in dependence upon a condition that is impermanent, be permanent?
Monks, one feels when touched; one intends when touched; one perceives when touched.
Thus, these phenomena are indeed unstable, precarious, impermanent, subject to change, and liable to become otherwise.
In this way, monks, consciousness arises dependent upon a dyad. Thus ends the tenth [discourse].
