Saḷavagga Adanta-aguttasutta: Untamed and Unguarded “Bhikkhus, the eye is untamed, unguarded, unrestrained, and uncontrolled; it leads to the arising of covetousness and displeasure in the world. If one does not train in its restraint, one will not attain the destruction of suffering. The ear is untamed... The nose is untamed... The tongue is untamed... The body is untamed... The mind is untamed, unguarded, unrestrained, and uncontrolled; it leads to the arising of covetousness and displeasure in the world. If one does not train in its restraint, one will not attain the destruction of suffering. But, bhikkhus, the eye is tamed, guarded, restrained, and controlled; it does not lead to the arising of covetousness and displeasure in the world. If one trains in its restraint, one will attain the destruction of suffering. The ear is tamed... The nose is tamed... The tongue is tamed... The body is tamed... The mind is tamed, guarded, restrained, and controlled; it does not lead to the arising of covetousness and displeasure in the world. If one trains in its restraint, one will attain the destruction of suffering.”
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
“Bhikkhus, these six bases of contact, when untamed, unguarded, unprotected, and unrestrained, bring about suffering.
Which six?
“Bhikkhus, the eye, a sphere of contact, if untamed, unguarded, unprotected, and unrestrained, brings about suffering … the tongue,
bhikkhus, a sphere of contact, if untamed, unguarded, unprotected, and unrestrained, brings about suffering … the mind,
bhikkhus, a sphere of contact, if untamed, unguarded, unprotected, and unrestrained, brings about suffering.”
“Monks, these six bases of contact, when untamed, unguarded, unprotected, and unrestrained, bring about suffering.
These six bases of contact, monks, when well-tamed, well-guarded, well-protected, and well-restrained, bring about happiness.
Which six?”
“Bhikkhus, the eye, as a sphere of contact, when well-tamed, well-guarded, well-protected, and well-restrained, brings about happiness….
The tongue, bhikkhus, as a sphere of contact, when well-tamed, well-guarded, well-protected, and well-restrained, brings about happiness….
The mind, bhikkhus, as a sphere of contact, when well-tamed, well-guarded, well-protected, and well-restrained, brings about happiness.”
“Monks, these six bases of contact, when well-tamed, well-guarded, well-protected, and well-restrained, lead to happiness.
Thus spoke the Blessed One; ... [as before] ...
the Teacher said this:
“Monks, there are these six bases of contact,
where one who is unrestrained meets with suffering;
and those who have understood their restraint— ”
Dwelling with faith as their companion, untainted by worldly desires,
they see forms that are pleasing to the mind,
and likewise, they see those that are unpleasing.
One should dispel the path of passion toward what is delightful,
and one should not harbor a mind of ill-will toward what is unlovely.
Having heard both kinds of sound— the pleasant and the unpleasant—
One should not be infatuated with pleasant sounds;
even toward the unpleasant, one should dispel thoughts of aversion,
and one should not let the mind become corrupted by thinking, "This is disagreeable."
Having smelled a fragrant and delightful scent,
and likewise having smelled what is impure and unpleasant,
one should dispel aversion toward that which is unpleasant.
One should not be led by desire nor be attached to what is pleasing.
Having experienced a taste that is unpalatable and sometimes even having experienced one that is sweet;
I shall not eat, clinging to delicious flavors;
I shall not savor what I have encountered as something disagreeable.
Touched by contact, I shall not become intoxicated by pleasure.
Though touched by suffering, he does not tremble;
he maintains equanimity toward both pleasant and painful contacts.
Unattached and unopposed to anyone, he remains free from conflict.
People with various perceptions,
being obsessed by mental proliferation, proceed with their perceptions;
[they grasp] everything consisting of mind and based on the household life.
Having dispelled [unwholesome thoughts], he dwells established in renunciation.
When the mind has been thus well-cultivated in regard to the six [sense bases],
his consciousness does not waver anywhere when touched by objects.
“Having overcome passion and hatred, O bhikkhus,
you have reached the further shore of birth and death. Thus ends the first [verse].

Saṁyutta Nikāya 35.95 (SN 35.95, PTS SN iv 72) 10. Saḷavagga Mālukyaputtasutta: To Māluṅkyaputta Then the Venerable Māluṅkyaputta approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said to him: “Venerable sir, it would be good if the Blessed One would clear up this ambiguity for me, this perplexity, regarding this matter that is open to doubt. What now, venerable sir, is identity? And what is non-identity? “Māluṅkyaputta, I shall clear up this ambiguity for you, this perplexity, regarding this matter that is open to doubt. Listen and attend closely; I will speak. “Yes, venerable sir,” the Venerable Māluṅkyaputta replied. The Blessed One said this: “Māluṅkyaputta, whatever kind of form there is—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—that is called ‘form. Whatever kind of feeling there is—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—that is called ‘feeling. Whatever kind of perception there is—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—that is called ‘perception. Whatever kind of volitional formations there are—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—that is called ‘volitional formations. Whatever kind of consciousness there is—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—that is called ‘consciousness. “This, Māluṅkyaputta, is called identity. And what is non-identity? Whatever is not yours, Māluṅkyaputta, abandon it. When you have abandoned it, that will lead to your welfare and happiness for a long time. And what is not yours? Form is not yours: abandon it. When you have abandoned it, that will lead to your welfare and happiness for a long time. Feeling is not yours... Perception is not yours... Volitional formations are not yours... Consciousness is not yours: abandon it. When you have abandoned it, that will lead to your welfare and happiness for a long time. “When, Māluṅkyaputta, a noble disciple has abandoned what is not his and has detached from it, he is called a noble disciple who is a stream-enterer, no longer bound to the nether world, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as his destination. “Suppose, Māluṅkyaputta, a person were to take a loan and invest it, and the profit he gained from that investment would be sufficient for him to support his mother and father, himself, and his wife and children, and to pay off the old debt and still have some left over for new expenses. Would that person be called a man who has made a good investment? “Yes, venerable sir. “In the same way, Māluṅkyaputta, when a noble disciple has abandoned what is not his and has detached from it, he is called a noble disciple who is a stream-enterer, no longer bound to the nether world, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as his destination. “Suppose, Māluṅkyaputta, a person were to construct a staircase for the roof of a house at a crossroads where four roads meet. Would that person be called a man who has built a staircase for the roof of a house? “Yes, venerable sir. “In the same way, Māluṅkyaputta, when a noble disciple has abandoned what is not his and has detached from it, he is called a noble disciple who is a stream-enterer, no longer bound to the nether world, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as his destination. When this was said, the Venerable Māluṅkyaputta said to the Blessed One: “Magnificent, venerable sir! Magnificent, venerable sir!... From today let the Blessed One remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus! “Venerable sir,” they replied. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, if anyone should say: ‘I will not lead the holy life under the Blessed One until the Blessed One declares to me: “The world is eternal”’—that would be a mere trifle for him, bhikkhus, that the Tathāgata should declare to him: ‘The world is eternal. “If anyone should say: ‘I will not lead the holy life under the Blessed One until the Blessed One declares to me: “The world is finite”’—that would be a mere trifle for him, bhikkhus, that the Tathāgata should declare to him: ‘The world is finite. “If anyone should say: ‘I will not lead the holy life under the Blessed One until the Blessed One declares to me: “The soul is the same as the body”’—that would be a mere trifle for him, bhikkhus, that the Tathāgata should declare to him: ‘The soul is the same as the body. “If anyone should say: ‘I will not lead the holy life under the Blessed One until the Blessed One declares to me: “The soul is one thing and the body another”’—that would be a mere trifle for him, bhikkhus, that the Tathāgata should declare to him: ‘The soul is one thing and the body another. “If anyone should say: ‘I will not lead the holy life under the Blessed One until the Blessed One declares to me:

“After death a Tathāgata exists”’—that would be a mere trifle for him, bhikkhus, that the Tathāgata should declare to him: ‘After death a Tathāgata exists. “If anyone should say: ‘I will not lead the holy life under the Blessed One until the Blessed One declares to me: “After death a Tathāgata does not exist”’—that would be a mere trifle for him, bhikkhus, that the Tathāgata should declare to him: ‘After death a Tathāgata does not exist. “If anyone should say: ‘I will not lead the holy life under the Blessed One until the Blessed One declares to me: “After death a Tathāgata both exists and does not exist”’—that would be a mere trifle for him, bhikkhus, that the Tathāgata should declare to him: ‘After death a Tathāgata both exists and does not exist. “If anyone should say: ‘I will not lead the holy life under the Blessed One until the Blessed One declares to me: “After death a Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist”’—that would be a mere trifle for him, bhikkhus, that the Tathāgata should declare to him: ‘After death a Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist. “Why is that? Because, bhikkhus, these things have not been declared by the Tathāgata; they are not relevant to the goal, not relevant to the Dhamma, and do not lead to disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, to Nibbāna. Therefore the Tathāgata has not declared them. “But, bhikkhus, if anyone should say: ‘I will lead the holy life under the Blessed One; and the Blessed One will teach me the Dhamma for the sake of which a clansman rightly goes forth from the household life into homelessness,’ then the Tathāgata would teach him that Dhamma. “And what, bhikkhus, is that Dhamma for the sake of which a clansman rightly goes forth from the household life into homelessness? It is: ‘Such is form, such its origin, such its passing away; such is feeling... such is perception... such are volitional formations... such is consciousness, such its origin, such its passing away. “When, bhikkhus, a noble disciple has clearly seen with correct wisdom as it really is this suffering, the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the way leading to the cessation of suffering, he here and now possesses four factors of stream-entry. “What four? Here, bhikkhus, a noble disciple possesses confirmed confidence in the Buddha thus: ‘The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Enlightened One, the Blessed One. “He possesses confirmed confidence in the Dhamma thus: ‘The Dhamma is well expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see,
Then the Venerable Māluṅkyaputta approached the Blessed One... [as before] ...and sitting to one side, the Venerable Māluṅkyaputta said this to the Blessed One:
“It would be well, Bhante, if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief, so that having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, I might dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute.
“In that case, Māluṅkyaputta, what shall we say to the young bhikkhus?”
“Indeed, monk, since you—being aged, old, advanced in years, having reached the end of your life’s span—request a brief instruction.

“Even though I am, venerable sir, aged, old, advanced in years, having reached the end of my life’s span, may the Blessed One teach me the Dhamma in brief; may the Sugata teach me the Dhamma in brief.”
"Perhaps I might come to understand the meaning of what has been spoken by the Blessed One; perhaps I might become an heir to what has been spoken by the Blessed One.
"What do you think, Māluṅkyaputta?

Regarding those forms cognizable by the eye that have not been seen, have never been seen before, which you do not see now, and for which you do not have the thought, 'May I see them'—is there in you any desire, passion, or affection for them?"
“No, venerable sir.

“Those sounds cognizable by the ear that you have not heard, have never before been heard, and you do not hear them now—do you not have the thought, ‘May I hear them’? Do you have any desire, lust, or affection for them?
“No, venerable sir.”

“Are there those odors cognizable by the nose that have not been smelled, nor smelled before, which you do not smell now, and for which you do not think, ‘May I smell them’? Is there in you any desire, lust, or affection for them?
“No, venerable sir.

“Are there those flavors cognizable by the tongue that have not been tasted, nor tasted before, which you do not taste now, and for which you do not think, ‘May I taste them’? Is there in you any desire, lust, or affection for them?”
“No, venerable sir.

“Those tangibles cognizable by the body that are not touched, have never been touched before, and you do not touch them now, nor do you think, ‘May I touch them’—do you have any desire, lust, or affection for them?
“No, venerable sir.”

“Are there those mental phenomena cognizable by the mind that you have not cognized, have never cognized before, which you do not cognize now, yet for which you do not think, ‘I might cognize them’? Do you have any desire, lust, or affection for them?
“No, venerable sir.
“In this case, Māluṅkyaputta, regarding those phenomena to be seen, heard, sensed, and cognized—regarding what has been seen, there is merely the seen.”

There will be merely what has been heard regarding what is heard; there will be merely what has been sensed regarding what is sensed; there will be merely what has been cognized regarding what is cognized.

But when, Māluṅkyaputta, regarding phenomena that are seen, heard, sensed, or cognized, there is merely what is seen regarding what is seen, merely what is heard regarding what is heard, merely what is sensed regarding what is sensed, and merely what is cognized regarding what is cognized;
Therefore, Māluṅkyaputta, you are not that.
Since, Māluṅkyaputta, you are not that,
therefore, Māluṅkyaputta, you are not there.
“Since you, Mālunkyāputta, do not exist there, therefore, Mālunkyāputta,
you are neither here, nor in the world beyond, nor in between the two.
This itself is the end of suffering.”
“Venerable sir, I understand in detail the meaning of what was stated by the Blessed One in brief thus:
‘When one has seen a form and mindfulness is lost,
attending to a pleasing sign;’”
With a mind full of lust he experiences it,
and he remains clinging to it.
His feelings increase.
Arising from many forms of beauty,
covetousness and cruelty cause the mind to be struck with grief.
For one who thus accumulates suffering,
it is said that Nibbāna is far away.
Having heard a sound, mindfulness is lost.
For one who attends to a pleasing sign,
the mind becomes impassioned; he experiences it and remains absorbed in it.
For him, various sensations arising from sounds increase—
both covetousness and ill will.
The mind is struck down by tears;
for one who thus accumulates suffering,
it is said that Nibbāna is far away.
Having smelled a fragrance,
mindfulness is lost as one attends to a pleasing sign;
with a mind full of passion, he experiences it.
And he remains having consumed it.
His sensations increase,
many of them arising from scents.
Covetousness and ill will—
by these the mind is struck;
thus does suffering accumulate for one who gathers it.
Nibbāna is called "far away" for one who has tasted it but whose mindfulness is lost while attending to a pleasing sign.
With a mind full of passion he experiences it,
and he remains clinging to it.
His feelings increase.
Arising from many flavors,
covetousness and cruelty cause the mind to be afflicted.
For one who thus accumulates suffering,
Nibbāna is said to be far away.
When contact is touched and mindfulness is lost,
For one who attends to a pleasing object,
the mind becomes impassioned; he experiences it and remains absorbed in it.
His feelings increase,
arising from manifold contacts:
covetousness and ill will.
The mind is struck by tears;
for one who thus accumulates suffering,
it is said that Nibbāna is far away.
Having understood the Dhamma,
mindfulness is lost for one who attends to a pleasing sign;
with a mind full of lust, he experiences [sensation].
And he remains absorbed in that.
His feelings increase,
arising from manifold phenomena.
Covetousness and ill will—
by these the mind is afflicted;
thus does one who accumulates suffering,
Nibbāna is called "far away.
He does not take delight in forms,
being mindful when seeing a form.
With a mind detached, one experiences [it],
yet one does not remain clinging to it.
Just as one perceives a form...
And even while experiencing feeling,
he is consumed by it and does not accumulate [kamma];
thus he dwells mindful.
For one who thus diminishes suffering,
Nibbāna is said to be near.
Such a person does not take delight in sounds.
Having heard a sound, being mindful,
he experiences it with a detached mind and does not remain clinging to it.
Just as for one who hears a sound and experiences the feeling that arises from it,
[the mind] wastes away and does not accumulate.
Thus he dwells mindful; thus, for one who is diminishing suffering,
it is said that Nibbāna is near.
He is not infatuated with odors,
being mindful when smelling an odor;
with a mind detached, he experiences it.
And he does not persist by relishing it.
Just as for one who smells a fragrance and experiences the feeling from partaking of it;
It diminishes and does not accumulate;
thus he fares mindful.
Thus, for one who is disintegrating suffering,
Nirvana is said to be near.
He does not take delight in flavors,
having tasted them with mindfulness.
With a mind detached, he experiences it,
and he does not remain clinging to it;
just as one who tastes a flavor.
Even while experiencing feeling,
he diminishes it and does not accumulate it;
thus he dwells mindfully.
For one who thus diminishes suffering,
Nibbāna is said to be near.
Such a person does not take delight in sense contacts.
Having touched a contact with clear comprehension,
one feels it with a mind detached from passion,
and one does not remain clinging to it.
Just as for one who touches contact and experiences feeling,
it diminishes and does not accumulate.
Thus he dwells mindful; thus, for one who is diminishing suffering,
it is said that Nibbāna is near.
He does not take delight in phenomena,
having understood phenomena and being mindful;
with a detached mind, he experiences them.
And he does not persist by clinging to that.
Just as for one who knows the Dhamma and experiences the feeling while practicing it;
It diminishes and does not accumulate;
thus he fares mindfully.
Thus, for one who is thus diminishing suffering,
“‘Nibbāna is said to be in one’s presence.
This, Bhante, is how I understand in detail the meaning of what was spoken by the Blessed One in brief.
“Excellent, excellent, Māluṅkyaputta!”
"It is good, Māluṅkyaputta, that you understand in detail the meaning of what was spoken by me in brief:
'When mindfulness is lost after seeing a form,
one attends to a pleasing sign.'"
With a mind full of lust he experiences it,
and he persists by cleaving to it.
His feelings increase.
Arising from many forms of beauty,
covetousness and cruelty cause the mind to be afflicted.
For one who thus accumulates suffering,
it is said that Nibbāna is far away.
…pe…
He does not take delight in phenomena,
having understood phenomena and being mindful;
with a detached mind, he experiences them.
And he does not persist by clinging to that.
Just as for one who understands the Dhamma and experiences the feeling of practicing it;
It diminishes and does not accumulate;
thus he fares mindfully.
Thus, for one who is discarding suffering,
“‘Nibbāna is said to be in one’s presence.
This, Māluṅkyaputta, is how the meaning of what was spoken by me in brief should be understood in detail.
Then the Venerable Māluṅkyaputta, having delighted and rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him to his right, departed.
Then, dwelling alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute, the Venerable Māluṅkyaputta, in no long time,

having realized for himself with direct knowledge in this very life that supreme goal of the holy life, for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness, entered and dwelt in it.
“Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being”—thus he directly knew.
And the Venerable Māluṅkyaputta became one of the arahants. This is the second [discourse].

Saṁyutta Nikāya 35.96 (SN 35.96, PTS SN iv 76) 10. Saḷavagga Parihānadhammasutta: The Discourse on the Nature of Decline “Bhikkhus, there are these six bases for decline. What six? (1) Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is one who destroys life; he is given to taking what is not given; he is of wrong view; he is one who dwells with a mind full of ill will; he is one who dwells with a mind obsessed by sloth and torpor; he is one who dwells with a mind obsessed by restlessness and remorse. These, bhikkhus, are the six bases for decline. (2) Furthermore, bhikkhus, there are these six bases for non-decline. What six? (1) Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu abstains from destroying life; he abstains from taking what is not given; he has right view; he dwells with a mind free from ill will; he dwells with a mind free from sloth and torpor; he dwells with a mind free from restlessness and remorse. These, bhikkhus, are the six bases for non-decline.”
“Monks, I will teach you what is subject to decline and what is not subject to decline, as well as the six bases of mastery.
Listen to that.
And how, monks, is one subject to decline?
In this case, monks, when a monk has seen a form with the eye, there arise evil, unwholesome, and fettering thoughts associated with relishing.
If that monk endures them, does not abandon them, does not dispel them, does not bring them to an end, and does not cause them to cease, it should be understood by that monk, monks:
"I am falling away from wholesome states."
"For this is called a falling away, as stated by the Blessed One...
...Furthermore, monks, having tasted a flavor with the tongue, there arise in a monk...
Furthermore, monks, having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, there arise in a monk evil, unwholesome, sensual thoughts that lead to fetters.
If a bhikkhu tolerates that [distraction], does not abandon it, does not dispel it, does not bring it to an end, and does not cause it to cease, then it should be understood by that bhikkhu:
"I am declining from wholesome states.
For this is called decline by the Blessed One.
In this way, monks, one is subject to decline.
And how, monks, is one not subject to decline?
Here, monks, when a monk sees a form with the eye, there arise in him evil, unwholesome, and fettering thoughts associated with the heart.
If a bhikkhu does not accept that [thought], but abandons it, dispels it, brings it to an end, and causes it to cease, then it should be understood by that bhikkhu:
“I am not falling away from wholesome states.
For this is called “non-falling away” by the Blessed One... (as above)...
Furthermore, monks, after a monk has tasted a flavor with the tongue, there arise ... [as before] ...
Furthermore, monks, after a monk has cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, there arise evil, unwholesome, sensual, and fettering thoughts.

If a monk does not tolerate them, but abandons them, dispels them, makes an end of them, and brings them to non-existence, it should be understood by that monk, monks: [that he is one who acts in accordance with the Dhamma].
‘I do not fall away from wholesome states.
For this is called ‘non-falling away’ by the Blessed One.
It is in this way, monks, that one is of a nature not to fall away.
And what, monks, are the six bases of mastery?
Here, monks, when a monk has seen a form with the eye, evil, unwholesome states of covetousness and dejection that are fetters do not arise.
It should be understood by that monk, monks:
‘This sphere has been mastered.
For this is called a ‘sphere of mastery’ by the Blessed One...
Furthermore, monks, when a monk has cognized a mental object with the mind, evil unwholesome states that are accompanied by latent tendencies and lead to fetters do not arise.
“Bhikkhus, it should be understood by a bhikkhu:
‘This sphere has been mastered.
For this is called a ‘sphere of mastery’ by the Blessed One.”
“Monks, these are called the six bases of mastery. Thus was the third [discourse].
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 35.97 (SN 35.97, PTS SN iv 78).
10. The Chapter on the Six (Saḷavagga) The Discourse on Dwelling in Negligence “Monks, I will teach you about one who dwells in negligence and one who dwells in diligence. Listen to that.”
Listen to that.
And how, monks, does one dwell in negligence?
For one who dwells with the faculty of the eye unguarded, the mind becomes defiled by forms cognizable by the eye.
For one whose mind is distracted, there is no gladness.
When there is no gladness, there is no rapture.
When there is no rapture, there is no tranquility.
In the absence of tranquility, there is suffering.
For one who suffers, the mind does not become concentrated.
When the mind is unconcentrated, phenomena do not become manifest.
Due to the non-manifestation of wholesome states, one comes to be reckoned as living in negligence...
For a monk who dwells with the tongue-faculty unguarded, the mind becomes drenched in tastes cognizable by the tongue;
for him whose mind is thus drenched... [and so on].
He comes to be reckoned as one who dwells in negligence...
Monks, for one who dwells with the faculty of mind unrestrained, the mind becomes defiled by mental phenomena cognizable by the mind;
when his mind is defiled, joy does not arise.
When there is no gladness, there is no rapture.
When there is no rapture, there is no tranquility.
When there is no tranquility, there is suffering.
One who is suffering does not attain concentration of mind.
When the mind is unconcentrated, phenomena do not become manifest.
Due to the non-manifestation of phenomena, one is reckoned as dwelling in negligence.
In this way, monks, one dwells in negligence.
And how, monks, does one dwell in diligence?
For one who dwells with the faculty of the eye restrained, the mind does not become drenched in the forms cognizable by the eye.
In one whose mind is undisturbed, joy arises.
In one who is joyful, rapture arises.
In one whose mind is rapturous, the body becomes tranquil.
One whose body is tranquil dwells in happiness.
The mind of one who is happy becomes concentrated.
When the mind is concentrated, phenomena become manifest.

Through the manifestation of these qualities, one comes to be reckoned as dwelling in heedfulness …pe… For a bhikkhu who dwells with the tongue-faculty restrained, the mind does not become defiled …pe… he comes to be reckoned as dwelling in heedfulness.
“Monks, for one who dwells with the faculty of mind restrained, the mind does not become defiled regarding mental phenomena cognizable by the mind.
For one whose mind is undefiled, gladness arises.
For one who is gladdened, rapture arises.”
The body of one whose mind is joyful becomes tranquil.
One whose body is tranquil dwells in happiness.
The mind of one who is happy becomes concentrated.
"When the mind is concentrated, phenomena become manifest.
Through the manifestation of these phenomena, one comes to be reckoned as 'dwelling in heedfulness.
It is in this way, monks, that one dwells in heedfulness."
The Fourth.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 35.98 (SN 35.98, PTS SN iv 79) 10.
Saḷavagga (The Chapter on the Six)
The Discourse on Restraint:
“Bhikkhus, I will teach you restraint and non-restraint.
Listen to that.”
And how, monks, is there non-restraint?
There are, monks, forms cognizable by the eye—desirable, lovely, pleasing, endearing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust.
If a monk delights in them, welcomes them, and remains attached to them, it should be understood by that monk, monks: [that he is unrestrained].
‘I am declining from wholesome states;
for this is called decline by the Blessed One.
… [and so on] … “Bhikkhus, there are tastes cognizable by the tongue …” and so on.
“Bhikkhus, there are mental phenomena cognizable by the mind that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust.
If a bhikkhu delights in them, welcomes them, and remains attached to them, it should be understood by that bhikkhu:
‘I am declining in wholesome states.’”
"For this, monks, has been called 'decline' by the Blessed One.
In this way, monks, there is non-restraint.
And how, monks, is there restraint?
“Bhikkhus, there are forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust.
If a bhikkhu does not delight in them, does not welcome them, and does not remain attached to them, it should be understood by that bhikkhu:
‘I am not declining in wholesome states.’”
"For this was said by the Blessed One: '... [as before] ...
There are, monks, tastes cognizable by the tongue ... [as before] ...
There are, monks, mental phenomena cognizable by the mind that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, endearing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust.'"
If a bhikkhu does not delight in that, does not welcome it, and does not remain clinging to it, he should understand:
"I am not falling away from wholesome states;
for this is called 'non-falling away' by the Blessed One."
“In this way, monks, there is restraint.
The fifth [discourse].
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 35.99. (SN 35.99, PTS SN iv 80)
10. The Chapter on the Six (Saḷavagga) The Discourse on Concentration (Samādhisutta):
“Bhikkhus, develop concentration.
“Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who is concentrated understands things as they really are.
And what does he understand as it really is?
He understands, ‘The eye is impermanent,’ as it really is.”
One understands as it really is: ‘Forms are impermanent’;
one understands as it really is: ‘Eye-consciousness is impermanent’;
one understands as it really is: ‘Eye-contact is impermanent.’
‘Whatever feeling arises conditioned by eye-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too is impermanent,’ he understands it as it really is.
…pe… ‘The mind is impermanent,’ he understands it as it really is. ‘Mental phenomena (dhammā) …’ [he understands them as they really are].
He understands as it really is: "Mind-consciousness... mind-contact...
and whatever feeling arises conditioned by mind-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too is impermanent."
“Develop concentration, bhikkhus.
A bhikkhu who is concentrated understands things as they really are.
The sixth.

Saṁyutta Nikāya 35.100 (SN 35.100, PTS SN iv 80) 10. Saḷavagga Paṭisallānasutta (The Discourse on Seclusion) “Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu is secluded, he is capable of understanding as it really is: ‘This is suffering. When a bhikkhu is secluded, he is capable of understanding as it really is: ‘This is the origin of suffering. When a bhikkhu is secluded, he is capable of understanding as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of suffering. When a bhikkhu is secluded, he is capable of understanding as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. When a bhikkhu is secluded, he is capable of understanding as it really is: ‘These are the taints. When a bhikkhu is secluded, he is capable of understanding as it really is: ‘This is the origin of the taints. When a bhikkhu is secluded, he is capable of understanding as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of the taints. When a bhikkhu is secluded, he is capable of understanding as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of the taints.’”
“Bhikkhus, apply yourselves to seclusion.
A bhikkhu who is secluded, bhikkhus, understands things as they really are.
And what does he understand as it really is?
‘The eye is impermanent,’ he understands it as it really is;
‘Forms are impermanent,’ he understands them as they really are;
‘Eye-consciousness is impermanent,’ he understands it as it really is.

“One understands as it really is: ‘Eye-contact is impermanent’ …pe… ‘Whatever feeling arises conditioned by mind-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too is impermanent.
Monks, apply yourselves to meditation in seclusion.”
“Secluded, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu understands things as they really are.
The seventh.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 35.101 (SN 35.101, PTS SN iv 81)
10. The Chapter on the Six (Saḷavagga) The First Discourse on What Does Not Belong to You:
“Monks, whatever does not belong to you, abandon that.
That which has been abandoned by you will lead to your welfare and happiness.
And what, monks, is not yours?
The eye, monks, is not yours.
Abandon that.
Its abandonment will lead to your welfare and happiness.
Forms are not yours.
Abandon them.
When they have been abandoned by you, they will lead to your welfare and happiness.
Eye-consciousness is not yours.
Abandon that.
When that is abandoned by you, it will lead to your welfare and happiness.
Eye-contact is not yours.
Abandon that.
When it is abandoned, it will lead to your welfare and happiness.
Furthermore, whatever feeling arises conditioned by eye-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too is not yours.
Abandon that.
That being abandoned will lead to your welfare and happiness.
…pe…
The tongue is not yours; abandon it.
When it is abandoned by you, it will lead to your welfare and happiness.
Tastes are not yours;
abandon them.
When they are abandoned by you, they will lead to your welfare and happiness.
Tongue-consciousness is not yours;
abandon it.
Its abandonment will lead to your welfare and happiness.
Tongue-contact is not yours;
abandon it.
When it is abandoned by you, it will lead to your welfare and happiness.
Whatever feeling arises conditioned by tongue-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too is not yours.
Abandon it. Its abandonment will lead to your welfare and happiness.
…pe… The mind is not yours.
Abandon that.
When it is abandoned, it will lead to your welfare and happiness.
Phenomena are not yours.
Abandon them.
When they are abandoned, they will lead to your welfare and happiness.
Mental consciousness is not yours.
Abandon that.
When that is abandoned by you, it will lead to your welfare and happiness.
Mental contact is not yours.
Abandon that.
When it is abandoned, it will lead to your welfare and happiness.
Whatever feeling arises conditioned by mind-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too is not yours.
Abandon that.
Its abandonment will lead to your welfare and happiness.
Monks, it would be just as if people were to carry away, burn, or do whatever they please with the grass, wood, branches, and foliage here in this Jeta Grove.
“Would it occur to you:
‘People are carrying us away, or burning us, or doing with us as they please’?
“Certainly not, Bhante.”
“And why is that? “Because this, Bhante, is neither our self nor what belongs to our self.
“In the same way, monks, the eye is not yours.”
Abandon that.
Its abandonment will lead to your welfare and happiness.
Forms are not yours...
Eye-consciousness... eye-contact...
and whatever feeling arises conditioned by mind-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too is not yours.
“Abandon that.
When that has been abandoned by you, it will lead to your welfare and happiness.
The eighth.

Saṁyutta Nikāya 35.102 (SN 35.102, PTS SN iv 82) 10. Saḷavagga Second Discourse on "Not Yours" "Bhikkhus, 'This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self'—in regard to form, bhikkhus, when one sees thus with right wisdom as it really is, one becomes disenchanted with form; through disenchantment, one becomes dispassionate; through dispassion, one is liberated; through liberation, there is the knowledge: 'It is liberated. "In regard to feeling... In regard to perception... In regard to volitional formations... In regard to consciousness, bhikkhus, when one sees thus with right wisdom as it really is, one becomes disenchanted with consciousness; through disenchantment, one becomes dispassionate; through dispassion, one is liberated; through liberation, there is the knowledge: 'It is liberated.'"
“Monks, whatever is not yours, abandon it.
When you have abandoned it, that will lead to your welfare and happiness.
And what, monks, is not yours?”
The eye, monks, is not yours;
abandon it.
Its abandonment will lead to your welfare and happiness.
Forms are not yours;
abandon them.
When they are abandoned by you, they will lead to your welfare and happiness.
Eye-consciousness is not yours;
abandon it.
Its abandonment will lead to your welfare and happiness.
Eye-contact is not yours;
abandon it. When it is abandoned by you, it will lead to your welfare and happiness... [and so on] ...
Whatever feeling arises conditioned by mind-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too is not yours.
Abandon it. When you have abandoned it, it will lead to your welfare and happiness.
“Monks, whatever is not yours, abandon it.
When that has been abandoned, it will lead to your welfare and happiness. Thus was the ninth [sutta].

Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.103 (SN 35.103, PTS SN iv 83) 10. The Chapter on the Six (Saḷavagga) The Discourse on Water (Udakasutta) “Bhikkhus, just as when water is poured from one vessel into another, not even a drop of water is lost, so too, bhikkhus, when a noble disciple possesses these five faculties, it is impossible that he should not attain final knowledge within seven years. What five? The faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom. It is impossible, bhikkhus, that a noble disciple who possesses these five faculties should not attain final knowledge within seven years. Just as, bhikkhus, when water is poured from one vessel into another, not even a drop of water is lost, so too, bhikkhus, when a noble disciple possesses these five faculties, it is impossible that he should not attain final knowledge within seven years.”
“Bhikkhus, Udaka Rāmaputta indeed spoke these words:
‘This one is truly a knower of all;
this one is truly an all-conqueror.’”
"This is merely scratching the root of the boil that has not yet been scratched. Yet, monks,
Udaka Rāmaputta, being one who is not actually a master of knowledge (*avedagu*), declares, "I am a master of knowledge (*vedagu*)."
While not being one who has gone beyond all, he says, "I am one who has gone beyond all"; while not having cut out the root of the tumor, he says, "The root of the tumor has been cut out by me.
In this regard, monks, a monk speaking rightly would say: [this is how it is].
‘This is indeed for one who has attained knowledge;
this is indeed for one who has conquered all;
this is indeed for one who has not yet scraped away [the defilements].’
"Digging up the root of the tumor.
And how, monks, is one a master of knowledge (vedagū)?
It is when, monks, a monk understands as they really are the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding the six bases of contact.
In this way, monks, a monk is a master of knowledge (*vedagū*).
And how, monks, is a monk a conqueror of all (*sabbajī*)?

When, monks, a monk—having understood as they really are the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding the six bases of contact—is liberated through non-clinging.
"In this way, monks, a monk is a 'scorcher of all' (sabbajī).
And how, monks, is the root of the boil scraped away for a monk who has not yet scraped it away?

'Boil,' monks, is a designation for this body composed of the four great elements, born of mother and father, nourished by boiled rice and porridge, subject to impermanence, rubbing, massaging, breaking up, and dissolution."
“‘The root of the boil,’ monks, is a designation for craving. When, monks,
a monk’s craving has been abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated so that it is no more subject to future arising—
in this way, monks, the unexcised root of the boil of a monk becomes excised.”
"Bhikkhus, Udaka Rāmaputta indeed spoke these words:
'This one is truly a master of knowledge;
this one is truly an all-conqueror.'"
‘This has never been scraped away before;
let us now scrape away the root of the tumor.
Yet, monks, Udaka Rāmaputta, being himself one who had not attained final knowledge (*avedagu*), spoke thus, saying, ‘I am one who has attained final knowledge (*vedagu*).’”
While not being one who has gone beyond all, he says, ‘I am one who has gone beyond all’; while not having even lanced the root of the boil, he says, ‘The root of my boil has been lanced.
In this case, monks, a bhikkhu speaking rightly would say: [‘This person is a liar’].”
“This is indeed the one who has known all;
this is indeed the one who has gone beyond all;
this is indeed the one who has not been scraped away.”
“Dig up the root of the tumor.
Tenth. The fifth chapter on the Six.
Its summary verse:
Two on being grouped together, decline,
dwelling in negligence, and restraint.
Concentration, seclusion,
and the two [types of] water that do not belong to you.
The second fifty-sections of the Chapter on the Six Sense Bases is completed.
Its summary of sections (vagguddāna) is:
Ignorance (avijjā), the Deer-net (migajāla),
the Sick (gilāna), the Thatched Hut (channa), and the fourth.
With the Saḷavagga, there are fifty;
thus ends the second fiftieth section.
This concludes the first hundred.

Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.104 (SN 35.104, PTS SN iv 84) 11. Yogakkhemivagga Yogakkhemisutta – The Discourse on the One Who Seeks Safety from Bondage “Bhikkhus, I shall teach you the one who seeks safety from bondage and the non-attainment of the one who seeks safety from bondage. Listen to that and attend closely; I will speak. “Yes, venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: “And how, bhikkhus, is one a seeker of safety from bondage? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu has abandoned lust, hatred, and delusion regarding the eye; he has cut them off at the root, made them like a palm stump, obliterated them so that they are no longer subject to future arising. He has abandoned lust, hatred, and delusion regarding the ear... regarding the nose... regarding the tongue... regarding the body... regarding the mind; he has cut them off at the root, made them like a palm stump, obliterated them so that they are no longer subject to future arising. This, bhikkhus, is called a bhikkhu who is a seeker of safety from bondage. “And how, bhikkhus, is one a non-attainer of the one who seeks safety from bondage? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu has not yet abandoned lust, hatred, and delusion regarding the eye; he has not cut them off at the root, nor made them like a palm stump, nor obliterated them so that they are no longer subject to future arising. He has not yet abandoned lust, hatred, and delusion regarding the ear... regarding the nose... regarding the tongue... regarding the body... regarding the mind; he has not cut them off at the root, nor made them like a palm stump, nor obliterated them so that they are no longer subject to future arising. This, bhikkhus, is called a bhikkhu who is a non-attainer of the one who seeks safety from bondage. “This, bhikkhus, is the one who seeks safety from bondage and the non-attainment of the one who seeks safety from bondage.”
At Sāvatthī.
"Monks, I will teach you a discourse on the Dhamma concerning the way to security from bondage.
Listen to it."
And what, monks, is the discourse on the Dhamma concerning the one who has attained security from bondage?
There are, monks, forms cognizable by the eye— desirable, lovely, pleasing, endearing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust—
which have been abandoned by the Tathāgata, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated so that they are no more subject to future arising.
And he has proclaimed the practice for their abandonment; therefore the Tathāgata is called "one who has attained security from bondage.
... There are, monks, mental phenomena cognizable by the mind that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, endearing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust.
These have been abandoned by the Tathāgata, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated so that they are no more subject to future arising.
And he proclaimed the practice for their abandonment; therefore, the Tathāgata is called "one who has attained security from bondage.
This, monks, is the discourse on the way to security from bondage, a discourse on the Dhamma. Thus was the first [sutta].

Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.105 (SN 35.105, PTS SN iv 85) 11. Yogakkhemivagga Upādāyasutta “Bhikkhus, it is by clinging that suffering arises; it is by not clinging that suffering ceases. When this was said, a certain bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “But, venerable sir, by clinging to what does suffering arise? By not clinging to what does suffering cease? “It is, bhikkhu, by clinging to form that suffering arises; it is by not clinging to form that suffering ceases. It is by clinging to feeling that suffering arises; it is by not clinging to feeling that suffering ceases. It is by clinging to perception that suffering arises; it is by not clinging to perception that suffering ceases. It is by clinging to volitional formations that suffering arises; it is by not clinging to volitional formations that suffering ceases. It is by clinging to consciousness that suffering arises; it is by not clinging to consciousness that suffering ceases. When this was said, that bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, is it only these five aggregates subject to clinging that are the basis for clinging, or is there another basis for clinging as well? “There is, bhikkhu, another basis for clinging as well. Whatever in the world has the nature to be clung to, whatever in the world is agreeable and pleasurable—this is the other basis for clinging. When this was said, that bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, why is it that some beings do not attain final Nibbāna in this very life? “Because they have not abandoned craving, bhikkhu, because they have not abandoned delight, because they have not abandoned lust, because they have not abandoned passion, because they have not abandoned fever, because they have not abandoned thirst, because they have not abandoned the underlying tendency toward conceit, because they have not abandoned ignorance, therefore some beings do not attain final Nibbāna in this very life. When this was said, that bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, why is it that some beings attain final Nibbāna in this very life? “Because they have abandoned craving, bhikkhu, because they have abandoned delight, because they have abandoned lust, because they have abandoned passion, because they have abandoned fever, because they have abandoned thirst, because they have abandoned the underlying tendency toward conceit, because they have abandoned ignorance, therefore some beings attain final Nibbāna in this very life. When this was said, that bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, how should one know, how should one see, so that, in regard to this body with its consciousness and all external signs, there is no I-making, mine-making, or underlying tendency toward conceit? “Bhikkhu, when one sees all phenomena as alien, as suffering, as a disease, as a tumor, as a barb, as a calamity, as an affliction, as alien, as disintegrating, as empty, as non-self, then one knows, one sees, so that in regard to this body with its consciousness and all external signs, there is no I-making, mine-making, or underlying tendency toward conceit. When this was said, that bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, how should one know, how should one see, so that, having seen rightly, one attains final Nibbāna in this very life? “Bhikkhu, when one sees the cessation of form, the cessation of feeling, the cessation of perception, the cessation of volitional formations, the cessation of consciousness, then one knows, one sees, so that, having seen rightly, one attains final Nibbāna in this very life. When this was said, that bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, how should one know, how should one see, so that, having seen rightly, one does not cling to anything in the world, and through non-clinging, being detached, through detachment, one attains final Nibbāna? “Bhikkhu, when one sees the cessation of the world, the cessation of the origin of the world, the cessation of the cessation of the world, the cessation of the path leading to the cessation of the world, then one knows, one sees, so that, having seen rightly, one does not cling to anything in the world, and through non-clinging, being detached, through detachment, one attains final Nibbāna. When this was said, that bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, how should one know, how should one see, so that, having seen rightly, one fully understands suffering, abandons the origin of suffering, realizes the cessation of suffering, and develops the path leading to the cessation of suffering? “Bhikkhu, when one sees the Noble Truth of Suffering as it really is, the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering as it really is, the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering as it really is, and the Noble Truth of the Path Leading to the Cessation of Suffering as it really is, then one knows, one sees, so that, having seen rightly, one fully understands suffering, abandons the origin of suffering, realizes the cessation of suffering, and develops the path leading to the cessation of suffering.

When this was said, that bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, how should one know, how should one see, so that, having seen rightly, one penetrates this Dhamma right here and now, and having penetrated it, one attains final Nibbāna in this very life? “Bhikkhu, when one sees the Noble Truth of Suffering as it really is, the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering as it really is, the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering as it really is, and the Noble Truth of the Path Leading to the Cessation of Suffering as it really is, then one knows, one sees, so that, having seen rightly, one penetrates this Dhamma right here and now, and having penetrated it, one attains final Nibbāna in this very life. When this was said, that bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, how should one know, how should one see, so that, having seen rightly, one becomes one who has reached the ultimate end, one who has done what was to be done, one who has laid down the burden, one who has lived the holy life, one who has accomplished his own goal, one whose fetters of existence are utterly destroyed, one who has attained final Nibbāna? “Bhikkhu, when one sees the Noble Truth of Suffering as it really is, the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering as it really is, the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering as it really is, and the Noble Truth of the Path Leading to the Cessation of Suffering as it really is, then one knows, one sees, so that, having seen rightly, one becomes one who has reached the ultimate end, one who has done what was to be done, one who has laid down the burden, one who has lived the holy life, one who has accomplished his own goal, one whose fetters of existence are utterly destroyed, one who has attained final Nibbāna. When this was said, that bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, how should one know, how should one see, so that, having seen rightly, one is a stream-enterer, no longer subject to perdition, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as one’s destination? “Bhikkhu, when one sees the Noble Truth of Suffering as it really is, the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering as it really is, the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering as it really is, and the Noble Truth of the Path Leading to the Cessation of Suffering as it really is, then one knows, one sees, so that, having seen rightly, one is a stream-enterer, no longer subject to perdition, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as one’s destination. When this was said, that bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, how should one know, how should one see, so that, having seen rightly, one is a once-returner, who, after coming back to this world only one more time, will make an end of suffering? “Bhikkhu, when one sees the Noble Truth of Suffering as it really is, the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering as it really is, the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering as it really is, and the Noble Truth of the Path Leading to the Cessation of Suffering as it really is, then one knows, one sees, so that, having seen rightly, one is a once-returner, who, after coming back to this world only one more time, will make an end of suffering. When this was said, that bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, how should one know, how should one see, so that, having seen rightly, one
“Monks, when what exists, by clinging to what, do internal pleasure and pain arise?
“Venerable sir, our teachings are rooted in the Blessed One...
“Monks, when the eye exists, by clinging to the eye, internal pleasure and pain arise...”
"When there is the mind, with the mind as its basis, internal pleasure and pain arise.
What do you think, monks,
is the eye permanent or impermanent?"
“Impermanent, venerable sir.
“But what is impermanent, is that suffering or happiness?
“Suffering, venerable sir.”
“But that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—would internal pleasure or pain arise through clinging to that?
“Certainly not, Bhante.
… “Is the tongue permanent or impermanent?”
“Impermanent, venerable sir.
“But what is impermanent, is that suffering or happiness?
“Suffering, venerable sir.”
“But that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—could internal pleasure or pain arise with regard to it through clinging?
“Certainly not, Bhante.
… “Is the mind permanent or impermanent?”
“Impermanent, venerable sir.
“But that which is impermanent, is it suffering or happiness?
“Suffering, venerable sir.”
“But what is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—could internal pleasure or pain arise with that as its basis?
“Certainly not, Bhante.
“Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the well-taught noble disciple becomes disenchanted with the eye... [and so on] ...he becomes disenchanted with the mind.”
“Through disenchantment, one becomes dispassionate; through dispassion, one is liberated. In liberation, the knowledge arises: ‘It is liberated. One understands:
‘Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.
This is the second [sutta].

Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.106 (SN 35.106, PTS SN iv 86) 11. Yogakkhemivagga Dukkhasamudayasutta (The Discourse on the Origin of Suffering) “Bhikkhus, I shall teach you the origin of suffering and the cessation of suffering. Listen to that, and pay close attention; I will speak. “Yes, venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: “And what, bhikkhus, is the origin of suffering? It is craving, which brings renewal of being, is accompanied by delight and lust, and delights in this and that; that is, craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence. This, bhikkhus, is called the origin of suffering. “And what, bhikkhus, is the cessation of suffering? It is the remainderless fading away and cessation of that same craving, the giving up and relinquishing of it, freedom from it, and non-reliance on it. This, bhikkhus, is called the cessation of suffering. “This, bhikkhus, is the noble truth of the origin of suffering. This, bhikkhus, is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering. This, bhikkhus, is the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering. “‘This is the noble truth of the origin of suffering’: thus, bhikkhus, in regard to things unheard before, there arose in me vision, knowledge, wisdom, true knowledge, and light. “‘This noble truth of the origin of suffering must be abandoned’: thus, bhikkhus, in regard to things unheard before, there arose in me vision, knowledge, wisdom, true knowledge, and light. “‘This noble truth of the origin of suffering has been abandoned’: thus, bhikkhus, in regard to things unheard before, there arose in me vision, knowledge, wisdom, true knowledge, and light. “‘This is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering’: thus, bhikkhus, in regard to things unheard before, there arose in me vision, knowledge, wisdom, true knowledge, and light. “‘This noble truth of the cessation of suffering must be realized’: thus, bhikkhus, in regard to things unheard before, there arose in me vision, knowledge, wisdom, true knowledge, and light. “‘This noble truth of the cessation of suffering has been realized’: thus, bhikkhus, in regard to things unheard before, there arose in me vision, knowledge, wisdom, true knowledge, and light. “‘This is the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering’: thus, bhikkhus, in regard to things unheard before, there arose in me vision, knowledge, wisdom, true knowledge, and light. “‘This noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering must be developed’: thus, bhikkhus, in regard to things unheard before, there arose in me vision, knowledge, wisdom, true knowledge, and light. “‘This noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering has been developed’: thus, bhikkhus, in regard to things unheard before, there arose in me vision, knowledge, wisdom, true knowledge, and light. “As long as, bhikkhus, my knowledge and vision of these four noble truths as they really are—through their three rounds and twelve aspects—was not thoroughly purified in this way, I did not claim to have awakened to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment in this world with its devas, Māra, and Brahmā, in this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans. But when my knowledge and vision of these four noble truths as they really are—through their three rounds and twelve aspects—was thoroughly purified in this way, then I claimed to have awakened to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment in this world with its devas, Māra, and Brahmā, in this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans. “The knowledge and vision arose in me: ‘Unshakable is my liberation of mind; this is my last birth; now there is no more renewed existence. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Elated, those bhikkhus delighted in the Blessed One’s words. (This concludes the Discourse on the Origin of Suffering.)
“Monks, I will teach you the origin and the passing away of suffering.
Listen to that.
And what, monks, is the origin of suffering?”
Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises. The meeting of the three is contact.
With contact as condition, there is feeling;
with feeling as condition, there is craving.
This is the origin of suffering...
[and so on] ...dependent on the tongue and tastes, tongue-consciousness arises. The meeting of the three is contact.
With contact as condition, feeling arises.
With feeling as condition, craving arises.
This is the origin of suffering …pe… Dependent on the mind and mental phenomena, mind-consciousness arises.
The meeting of these three is contact.
With contact as condition, feeling arises;
with feeling as condition, craving arises.

And what, monks, is the cessation of suffering?
Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises. The meeting of the three is contact.
With contact as condition, feeling arises.
With feeling as condition, craving arises.
With the remainderless fading away and cessation of that very craving comes the cessation of clinging;
with the cessation of clinging comes the cessation of existence.
With the cessation of existence, birth ceases;
with the cessation of birth, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair cease.

Saṁyutta Nikāya 35.107 (SN 35.107, PTS SN iv 87) 11. Yogakkhemivagga Lokasamudayasutta: The Arising of the World "Bhikkhus, I will teach you the arising of the world. Listen to that. This, bhikkhus, is called the arising of the world. [The same is repeated for the ear and sounds, the nose and odors, the tongue and flavors, the body and tangibles,] ...Dependent on the mind and mental phenomena, mind-consciousness arises; the meeting of the three is contact; with contact as condition, feeling; with feeling as condition, craving; with craving as condition, clinging; with clinging as condition, existence; with existence as condition, birth; with birth as condition, aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise. This, bhikkhus, is called the arising of the world."

Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.108 (SN 35.108, PTS SN iv 88) 11. Yogakkhemivagga Seyyohamasmi Sutta: "I am Superior" At Sāvatthī. "Bhikkhus, there are these three kinds of persons found existing in the world. What three? The person who thinks, 'I am superior,' the person who thinks, 'I am equal,' and the person who thinks, 'I am inferior. And how, bhikkhus, is one a person who thinks, 'I am superior'? Here, bhikkhus, a noble disciple possesses confirmed confidence in the Buddha thus: 'The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Enlightened One, the Blessed One. He possesses confirmed confidence in the Dhamma thus: 'The Dhamma is well expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally experienced by the wise. He possesses confirmed confidence in the Saṅgha thus: 'The Saṅgha of the Blessed One's disciples is practicing the good way, practicing the straight way, practicing the true way, practicing the proper way; that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals—this Saṅgha of the Blessed One's disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. He possesses the virtues dear to the noble ones, unbroken, untorn, unblemished, unmottled, freeing, praised by the wise, ungrasped, leading to concentration. It is in this way, bhikkhus, that one is a person who thinks, 'I am superior. "And how, bhikkhus, is one a person who thinks, 'I am equal'? Here, bhikkhus, a noble disciple possesses confirmed confidence in the Buddha... in the Dhamma... in the Saṅgha... and he possesses the virtues dear to the noble ones... It is in this way, bhikkhus, that one is a person who thinks, 'I am equal. "And how, bhikkhus, is one a person who thinks, 'I am inferior'? Here, bhikkhus, a noble disciple possesses confirmed confidence in the Buddha... in the Dhamma... in the Saṅgha... and he possesses the virtues dear to the noble ones... It is in this way, bhikkhus, that one is a person who thinks, 'I am inferior. “Bhikkhus, when what exists, by clinging to what, by adhering to what, does the thought ‘I am superior’ arise, or the thought ‘I am equal,’ or the thought ‘I am inferior’?

“Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the well-taught noble disciple becomes disenchanted with the eye … [and so on] … he becomes disenchanted with the mind.

Fifth. Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.109 (SN 35.109, PTS SN iv 89) 11. Yogakkhemivagga (The Chapter on the One Who Has Attained Security from Bondage)
The Discourse on the Things that Conduce to Fettering: “Monks, I will teach you the things that conduce to fettering and the fetter itself.
Listen to that.”
"And what, bhikkhus, are the things that fetter, and what is the fetter?
The eye, bhikkhus, is a thing that fetters.
The desire and lust for it—that is the fetter there... [and so on for the other sense bases]."
The tongue is a phenomenon that fetters; ... [and so on] ...
the mind is a phenomenon that fetters.
Whatever desire and lust there is therein, that is the fetter therein.
“Monks, these are called the things that fetter; this is the fetter.
The sixth [discourse]. Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.110 (SN 35.110, PTS SN iv 89)
11. The Chapter on the One Who Seeks Security from Bondage (Yogakkhemivagga).
Discourse on Clinging (Upādāniyasutta): “Monks, I will teach you the things that lead to clinging and clinging itself.”
Listen to that.
And what, monks, are the phenomena subject to clinging, and what is clinging?
The eye, monks, is a phenomenon subject to clinging.
Whatever desire and lust there is for that, that is clinging therein … the tongue is a phenomenon subject to clinging … the mind is a phenomenon subject to clinging.
Whatever desire and lust there is for them, that is clinging in regard to them.
These, monks, are called the things subject to clinging; this is clinging.
Thus ends the seventh [sutta].

Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.111 (SN 35.111, PTS SN iv 89) 11. Yogakkhemivagga Ajjhattikāyatanaparijānanasutta: The Discourse on the Full Understanding of the Internal Bases "Bhikkhus, I shall teach you the full understanding of the internal bases. Listen to it and attend closely; I will speak. "Yes, venerable sir," those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: "And what, bhikkhus, is the full understanding of the internal bases? It is the knowledge of the eye as it really is, its arising, its cessation, and the way leading to its cessation; the knowledge of forms as they really are, their arising, their cessation, and the way leading to their cessation; the knowledge of eye-consciousness as it really is, its arising, its cessation, and the way leading to its cessation; the knowledge of eye-contact as it really is, its arising, its cessation, and the way leading to its cessation; and the knowledge of whatever feeling arises with eye-contact as condition—as pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—as it really is, its arising, its cessation, and the way leading to its cessation. "The knowledge of the ear as it really is... the knowledge of the nose as it really is... the knowledge of the tongue as it really is... the knowledge of the body as it really is... the knowledge of the mind as it really is, its arising, its cessation, and the way leading to its cessation; the knowledge of mental phenomena as they really are, their arising, their cessation, and the way leading to their cessation; the knowledge of mind-consciousness as it really is, its arising, its cessation, and the way leading to its cessation; the knowledge of mind-contact as it really is, its arising, its cessation, and the way leading to its cessation; and the knowledge of whatever feeling arises with mind-contact as condition—as pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—as it really is, its arising, its cessation, and the way leading to its cessation. "This, bhikkhus, is called the full understanding of the internal bases."
“Bhikkhus, without directly knowing the eye, without fully understanding it, without becoming dispassionate toward it, and without abandoning it, one is incapable of the destruction of suffering.
[The same applies to] the ear … the nose …”

Without directly knowing and fully understanding the tongue … the body … the mind, without becoming dispassionate toward it and without abandoning it, one is incapable of the destruction of suffering.
“Monks, by directly knowing the eye, fully understanding it, fading away toward it, and abandoning it, one is capable of the destruction of suffering … [and so on] … the tongue … the body …”
“By directly knowing the mind, by fully understanding it, by making it fade away, and by abandoning it, one is capable of the destruction of suffering.
Thus was the eighth [discourse]. *Saṃyutta Nikāya* 35.112.
11. The Chapter on the One Who Seeks Safety in Yoga (Yogakkhemivagga) The Discourse on Fully Understanding the External Sense-Bases “Bhikkhus,
one who does not directly know forms, does not fully understand them, does not become dispassionate toward them, and does not abandon them, is incapable of the destruction of suffering.
In sounds … in odors … in tastes …

“Monks, one who does not directly know and fully understand tactile objects, and who does not become dispassionate toward them or abandon them, is incapable of the destruction of suffering. But, monks,
one who directly knows and fully understands forms, and who becomes dispassionate toward them and abandons them, is capable of the destruction of suffering.”
In sounds … in odors … in tastes …
“By directly knowing and fully understanding tangible objects… mental phenomena, by removing passion for them and abandoning them, one is capable of the destruction of suffering.
Thus ends the ninth [discourse].

Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.113 (SN 35.113, PTS SN iv 90) 11. Yogakkhemivagga Upassutisutta – The Discourse on Eavesdropping At Sāvatthī. At that time, several bhikkhus were sitting together in the assembly hall, engaged in a discussion concerning the Dhamma. Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and reported to the Blessed One what those bhikkhus had been discussing. “Good, good, Ānanda! It is fitting for you to encourage the bhikkhus with such a talk on the Dhamma. For it is by means of such talk on the Dhamma that the Tathāgata encourages the bhikkhus. Ānanda, when a bhikkhu is practicing for the attainment of the security from bondage, he should attend closely to this: ‘Do my body, speech, and mind become more refined through this practice, or do they not? Is aversion being abandoned in me, or is it not? Am I attaining temporary liberation, or am I not? If, while attending closely, a bhikkhu understands: ‘Through this practice, my body, speech, and mind become more refined; aversion is being abandoned in me; and I am attaining temporary liberation,’ then he should practice that same thing more frequently. But if, while attending closely, a bhikkhu understands: ‘Through this practice, my body, speech, and mind do not become more refined; aversion is not being abandoned in me; and I am not attaining temporary liberation,’ then he should abandon that practice and pursue another. Suppose, Ānanda, there was a person who, wishing to see a great tree, would go to the foot of that great tree and stand there. While standing there, he would think: ‘I hope this great tree does not have its roots growing upwards, its branches and foliage growing downwards. And as he stands there, he sees that the great tree indeed has its roots growing upwards and its branches and foliage growing downwards. He thinks: ‘Alas, this great tree has its roots growing upwards and its branches and foliage growing downwards! It will not long endure! In the same way, Ānanda, when a bhikkhu is practicing for the attainment of the security from bondage, he should attend closely to this: ‘Do my body, speech, and mind become more refined through this practice, or do they not? Is aversion being abandoned in me, or is it not? Am I attaining temporary liberation, or am I not? If, while attending closely, a bhikkhu understands: ‘Through this practice, my body, speech, and mind become more refined; aversion is being abandoned in me; and I am attaining temporary liberation,’ then he should practice that same thing more frequently. But if, while attending closely, a bhikkhu understands: ‘Through this practice, my body, speech, and mind do not become more refined; aversion is not being abandoned in me; and I am not attaining temporary liberation,’ then he should abandon that practice and pursue another. Suppose, Ānanda, there was a person who, wishing to see a great tree, would go to the foot of that great tree and stand there. While standing there, he would think: ‘I hope this great tree does not have its roots growing downwards, its branches and foliage growing upwards. And as he stands there, he sees that the great tree indeed has its roots growing downwards and its branches and foliage growing upwards. He thinks: ‘Alas, this great tree has its roots growing downwards and its branches and foliage growing upwards! It will long endure! In the same way, Ānanda, when a bhikkhu is practicing for the attainment of the security from bondage, he should attend closely to this: ‘Do my body, speech, and mind become more refined through this practice, or do they not? Is aversion being abandoned in me, or is it not? Am I attaining temporary liberation, or am I not? If, while attending closely, a bhikkhu understands: ‘Through this practice, my body, speech, and mind become more refined; aversion is being abandoned in me; and I am attaining temporary liberation,’ then he should practice that same thing more frequently. But if, while attending closely, a bhikkhu understands: ‘Through this practice, my body, speech, and mind do not become more refined; aversion is not being abandoned in me; and I am not attaining temporary liberation,’ then he should abandon that practice and pursue another.”

“Bhikkhus, there are forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, lovely, pleasing, dear, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust.

If a bhikkhu delights in that, welcomes it, and remains clinging to it, then, monks, this bhikkhu is said to have entered Māra’s domain, to have come under Māra’s control, and to have had Māra’s snare fastened upon him.
He is bound by Māra’s fetter; he may be done with at will by the Evil One... [as before]...
"There are, monks, flavors cognizable by the tongue that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual pleasure, and provocative of lust.

If a monk delights in them, welcomes them, and remains clinging to them, this monk, monks, is said to have come into Māra’s domain, fallen under Māra’s power, and has had Māra’s snare fastened upon him. He is bound by Māra’s fetter... [as before].
“Monks, there are mental phenomena cognizable by the mind that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust.
If a monk delights in them, welcomes them, and remains attached to them, this monk, monks,
is said to have come into Māra’s dwelling, has fallen under Māra’s control, and has been bound by Māra’s snare.”
He is bound by the bond of Māra, subject to the doing with him as the Evil One wishes...
But there are, monks, forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, lovely, pleasing, dear, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust.

“Monks, this monk is called one who is bound to forms cognizable by the eye, who has come to Māra’s dwelling, who has fallen under Māra’s power, and for whom Māra’s snare is fastened.
He is bound by Māra’s fetter and is subject to the doing with him as the Evil One wishes...
There are, monks, tastes cognizable by the tongue... [as before]...”
"There are, bhikkhus, mental phenomena cognizable by the mind that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust.

If a bhikkhu delights in them, welcomes them, and remains clinging to them, this bhikkhu is called one who is bound to mental phenomena cognizable by the mind; he has come under Māra’s dwelling, fallen under Māra’s power, and is caught in Māra’s snare."
He is bound by the bond of Māra; he is at the disposal of the Evil One...
There are, however, monks, forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, lovely, pleasing, dear, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust.
If a monk does not delight in them, does not welcome them, and does not remain clinging to them—

“Monks, this monk is called one who is freed from forms cognizable by the eye, who has not come under Māra’s control, who has not fallen into Māra’s power, and for whom Māra’s snare has been cast off.
He is freed from Māra’s bondage and is no longer subject to the Evil One’s doing as he wishes...
There are, monks, tastes cognizable by the tongue... (and so on).
“Bhikkhus, there are mind-objects cognizable by the mind that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust.

If a bhikkhu does not delight in them, does not welcome them, and does not remain holding to them, he is called a bhikkhu who is freed from mind-objects cognizable by the mind; he has not come under Māra’s dwelling, he has not come under Māra’s control, and the snare of Māra has been cast off.”
"He is freed from the bonds of Māra; he is no longer subject to the doing of his will by the Evil One.
Second.

"This Venerable Ānanda is indeed praised by the Teacher and esteemed by his wise fellow-celibates."
“The Venerable Ānanda is capable of analyzing in detail the meaning of this brief summary given by the Blessed One, the meaning of which has not yet been analyzed in detail.
