The Chapter on the World and the Strands of Sensual Pleasure The Discourse on the Questions of Sakka At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. Then the deva-king Sakka approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and stood to one side. Standing there, he addressed the Blessed One in verse: “How does one know, how does one see, friend Gotama, so that this world does not become bewildered, nor does it fall into confusion regarding the true nature of things? “By knowing form as it really is, friend, by knowing feeling as it really is, by knowing perception as it really is, by knowing volitional formations as they really are, and by knowing consciousness as it really is—thus one knows, thus one sees, friend, so that this world does not become bewildered, nor does it fall into confusion regarding the true nature of things. “But what is form, friend? What is feeling? What is perception? What are volitional formations? And what is consciousness? “Whatever form there is, friend, whether past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near—it is all considered as it really is with right wisdom: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self. Whatever feeling there is... Whatever perception there is... Whatever volitional formations there are... Whatever consciousness there is, whether past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near—it is all considered as it really is with right wisdom: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self. When one knows form as it really is, friend, when one knows feeling as it really is, when one knows perception as it really is, when one knows volitional formations as they really are, and when one knows consciousness as it really is, then one does not cling to anything in the world; not clinging, one is not agitated; being unagitated, one personally attains Nibbāna. One understands: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being. When this was said, the deva-king Sakka said to the Blessed One: “Magnificent, venerable sir! Magnificent, venerable sir! Just as one might set upright what was overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who was lost, or bring an oil lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms, even so has the Dhamma been declared by the Blessed One in many ways. I go for refuge to the Blessed One, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. May the Blessed One accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life shall last. Then the deva-king Sakka, having delighted and rejoiced in the words of the Blessed One, paid homage to him, circumambulated him keeping the right side toward him, and vanished right there. "There are, O Lord of Devas, tastes cognizable by the tongue...
There are, O Lord of Devas, mental phenomena cognizable by the mind that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual pleasure, and provocative of lust.
If a bhikkhu does not delight in them, does not welcome them, and does not remain clinging to them, [he is said to dwell detached from them]."
When one does not delight in that, does not welcome it, and does not remain clinging to it, consciousness is no longer dependent on it and does not take it as its fuel.
O Lord of Devas, a bhikkhu who is without fuel attains final nibbāna.
This, O Lord of Devas, is the cause, this is the condition by which some beings here attain final nibbāna in this very life.”
Fifth. Saṁyutta Nikāya 35.119 (SN 35.119, PTS SN iv 103) 12. The Chapter on the World and the Strands of Sensual Pleasure (Lokakāmaguṇavagga)
The Discourse to Pañcasikha.
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha on Vulture Peak Mountain.
Then Pañcasikha, the son of the gandhabba deities, approached the Blessed One; having approached, he...
Having paid homage to the Blessed One, he stood to one side. Standing to one side, Pañcasikha the gandhabba-deva son addressed the Blessed One thus:
"What, venerable sir, is the cause, what is the reason why some beings here do not attain final nibbāna in this very life?"
"But what, venerable sir, is the cause, what is the reason why some beings here attain final nibbāna in this very life?
"There are, Pañcasikha, forms cognizable by the eye...
[and so on] ...there are, Pañcasikha, mental phenomena cognizable by the mind, which are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual pleasure, and provocative of lust."
If a bhikkhu delights in that, welcomes it, and remains clinging to it,
then as he delights in it, welcomes it, and remains clinging to it, his consciousness becomes dependent upon it and takes it as its fuel.
With such fuel, Pañcasikha, a bhikkhu does not attain final Nibbāna.
"This, Pañcasikha, is the cause, this is the condition, why some beings here do not attain final nibbāna in this very life.
There are, Pañcasikha, forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, lovely, pleasing...
[and so on] ...There are, Pañcasikha, mental phenomena cognizable by the mind that are desirable, lovely, pleasing, endearing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust."

If a bhikkhu does not delight in that, does not welcome it, and does not remain clinging to it, then for him who does not delight in it, does not welcome it, and does not remain clinging to it, consciousness is no longer dependent on it and does not take it as its fuel.
Being without fuel, Pañcasikha, a bhikkhu attains final Nibbāna.
This, Pañcasikha, is the cause, this is the condition by which some beings here attain final Nibbāna in this very life.”
The Sixth.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 35.120 (SN 35.120, PTS SN iv 103) 12. The Chapter on the World and the Strands of Sensual Pleasure (Lokakāmaguṇavagga)
The Discourse on the Co-resident of Venerable Sāriputta.
On one occasion, the Venerable Sāriputta was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Then a certain bhikkhu approached the Venerable Sāriputta; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Venerable Sāriputta.
Having exchanged greetings and pleasantries, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, that bhikkhu said to the Venerable Sāriputta:
"Friend Sāriputta, my co-resident bhikkhu has renounced the training and returned to the lower life.
"It is just so, friend, for one who does not guard the doors of the sense faculties, who is immoderate in eating, and who is not devoted to wakefulness."

"Friends, it is impossible that a bhikkhu who guards not the doors of the sense faculties, who is immoderate in eating, and who is not devoted to wakefulness should maintain the holy life in its full perfection and purity for as long as life lasts.

But, friends, it is possible that a bhikkhu who guards the doors of the sense faculties, who is moderate in eating, and who is devoted to wakefulness should maintain the holy life in its full perfection and purity for as long as life lasts.
And how, friends, does one guard the doors of the sense faculties?"
Here, friends, having seen a form with the eye, a bhikkhu does not grasp at its signs or its secondary characteristics.
Since, if he were to dwell with this faculty unrestrained, covetousness and dejection—evil, unwholesome states—might flow in upon him, he practices for its restraint;
he guards the eye-faculty and achieves restraint over the eye-faculty.
Having heard a sound with the ear...
having smelled an odor with the nose...
having tasted a flavor with the tongue...
Having touched a tangible object with the body...
having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, one does not grasp at its signs nor grasp at its secondary characteristics.
For if one dwells with this faculty of mind unguarded, covetousness and dejection—evil, unwholesome states—[arise].

If, when he has gone to the forest, to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut, thoughts connected with desire, aversion, or delusion were to flow into him, he practices for their restraint; he guards the mind-faculty and attains restraint over the mind-faculty.
It is in this way, friends, that one is guarded in the doors of the sense faculties.
And how, friends, is one moderate in eating?
In this case, friends, a bhikkhu reflects wisely before taking food:

"Neither for amusement, nor for intoxication, nor for physical beauty, nor for adornment, but only for the maintenance and preservation of this body, for the allaying of hunger, and for supporting the holy life;
thus I shall put an end to old feelings [of hunger] and..."
"I shall not give rise to new feeling; I shall maintain myself, be blameless, and dwell at ease.
In this way, friends, one is moderate in eating.
And how, friends, is one devoted to wakefulness?
Here, friends, during the day a bhikkhu purifies his mind of obstructive states while walking back and forth and sitting.
During the first watch of the night, he purifies his mind of obstructive states while walking back and forth and sitting.

During the middle watch of the night, he lies down on his right side in the lion’s posture, with one foot overlapping the other, mindful and clearly comprehending, having fixed his mind on the thought of rising.
Rising during the last watch of the night, he purifies his mind of obstructive states while walking and sitting.
It is in this way, friends, that one is devoted to wakefulness.
Therefore, friends, you should train yourselves thus:
‘We shall guard the doors of the sense faculties, we shall be moderate in eating, and we shall be devoted to wakefulness.
In this way, friends, you should train yourselves.
This is the seventh [sutta].

Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.121 (SN 35.121, PTS SN iv 105) 12. The Chapter on the World and the Strands of Sensual Pleasure The Discourse of Advice to Rāhula At Sāvatthī. There, the Blessed One said this to the Venerable Rāhula: “Rāhula, what do you think? Is the eye permanent or impermanent? “Impermanent, Bhante. “But is that which is impermanent suffering or happiness? “Suffering, Bhante. “But is it fitting to regard what is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change as: ‘This is mine; this I am; this is my self’? “No, Bhante. “Rāhula, what do you think? Is the ear... the nose... the tongue... the body... the mind permanent or impermanent? “Impermanent, Bhante. “But is that which is impermanent suffering or happiness? “Suffering, Bhante. “But is it fitting to regard what is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change as: ‘This is mine; this I am; this is my self’? “No, Bhante. “Therefore, Rāhula, whatever is internal, belonging to oneself, and considered as one’s own—whether it be form, feeling, perception, volitional formations, or consciousness—that is impermanent. That which is impermanent is suffering. That which is suffering is not mine, is not I, is not my self. This is how it should be seen with right wisdom, just as it actually is. When one sees it thus with right wisdom, just as it actually is, one becomes disenchanted with the eye, disenchanted with the ear, disenchanted with the nose, disenchanted with the tongue, disenchanted with the body, and disenchanted with the mind. Being disenchanted, one becomes dispassionate. Through dispassion, one is liberated. Through liberation, there is the knowledge: ‘It is liberated. One understands: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Having said this, the Sublime One rose from his seat and went into his dwelling. Then, not long after the Blessed One had left, the Venerable Rāhula addressed the bhikkhus: “Friends, bhikkhus! “Friend! those bhikkhus replied to the Venerable Rāhula. The Venerable Rāhula said this: “Friends, the Blessed One taught me this Dhamma: ‘Rāhula, what do you think? Is the eye permanent or impermanent? ... [as above] ... ‘When one sees it thus with right wisdom, just as it actually is, one becomes disenchanted with the eye... and understands: “There is no more for this state of being. Friends, when the Blessed One taught me this Dhamma, I understood it thus: ‘If I were to attain final Nibbāna even today, that would be appropriate for me. “Indeed, friend Rāhula, the Blessed One taught you this Dhamma:

‘Rāhula, what do you think? Is the eye permanent or impermanent? ... [as above] ... ‘When one sees it thus with right wisdom, just as it actually is, one becomes disenchanted with the eye... and understands: “There is no more for this state of being. Indeed, friend Rāhula, the Blessed One taught you this Dhamma, and you understood it thus: ‘If I were to attain final Nibbāna even today, that would be appropriate for me. Then the Venerable Rāhula approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and reported to the Blessed One everything that had occurred. “Good, good, Rāhula! It is good that you have understood this Dhamma taught by me thus. Indeed, Rāhula, if a bhikkhu should dwell in such a way for seven years, he may, through the destruction of the taints, realize for himself with direct knowledge in this very life, enter and dwell in the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, having realized it for himself with direct knowledge. But, Rāhula, let alone seven years. If a bhikkhu should dwell in such a way for six years... five years... four years... three years... two years... one year, he may, through the destruction of the taints, realize for himself with direct knowledge in this very life, enter and dwell in the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, having realized it for himself with direct knowledge. But, Rāhula, let alone one year. If a bhikkhu should dwell in such a way for seven months... six months... five months... four months... three months... two months... one month... half a month, he may, through the destruction of the taints, realize for himself with direct knowledge in this very life, enter and dwell in the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, having realized it for himself with direct knowledge. But, Rāhula, let alone half a month. If a bhikkhu should dwell in such a way for seven days and nights, he may, through the destruction of the taints, realize for himself with direct knowledge in this very life, enter and dwell in the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, having realized it for himself with direct knowledge. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Elated, the Venerable Rāhula delighted in the words of the Blessed One. (This concludes the Discourse of Advice to Rāhula.)
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Then, while the Blessed One was alone in seclusion, this reflection arose in his mind:
“The qualities that ripen for liberation have indeed reached maturity in Rāhula.”
"What if I were to further train Rāhula in the destruction of the taints?
Then, having dressed in the morning and taken his bowl and robe, the Blessed One went into Sāvatthī for alms.
Having walked for alms in Sāvatthī and returned from his almsround after the meal, he addressed the Venerable Rāhula:
“Take your sitting mat, Rāhula;
we will go to the Blind Men’s Grove for the day’s abiding.
“Very well, Bhante,” the Venerable Rāhula replied to the Blessed One, and taking his sitting mat, he followed closely behind the Blessed One.
Now at that time, many thousands of deities followed after the Blessed One, thinking:
"Today the Blessed One will further discipline the Venerable Rāhula in the destruction of the taints.
Then the Blessed One, having entered deep into the Andhavana grove, sat down on a seat prepared at the foot of a certain tree.
The Venerable Rāhula also paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side.
As the Venerable Rāhula was sitting there, the Blessed One said this to him:
“What do you think, Rāhula?”
“Is the eye permanent or impermanent?
“Impermanent, venerable sir.
“But that which is impermanent, is it suffering or happiness?”
“It is suffering, venerable sir.
“But that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—is it fitting to regard it thus:
‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?”
“No, venerable sir.
(…) “Are forms permanent or impermanent?
“Impermanent, venerable sir. …pe…
“Is eye-consciousness permanent or impermanent?
“Impermanent, venerable sir.
… [and so on] … “Is eye-contact permanent or impermanent?”
“Impermanent, Bhante.
… [as before] … “And as for this feeling, perception, volitional formations, and consciousness that arise conditioned by eye-contact: are they permanent or impermanent?
“Impermanent, Bhante.”
“But that which is impermanent, is it suffering or happiness?”—
“Suffering, Bhante.”—
“But that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change— is it fitting to regard it thus:”
‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?
— “Certainly not, Bhante.
… “Is the tongue permanent or impermanent?”
“Impermanent, venerable sir.
… [as before] … “Is tongue-consciousness permanent or impermanent?
“Impermanent, venerable sir. … [as before] …
“Is tongue-contact permanent or impermanent?
“Impermanent, venerable sir.
… [as before] … “And as for this feeling, perception, volitional formations, and consciousness that arise conditioned by tongue-contact—are they permanent or impermanent?”
“Impermanent, venerable sir.
“But what is impermanent, is that suffering or happiness?
“Suffering, venerable sir.”
“But that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—is it fitting to regard it thus:
‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?
“Certainly not, Bhante. …pe…
“Is the mind permanent or impermanent?
“Impermanent, venerable sir.
“But that which is impermanent, is it suffering or happiness?”
“It is suffering, venerable sir.
“But that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—is it fitting to regard it thus:
‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?”
“No, venerable sir.
“Are phenomena permanent or impermanent?
“Impermanent, venerable sir. … [as before] …
“Is mind-consciousness permanent or impermanent?
“Impermanent, venerable sir.
… [as before] … “Is mind-contact permanent or impermanent?”
“Impermanent, venerable sir.
… [as before] … “And that which arises conditioned by mind-contact—whether it be feeling, perception, volitional formations, or consciousness—is that permanent or impermanent?
“Impermanent, venerable sir.”
“But what is impermanent, is that suffering or happiness?”—
“Suffering, venerable sir.”—
“But what is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change— is it fitting to regard it thus:”
‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?”—
“Certainly not, Bhante.”—
“Seeing thus, Rāhula, the well-taught noble disciple becomes disenchanted with the eye, and he becomes disenchanted with forms.”

One becomes disenchanted with eye-consciousness; one becomes disenchanted with eye-contact; and one becomes disenchanted with whatever feeling, perception, volitional formations, and consciousness arise conditioned by that eye-contact.
…pe… One becomes disenchanted with the tongue; one becomes disenchanted with tastes; one becomes disenchanted with tongue-consciousness; and one becomes disenchanted with tongue-contact.

One becomes disenchanted; one becomes disenchanted with whatever feeling, perception, volitional formations, and consciousness arise conditioned by tongue-contact …pe… One becomes disenchanted with the mind,
disenchanted with mental phenomena, disenchanted with mind-consciousness, and disenchanted with mind-contact.
One becomes disenchanted with it; one becomes disenchanted with whatever feeling, perception, volitional formations, and consciousness arise conditioned by mental contact.
Being disenchanted, one becomes dispassionate; through dispassion, one is liberated. In liberation, the knowledge arises: "It is liberated."
‘Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
The Venerable Rāhula, glad at heart, rejoiced in the words of the Blessed One.
And while this exposition was being spoken, the mind of the Venerable Rāhula was liberated from the taints through non-clinging.
And in many thousands of deities, the dustless, stainless Dhamma-eye arose:
"Whatever is subject to origination, all that is subject to cessation."
The Eighth.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 35.122 (SN 35.122, PTS SN iv 107) 12. The Chapter on the World and the Strands of Sensual Pleasure (Lokakāmaguṇavagga)
Saṁyojaniyadhammasutta:
“Monks, I will teach you the things that fetter and the fetter itself.
Listen to that.”
"And what, monks, are the things that fetter, and what is the fetter?
There are, monks, forms cognizable by the eye—desirable, lovely, pleasing, endearing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust.
These, monks, are called the things that fetter."
Whatever desire and lust there is for that, that is the fetter there...
There are, monks, tastes cognizable by the tongue...
There are, monks, mental phenomena cognizable by the mind that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual pleasure, and provocative of passion.
“Monks, these are called the things that fetter.
The desire and lust for them—that is the fetter therein.
Thus ends the ninth [sutta].

What phenomena, bhikkhus, are subject to clinging? The eye, bhikkhus, is a phenomenon subject to clinging; forms are phenomena subject to clinging; eye-consciousness is a phenomenon subject to clinging; eye-contact is a phenomenon subject to clinging; and whatever feeling arises with eye-contact as its condition—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too is a phenomenon subject to clinging. “The ear is a phenomenon subject to clinging; sounds are phenomena subject to clinging; ear-consciousness is a phenomenon subject to clinging; ear-contact is a phenomenon subject to clinging; and whatever feeling arises with ear-contact as its condition... that too is a phenomenon subject to clinging. “The nose is a phenomenon subject to clinging; odors are phenomena subject to clinging; nose-consciousness is a phenomenon subject to clinging; nose-contact is a phenomenon subject to clinging; and whatever feeling arises with nose-contact as its condition... that too is a phenomenon subject to clinging. “The tongue is a phenomenon subject to clinging; tastes are phenomena subject to clinging; tongue-consciousness is a phenomenon subject to clinging; tongue-contact is a phenomenon subject to clinging; and whatever feeling arises with tongue-contact as its condition... that too is a phenomenon subject to clinging. “The body is a phenomenon subject to clinging; tangibles are phenomena subject to clinging; body-consciousness is a phenomenon subject to clinging; body-contact is a phenomenon subject to clinging; and whatever feeling arises with body-contact as its condition... that too is a phenomenon subject to clinging. “The mind is a phenomenon subject to clinging; mental phenomena are phenomena subject to clinging; mind-consciousness is a phenomenon subject to clinging; mind-contact is a phenomenon subject to clinging; and whatever feeling arises with mind-contact as its condition—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too is a phenomenon subject to clinging. “These, bhikkhus, are the phenomena subject to clinging.”
“Monks, I will teach you the things that are conducive to clinging and clinging itself.
Listen to that.
And what, monks, are the things conducive to clinging, and what is clinging?

“Bhikkhus, there are forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust. These, bhikkhus, are called things that can be clung to. The desire and lust for them: that is clinging therein. … [as above] … “Bhikkhus, there are sounds cognizable by the ear … smells cognizable by the nose … tastes cognizable by the tongue … tactile objects cognizable by the body … mental phenomena cognizable by the mind that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust. These, bhikkhus, are called things that can be clung to. That which is the absence of clinging, the fading away of clinging, the cessation of clinging, the relinquishing of clinging, the abandoning of clinging: this is called Nibbāna. … [as above] … “Bhikkhus, there are sounds cognizable by the ear … smells cognizable by the nose … tastes cognizable by the tongue … tactile objects cognizable by the body … mental phenomena cognizable by the mind that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust. Saṁyutta Nikāya 35.124 (SN 35.124, PTS SN iv 109) 13.
Gahapativagga (The Chapter on Householders)
The Vesālī Sutta On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Vesālī in the Great Wood, in the Gabled Hall.
Then Ugga, the householder of Vesālī, approached the Blessed One; having approached, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, Ugga, the householder of Vesālī, said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, what is the cause, what is the reason why some beings here do not attain final nibbāna in this very life?
But what, venerable sir, is the cause, what is the reason why some beings here do attain final nibbāna in this very life?
“Householder, there are forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, lovely, pleasing, dear, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust.

If a bhikkhu delights in that, welcomes it, and remains clinging to it, then for him who delights in it, welcomes it, and remains clinging to it, consciousness becomes dependent on that and takes that as its fuel.
A bhikkhu with fuel, householder, does not attain final nibbāna...
There are, householder, flavors cognizable by the tongue... [and so forth].
"There are, householder, mental phenomena cognizable by the mind that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust.
If a bhikkhu delights in them, welcomes them, and remains attached to them, then his consciousness becomes dependent on them and takes them as its sustenance.
Householder, a bhikkhu who has such sustenance does not attain final nibbāna."
"This, householder, is the cause, this is the condition why some beings here do not attain final nibbāna in this very life.
There are, householder, forms cognizable by the eye—desirable, lovely, pleasing, endearing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust.
If a bhikkhu does not delight in them, does not welcome them, and does not remain clinging to them, then his consciousness is not dependent on them and does not take them as its fuel.
“Householder, a bhikkhu who is without clinging attains final Nibbāna...
There are, householder, tastes cognizable by the tongue...
There are, householder, mental phenomena cognizable by the mind that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual pleasure, and provocative of lust.”

“If a bhikkhu does not delight in that, does not welcome it, and does not remain clinging to it, then for him who does not delight in it, does not welcome it, and does not remain clinging to it, consciousness is no longer dependent on that and does not take up that as its fuel.
Being without fuel, householder, a bhikkhu attains final nibbāna.
This, householder, is the cause, this is the condition, by which some beings here attain final nibbāna in this very life.”
First.

Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.127 (SN 35.127, PTS SN iv 110) 13. Gahapativagga Bhāradvājasutta Then the Venerable Bhāradvāja approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it would be good if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief, so that, having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, I might dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute. “Bhāradvāja, when one has not seen much of the noble ones, and one’s view is not aligned with theirs, and one has not been trained in their Dhamma, it is impossible for one to know: ‘This is suffering,’ ‘This is the origin of suffering,’ ‘This is the cessation of suffering,’ and ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. “But, venerable sir, when one has seen much of the noble ones, and one’s view is aligned with theirs, and one has been well-trained in their Dhamma, is it possible for one to know: ‘This is suffering,’ ‘This is the origin of suffering,’ ‘This is the cessation of suffering,’ and ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering’? “Yes, Bhāradvāja, it is possible. “Venerable sir, how does one come to know: ‘This is suffering,’ ‘This is the origin of suffering,’ ‘This is the cessation of suffering,’ and ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering’? “Bhāradvāja, form is suffering; this is how one comes to know: ‘This is suffering. The origin of form is the origin of suffering; this is how one comes to know: ‘This is the origin of suffering. The cessation of form is the cessation of suffering; this is how one comes to know: ‘This is the cessation of suffering. The way leading to the cessation of form is the way leading to the cessation of suffering; this is how one comes to know: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. Feeling is suffering... Perception is suffering... Volitional formations are suffering... Consciousness is suffering; this is how one comes to know: ‘This is suffering. The origin of consciousness is the origin of suffering; this is how one comes to know: ‘This is the origin of suffering. The cessation of consciousness is the cessation of suffering; this is how one comes to know: ‘This is the cessation of suffering. The way leading to the cessation of consciousness is the way leading to the cessation of suffering; this is how one comes to know: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. When, Bhāradvāja, one knows thus and sees thus, one abandons lust for form, abandons lust for feeling, abandons lust for perception, abandons lust for volitional formations, and abandons lust for consciousness. By abandoning lust, one is liberated. When liberated, there is the knowledge: ‘It is liberated. One understands: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more coming to any state of being. When this was said, the Venerable Bhāradvāja said to the Blessed One: “Magnificent, venerable sir! Magnificent, venerable sir! Just as if one were to set upright what was overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who was lost, or bring a lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms, even so has the Blessed One—through many lines of reasoning—made the Dhamma clear. I go to the Blessed One for refuge, and to the Dhamma, and to the Sangha of bhikkhus. May the Blessed One accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life shall last.”
On one occasion the Venerable Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja was dwelling at Kosambī in Ghosita’s Park.
Then King Udena approached the Venerable Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja and exchanged greetings with him.
When they had concluded their polite and courteous conversation, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, King Udena said this to the Venerable Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja:
“Master Bhāradvāja, what is the cause, what is the reason, why these young bhikkhus— well-built, with black hair, endowed with the beauty of youth,

in the prime of their lives, and who have not dallied with sensual pleasures— lead the holy life (brahmacariya) completely fulfilled and pure for as long as life lasts, and carry it on for a long duration?”
“Indeed, Great King, this was said by that Blessed One—the one who knows, the one who sees, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One:

‘Come, monks, toward those who are merely mothers, establish the thought of a mother; toward those who are merely sisters, establish the thought of a sister; toward those who are merely daughters, establish the thought of a daughter.
This, Great King, is the cause, this is the reason why these young bhikkhus—handsome, with black hair and in the prime of their youth—[are so well-behaved].”
“Endowed with youth, in the prime of life, having not yet sported with sensual pleasures,
they lead the holy life (brahmacariya) throughout their lives— complete and pure— and they persist in it for a long duration.
“The mind, Master Bhāradvāja, is indeed fickle.”

“Sometimes, Master Bhāradvāja, thoughts of lust arise even toward one’s mother’s sister; thoughts of lust arise even toward one’s own sister; thoughts of lust arise even toward one’s daughter’s sister.
Is there, Master Bhāradvāja, some other cause and some other condition by which these young bhikkhus—tall, dark-haired, endowed with the faculties of youth... [and so on]... travel great distances?
“It has been said, Great King, by that Blessed One, the Knower, the Seer, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One:”
"Come, monks, contemplate this very body, from the soles of the feet upwards and from the hair of the head downwards, bounded by the skin, as full of various kinds of impurity:
'In this body there are head-hairs, body-hairs, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews,
bones, bone-marrow, kidneys, heart, liver, midriff, spleen, lungs, intestines, mesentery, gorge, feces, bile..."
“Phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, fat, tears, grease, spittle, snot, synovial fluid, and urine.
This too, Great King, is the cause, this is the condition by which these young bhikkhus—well-built, with black hair... [and so on] ...are able to travel great distances.
“But for those bhikkhus, Master Bhāradvāja, who have developed the body, developed virtue, developed the mind, and developed wisdom, it is easy for them.”
"But for those monks, Master Bhāradvāja, who have not developed the body, have not developed virtue, have not developed the mind, and have not developed wisdom—that is difficult for them.
Sometimes, Master Bhāradvāja, when one thinks, 'I will attend to the unattractive,' what is attractive instead comes to mind.
Is there, Master Bhāradvāja, some other cause and some other condition by which these young monks, who are well-fleshed, with black hair... [and so on]... travel the long journey?"
“Great King, this was said by that Blessed One—the one who knows, the one who sees, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One:
‘Come, monks, dwell with the doors of the sense faculties guarded.
Having seen a form with the eye, do not grasp at its signs, do not grasp at its secondary characteristics.’”
Since, if one dwells with this faculty of the eye unrestrained, covetousness and dejection—evil, unwholesome states—might flow in upon him, you should practice for its restraint.
Guard the faculty of the eye; attain restraint over the faculty of the eye.
Having heard a sound with the ear... [and so on].
Having smelled an odor with the nose...
having tasted a flavor with the tongue...
having touched a tangible object with the body...
Having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, do not grasp at its signs, do not grasp at its secondary characteristics.

Since covetousness and dejection—evil, unwholesome states—might flow in upon one who dwells with this faculty of the mind unrestrained, you should practice for its restraint. Guard the faculty of the mind; [guard] the faculty of the mind.
‘Enter upon the restraint. This, great king, is the cause, this is the condition why these young bhikkhus— well-fleshed, with black hair,
endowed with the excellence of youth, in the prime of their lives, and who have not dallied with sensual pleasures— [live] for as long as life lasts in full perfection.
“They lead the holy life in complete purity and travel the path for its duration.
“It is wonderful, Master Bhāradvāja! It is marvelous, Master Bhāradvāja!
How well this has been spoken by the Blessed One—the one who knows, the one who sees, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One!”
This, Master Bhāradvāja, is the cause, this is the reason why these young bhikkhus— handsome, with black hair, endowed with the blessing of youth,
in the prime of their lives, and who have not yet dallied with sensual pleasures—
lead the holy life (brahmacariya) completely fulfilled and pure for as long as life lasts, and carry it on for a long duration.
"Indeed, Master Bhāradvāja, on whatever occasion I enter the inner palace with body unguarded,
speech unguarded, mind unguarded, mindfulness unestablished, and the sense faculties unrestrained,
at that time lustful states overwhelm me exceedingly."
But at whatever time, Master Bhāradvāja, I enter the inner palace with body guarded,
speech guarded, mind guarded, mindfulness established, and sense faculties restrained,
at that time lustful states do not overwhelm me.
“Excellent, Master Bhāradvāja! Excellent, Master Bhāradvāja!

Just as one might set upright what had been overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who was lost, or bring an oil lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms—[so has this been made clear by Master Bhāradvāja].”
"will see," so too has the Dhamma been proclaimed by Master Bhāradvāja in many ways.
Therefore, Master Bhāradvāja, I go for refuge to that Blessed One, and to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
May Master Bhāradvāja accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life shall last."
The Fourth.
Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.128 (SN 35.128, PTS SN iv 113) 13.

The Soṇa Sutta.
