13. Gahapativagga Ghositasutta.
On one occasion the Venerable Ānanda was dwelling at Kosambī in Ghosita’s Park.
Then the householder Ghosita approached the Venerable Ānanda... [as before] ...and sitting to one side, the householder Ghosita said this to the Venerable Ānanda:
"Venerable Ānanda, it is said: ‘the diversity of elements, the diversity of elements.
To what extent, venerable sir, has the diversity of elements been spoken of by the Blessed One?"
“Householder, there exists the eye-element, and there are pleasing forms, and there is eye-consciousness to be experienced as pleasant.
Dependent on contact, a pleasant feeling arises.
Householder, there exists the eye-element, and there are unpleasing forms, and there is eye-consciousness to be experienced as painful.”
Dependent on contact, painful feeling arises.
Householder, there exists the eye-element, and forms that are agreeable and to be experienced with equanimity, and eye-consciousness that is to be experienced as neither-painful-nor-pleasant.
Dependent on contact, neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling arises... [and so on].
"There exists, householder, the tongue-element, agreeable tastes, and tongue-consciousness to be experienced as pleasant.
Dependent on contact, a pleasant feeling arises.
There exists, householder, the tongue-element, disagreeable tastes, and tongue-consciousness to be experienced as painful."
Dependent on contact, painful feeling arises.
Householder, there exists the tongue-element, tastes that are to be experienced with equanimity, and tongue-consciousness that is to be experienced as neither-painful-nor-pleasant.
Dependent on contact, neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling arises... [and so forth]...
"Householder, there exists the mind-element, agreeable mental phenomena, and mind-consciousness to be experienced as pleasant;
dependent on contact, a pleasant feeling arises.
Householder, there exists the mind-element, disagreeable mental phenomena, and mind-consciousness to be experienced as painful."
Dependent on contact, painful feeling arises.
Householder, the mind-element exists, and there are mental phenomena to be experienced with equanimity, and mind-consciousness to be experienced as neither-painful-nor-pleasant.
Dependent on contact, neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling arises.
"To this extent, householder, has the diversity of elements been taught by the Blessed One.
The sixth.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 35.130 (SN 35.130, PTS SN iv 115)
13. Gahapativagga:
The Discourse to Hāliddikāni On one occasion the Venerable Mahākaccāna was dwelling among the Avantis at Kuraraghara on the Papāta mountain.
Then the householder Hāliddikāni approached the Venerable Mahākaccāna... [as before] ...and sitting to one side, the householder Hāliddikāni said this to the Venerable Mahākaccāna:
"It was said, Bhante, by the Blessed One:
'Dependent upon the diversity of elements arises the diversity of contacts; dependent upon the diversity of contacts arises the diversity of feelings.'"
“Venerable sir, how is it that, dependent on the diversity of elements, there arises the diversity of contact; and dependent on the diversity of contact, there arises the diversity of feeling?
“In this case, householder, a bhikkhu, having seen a form with the eye, understands: ‘This is agreeable,’ and he knows the eye-consciousness to be associated with pleasant feeling.
Dependent on that contact, a pleasant feeling arises.”
Furthermore, having seen a form with the eye, one understands: "This is indeed unpleasant," and the eye-consciousness is to be experienced as painful.
Dependent on contact, a painful feeling arises.
Furthermore, having seen a form with the eye, one understands: "This is indeed a basis for equanimity," and the eye-consciousness is to be experienced as neither-painful-nor-pleasant.
In dependence on contact, neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling arises.
Furthermore, householder, when a bhikkhu has heard a sound with the ear … [and so on] … has smelled an odor with the nose … [and so on] …
Having tasted a flavor with the tongue …pe… having touched a tangible object with the body …pe… having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind,
one understands: "This is indeed agreeable," and the mind-consciousness is to be experienced as pleasant.
Dependent on contact, pleasant feeling arises.
Furthermore, having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, one understands: "This is indeed unpleasant," and the mind-consciousness is to be experienced as painful.
Dependent on that contact, painful feeling arises.
"But having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, one understands: 'This is a basis for equanimity,' and one experiences mental consciousness as neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
Dependent on contact, neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling arises.
Thus, householder, dependent on the diversity of elements, there arises the diversity of contacts; dependent on the diversity of contacts, there arises the diversity of feelings."
Seventh.
Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.131 (SN 35.131, PTS SN iv 116) 13.
Gahapativagga (The Chapter on Householders)
The Discourse to Nakulapita On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Bhaggas at Suṃsumāragira, in the Bhesakaḷā Grove, the Deer Park.
Then Nakulapita the householder approached the Blessed One... [as above] ...and sat down to one side. Seated there, Nakulapita the householder said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, what is the cause, what is the reason why some beings here do not attain final nibbāna in this very life?
But what, venerable sir, is the cause, what is the reason why some beings here do attain final nibbāna in this very life?
“Householder, there are forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, lovely, pleasing, dear, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust.

If a bhikkhu delights in that, welcomes it, and remains clinging to it, then for him who delights in it, welcomes it, and remains clinging to it, consciousness becomes dependent upon that and takes up that as its fuel.
With such fuel, householder, the bhikkhu does not attain final Nibbāna... [as before] ...
"There are, householder, tastes cognizable by the tongue...
There are, householder, mental phenomena cognizable by the mind that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, dear, connected with sensual pleasure, and provocative of lust.
If a bhikkhu delights in them, welcomes them, and remains clinging to them..."
For one who delights in that, welcomes it, and persists in clinging to it, consciousness becomes dependent on that and takes up that as its fuel.
Householder, a bhikkhu who has such fuel does not attain final nibbāna.
This, householder, is the cause, this is the condition, why some beings here do not attain final nibbāna in this very life.
Furthermore, householder, there are forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, lovely, pleasing, dear, connected with sensual desire,
and provocative of lust. If a bhikkhu does not delight in them, does not welcome them, and does not remain clinging to them,
then his consciousness is not supported by them, nor does it take them as its fuel.
“Householder, a bhikkhu who is without clinging attains final Nibbāna...
There are, householder, tastes cognizable by the tongue...
There are, householder, mental phenomena cognizable by the mind that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust.”
If a bhikkhu does not delight in that, does not welcome it, and does not remain clinging to it,
then for him who does not delight in it, does not welcome it, and does not remain clinging to it, consciousness is not dependent upon it and does not take it as its fuel.
Being without fuel, householder, a bhikkhu attains final nibbāna.
“This, householder, is the cause, this is the condition, by which some beings here attain final nibbāna in this very life.
The eighth.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 35.132. (SN 35.132, PTS SN iv 116)
13. Gahapativagga:
Lohiccasutta.
On one occasion the Venerable Mahākaccāna was dwelling among the Avantīs at Makkarakata in a forest hut.
Then many young brahmin students of Lohicca, who were wood-gatherers,
approached the forest hut where the Venerable Mahākaccāna was staying. Having approached, they walked back and forth and wandered about all around the hut,
making a great clamor and loud noise, shouting various cries of "seleyyaka."
“But these shavelings, these wretched little ascetics—outcasts, dark fellows, the descendants of our kinsman’s feet—are honored, revered, esteemed, worshipped, and venerated by these Bharatas.
Then the Venerable Mahākaccāna came out from his dwelling and said this to those young brahmins:
“Do not make a noise, young men!”
“I shall speak the Dhamma to you.
When this was said, those young brahmins became silent.
Then the Venerable Mahākaccāna addressed those young brahmins in verses:
“Those who remembered the ancient tradition were the brahmins of old, supreme in virtue;
their sense-doors were well-guarded.”
They had overcome anger;
they were devoted to the Dhamma and to meditative absorption—
those brahmins who remember the ancient tradition.
And these, having departed, revile [others];
intoxicated by their divine status, they act unjustly;
overcome by anger, they inflict various punishments upon others.
Though they exert themselves among those who are free from craving,
for one whose senses are unguarded, their efforts are in vain—
like wealth acquired in a dream by a man.
Fasting, sleeping on the bare ground,
bathing at dawn, the three Vedas,
the rough antelope skin, matted hair, and mud— these are not the means for purification.
Pride, rules and observances, asceticism,
hypocrisy, crooked staves,
and ritual rinsings with water;
These are the mere outward marks of brahmins,
fashioned for the sake of some small gain;
but the mind is well-composed.
Clear, undisturbed,
and free from harshness toward all beings—
that is the path for attaining Brahman.
Then those young brahmins, angry and displeased, approached the brahmin Lohicca; having approached him, they said this to the brahmin Lohicca:
"Sire, you should know that the ascetic Mahākaccāna utterly disparages and reviles the mantras of the brahmins.
When this was said, the brahmin Lohicca became angry and displeased.
Then it occurred to the brahmin Lohicca:
"It is not fitting for me to revile and abuse the ascetic Mahākaccāna merely on hearing what other young men have said.
Suppose I were to approach him and question him?"
Then the brahmin Lohicca, together with those young brahmin students, approached the Venerable Mahākaccāna. Having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Venerable Mahākaccāna.
When they had concluded their polite and friendly conversation, he sat down to one side. Sitting there, the brahmin Lohicca said this to the Venerable Mahākaccāna:
"Master Kaccāna, have many of our resident young brahmin students who were gathering firewood come here?"
“Did those many young brahmin students who were wood-gatherers come here, brahmin?
“But did you have any conversation with those young men, Master Kaccāna?
“I did indeed have some conversation with those young men, brahmin.”
“But how, Master Kaccāna, was your conversation with those young brahmins?
“In this way, brahmin, my conversation with those young brahmins was as follows:
‘Those of old were preeminent in virtue;’”
Those brahmins who remember the ancient tradition...
[and so on] ...who are free from harshness toward all beings.
“...that is the path for attaining the state of a brahmin. This, brahmin, was the conversation I had with those young men.
“Master Kaccāna said, ‘One who does not guard the doors of the senses.’”
“To what extent, Master Kaccāna, is one said to have ‘unguarded sense doors’?
“Here, brahmin, someone, having seen a form with the eye, becomes obsessed with a pleasing form and feels aversion toward an unpleasing form.

He dwells without mindfulness established in the body, with a limited mind, and does not understand, as it really is, that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom wherein those arisen evil, unwholesome states cease without remainder.”
Having heard a sound with the ear...
having smelled an odor with the nose...
having tasted a flavor with the tongue...
Having touched a tangible object with the body...
having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, one becomes obsessed with agreeable phenomena and feels aversion toward disagreeable phenomena.

One dwells without established mindfulness of the body, with a limited mind, and does not understand as it really is that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom wherein those arisen evil unwholesome states cease without remainder.
“In this way, brahmin, one is one whose sense doors are unguarded.
“It is wonderful, Master Kaccāna! It is marvelous, Master Kaccāna!
To what extent Master Kaccāna has declared that one who is actually one whose sense doors are unguarded is indeed ‘one whose sense doors are unguarded’!”
“‘One who guards the doors of the sense-faculties,’ so said Master Kaccāna.
To what extent, Master Kaccāna, is one a guardian of the doors of the sense-faculties?

“In this case, brahmin, having seen a form with the eye, a bhikkhu is not infatuated with a pleasing form, nor does he feel aversion toward an unpleasing form. He dwells with mindfulness established in the body and with a mind immeasurable.”
And he understands, as it really is, that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom wherein those arisen evil, unwholesome states cease without remainder.
Having heard a sound with the ear...
having smelled an odor with the nose...
Having tasted a flavor with the tongue...
having touched a tangible object with the body...

having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, one is not obsessed with agreeable phenomena and does not feel aversion toward disagreeable phenomena; one dwells with mindfulness established in the body and with a mind of immeasurable scope.
And he understands, as it really is, that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom wherein those arisen evil, unwholesome states cease without remainder.
It is in this way, brahmin, that one is guarded at the doors of the senses.
“It is wonderful, Master Kaccāna! It is marvelous, Master Kaccāna!”
To this extent, Master Kaccāna, you have indeed declared one who has guarded doors to be "one with guarded doors.
Excellent, Master Kaccāna! Excellent, Master Kaccāna!
It is as if, Master Kaccāna, one were to set upright what had been overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who was lost.
Or as one might show the way to one who has lost his path, or as one might hold up an oil lamp in the darkness so that those with eyes may see forms—
even so has the Dhamma been elucidated by Master Kaccāna in many ways.
Therefore, Master Kaccāna, I go for refuge to the Blessed One, and to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
"May Master Kaccāna accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forward for as long as life lasts.
And just as Master Kaccāna visits the families of lay followers in Makkarakata, so may he visit the Lohicca family.
There, whatever young men or young women pay homage to Master Kaccāna, rise up for him, or offer him a seat or water—for them that will lead to their welfare and happiness for a long time."
Ninth. Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.133 (SN 35.133, PTS SN iv 121) 13.
The Chapter on Householders (Gahapativagga)
The Discourse to Verañjā’s Son.
On one occasion the Venerable Udāyī was dwelling at Kāmaṇḍā in the mango grove of the brahmin Todeyya.
Then a young brahmin student, a pupil of the brahmin lady of the Verañjā clan, approached the Venerable Udāyī; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Venerable Udāyī.
Having exchanged polite and courteous greetings, he sat down to one side.
As the young brahmin sat there, the Venerable Udāyī instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened him with a discourse on the Dhamma.
Then that young brahmin, having been instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened by the Venerable Udāyī with a discourse on the Dhamma...
Having been thus praised, he rose from his seat and approached the brahmin lady of the Verahaccāni clan;
having approached her, he said this to the brahmin lady of the Verahaccāni clan:
"Come now, madam, you should know."

“The ascetic Udāyī teaches the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end; he proclaims the holy life, both in its meaning and in its phrasing, entirely complete and pure.
“Well then, young man, invite the ascetic Udāyī on my behalf for a meal tomorrow.
“Yes, sir,” the young man replied to the brahmin lady of the Verahaccāni clan. He then approached the Venerable Udāyī and, having approached him, said this to the Venerable Udāyī:
“May the venerable Udāyī please accept tomorrow’s meal from our teacher’s wife, the brahmin lady of the Verahaccāni clan.
The venerable Udāyī consented by remaining silent.
Then, at the end of that night, in the morning, the venerable Udāyī dressed, took his bowl and outer robe, and departed.
He went to the residence of the brahmin lady of the Verahaccāni clan; having arrived, he sat down on the prepared seat.
Then the brahmin lady of the Verahaccāni clan, with her own hands, served and satisfied the Venerable Udāyī with excellent hard and soft foods.

When the Venerable Udāyī had finished his meal and had removed his hand from the bowl, the brahmin lady of the Verahaccāni clan put on her sandals, sat down on a high seat, covered her head, and said this to the Venerable Udāyī:
“Speak, ascetic, of the Dhamma!
“There will be a time, sister,” he said, and rising from his seat, he departed.
A second time, that young brahmin approached the Venerable Udāyī; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Venerable Udāyī.
Having exchanged greetings and pleasant, courteous conversation, he sat down to one side.
As he was sitting there, the Venerable Udāyī instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened that young brahmin with a discourse on the Dhamma.
A second time, that young brahmin was instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened by the Venerable Udāyī with a discourse on the Dhamma.
Encouraged and gladdened, he rose from his seat and approached the brahmin lady of the Verahaccāni clan;
having approached her, he said this to the brahmin lady of the Verahaccāni clan:
"Indeed, madam, you should know."
“The ascetic Udāyī teaches the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end; he proclaims the holy life, complete and pure, with its meaning and its phrasing.
“But, young man, you speak in praise of the ascetic Udāyī in this way.
Yet when the ascetic Udāyī was told, ‘Speak, ascetic, on the Dhamma,’ he said, ‘There will be a time, sister,’ and having spoken, he rose from his seat and departed.”
“Indeed, lady, it was because you had put on sandals, were seated on a high seat, and had covered your head that you said:
‘Speak, ascetic, speak the Dhamma.
For these gentlemen are reverent toward the Dhamma and cherish the Dhamma.”
“In that case, young man, invite the ascetic Udāyī on my behalf for tomorrow’s meal.
“Very well, madam,” the young man replied to the brahmin woman of the Verahaccāni clan. He then approached the Venerable Udāyī and said to him:
“May the venerable Udāyī please accept tomorrow’s meal from our teacher’s wife, the brahmin woman of the Verahaccāni clan.”
The Venerable Udāyī consented by remaining silent.

Then, when that night had passed, the Venerable Udāyī dressed in the morning, took his bowl and robe, and went to the residence of the brahmin woman of the Verahaccāni clan. Having arrived, he sat down on the prepared seat.
Then the brahmin lady of the Verahaccāni clan, with her own hands, served and satisfied the Venerable Udāyī with excellent hard and soft foods.

When the Venerable Udāyī had finished eating and had withdrawn his hand from the bowl, the brahmin lady of the Verahaccāni clan removed her sandals, sat down on a low seat, uncovered her head, and said this to the Venerable Udāyī:
"Venerable sir, when what exists do the Arahants describe pleasure and pain; and when what does not exist do the Arahants not describe pleasure and pain?"
“Sister, when there is the eye, the Arahants describe pleasure and pain; when there is no eye, the Arahants do not describe pleasure and pain...
[and so on] ...when there is the tongue, the Arahants describe pleasure and pain; when there is no tongue, the Arahants do not describe pleasure and pain...
[and so on] ...when there is the mind, the Arahants describe pleasure and pain; when there is no mind, the Arahants do not describe pleasure and pain.”
When this was said, the brahmin lady of the Verahaccāni clan said this to the Venerable Udāyin:
“Excellent, Bhante! Excellent, Bhante!
Just as, Bhante, one might set upright what had been overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who was lost...”
Or one might show the way, or hold up a lamp in the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms;
even so has the Dhamma been elucidated by the venerable Udāyin in many ways.
Therefore, venerable Udāyin, I go for refuge to the Blessed One, and to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
“May the venerable Udāyī accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life lasts.
The tenth.
The third section on householders.
Its summary verse:
Vesālī, Vajjī, Nāḷandā,
Bhāradvāja, Soṇa, and Ghosita.
Hāliddikāni the father of Nakula,
and Lohicca the son of Verahaccāni.
*Saṁyutta Nikāya* 35.134 (SN 35.134, PTS SN iv 124).
14. Devadaha Chapter: The Discourse at Devadaha.
At one time the Blessed One was dwelling among the Sakyans at a town of the Sakyans named Devadaha.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
"Bhikkhus, I do not say that all bhikkhus must apply diligence regarding the six bases of contact;
nor, bhikkhus, do I say that all bhikkhus must not apply diligence regarding the six bases of contact."
“Bhikkhus, as for those bhikkhus who are arahants— whose taints are destroyed, who have lived the holy life, done what was to be done,
laid down the burden, attained their own goal, utterly destroyed the fetters of existence, and are completely liberated through final knowledge—
I say that for those bhikkhus there is nothing further to be done by way of diligence regarding the six bases of contact.”
For what reason?
Because they have accomplished their task through diligence; they are incapable of negligence.
And as for those monks, bhikkhus, who are still in training (*sekkha*), who have not yet attained their goal, and who aspire to the unsurpassed security from bondage—
"Bhikkhus, for those bhikkhus who dwell thus, I say that they must apply themselves with diligence regarding the six bases of contact. Why is that?
Bhikkhus, there are forms cognizable by the eye that are pleasing and also unpleasing."
As they repeatedly touch these [objects], their minds do not remain obsessed by them.
Because the mind is not obsessed, energy is aroused and unflagging, mindfulness is established and unconfused, the body is tranquil and untroubled, and the mind is concentrated and one-pointed.
Seeing this fruit of diligence, monks, I say that those bhikkhus must practice with diligence regarding the six bases of contact. …pe…
“Bhikkhus, there are mental phenomena cognizable by the mind that are both pleasing and unpleasing.
As he encounters them again and again, they do not obsess his mind.

Because his mind is not obsessed, energy is aroused and does not flag; mindfulness is established and is not muddled; the body is tranquil and not agitated; and the mind is concentrated and one-pointed.”
"Seeing this fruit of diligence, monks, I say that these bhikkhus must apply diligence regarding the six bases of contact.
Thus was the first [discourse]. *Saṃyutta Nikāya* 35.135.
14. Devadaha Chapter. The Discourse on the Moment:
“It is a gain for you, bhikkhus; it is well-gained by you, bhikkhus.”
The opportunity has been obtained by you for living the holy life.
Monks, I have seen the hells called "the Six Bases of Contact.
There, whatever form one sees with the eye, one sees only what is undesirable, not what is desirable; only what is unlovely, not what is lovely; only what is disagreeable, not what is agreeable.
Whatever sound one hears with the ear...
whatever odor one smells with the nose...
whatever flavor one tastes with the tongue... [and so on].
Whatever tangible object one touches with the body... pe...

whatever mental phenomenon one cognizes with the mind, one cognizes only what is undesirable, not what is desirable; one cognizes only what is unlovely, not what is lovely; one cognizes only what is disagreeable, not what is agreeable.
It is a gain for you, monks! It is a great fortune for you, monks!
The opportunity has been obtained by you for living the holy life.
Monks, I have seen the heavens called the Six Realms of Sense-Contact.

There, whatever form one sees with the eye, one sees only a desirable form, not an undesirable form; one sees only a pleasing form, not a displeasing form; one sees only a lovely form, not an unlovely form... [and so on].
Whatever taste one tastes with the tongue... pe...

whatever mental phenomenon one cognizes with the mind, one cognizes only what is desirable, not what is undesirable; one cognizes only what is lovely, not what is unlovely; one cognizes only what is agreeable, not what is disagreeable.
It is a gain for you, monks! It is a great acquisition for you, monks!
“The opportune moment has been obtained by you for living the holy life.
Second.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 35.136 (SN 35.136, SN 35.136a, PTS SN iv 126).
14. Devadaha Chapter.
First Discourse on Delighting in Form:
“Monks, gods and humans delight in form, rejoice in form, and exult in form.”
“Monks, with the change, fading away, and cessation of forms, gods and humans dwell in suffering.
Monks, gods and humans delight in sounds, rejoice in sounds, and exult in sounds.
With the change, fading away, and cessation of sounds, monks, gods and humans dwell in suffering.”
...delighting in odors ...
delighting in tastes ...
delighting in tangibles ...
“Monks, gods and humans delight in the Dhamma, rejoice in the Dhamma, and exult in the Dhamma.
Yet, monks, with the change, fading away, and cessation of the Dhamma, gods and humans dwell in suffering.

But the Tathāgata, monks—the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One—having understood, as they truly are, the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding forms, does not delight in forms, does not rejoice in forms, and does not exult in forms.”
“Through the change, fading away, and cessation of forms, monks, the Tathāgata dwells in happiness.
[The same applies to] sounds… scents…”

Having understood, as they really are, the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena, he does not delight in mental phenomena, does not rejoice in mental phenomena, and does not exult in mental phenomena.
“Through the change, fading away, and cessation of phenomena, monks, the Tathāgata dwells in happiness.
This is what the Blessed One said.
Having said this, the Sublime One, the Teacher, further spoke as follows:
“Forms, sounds, tastes, smells,
tangibles, and all mental objects—
those that are desirable, lovely, and pleasing,”
As long as they exist,
these are considered by you to be sources of happiness in this world together with its devas.
And where these cease,
that is considered by them to be suffering;
this happiness has been seen by the Noble Ones.
The cessation of personal existence—
this is contrary to what is seen by the entire world.
That which others call happiness,
the Noble Ones call suffering;
that which others call suffering, [the Noble Ones call happiness].
The Noble Ones know that as happiness.
Behold this Dhamma so difficult to understand;
here the ignorant are utterly deluded.
For those who are covered, there is darkness;
for those who do not see, there is blind gloom.
But for the wise, it is opened wide.
Light is as it were for those who see;
but those who are unskilled in the Dhamma do not recognize the path even when it is near.
By those who are overcome by passion for existence,
who follow after passion for existence,
and who have fallen into the realm of Māra.
This Dhamma is not easily awakened to.
Who indeed, other than the Noble Ones,
is able to awaken to this state?
Having fully understood that state,
those free from taints attain final Nibbāna. Thus ends the third [verse].

Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.137 (SN 35.137, SN 35.136b, PTS SN iv 128) 14. Devadaha Vagga Second Discourse on Delighting in Form At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, if one were to say: ‘I do not see even a single thing that, when clung to, leads to such great suffering as the form-aggregate does,’ that would be fitting. If one were to say: ‘I do not see even a single thing that, when clung to, leads to such great suffering as the feeling-aggregate does… the perception-aggregate does… the volitional formations-aggregate does… the consciousness-aggregate does,’ that would be fitting. Why is that? Because, bhikkhus, this form-aggregate is the basis for lust, the basis for hatred, the basis for delusion; it is the basis for grief, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair. This feeling-aggregate… this perception-aggregate… this volitional formations-aggregate… this consciousness-aggregate is the basis for lust, the basis for hatred, the basis for delusion; it is the basis for grief, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair. Therefore, bhikkhus, you should abandon desire for form, abandon lust for form, abandon the underlying tendency toward form, and cultivate revulsion toward form, cultivate dispassion toward form, and attain liberation from form. You should abandon desire for feeling… perception… volitional formations… consciousness, abandon lust for consciousness, abandon the underlying tendency toward consciousness, and cultivate revulsion toward consciousness, cultivate dispassion toward consciousness, and attain liberation from consciousness. When, bhikkhus, a noble disciple has abandoned desire for form, abandoned lust for form, abandoned the underlying tendency toward form, and has cultivated revulsion toward form, cultivated dispassion toward form, and attained liberation from form; when he has abandoned desire for feeling… perception… volitional formations… consciousness, abandoned lust for consciousness, abandoned the underlying tendency toward consciousness, and has cultivated revulsion toward consciousness, cultivated dispassion toward consciousness, and attained liberation from consciousness—then he is called a noble disciple who has cut off craving, stripped off the fetter, and by completely breaking through conceit, has made an end of suffering.”
“Bhikkhus, gods and humans delight in forms, rejoice in forms, and exult in forms.
With the change, fading away, and cessation of forms, bhikkhus, gods and humans dwell in suffering.
They delight in sounds….”
...delighting in odors ...
delighting in tastes ...
delighting in tangibles ...
“Monks, gods and humans delight in the Dhamma, rejoice in the Dhamma, and exult in the Dhamma.
Monks, gods and humans dwell in suffering because of the change, fading away, and cessation of the Dhamma.

But the Tathāgata, monks—the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One—having understood, as they really are, the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding forms, does not delight in forms, does not rejoice in forms, and does not exult in forms.”
“Monks, through the change, fading away, and cessation of forms, the Tathāgata dwells in happiness. [Through the change, fading away,
and cessation] of sounds… of odors…”

Having understood, as they truly are, the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena, he does not delight in mental phenomena, does not rejoice in mental phenomena, and does not exult in mental phenomena.
“With the change, fading away, and cessation of phenomena, monks, the Tathāgata dwells in happiness.
This was the fourth.
*Saṁyutta Nikāya* 35.138. (SN 35.138, SN 35.137, PTS SN iv 128)
14. Devadaha Chapter. First Discourse on What Does Not Belong to You:
“Bhikkhus, whatever does not belong to you, abandon that.
That which has been abandoned by you will lead to your welfare and happiness.
And what, monks, is not yours?
The eye, monks, is not yours; abandon it.
That which has been abandoned by you will lead to your welfare and happiness...
[and so on] ...The tongue is not yours; abandon it.
That which has been abandoned by you will lead to your welfare and happiness... [and so on].
The mind is not yours; abandon it.
When it is abandoned, it will lead to your welfare and happiness.
Monks, suppose people were to carry away the grass, wood, branches, and foliage in this Jeta Grove, or burn them, or do with them as they please—would you think: [“This is ours”]?
“Does anyone carry us off, or burn us, or do with us as they please?”—
“Certainly not, Bhante.”—
“And for what reason?”
“Certainly not, Bhante; this is neither our self nor what belongs to our self.
“In the same way, monks, the eye is not yours; abandon it.
When it is abandoned by you, that will lead to your welfare and happiness … [and so on] …”
The tongue is not yours; abandon it.
When abandoned by you, it will lead to your welfare and happiness.
…pe… The mind is not yours; abandon it.
“Thus, when this is abandoned by you, it will lead to your welfare and happiness.
The fifth.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 35.139 (SN 35.139, SN 35.138, PTS SN iv 129).
14. Devadaha Chapter.
Second Discourse on What Belongs to You:
“Bhikkhus, whatever does not belong to you, abandon that.
That which has been abandoned by you will lead to your welfare and happiness.
And what, monks, is not yours?
Form, monks, is not yours;

Abandon them. When they are abandoned by you, they will lead to your welfare and happiness. Sounds... smells... [tastes... tactile objects... mental phenomena... abandon them. When they are abandoned by you, they will lead to your welfare and happiness.
Tastes … tangibles … mental phenomena are not yours; abandon them.
When these have been abandoned, they will lead to your welfare and happiness.
Just as, monks, whatever grass, wood, ... [and so on] ...
in this Jeta’s Grove, even so, monks, forms are not yours; abandon them.
“When these have been abandoned by you, they will lead to your welfare and happiness.
… The sixth.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 35.140 (SN 35.140, SN 35.139, PTS SN iv 129)
14. Devadaha Chapter:
The Discourse on the Internal Impermanent Cause “Bhikkhus, the eye is impermanent.”
Whatever cause and whatever condition there is for the arising of the eye, that too is impermanent.
Monks, how could the eye, being born of what is impermanent, be permanent?
… [and so on] … the tongue is impermanent.
Whatever cause and whatever condition there is for the arising of the tongue, that too is impermanent.
Monks, since the tongue is born of what is impermanent, how could it be permanent?
… [and so on] … the mind is impermanent.
“Monks, whatever cause and whatever condition there is for the arising of the mind, that too is impermanent.
Since the mind, monks, is born of what is impermanent, how could it be permanent?
Seeing thus, monks, the well-taught noble disciple becomes disenchanted with the eye... [and so on] ...becomes disenchanted with the ear, the nose, the tongue, the body, and the mind.”
“Through disenchantment, he becomes dispassionate; through dispassion, he is liberated. When liberated, the knowledge arises:
‘It is liberated. He understands: ‘Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.
This is the seventh [sutta].

Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.141 (SN 35.141, SN 35.140, PTS SN iv 130) 14. Devadaha Vagga Ajjhattadukkhahetusutta: The Discourse on the Internal Cause of Suffering At Devadaha, the Blessed One addressed the monks: “Monks! “Venerable sir,” those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: “Monks, what is the cause, what is the condition, for the arising of suffering internally? How does it come about that there is the arising of suffering internally? “Venerable sir, our teachings have the Blessed One as their root, the Blessed One as their guide, the Blessed One as their authority. It would be well if the Blessed One would clarify the meaning of this. Having heard it from the Blessed One, the monks will remember it. “Then listen, monks, and attend closely; I shall speak. “Yes, venerable sir,” those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: “Monks, contact is the cause, contact is the condition, for the arising of suffering internally. It is in this way that there is the arising of suffering internally. And how, monks, does there come to be the arising of suffering internally? Here, monks, one touches a form with the eye. Because of that contact, there arises in one feeling—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant. That feeling, being felt, is experienced internally. That experience of feeling is the cause, that experience of feeling is the condition, for the arising of suffering internally. It is in this way that there is the arising of suffering internally. One touches a sound with the ear... one touches an odor with the nose... one touches a taste with the tongue... one touches a tactile object with the body... one touches a mental phenomenon with the mind. Because of that contact, there arises in one feeling—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant. That feeling, being felt, is experienced internally. That experience of feeling is the cause, that experience of feeling is the condition, for the arising of suffering internally. It is in this way that there is the arising of suffering internally. Thus, monks, contact is the cause, contact is the condition, for the arising of suffering internally. It is in this way that there is the arising of suffering internally.”
“Bhikkhus, the eye is suffering.
Whatever cause and whatever condition there is for the arising of the eye, that too is suffering.
Since the eye, bhikkhus, is born of suffering, how could it be happiness? …” [and so on]
The tongue is suffering.
Whatever cause, whatever condition there is for the arising of the tongue, that too is suffering.
Since the tongue, monks, is born of suffering, how could it be happiness? …pe…
The mind is suffering.
Whatever cause and whatever condition there is for the arising of the mind, that too is suffering.
Since the mind, monks, is born of suffering, how could it be happy?
"Seeing thus...
he understands: ‘...there is no further state of being.
(The eighth.)

Saṁyutta Nikāya 35.142 (SN 35.142, SN 35.141, PTS SN iv 130) 14. Devadaha Chapter The Discourse on the Internal Non-Self as Cause At Devadaha, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus! “Venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, when what exists, by what being present, does identity view arise? And how does identity view come to be? “Venerable sir, our teachings are rooted in the Blessed One, guided by the Blessed One, and take recourse in the Blessed One. It would be good if the Blessed One would clarify the meaning of this statement. Having heard it from the Blessed One, the bhikkhus will remember it. “Then listen, bhikkhus, and attend closely. I shall speak. “Yes, venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, when there is form, by the presence of form, identity view arises; and thus identity view comes to be. When there is feeling … perception … volitional formations … consciousness, by the presence of consciousness, identity view arises; and thus identity view comes to be. “If one were to say, ‘Identity view arises dependent upon something other than form,’ that would not be tenable. Why is that? Because identity view has form as its cause, form as its source, form as its origin, and form as its condition. “If one were to say, ‘Identity view arises dependent upon something other than feeling … perception … volitional formations … consciousness,’ that would not be tenable. Why is that? Because identity view has consciousness as its cause, consciousness as its source, consciousness as its origin, and consciousness as its condition. “Bhikkhus, when what exists, by what being present, does the conceit ‘I am’ arise? And how does the conceit ‘I am’ come to be? [As above, substituting the conceit ‘I am’ for identity view. “Bhikkhus, when what exists, by what being present, do the underlying tendencies to lust, aversion, and ignorance arise? And how do the underlying tendencies to lust, aversion, and ignorance come to be? [As above, substituting the underlying tendencies for the conceit ‘I am. “Bhikkhus, when what exists, by what being present, do the obsessions with lust, aversion, and ignorance arise? And how do the obsessions with lust, aversion, and ignorance come to be? [As above, substituting the obsessions for the underlying tendencies. “Bhikkhus, when what exists, by what being present, do the obsessions with lust, aversion, and ignorance become bound up? And how do the obsessions with lust, aversion, and ignorance become bound up? [As above, substituting ‘become bound up’ for ‘arise. “Bhikkhus, when what exists, by what being present, do the obsessions with lust, aversion, and ignorance become manifest? And how do the obsessions with lust, aversion, and ignorance become manifest? [As above, substituting ‘become manifest’ for ‘become bound up. “Bhikkhus, when what exists, by what being present, do the obsessions with lust, aversion, and ignorance become established? And how do the obsessions with lust, aversion, and ignorance become established? [As above, substituting ‘become established’ for ‘become manifest. “Bhikkhus, when what exists, by what being present, do the obsessions with lust, aversion, and ignorance become consolidated? And how do the obsessions with lust, aversion, and ignorance become consolidated? [As above, substituting ‘become consolidated’ for ‘become established. “Bhikkhus, when what exists, by what being present, do the obsessions with lust, aversion, and ignorance become firmly rooted? And how do the obsessions with lust, aversion, and ignorance become firmly rooted? [As above, substituting ‘become firmly rooted’ for ‘become consolidated. “Bhikkhus, when what exists, by what being present, do the obsessions with lust, aversion, and ignorance become deeply embedded? And how do the obsessions with lust, aversion, and ignorance become deeply embedded? [As above, substituting ‘become deeply embedded’ for ‘become firmly rooted. “Bhikkhus, when what exists, by what being present, do the obsessions with lust, aversion, and ignorance become difficult to remove? And how do the obsessions with lust, aversion, and ignorance become difficult to remove? [As above, substituting ‘become difficult to remove’ for ‘become deeply embedded. “Bhikkhus, when what exists, by what being present, do the obsessions with lust, aversion, and ignorance become difficult to eradicate? And how do the obsessions with lust, aversion, and ignorance become difficult to eradicate? [As above, substituting ‘become difficult to eradicate’ for ‘become difficult to remove. “Bhikkhus, when what exists, by what being present, do the obsessions with lust, aversion, and ignorance become difficult to pull out? And how do the obsessions with lust, aversion, and ignorance become difficult to pull out? [As above, substituting ‘become difficult to pull out’ for ‘become difficult to eradicate. “Bhikkhus, when what exists, by what being present, do the obsessions with lust, aversion, and ignorance become difficult to bring to an end?

And how do the obsessions with lust, aversion, and ignorance become difficult to bring to an end? [As above, substituting ‘become difficult to bring to an end’ for ‘become difficult to pull out. “Bhikkhus, when what exists, by what being present, do the obsessions with lust, aversion, and ignorance become difficult to abandon? And how do the obsessions with lust, aversion, and ignorance become difficult to abandon? [As above, substituting ‘become difficult to abandon’ for ‘become difficult to bring to an end. “Bhikkhus, when what exists, by what being present, do the obsessions with lust, aversion, and ignorance become difficult to relinquish? And how do the obsessions with lust, aversion, and ignorance become difficult to relinquish? [As above, substituting ‘become difficult to relinquish’ for ‘become difficult to abandon. “Bhikkhus, when what exists, by what being present, do the obsessions with lust, aversion, and ignorance become difficult to escape? And how do the obsessions with lust, aversion, and ignorance become difficult to escape? Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.143 (SN 35.143, SN 35.142, PTS SN iv 131) 14. Devadaha Chapter The Discourse on External Impermanent Causes At Devadaha, the Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, I shall teach you the impermanent external causes and conditions for form, feeling, perception, volitional formations, and consciousness. When this was said, a certain bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “But how, Bhante, are there impermanent external causes and conditions for form, feeling, perception, volitional formations, and consciousness? “Here, bhikkhu, one might think: ‘May my external forms be thus; may my external forms not be thus. Yet it does not happen according to one’s wish: ‘May my external forms be thus; may my external forms not be thus. Thus, bhikkhu, there are impermanent external causes and conditions for form. One might think: ‘May my external feelings... external perceptions... external volitional formations... external consciousness be thus; may my external consciousness not be thus. Yet it does not happen according to one’s wish: ‘May my external consciousness be thus; may my external consciousness not be thus. Thus, bhikkhu, there are impermanent external causes and conditions for consciousness. Bhikkhus, when one sees thus with right wisdom as it really is, one abandons craving for form, abandons craving for feeling, abandons craving for perception, abandons craving for volitional formations, and abandons craving for consciousness. Through the abandoning of craving, one is liberated from passion; through liberation from passion, one is liberated; through liberation, one knows: ‘It is liberated. One understands: ‘Destroyed is birth, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being. This is what the Blessed One said. Elated, those bhikkhus delighted in the Blessed One’s words. (This discourse is identical to SN 35.142, differing only in the introductory setting.)
“Bhikkhus, forms are impermanent.
Whatever cause and whatever condition there is for the arising of forms, that too is impermanent.
Since forms, bhikkhus, are born of what is impermanent, how could they be permanent?
Sounds … odors … tastes …
Tangible objects...
mental phenomena are impermanent.
Whatever cause, whatever condition there is for the arising of phenomena, that too is impermanent.
“Bhikkhus, since phenomena have arisen from the impermanent, how could they be permanent?
Seeing thus...
[as before] ...he understands: ‘There is no further state of being.’”
The Tenth.

Devadaha Chapter

Seeing thus... [as before]...

14. Devadaha Chapter.
Discourse on External Non-Self as Cause:
"Bhikkhus, forms are non-self."
Whatever cause and whatever condition there is for the arising of forms, that too is non-self.
Since forms, monks, are born of what is non-self, how could they be self? [The same applies to] sounds...
Odors … tastes … tangibles …
Phenomena are non-self.
Whatever cause, whatever condition there is for the arising of phenomena, that too is non-self.
Since phenomena arise from what is non-self, monks, how could they be self?

"Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the well-taught noble disciple becomes disenchanted with forms, disenchanted with sounds, disenchanted with odors, disenchanted with tastes, disenchanted with tangibles, and disenchanted with mental phenomena.

*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 35.146 (SN 35.146, SN 35.145, PTS SN iv 132) 15.
Navapurāṇavagga (The Chapter on the New and the Old)
The Discourse on the Cessation of Kamma:
“Monks, I will teach you new and old kamma, the cessation of kamma, and the practice leading to the cessation of kamma.
Listen to that and attend closely; I will speak.”
And what, monks, is past kamma? The eye, monks, is to be seen as past kamma— wrought, volitionally produced,
and to be felt …pe… the tongue is to be seen as past kamma— wrought, volitionally produced, and to be felt …pe…
The mind, conditioned and intended by past karma, should be seen as something to be experienced.
This, monks, is called past karma.
And what, monks, is new karma?
Whatever action one performs now by way of body, speech,
or mind, monks, this is called new karma.
And what, monks, is the cessation of karma?
“Monks, whoever touches liberation through the cessation of bodily action, verbal action, and mental action— this, monks,
is called the cessation of karma. And what, monks,
is the practice leading to the cessation of karma?”
This very Noble Eightfold Path, namely: right view, right intention,
right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration— this, monks,
is called the practice leading to the cessation of karma.
"Thus, monks, have I taught you past karma, have I taught you new karma, have I taught you the cessation of karma, and have I taught you the practice leading to the cessation of karma.
Whatever, monks, ought to be done by a Teacher who seeks the welfare of his disciples and has compassion for them, out of compassion—that has been done by me for you.
Here, monks, are the roots of trees; here are empty huts. Meditate, monks, do not be negligent; do not later fall into regret. This is my instruction to you."
First.
Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.147 (SN 35.147, SN 35.146, PTS SN iv 133) 15.
Navapurāṇavagga (The Chapter on the New and the Old)
The Discourse on What is Conducive to Nibbāna and Impermanence:
“Monks, I will teach you the practice that is conducive to Nibbāna.
Listen to that …” [as before] …
And what, monks, is that practice conducive to Nibbāna?
Here, monks, a monk sees the eye as impermanent; he sees forms as impermanent; he sees eye-consciousness as impermanent;
he sees eye-contact as impermanent. Whatever [feeling] arises conditioned by this eye-contact...
Whatever feeling arises—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—he sees that as impermanent.
…pe… He sees the tongue as impermanent; he sees tastes as impermanent; he sees tongue-consciousness as impermanent; he sees tongue-contact as impermanent;
and whatever feeling arises conditioned by tongue-contact—whether pleasant or painful—[he sees that as impermanent].
or neither-painful-nor-pleasant, he sees that too as impermanent …pe… he sees the mind as impermanent,
he sees mental phenomena as impermanent, he sees mind-consciousness as impermanent, he sees mind-contact as impermanent,
and whatever feeling arises conditioned by mind-contact— whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant— he sees that too as impermanent.
Or whether it be neither-painful-nor-pleasant, one sees that too as impermanent.
This, monks, is the practice conducive to Nibbāna.

15. Navapurāṇavagga Nibbānasappāyapaṭipadāsutta “Monks, I will teach you the practice conducive to Nibbāna. Listen and pay close attention; I shall speak. “Yes, venerable sir,” those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: “Monks, what is the practice conducive to Nibbāna? It is this: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. This, monks, is the practice conducive to Nibbāna.”
Listen to that...
[as before] ...And what, monks, is the practice conducive to Nibbāna?
What do you think, monks?
“Is the eye permanent or impermanent?
“Impermanent, venerable sir.
“But that which is impermanent, is it suffering or happiness?”
“It is suffering, Bhante.
“But that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—is it fitting to regard it thus:
‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?”
“No, venerable sir.
“Are forms permanent or impermanent?
“Impermanent, venerable sir.”
“Is eye-consciousness … eye-contact … and whatever feeling arises conditioned by mind-contact— whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant— that too permanent or impermanent?”
“Impermanent, venerable sir.
“But what is impermanent, is that suffering or happiness?
“Suffering, venerable sir.”
“But that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—is it fitting to regard it thus:
‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?
“Certainly not, venerable sir.”

Navapurāṇavagga Antevāsikasutta “Bhikkhus, when a disciple dwells in dependence upon a teacher who possesses five qualities, it is not easy for that disciple to fall away from the supreme goal of the holy life for which clansmen rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness. What five? Here, bhikkhus, a teacher instructs, exhorts, inspires, and gladdens his disciples with a talk on the Dhamma; he is one who patiently endures being reproved and corrected by his disciples; he is one who does not conceal his own faults; he is one who reveals the Dhamma to others as he has heard it and learned it; and he is one who lives the holy life for the sake of his own higher knowledge. When a disciple dwells in dependence upon a teacher who possesses these five qualities, it is not easy for that disciple to fall away from the supreme goal of the holy life for which clansmen rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness.”
“Bhikkhus, this holy life is lived without a pupil and without a teacher.
A bhikkhu who has a pupil and a teacher, bhikkhus, dwells in suffering and discomfort.
A bhikkhu who has no pupil and no teacher, bhikkhus, dwells happily and in comfort.”
And how, bhikkhus, does one who lives with a teacher and dwells with a preceptor live in suffering and discomfort?
Here, bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu has seen a form with the eye, there arise in him evil unwholesome states that are accompanied by longing and are fetters.
They dwell within him; because evil unwholesome states dwell within him, he is said to "live with a teacher and dwell with a preceptor."
Therefore he is called "one who has disciples.
They treat him with familiarity; evil, unwholesome states treat him with familiarity.
Therefore he is called "one who has a teacher" ... [and so on] ...
Furthermore, monks, when a bhikkhu has tasted a flavor with the tongue, there arise in him evil unwholesome states that are accompanied by intention and are conducive to fetters.

They assail him; evil, unwholesome states assail him. Therefore he is called "one who has a teacher. ...

They dwell within him; evil, unwholesome states dwell within him.

They treat him with familiarity; evil, unwholesome states treat him with familiarity.

Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.152 (SN 35.152, SN 35.151, PTS SN iv 138) 15. Navapurāṇavagga Kimatthiyabrahmacariyasutta (The Discourse on the Purpose of the Holy Life) “Bhikkhus, for what purpose is the holy life lived under the Blessed One? “Venerable sir, it is for the sake of full understanding of suffering that the holy life is lived under the Blessed One. “Bhikkhus, it is indeed for the sake of full understanding of suffering that the holy life is lived under me. And how, bhikkhus, is there full understanding of suffering? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu understands as it really is: ‘This is suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the origin of suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. It is in this way, bhikkhus, that there is full understanding of suffering. It is for the sake of full understanding of suffering that the holy life is lived under me. And how, bhikkhus, is there full understanding of suffering? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu understands as it really is: ‘All formations are impermanent’; he understands as it really is: ‘All formations are suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘All phenomena are non-self. It is in this way, bhikkhus, that there is full understanding of suffering. It is for the sake of full understanding of suffering that the holy life is lived under me. And how, bhikkhus, is there full understanding of suffering? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu understands as it really is: ‘This is the noble truth of suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the noble truth of the origin of suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering. It is in this way, bhikkhus, that there is full understanding of suffering. It is for the sake of full understanding of suffering that the holy life is lived under me. And how, bhikkhus, is there full understanding of suffering? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu understands as it really is: ‘The noble truth of suffering has been fully understood by me’; he understands as it really is: ‘The noble truth of the origin of suffering has been abandoned by me’; he understands as it really is: ‘The noble truth of the cessation of suffering has been realized by me’; he understands as it really is: ‘The noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering has been developed by me. It is in this way, bhikkhus, that there is full understanding of suffering. It is for the sake of full understanding of suffering that the holy life is lived under me. And how, bhikkhus, is there full understanding of suffering? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu understands as it really is: ‘The noble truth of suffering is to be fully understood’; he understands as it really is: ‘The noble truth of the origin of suffering is to be abandoned’; he understands as it really is: ‘The noble truth of the cessation of suffering is to be realized’; he understands as it really is: ‘The noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering is to be developed. It is in this way, bhikkhus, that there is full understanding of suffering. It is for the sake of full understanding of suffering that the holy life is lived under me. And how, bhikkhus, is there full understanding of suffering? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu understands as it really is: ‘The noble truth of suffering has been fully understood’; he understands as it really is: ‘The noble truth of the origin of suffering has been abandoned’; he understands as it really is: ‘The noble truth of the cessation of suffering has been realized’; he understands as it really is: ‘The noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering has been developed. It is in this way, bhikkhus, that there is full understanding of suffering. It is for the sake of full understanding of suffering that the holy life is lived under me. And how, bhikkhus, is there full understanding of suffering? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu understands as it really is: ‘Suffering is to be fully understood’; he understands as it really is: ‘The origin of suffering is to be abandoned’; he understands as it really is: ‘The cessation of suffering is to be realized’; he understands as it really is: ‘The way leading to the cessation of suffering is to be developed. It is in this way, bhikkhus, that there is full understanding of suffering.

It is for the sake of full understanding of suffering that the holy life is lived under me. And how, bhikkhus, is there full understanding of suffering? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu understands as it really is: ‘Suffering has been fully understood’; he understands as it really is: ‘The origin of suffering has been abandoned’; he understands as it really is: ‘The cessation of suffering has been realized’; he understands as it really is: ‘The way leading to the cessation of suffering has been developed. It is in this way, bhikkhus, that there is full understanding of suffering. It is for the sake of full understanding of suffering that the holy life is lived under me. And how, bhikkhus, is there full understanding of suffering? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu understands as it really is: ‘The eye is impermanent’; he understands as it really is: ‘Forms are impermanent’; he understands as it really is: ‘Eye-consciousness is impermanent’; he understands as it really is: ‘Eye-contact is impermanent’; he understands as it really is: ‘Whatever feeling arises with eye-contact as its condition—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too is impermanent. He understands as it really is: ‘The ear is impermanent’... ‘The nose is impermanent’... ‘The tongue is impermanent’... ‘The body is impermanent’... ‘The mind is impermanent’; he understands as it really is: ‘Mental phenomena are impermanent’; he understands as it really is: ‘Mind-consciousness is impermanent’; he understands as it really is: ‘Mind-contact is impermanent’; he understands as it really is: ‘Whatever feeling arises with mind-contact as its condition—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too is impermanent. It is in this way, bhikkhus, that there is full understanding of suffering. It is for the sake of full understanding of suffering that the holy life is lived under me. And how, bhikkhus, is there full understanding of suffering? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu understands as it really is: ‘The eye is suffering’... ‘The ear is suffering’... ‘The nose is suffering’... ‘The tongue is suffering’... ‘The body is suffering’... ‘The mind is suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘Mental phenomena are suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘Mind-consciousness is suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘Mind-contact is suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘Whatever feeling arises with mind-contact as its condition—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too is suffering. It is in this way, bhikkhus, that there is full understanding of suffering. It is for the sake of full understanding of suffering that the holy life is lived under me. And how, bhikkhus, is there full understanding of suffering? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu understands as it really is: ‘The eye is non-self’... ‘The ear is non-self’... ‘The nose is non-self’... ‘The tongue is non-self’... ‘The body is non-self’... ‘The mind is non-self’; he understands as it really is: ‘Mental phenomena are non-self’; he understands as it really is: ‘Mind-consciousness is non-self’; he understands as it really is: ‘Mind-contact is non-self’; he understands as it really is: ‘Whatever feeling arises with mind-contact as its condition—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too is non-self. It is in this way, bhikkhus, that there is full understanding of suffering. It is for the sake of full understanding of suffering that the holy life is lived under me. And how, bhikkhus, is there full understanding of suffering? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu understands as it really is: ‘The eye is impermanent’; he understands as it really is: ‘The arising of the eye is impermanent’; he understands as it really is: ‘The passing away of the eye is impermanent’; he understands as it really is: ‘The arising and passing away of the eye is impermanent. He understands as it really is: ‘The ear is impermanent’... ‘The nose is impermanent’... ‘The tongue is imper
“Bhikkhus, if wanderers of other sects should ask you:
‘For what purpose, friends, is the holy life lived under the ascetic Gotama?’—
being asked thus, bhikkhus, you should answer those wanderers of other sects in this way:”
“‘Indeed, friends, the holy life is lived under the Blessed One for the full understanding of suffering.
But if, monks, wanderers of other sects should ask you:
‘But what, friends, is that suffering for the full understanding of which the holy life is lived under the ascetic Gotama?’”
Being asked thus, monks, you should answer those wanderers of other sects as follows:
"Friends, the eye is suffering;
it is for the full understanding of that that the holy life is lived under the Blessed One."
Forms are suffering;
for their full understanding, the holy life is lived under the Blessed One.
Eye-consciousness is suffering.
The holy life is lived under the Blessed One for the full understanding of that.
Eye-contact is suffering;
the holy life is lived under the Blessed One for the full understanding of that.
Whatever feeling arises conditioned by eye-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too is suffering.
It is for the full understanding of that [suffering] that the holy life is lived under the Blessed One. … [The same applies to] the ear … the nose … the tongue is suffering … [and so on].
The mind is suffering;
for its full understanding, the holy life is lived under the Blessed One.
... Whatever feeling arises conditioned by mind-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too is suffering.
“It is for the full understanding of that, friend, that the holy life is lived under the Blessed One.
This, friend, is suffering;
it is for the full understanding of this that the holy life is lived under the Blessed One.”
“Being asked thus, monks, you should answer those wanderers of other sects in this way.
The seventh.

15. Navapurāṇavagga:
Atthinukhopariyāyasutta “Bhikkhus, is there a method by means of which a bhikkhu, apart from faith, [can know for himself that]...”

“Could one declare final knowledge—‘I understand: birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being’—except through personal preference, except through hearsay, except through reasoned reflection, and except through approval based on a view?
“Venerable sir, our teachings are rooted in the Blessed One, guided by the Blessed One, and have the Blessed One as their refuge. It would be well indeed...”
“Venerable sir, let the Blessed One himself explain the meaning of these words; having heard it from the Blessed One, the bhikkhus will remember it.
“In that case, bhikkhus, listen and attend closely; I shall speak.
“Yes, venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this: “There is, bhikkhus,
a method by means of which a bhikkhu, apart from faith, apart from personal preference,
apart from oral tradition, apart from reasoned reflection, and apart from acceptance of a view after pondering it, might declare final knowledge:”
‘“Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being”—this I understand.
And what, bhikkhus, is that method by means of which a bhikkhu, apart from faith... apart from the acceptance of views after reflection, declares final knowledge:
‘Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being’?”
‘What was to be done has been done; there is no more of this state of being,’ do you understand thus?
Here, monks, when a monk sees a form with the eye, if lust, hatred, and delusion are present within him, he understands: ‘Lust, hatred, and delusion are present within me’;
or if lust, hatred, and delusion are not present within him, he understands: ‘Lust, hatred, and delusion are not present within me.’
“Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu, having seen a form with the eye, understands:
‘There is lust, hatred, and delusion in me’ if they are present within him; or understands:
‘There is no lust, hatred, and delusion in me’ if they are absent within him—should these things, bhikkhus, be understood by me through faith?”
“Are they to be known through preference, or known through oral tradition, or known through reasoned reflection, or known through acceptance based on contemplation of views?”—
“Certainly not, Bhante.”— “Then, monks,
are these phenomena not to be known by seeing them with wisdom?”
“Yes, venerable sir. “This, monks,
is the method by means of which a monk, apart from faith, apart from personal preference,
apart from oral tradition, apart from reasoned reflection, and apart from acceptance of a view after pondering it, declares final knowledge:”
‘“Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being,” thus I understand.

15. Navapurāṇavagga:
Indriyasampannasutta Then a certain bhikkhu approached the Blessed One... [as before] ...and sitting to one side, that bhikkhu said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, it is said, ‘one endowed with the faculties, one endowed with the faculties.
To what extent, venerable sir, is one endowed with the faculties?
“If, bhikkhu, while dwelling in contemplation of the arising and passing away of the eye-faculty, one becomes disenchanted with the eye-faculty… [and so on]…”

If, bhikkhu, while dwelling in contemplation of the arising and passing away of the tongue-faculty, one becomes disenchanted with the tongue-faculty … [and so on] … if, bhikkhu, while dwelling in contemplation of the arising and passing away of the mind-faculty, one becomes disenchanted with the mind-faculty.
Through disenchantment, passion fades away … [and so on] … when liberated, the knowledge arises: "It is liberated."
‘Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.
To this extent, monk, one is endowed with the faculties.

Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.155 (SN 35.155, SN 35.154, PTS SN iv 141) 15. Navapurāṇavagga Dhammakathikapucchasutta (The Discourse on the Questions of the Preacher of the Dhamma) At Sāvatthī. There, the Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu is a preacher of the Dhamma, he should question himself thus: ‘Do I speak in accordance with the Dhamma, or do I not? Do my words lead to the realization of the goal, or do they not? When this was said, a certain bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, how does a bhikkhu who is a preacher of the Dhamma speak in accordance with the Dhamma? “Bhikkhu, when a bhikkhu who is a preacher of the Dhamma speaks thus: ‘Form is impermanent; feeling is impermanent; perception is impermanent; volitional formations are impermanent; consciousness is impermanent’—this is called speaking in accordance with the Dhamma. Furthermore, when he speaks thus: ‘Form is suffering; feeling is suffering; perception is suffering; volitional formations are suffering; consciousness is suffering’—this too is called speaking in accordance with the Dhamma. Furthermore, when he speaks thus: ‘Form is non-self; feeling is non-self; perception is non-self; volitional formations are non-self; consciousness is non-self’—this too is called speaking in accordance with the Dhamma. Furthermore, when he speaks thus: ‘Form is subject to cessation; feeling is subject to cessation; perception is subject to cessation; volitional formations are subject to cessation; consciousness is subject to cessation’—this too is called speaking in accordance with the Dhamma. Furthermore, when he speaks thus: ‘I am not, what belongs to me is not’—this too is called speaking in accordance with the Dhamma. Furthermore, when he speaks thus: ‘I shall not be, what belongs to me shall not be’—this too is called speaking in accordance with the Dhamma. Furthermore, when he speaks thus: ‘Let me not be, let there be nothing belonging to me’—this too is called speaking in accordance with the Dhamma. Furthermore, when he speaks thus: ‘This is peace, this is sublime, namely, the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all attachments, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna’—this too is called speaking in accordance with the Dhamma. Bhikkhu, when a bhikkhu who is a preacher of the Dhamma speaks in this way, he is one who speaks in accordance with the Dhamma. When this was said, that bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, how does a bhikkhu who is a preacher of the Dhamma speak so as to lead to the realization of the goal? “Bhikkhu, when a bhikkhu who is a preacher of the Dhamma speaks thus: ‘This is suffering’—this is called speaking so as to lead to the realization of the goal. When he speaks thus: ‘This is the origin of suffering’—this too is called speaking so as to lead to the realization of the goal. When he speaks thus: ‘This is the cessation of suffering’—this too is called speaking so as to lead to the realization of the goal. When he speaks thus: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering’—this too is called speaking so as to lead to the realization of the goal. Bhikkhu, when a bhikkhu who is a preacher of the Dhamma speaks in this way, he is one who speaks so as to lead to the realization of the goal. When this was said, that bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, how does a bhikkhu who is a preacher of the Dhamma speak so that his words lead to the realization of the goal? “Bhikkhu, when a bhikkhu who is a preacher of the Dhamma speaks thus: ‘This is suffering’—this is called speaking so that his words lead to the realization of the goal. When he speaks thus: ‘This is the origin of suffering’—this too is called speaking so that his words lead to the realization of the goal. When he speaks thus: ‘This is the cessation of suffering’—this too is called speaking so that his words lead to the realization of the goal. When he speaks thus: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering’—this too is called speaking so that his words lead to the realization of the goal. Bhikkhu, when a bhikkhu who is a preacher of the Dhamma speaks in this way, his words lead to the realization of the goal. When this was said, that bhikkhu said to the Blessed One:

“Venerable sir, how does a bhikkhu who is a preacher of the Dhamma speak so that his words are in accordance with the Dhamma and lead to the realization of the goal? “Bhikkhu, when a bhikkhu who is a preacher of the Dhamma speaks thus: ‘This is suffering’—this is called speaking so that his words are in accordance with the Dhamma and lead to the realization of the goal. When he speaks thus: ‘This is the origin of suffering’—this too is called speaking so that his words are in accordance with the Dhamma and lead to the realization of the goal. When he speaks thus: ‘This is the cessation of suffering’—this too is called speaking so that his words are in accordance with the Dhamma and lead to the realization of the goal. When he speaks thus: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering’—this too is called speaking so that his words are in accordance with the Dhamma and lead to the realization of the goal. Bhikkhu, when a bhikkhu who is a preacher of the Dhamma speaks in this way, his words are in accordance with the Dhamma and lead to the realization of the goal. When this was said, that bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, how does a bhikkhu who is a preacher of the Dhamma speak so that his words are in accordance with the Dhamma, lead to the realization of the goal, and are conducive to the opening of the heart? “Bhikkhu, when a bhikkhu who is a preacher of the Dhamma speaks thus: ‘This is suffering’—this is called speaking so that his words are in accordance with the Dhamma, lead to the realization of the goal, and are conducive to the opening of the heart. When he speaks thus: ‘This is the origin of suffering’—this too is called speaking so that his words are in accordance with the Dhamma, lead to the realization of the goal, and are conducive to the opening of the heart. When he speaks thus: ‘This is the cessation of suffering’—this too is called speaking so that his words are in accordance with the Dhamma, lead to the realization of the goal, and are conducive to the opening of the heart. When he speaks thus: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering’—this too is called speaking so that his words are in accordance with the Dhamma, lead to the realization of the goal, and are conducive to the opening of the heart. Bhikkhu, when a bhikkhu who is a preacher of the Dhamma speaks in this way, his words are in accordance with the Dhamma, lead to the realization of the goal, and are conducive to the opening of the heart. When this was said, that bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, how does a bhikkhu who is a preacher of the Dhamma speak so that his words are in accordance with the Dhamma, lead to the realization of the goal, are conducive to the opening of the heart, and are spoken with a mind that is free from attachment? “Bhikkhu, when a bhikkhu who is a preacher of the Dhamma speaks thus: ‘This is suffering’—this is called speaking so that his words are in accordance with the Dhamma, lead to the realization of the goal, are conducive to the opening of the heart, and are spoken with a mind that is free from attachment. When he speaks thus: ‘This is the origin of suffering’—this too is called speaking so that his words are in accordance with the Dhamma, lead to the realization of the goal, are conducive to the opening of the heart, and are spoken with a mind that is free from attachment. When he speaks thus: ‘This is the cessation of suffering’—this too is called speaking so that his words are in accordance with the Dhamma, lead to the realization of the goal, are conducive to the opening of the heart, and are spoken with a mind that is free from attachment. When he speaks thus: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering’—this too is called speaking so that his words are in accordance with the Dhamma, lead to the realization of the goal, are conducive to the opening of the heart, and are spoken with a mind that is
Then a certain bhikkhu approached the Blessed One... and sitting to one side, that bhikkhu said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable sir, it is said, 'a speaker on the Dhamma, a speaker on the Dhamma.
In what way, venerable sir, is one a speaker on the Dhamma?"

“Bhikkhu, if one teaches the Dhamma for the sake of disenchantment with the eye, for its fading away, and for its cessation, it is sufficient to call such a person ‘a bhikkhu who is a speaker of the Dhamma.

Bhikkhu, if one practices for the sake of disenchantment with the eye, for its fading away, and for its cessation, it is sufficient to call such a person ‘a bhikkhu who practices in accordance with the Dhamma.

… [and so on] … If, bhikkhu, one teaches the Dhamma for the sake of disenchantment with, for the fading away of lust for, and for the cessation of the mind, one is fit to be called a “bhikkhu who is a preacher of the Dhamma.

If, bhikkhu, one practices for the sake of disenchantment with, for the fading away of lust for, and for the cessation of the mind, one is fit to be called a “bhikkhu who practices in accordance with the Dhamma.”

“If, bhikkhu, through disenchantment with mind, through its fading away, and through its cessation, one is liberated by non-clinging, it is sufficient to say: ‘This bhikkhu has attained Nibbāna in this very life.
The tenth [sutta].
The fifth chapter on the Old and the New is finished.
Its summary verse:
Action, the four suitable things,
the one without a pupil, and for what purpose?

Gahapati and Devadaha.
