when a bhikkhu sees the eye as simply impermanent, that is his right view.
Seeing rightly, one becomes disenchanted.
With the destruction of delight comes the destruction of lust;
with the destruction of lust comes the destruction of delight.
“With the destruction of delight and lust, the mind is said to be well-liberated … Monks,
when a monk sees the tongue as impermanent, that is his right view.

With the destruction of delight comes the destruction of lust;
with the destruction of lust, [the mind] is said to be well-liberated... pe ... [as before] ...pe ... it is said that the mind is well-liberated.
"Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu sees the mind as simply impermanent, that is his right view.

Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.157 (SN 35.157, SN 35.156, PTS SN iv 142) 16. Nandikkhaya-vagga Bāhiranandikkhaya-sutta: The Discourse on the Destruction of External Delight “Monks, I shall teach you the destruction of delight in the external. Listen and pay close attention; I will speak. “Yes, venerable sir,” those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: “And what, monks, is the destruction of delight in the external? Here, monks, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings... mind in the mind... phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. This, monks, is called the destruction of delight in the external. [The Buddha then elaborates on the contemplation of the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena, concluding: “When, monks, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body... feelings in feelings... mind in the mind... phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world, he does not delight in the external. When he does not delight in the external, he does not take up [grasping] in the external. When he does not take up [grasping] in the external, he is not established upon the foundation for the arising of suffering. When he is not established upon the foundation for the arising of suffering, he is not bound by the bond of craving. When he is not bound by the bond of craving, he is liberated. Being liberated, he knows: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being. “This, monks, is called the destruction of delight in the external.”
“Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu sees forms as impermanent in what is indeed impermanent, that is his right view.
Seeing rightly, he becomes disenchanted.
With the destruction of delight comes the destruction of lust;”
With the destruction of lust comes the destruction of delight.
With the destruction of delight and lust, the mind is said to be well-liberated.
Monks, it is precisely regarding sounds that a monk [perceives impermanence]...
In odors … in tastes … in tangibles …
When one sees phenomena as impermanent, that is one's right view.
Seeing rightly, one becomes disenchanted.
With the destruction of delight comes the destruction of lust.
With the destruction of lust comes the destruction of delight.
With the destruction of lust and delight, the mind is said to be well-liberated. Thus ends the second [sutta].

Saṁyutta Nikāya 35.158 (SN 35.158, SN 35.157, PTS SN iv 142) 16. Nandikkhayavagga: Ajjhatta-anicca-nandikkhaya-sutta (The Discourse on the Destruction of Delight in the Impermanent Internally) "Bhikkhus, when one sees with correct wisdom as it really is: ‘This is suffering,’ delight in the internal ceases. When delight has ceased, passion ceases. With the cessation of passion, one is liberated. One who is liberated possesses the knowledge: ‘I am liberated. When one sees with correct wisdom as it really is: ‘This is the origin of suffering,’ delight in the internal ceases... When one sees with correct wisdom as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of suffering,’ delight in the internal ceases... When one sees with correct wisdom as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering,’ delight in the internal ceases. When delight has ceased, passion ceases. With the cessation of passion, one is liberated. One who is liberated possesses the knowledge: ‘I am liberated.’"
“Bhikkhus, attend wisely to the eye and contemplate the impermanence of the eye as it really is.
Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu attends wisely to the eye and contemplates the impermanence of the eye as it really is, he becomes disenchanted with the eye.
With the destruction of delight comes the destruction of lust.”
With the destruction of lust comes the destruction of delight.
With the destruction of lust and delight, the mind is said to be well-liberated.
Attend to the ear, bhikkhus, with wise attention...
“Monks, attend wisely to the nose… to the tongue, monks, and contemplate the impermanence of the tongue as it really is.
By attending wisely to the tongue, monks, and contemplating the impermanence of the tongue as it really is, a monk becomes disenchanted with the tongue.”
With the destruction of delight comes the destruction of lust; with the destruction of lust comes the destruction of delight.

“Bhikkhus, attend wisely to the body… to the mind, and contemplate the impermanence of the mind as it really is.

With the destruction of delight comes the destruction of lust; with the destruction of lust comes the destruction of delight.
With the destruction of both delight and lust, the mind is said to be well-liberated.”

that too is seen as it really is as impermanent … pe … the tongue is seen as it really is as impermanent … pe …

Whatever feeling arises conditioned by mind-contact, whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant, that too is impermanent—this is seen as it really is.
Monks, develop concentration.
“Bhikkhus, for a bhikkhu who is concentrated, things become manifest as they really are.

Discourse on Seclusion in Jīvaka’s Mango Grove.

There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
“… ‘Bhikkhus, apply yourselves to seclusion.
For a bhikkhu who is secluded, things become manifest as they really are.’”
And what is seen as it really is?
It is seen as it really is that the eye is impermanent; it is seen as it really is that forms are impermanent;
it is seen as it really is that eye-consciousness is impermanent; it is seen as it really is that eye-contact is impermanent.
Whatever feeling arises conditioned by eye-contact— whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—
that too is seen as it really is as impermanent … [and so on] … the mind is seen as it really is as impermanent; mental phenomena …
"Mind-consciousness...
mind-contact...
and whatever feeling—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—arises conditioned by mind-contact, that too is impermanent," thus it is seen as it really is.
“Apply yourselves, bhikkhus, to seclusion.

Saṁyutta Nikāya 35.162 (SN 35.162, SN 35.161, PTS SN iv 145) 16. Nandikkhayavagga Koṭṭhika-anicca Sutta: To Koṭṭhita on Impermanence At Sāvatthī. Then the Venerable Koṭṭhita approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it was said: ‘The destruction of craving, the cessation of craving, the relinquishing of craving, the abandoning of craving. In what way, venerable sir, has this been said? “Koṭṭhita, form is impermanent; its change, transformation, fading away, and cessation are the destruction of craving for form. Feeling is impermanent... Perception is impermanent... Volitional formations are impermanent... Consciousness is impermanent; its change, transformation, fading away, and cessation are the destruction of craving for consciousness. It is in this way, Koṭṭhita, that it has been said: ‘The destruction of craving, the cessation of craving, the relinquishing of craving, the abandoning of craving. When this was said, the Venerable Koṭṭhita said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it was said: ‘The destruction of clinging, the cessation of clinging, the relinquishing of clinging, the abandoning of clinging. In what way, venerable sir, has this been said? “Koṭṭhita, form is impermanent; its change, transformation, fading away, and cessation are the destruction of clinging to form. Feeling is impermanent... Perception is impermanent... Volitional formations are impermanent... Consciousness is impermanent; its change, transformation, fading away, and cessation are the destruction of clinging to consciousness. It is in this way, Koṭṭhita, that it has been said: ‘The destruction of clinging, the cessation of clinging, the relinquishing of clinging, the abandoning of clinging. When this was said, the Venerable Koṭṭhita said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it was said: ‘The destruction of the taints, the cessation of the taints, the relinquishing of the taints, the abandoning of the taints. In what way, venerable sir, has this been said? “Koṭṭhita, form is impermanent; its change, transformation, fading away, and cessation are the destruction of the taints regarding form. Feeling is impermanent... Perception is impermanent... Volitional formations are impermanent... Consciousness is impermanent; its change, transformation, fading away, and cessation are the destruction of the taints regarding consciousness. It is in this way, Koṭṭhita, that it has been said: ‘The destruction of the taints, the cessation of the taints, the relinquishing of the taints, the abandoning of the taints. When this was said, the Venerable Koṭṭhita said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it was said: ‘The destruction of identity, the cessation of identity, the relinquishing of identity, the abandoning of identity. In what way, venerable sir, has this been said? “Koṭṭhita, form is impermanent; its change, transformation, fading away, and cessation are the destruction of identity in form. Feeling is impermanent... Perception is impermanent... Volitional formations are impermanent... Consciousness is impermanent; its change, transformation, fading away, and cessation are the destruction of identity in consciousness. It is in this way, Koṭṭhita, that it has been said: ‘The destruction of identity, the cessation of identity, the relinquishing of identity, the abandoning of identity. When this was said, the Venerable Koṭṭhita said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it was said: ‘The destruction of the conceit “I am,” the cessation of the conceit “I am,” the relinquishing of the conceit “I am,” the abandoning of the conceit “I am. In what way, venerable sir, has this been said? “Koṭṭhita, form is impermanent; its change, transformation, fading away, and cessation are the destruction of the conceit ‘I am’ in form. Feeling is impermanent... Perception is impermanent... Volitional formations are impermanent... Consciousness is impermanent; its change, transformation, fading away, and cessation are the destruction of the conceit ‘I am’ in consciousness. It is in this way, Koṭṭhita, that it has been said: ‘The destruction of the conceit “I am,” the cessation of the conceit “I am,” the relinquishing of the conceit “I am,” the abandoning of the conceit “I am. When this was said, the Venerable Koṭṭhita said to the Blessed One: “Magnificent, venerable sir! Magnificent, venerable sir!

It is as if he were to set upright what had been overturned, or to reveal what was hidden, or to show the way to one who was lost, or to carry a lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms. Thus has the Dhamma been made clear by the Blessed One in many ways. I go for refuge to the Blessed One, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. May I receive the going forth under the Blessed One, may I receive the full admission. “Koṭṭhita, whoever has previously belonged to another sect and desires the going forth and the full admission in this Dhamma and Discipline must wait four months; at the end of four months, having satisfied the bhikkhus, they will receive the going forth and the full admission. However, there is an exception in the case of one possessed of special qualities. “I am possessed of special qualities, venerable sir. Then the Venerable Koṭṭhita received the going forth under the Blessed One, and he received the full admission. Not long after his full admission, dwelling alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute, the Venerable Koṭṭhita, by realizing it for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life entered and dwelt in that unsurpassed goal of the holy life for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness. He directly knew: “Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more coming to any state of being. And the Venerable Koṭṭhita became one of the arahants.
Then the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhita approached the Blessed One... [as before] ...and sitting to one side, the Venerable Koṭṭhita said this to the Blessed One:
“It would be well, Bhante, if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief, so that having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, I might dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute.
“Koṭṭhita, whatever is impermanent, you should abandon desire for that.”
And what, Koṭṭhika, is impermanent?
The eye, Koṭṭhika, is impermanent; you should abandon desire for it.
Forms are impermanent; you should abandon desire for them.
Eye-consciousness is impermanent; you should abandon desire for it.
Eye-contact is impermanent; you should abandon desire for it.
And whatever feeling arises conditioned by eye-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too is impermanent; you should abandon desire for it... [and so on].
The tongue is impermanent; you should abandon desire for it.
Tastes are impermanent; you should abandon desire for them.
Tongue-consciousness is impermanent; you should abandon desire for it.
Tongue-contact is impermanent; you should abandon desire for it.
Whatever feeling arises conditioned by tongue-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too is impermanent; you should abandon desire for it.
…pe… Mind is impermanent; you should abandon desire for it.
Mental phenomena are impermanent; in regard to them, desire should be abandoned.
Mind-consciousness is impermanent; in regard to it, desire should be abandoned.
Mind-contact is impermanent; in regard to it, desire should be abandoned.
Whatever feeling arises conditioned by mind-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too is impermanent; you should abandon desire for that.
For whatever is impermanent, Koṭṭhika, you should abandon desire for that. Thus it was said.
The seventh.

Saṁyutta Nikāya 35.163 (SN 35.163, SN 35.162, PTS SN iv 146) 16. Nandikkhayavagga Koṭṭhika on Suffering At Sāvatthī. Then the Venerable Koṭṭhita approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it was said: ‘Suffering, suffering. In what way, venerable sir, has this been said? “Koṭṭhita, form is suffering; thus, Koṭṭhita, it has been said: ‘Suffering, suffering. Feeling is suffering... Perception is suffering... Volitional formations are suffering... Consciousness is suffering; thus, Koṭṭhita, it has been said: ‘Suffering, suffering. “But, venerable sir, why has it been said that form is suffering? Why has it been said that feeling is suffering... perception is suffering... volitional formations are suffering... consciousness is suffering? “Koṭṭhita, form is impermanent; because it is impermanent, it is suffering. Feeling is impermanent... perception is impermanent... volitional formations are impermanent... consciousness is impermanent; because it is impermanent, it is suffering. It is in this way, Koṭṭhita, that it has been said: ‘Form is suffering... consciousness is suffering. “But, venerable sir, why is form impermanent? Why is feeling impermanent... perception is impermanent... volitional formations are impermanent... why is consciousness impermanent? “Koṭṭhita, form arises from conditions and ceases due to conditions. Feeling arises from conditions and ceases due to conditions... perception arises from conditions and ceases due to conditions... volitional formations arise from conditions and cease due to conditions... consciousness arises from conditions and ceases due to conditions. It is in this way, Koṭṭhita, that form is impermanent... feeling is impermanent... perception is impermanent... volitional formations are impermanent... consciousness is impermanent. “Venerable sir, it is wonderful, it is marvelous! How well this has been stated by the Blessed One: ‘Form is impermanent; because it is impermanent, it is suffering. Feeling is impermanent... perception is impermanent... volitional formations are impermanent... consciousness is impermanent; because it is impermanent, it is suffering. Now, venerable sir, when one sees with right wisdom according to reality as it is—‘This is suffering’; when one sees with right wisdom according to reality as it is—‘This is the origin of suffering’; when one sees with right wisdom according to reality as it is—‘This is the cessation of suffering’; when one sees with right wisdom according to reality as it is—‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering’—then, venerable sir, for one who sees thus, does the mind incline toward seclusion, becomes dispassionate, and finds release in Nibbāna? “Yes, Koṭṭhita, when one sees with right wisdom according to reality as it is—‘This is suffering’... ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering’—then, Koṭṭhita, for one who sees thus, the mind inclines toward seclusion, becomes dispassionate, and finds release in Nibbāna. “Venerable sir, how does one know, how does one see, so that in regard to this body with its consciousness and all external phenomena, there is no more I-making, mine-making, or the underlying tendency to conceit? “Koṭṭhita, when one sees with right wisdom according to reality as it is: ‘All phenomena are non-self,’ then, Koṭṭhita, one knows, one sees, so that in regard to this body with its consciousness and all external phenomena, there is no more I-making, mine-making, or the underlying tendency to conceit. “It is wonderful, venerable sir, it is marvelous! How well this has been stated by the Blessed One: ‘When one sees with right wisdom according to reality as it is: “All phenomena are non-self,” then one knows, one sees, so that in regard to this body with its consciousness and all external phenomena, there is no more I-making, mine-making, or the underlying tendency to conceit. Venerable sir, suppose a man were to let go of a very large bundle of grass and sticks, thinking: ‘It is heavy, it is burdensome! and another man were to let go of a small bundle of grass and sticks, thinking: ‘It is light, it is not burdensome! In the same way, venerable sir, this Dhamma has been well-expounded by the Blessed One, and it is clear that those who have entered the stream have abandoned the heavy burden and taken up the light burden. “It is wonderful, venerable sir, it is marvelous! How well this has been stated by the Blessed One. And now, venerable sir, we depart; we are busy and have much to do. “You may go, Koṭṭhita, at your own convenience. Then the Venerable Koṭṭhita, having delighted and rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him on his right, departed. Not long after he had left, the Venerable Koṭṭhita attained final Nibbāna. Then a number of bhikkhus approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, the Venerable Koṭṭhita has attained final Nibbāna. When he was asked about the meaning of this, he did not answer.

What is the cause, what is the reason, why the Venerable Koṭṭhita did not answer? “Bhikkhus, if anyone had answered me when asked about the meaning of this, it would have been hard for them to do so. For Koṭṭhita, bhikkhus, had fully understood this Dhamma even to the point of subtlety. Then the Venerable Ānanda thought: “It is wonderful, it is marvelous! How well this has been stated by the Blessed One: ‘For Koṭṭhita, bhikkhus, had fully understood this Dhamma even to the point of subtlety. Now, venerable sir, how far does this Dhamma extend in its subtlety? “Ānanda, if anyone were to say: ‘I will declare the limit of the extent to which this Dhamma extends in its subtlety,’ they would be speaking of something beyond their range. For even the Tathāgata, Ānanda, does not declare the limit of the extent to which this Dhamma extends in its subtlety. Suppose, Ānanda, a cowherd were to drive cattle from one pasture to another. He would know: ‘These cattle have gone from this pasture to that pasture,’ but he would not know: ‘These cattle have gone this far. Even so, Ānanda, if anyone were to say: ‘I will declare the limit of the extent to which this Dhamma extends in its subtlety,’ they would be speaking of something beyond their range. For even the Tathāgata, Ānanda, does not declare the limit of the extent to which this Dhamma extends in its subtlety. Nandikkhayavagga Attānudiṭṭhipahānasutta – The Discourse on the Abandoning of the View of Self “Bhikkhus, when what exists, by clinging to what, with the arising of what, does the view ‘self’ arise? “Venerable sir, our teachings are rooted in the Blessed One, guided by the Blessed One, and take recourse in the Blessed One. It would be good if the Blessed One himself would clarify the meaning of this statement. Having heard it from him, the bhikkhus will remember it. “Then listen, bhikkhus, and attend closely. I will speak. “Yes, venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied. The Blessed One said this: “When there is form, bhikkhus, by clinging to form, with the arising of form, the view ‘self’ arises. When there is feeling … perception … volitional formations … consciousness, by clinging to consciousness, with the arising of consciousness, the view ‘self’ arises. When there is no form, bhikkhus, by not clinging to form, with the cessation of form, the view ‘self’ ceases. When there is no feeling … perception … volitional formations … consciousness, by not clinging to consciousness, with the cessation of consciousness, the view ‘self’ ceases. “Bhikkhus, when what exists, by clinging to what, with the arising of what, do the views ‘I am form,’ ‘form is mine,’ ‘I am in form,’ ‘form is my self’ arise? … [and so on for feeling, perception, volitional formations, and consciousness] … “Bhikkhus, when what exists, by clinging to what, with the arising of what, do the views ‘I am other than form,’ ‘other than form is mine,’ ‘I am in what is other than form,’ ‘what is other than form is my self’ arise? … [and so on for feeling, perception, volitional formations, and consciousness] … “Bhikkhus, when what exists, by clinging to what, with the arising of what, do the views ‘I am form and other than form,’ ‘form and other than form are mine,’ ‘I am in form and other than form,’ ‘form and other than form are my self’ arise? … [and so on for feeling, perception, volitional formations, and consciousness] … “Bhikkhus, when what exists, by clinging to what, with the arising of what, do the views ‘I am not form,’ ‘form is not mine,’ ‘I am not in form,’ ‘form is not my self’ arise? … [and so on for feeling, perception, volitional formations, and consciousness] … “Bhikkhus, when what exists, by clinging to what, with the arising of what, do the views ‘I am not other than form,’ ‘other than form is not mine,’ ‘I am not in what is other than form,’ ‘what is other than form is not my self’ arise? … [and so on for feeling, perception, volitional formations, and consciousness] … “Bhikkhus, when what exists, by clinging to what, with the arising of what, do the views ‘I am form and other than form,’ ‘form and other than form are not mine,’ ‘I am in form and other than form,’ ‘form and other than form are not my self’ arise? … [and so on for feeling, perception, volitional formations, and consciousness] … “Bhikkhus, when what exists, by clinging to what, with the arising of what, do the views ‘I might be form after death,’ ‘I might be feeling after death,’ ‘I might be perception after death,’ ‘I might be volitional formations after death,’ ‘I might be consciousness after death’ arise? … [and so on for each aggregate] … “Bhikkhus, when what exists, by clinging to what, with the arising of what, do the views ‘I might be formless after death,’ ‘I might be percipient after death,’ ‘I might be non-percipient after death,’ ‘I might be neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient after death’ arise? … [and so on for each aggregate] … “Bhikkhus, when what exists, by clinging to what, with the arising of what, do the views ‘I might be finite after death,’ ‘I might be infinite after death,’ ‘I might be finite and infinite after death,’ ‘I might be neither finite nor infinite after death’ arise? … [and so on for each aggregate] … “Bhikkhus, when what exists, by clinging to what, with the arising of what, do the views ‘I might be of one mode of existence after death,’ ‘I might be of various modes of existence after death,’ ‘I might be of limited power after death,’ ‘I might be of unlimited power after death,’ ‘I might be lord after death,’ ‘I might not be lord after death,’ ‘I might be conscious after death,’ ‘I might be unconscious after death,’ ‘I might be neither-conscious-nor-unconscious after death’ arise?

… [and so on for each aggregate] … “Bhikkhus, when what exists, by clinging to what, with the arising of what, do the views ‘That which is the self is the world; having passed away, that I shall be—permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change’ arise? … [and so on for each aggregate] … “Bhikkhus, when what exists, by clinging to what, with the arising of what, do these sixty-two speculative views arise? … [and so on for each aggregate] … “Bhikkhus, when what exists, by clinging to what, with the arising of what, do these sixty-two speculative views cease? … [and so on for each aggregate] … “Bhikkhus, when what exists, by clinging to what, with the arising of what, do these sixty-two speculative views arise? With the cessation of consciousness, they cease. “Venerable sir, it is wonderful, it is marvelous! Such is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering. “It is because, bhikkhus, this has been seen as it really is by means of right wisdom thus: ‘The cessation of ignorance is nibbāna,’ that with the cessation of ignorance comes the cessation of volitional formations … such is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering. “It is because, bhikkhus, this has been seen as it really is by means of right wisdom thus: ‘This is suffering,’ that with the cessation of ignorance comes the cessation of volitional formations … such is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering. “It is because, bhikkhus, this has been seen as it really is by means of right wisdom thus: ‘This is the origin of suffering’ … ‘This is the cessation of suffering’ … ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering,’ that with the cessation of ignorance comes the cessation of volitional formations … such is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering. “It is because, bhikkhus, this has been seen as it really is by means of right wisdom thus: ‘These are volitional formations’ … ‘This is the origin of volitional formations’ … ‘This is the cessation of volitional formations’ … ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of volitional formations’ … ‘This is consciousness’ … ‘This is the origin of consciousness’ … ‘This is the cessation of consciousness’ … ‘This is name-and-form’ … ‘This is the origin of name-and-form’ … ‘This is the cessation of name-and-form’ … ‘These are the six sense bases’ … ‘This is the origin of the six sense bases’ … ‘This is the cessation of the six sense bases’ … ‘This is contact’ … ‘This is the origin of contact’ … ‘This is the cessation of contact’ … ‘This is feeling’ … ‘This is the origin of feeling’ … ‘This is the cessation of feeling’ … ‘This is craving’ … ‘This is the origin of craving’ … ‘This is the cessation of craving’ … ‘This is clinging’ … ‘This is the

Saṭṭhipeyyālavagga Ajjhatta-anicca-chandasutta “Bhikkhus, whatever desire, lust, delight, craving, affection, or fever there is regarding the internal eye—this is called suffering in the Noble One’s Discipline. Whatever desire, lust, delight, craving, affection, or fever there is regarding the internal ear... nose... tongue... body... mind—this is called suffering in the Noble One’s Discipline. “Bhikkhus, when one sees this thus as it really is with correct wisdom, that which is the desire for the cessation of this very suffering ceases; the desire for its non-arising ceases; the desire for its abandonment ceases; the desire for its relinquishment ceases. “Bhikkhus, whatever is impermanent, you should abandon desire for it.

the mind is impermanent; therein you must abandon desire.

Saṁyutta Nikāya 35.169 (SN 35.169, SN 35.167b, PTS SN iv 149) 17. Saṭṭhipeyyālavagga Ajjhatta-anicca-rāgasutta (The Discourse on Lust for the Internal as Impermanent) “Bhikkhus, whatever kind of lust there is for the internal as impermanent, that is called ‘lust for the internal. Whatever kind of lust there is for the external as impermanent, that is called ‘lust for the external. “Bhikkhus, whatever kind of lust there is for the internal as impermanent, that is unwholesome; whatever kind of lust there is for the external as impermanent, that is unwholesome. “Bhikkhus, whatever kind of lust there is for the internal as impermanent, that leads to suffering; whatever kind of lust there is for the external as impermanent, that leads to suffering. “Bhikkhus, whatever kind of lust there is for the internal as impermanent, that is not the goal; whatever kind of lust there is for the external as impermanent, that is not the goal. “Bhikkhus, whatever kind of lust there is for the internal as impermanent, that is not the Dhamma; whatever kind of lust there is for the external as impermanent, that is not the Dhamma. “Bhikkhus, whatever kind of lust there is for the internal as impermanent, that is not the Vinaya; whatever kind of lust there is for the external as impermanent, that is not the Vinaya. “Bhikkhus, whatever kind of lust there is for the internal as impermanent, that is not conducive to the attainment of the fruit of stream-entry; whatever kind of lust there is for the external as impermanent, that is not conducive to the attainment of the fruit of stream-entry. “Bhikkhus, whatever kind of lust there is for the internal as impermanent, that is not conducive to the attainment of the fruit of once-returning; whatever kind of lust there is for the external as impermanent, that is not conducive to the attainment of the fruit of once-returning. “Bhikkhus, whatever kind of lust there is for the internal as impermanent, that is not conducive to the attainment of the fruit of non-returning; whatever kind of lust there is for the external as impermanent, that is not conducive to the attainment of the fruit of non-returning. “Bhikkhus, whatever kind of lust there is for the internal as impermanent, that is not conducive to the attainment of the fruit of arahantship; whatever kind of lust there is for the external as impermanent, that is not conducive to the attainment of the fruit of arahantship. “Bhikkhus, whatever kind of lust there is for the internal as impermanent, that is not conducive to revulsion, dispassion, cessation, peace, direct knowledge, enlightenment, and Nibbāna; whatever kind of lust there is for the external as impermanent, that is not conducive to revulsion, dispassion, cessation, peace, direct knowledge, enlightenment, and Nibbāna.”
“Monks, whatever is impermanent, therein you must abandon lust.
And what, monks, is impermanent?
The eye, monks, is impermanent.”
In that regard, lust for you must be abandoned … [as before] … the tongue is impermanent;
in that regard, lust for you must be abandoned … [as before] …
“The mind is impermanent;
therein you must abandon lust.
Whatever is impermanent, bhikkhus, therein you must abandon lust.”

Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.170 (SN 35.170, SN 35.167c, PTS SN iv 149) 17. Saṭṭhipeyyālavagga Ajjhatta-anicca-chanda-rāga-sutta “Bhikkhus, whatever kind of desire and lust there is for the internal, that is impermanent;

it is subject to cessation, vanishing, fading away, and ceasing. Whatever kind of desire and lust there is for the external, that too is impermanent; it is subject to cessation, vanishing, fading away, and ceasing.”
“Bhikkhus, whatever is impermanent, therein you should abandon desire and lust.
And what, bhikkhus, is impermanent?
The eye, bhikkhus, is impermanent.”
In that regard, desire and lust for it must be abandoned … [and so on] … the tongue is impermanent;
in that regard, desire and lust for it must be abandoned … [and so on] …
“The mind is impermanent;
therein you must abandon desire and lust.
Monks, whatever is impermanent, therein you must abandon desire and lust.”

Saṁyutta Nikāya 35.174–176 (SN 35.174, SN 35.169a, PTS SN iv 150) 17. Saṭṭhipeyyālavagga Anattachandādisutta “Bhikkhus, whatever desire, lust, delight, craving, affection, passion, and fetter there is regarding form: that is what makes form ‘self. Whatever desire, lust, delight, craving, affection, passion, and fetter there is regarding feeling... perception... volitional formations... consciousness: that is what makes consciousness ‘self. “If, bhikkhus, one does not have desire, lust, delight, craving, affection, passion, and fetter regarding form, then form is not ‘self’ for one. If one does not have desire, lust, delight, craving, affection, passion, and fetter regarding feeling... perception... volitional formations... consciousness, then consciousness is not ‘self’ for one. “Bhikkhus, when one does not regard anything as self, one does not cling to anything in the world. When one does not cling to anything in the world, one is not agitated by it. When one is not agitated by it, one attains Nibbāna in the present life. One understands: ‘Birth has been eradicated, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being.’”
“Monks, whatever is not-self, therein you should abandon desire, abandon lust, and abandon desire-and-lust.
And what, monks, is not-self?
The eye, monks, is not-self; therein you should abandon desire, abandon lust, and abandon desire-and-lust … [and so on for the other sense bases] …”
“The tongue is not-self; therein you must abandon desire, abandon lust, abandon desire and lust.
… The mind is not-self; therein you must abandon desire, abandon lust, abandon desire and lust.
Whatever, bhikkhus, is not-self, therein you must abandon desire, abandon lust, abandon desire and lust.”

Saṁyutta Nikāya 35.177–179 (SN 35.177, SN 35.170a, PTS SN iv 150) 17. Saṭṭhipeyyālavagga Bāhirāniccachandādisutta “Bhikkhus, whatever external forms there are—whether past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near—all those forms are not yours; you should abandon them by means of right wisdom, seeing them as they really are. Whatever external sounds... Whatever external odors... Whatever external tastes... Whatever external tactile objects... Whatever external phenomena there are—whether past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near—all those phenomena are not yours; you should abandon them by means of right wisdom, seeing them as they really are. When one sees this thus as it really is with correct wisdom, one becomes disenchanted with form, disenchanted with sound, disenchanted with odor, disenchanted with taste, disenchanted with tactile object, and disenchanted with phenomena. Being disenchanted, one becomes dispassionate. Through dispassion, one is liberated. Through liberation, there is the knowledge: ‘It is liberated. One understands: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being.’”
“Bhikkhus, whatever is impermanent, therein you must abandon desire, abandon lust, and abandon desire-and-lust.
And what, bhikkhus, is impermanent?
Material form, bhikkhus, is impermanent; therein you must abandon desire, abandon lust, and abandon desire-and-lust.”
Sounds are impermanent; therein you must abandon desire, abandon lust, and abandon desire-and-lust.
Odors are impermanent; therein you must abandon desire, abandon lust, and abandon desire-and-lust.
Tastes are impermanent; therein you must abandon desire, abandon lust, and abandon desire-and-lust.
“Tangible objects are impermanent; therein you should abandon desire, abandon lust, and abandon desire-and-lust.
Mental phenomena are impermanent; therein you should abandon desire, abandon lust, and abandon desire-and-lust.
Whatever, monks, is impermanent—therein you should abandon desire, abandon lust, and abandon desire-and-lust.”

Saṁyutta Nikāya 35.180–182 (SN 35.180, SN 35.171a, PTS SN iv 150) 17. Saṭṭhipeyyālavagga Bāhiradukkhachandādisutta “Bhikkhus, there are these three kinds of suffering that are external. What three? Suffering born of desire, suffering born of aversion, and suffering born of delusion. These are the three kinds of suffering that are external. “There are these three kinds of craving that are external. What three? Craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence. These are the three kinds of craving that are external. “There are these three kinds of clinging that are external. What three? Clinging to sensual pleasures, clinging to views, and clinging to rules and observances. These are the three kinds of clinging that are external. “There are these three kinds of taints that are external. What three? The taint of sensuality, the taint of existence, and the taint of ignorance. These are the three kinds of taints that are external. “There are these three kinds of fires that are external. What three? The fire of lust, the fire of hatred, and the fire of delusion. These are the three kinds of fires that are external. “There are these three kinds of arrows that are external. What three? The arrow of lust, the arrow of hatred, and the arrow of delusion. These are the three kinds of arrows that are external. “There are these three kinds of barbs that are external. What three? The barb of lust, the barb of hatred, and the barb of delusion. These are the three kinds of barbs that are external. “There are these three kinds of fevers that are external. What three? The fever of lust, the fever of hatred, and the fever of delusion. These are the three kinds of fevers that are external. “There are these three kinds of stains that are external. What three? The stain of lust, the stain of hatred, and the stain of delusion. These are the three kinds of stains that are external. “There are these three kinds of bonds that are external. What three? The bond of lust, the bond of hatred, and the bond of delusion. These are the three kinds of bonds that are external. “There are these three kinds of shackles that are external. What three? The shackle of lust, the shackle of hatred, and the shackle of delusion. These are the three kinds of shackles that are external. “There are these three kinds of obsessions that are external. What three? The obsession of lust, the obsession of hatred, and the obsession of delusion. These are the three kinds of obsessions that are external. “There are these three kinds of underlying tendencies that are external. What three? The underlying tendency to lust, the underlying tendency to hatred, and the underlying tendency to delusion. These are the three kinds of underlying tendencies that are external.”
“Bhikkhus, whatever is suffering, you should abandon desire for it, abandon lust for it, abandon desire-and-lust for it.
And what, bhikkhus, is suffering?
Forms, bhikkhus, are suffering; you should abandon desire for them, abandon lust for them, abandon desire-and-lust for them.”
Sounds … odors … tastes …
“Tangible objects … mental phenomena are suffering; in regard to them, desire must be abandoned, lust must be abandoned, and desire-and-lust must be abandoned.
Monks, in whatever is suffering, desire must be abandoned, lust must be abandoned, and desire-and-lust must be abandoned.”

Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.183–185 (SN 35.183, SN 35.172a, PTS SN iv 151) 17. Saṭṭhipeyyālavagga Bāhirānattachandādisutta (Discourse on External Non-Self and Desire, etc. “Monks, those ascetics and brahmins who do not understand as they really are the gratification, the danger, and the escape in the case of external forms, they cannot transcend craving for external forms; they cannot transcend desire for them, affection for them, thirst for them, passion for them, fever for them, and the underlying tendency toward them. Those ascetics and brahmins who do not understand as they really are the gratification, the danger, and the escape in the case of external sounds... external odors... external tastes... external tactile objects... external mental phenomena, they cannot transcend craving for external mental phenomena; they cannot transcend desire for them, affection for them, thirst for them, passion for them, fever for them, and the underlying tendency toward them. But, monks, those ascetics and brahmins who understand as they really are the gratification, the danger, and the escape in the case of external forms, they can transcend craving for external forms; they can transcend desire for them, affection for them, thirst for them, passion for them, fever for them, and the underlying tendency toward them. Those ascetics and brahmins who understand as they really are the gratification, the danger, and the escape in the case of external sounds... external odors... external tastes... external tactile objects... external mental phenomena, they can transcend craving for external mental phenomena; they can transcend desire for them, affection for them, thirst for them, passion for them, fever for them, and the underlying tendency toward them.”
“Bhikkhus, whatever is not-self, therein you should abandon desire, abandon lust, abandon desire-and-lust.
And what, bhikkhus, is not-self?
Form, bhikkhus, is not-self; therein you should abandon desire, abandon lust, abandon desire-and-lust.”
Sounds … odors … tastes …
“Tangible objects … mental phenomena are non-self; therein you must abandon desire, abandon lust, and abandon desire-and-lust.
Monks, whatever is non-self, therein you must abandon desire, abandon lust, and abandon desire-and-lust.”

Saṁyutta Nikāya 35.186 (SN 35.186, SN 35.173a, PTS SN iv 151) 17. Saṭṭhipeyyālavagga Ajjhattātītāniccasutta (The Discourse on the Internal and Past as Impermanent) "Bhikkhus, whatever is impermanent, whether internal or external, past or future, that is suffering. That which is suffering is not-self. That which is not-self should be seen with right wisdom as it really is: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self. When this was said, a certain bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: "Venerable sir, what now is the internal, and what is the external? "Bhikkhu, the eye is internal; forms are external. The ear is internal; sounds are external. The nose is internal; odors are external. The tongue is internal; tastes are external. The body is internal; tangibles are external. The mind is internal; mental phenomena are external. "Bhikkhus, whatever is impermanent, whether internal or external, past or future, that is suffering. That which is suffering is not-self. That which is not-self should be seen with right wisdom as it really is: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self. Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the instructed noble disciple experiences revulsion toward the eye, revulsion toward forms, revulsion toward the ear, revulsion toward sounds, revulsion toward the nose, revulsion toward odors, revulsion toward the tongue, revulsion toward tastes, revulsion toward the body, revulsion toward tangibles, and revulsion toward the mind, revulsion toward mental phenomena. Experiencing revulsion, he becomes dispassionate. Through dispassion, he is liberated. When liberated, there comes the knowledge: ‘It is liberated. He understands: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being.’"
“Bhikkhus, the eye of the past is impermanent … [and so on] … the tongue of the past is impermanent … [and so on] … the mind of the past is impermanent.
Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the well-taught noble disciple becomes disenchanted with the eye … [and so on] … becomes disenchanted with the tongue … [and so on] … becomes disenchanted with the mind.
Through disenchantment, he becomes dispassionate; through dispassion, he is liberated. When liberated, there arises the knowledge: ‘It is liberated.’”
“He understands: ‘Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.

Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.205 (SN 35.205, SN 35.179b, PTS SN iv 153) 17. Saṭṭhipeyyālavagga Ajjhattānāgatayadaniccasutta (The Discourse on Whatever is Impermanent Internally in the Future) "Bhikkhus, whatever is impermanent internally in the future: that is not mine, I am not that, that is not my self. This, bhikkhus, is how it should be seen with right wisdom as it really is: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self. When one sees it thus with right wisdom as it really is, one becomes disenchanted with what is impermanent internally in the future; one detaches from it; by detaching, one is liberated; when liberated, there comes the knowledge: ‘It is liberated. One understands: ‘Destroyed is birth, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being.’"
“Bhikkhus, the eye that has not yet arisen is impermanent.
What is impermanent is suffering;
what is suffering is non-self.”
That which is not-self should be seen as it really is with correct wisdom thus: "This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.

The Koṭṭhika Sutta.
On one occasion the Venerable Sāriputta and the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhika were dwelling at Bārāṇasī in the Deer Park at Isipatana.
Then, in the evening, the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhika emerged from seclusion and approached the Venerable Sāriputta; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Venerable Sāriputta.
Having exchanged courteous and memorable greetings, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhika said to the Venerable Sāriputta:
“Friend Sāriputta, is the eye the fetter of forms, or are forms the fetter of the eye?
… [and so on] … is the tongue the fetter of tastes, or are tastes the fetter of the tongue? … [and so on] …
“Is the mind the fetter of mental phenomena, or are mental phenomena the fetter of the mind?
“Friend Koṭṭhika, the eye is not the fetter of forms, nor are forms the fetter of the eye.
Rather, the desire and lust that arise there in dependence upon both of them—that is the fetter there... [and so on for the other sense bases].”
The tongue is not the fetter of tastes, nor are tastes the fetter of the tongue.

Rather, the desire and lust that arise there dependent upon both of them—that is the fetter there. … [and so on] … The mind is not the fetter of mental phenomena, nor are mental phenomena the fetter of the mind. Rather, the desire and lust that arise there dependent upon both of them—that is the fetter there.
And whatever desire and lust arise there in dependence upon both of those—that is the fetter there.
Just as, friends, a black ox and a white ox might be tied together by a single rope or yoke;
and someone were to say:
“If one were to say, ‘A black ox is the fetter for a white ox; a white ox is the fetter for a black ox,’ would he be speaking correctly?
“Certainly not, friend.
“Indeed, friend, a black ox is not the fetter for a white ox, nor is a white ox the fetter for a black ox.”
But that by which they are bound together—whether by a single rope or a cord—that is the fetter there.
In the same way, friends, the eye is not the fetter of forms, nor are forms the fetter of the eye.
Rather, the desire and lust that arise dependent upon both of them—that is the fetter there... [and so on for the other sense bases].
The tongue is not the fetter for tastes, nor are tastes the fetter for the tongue;
the mind is not the fetter for mental phenomena, nor are mental phenomena the fetter for the mind.
Whatever desire and lust arise there in dependence upon both of them—that is the fetter therein.
"Friends, if the eye were the fetter for forms, or if forms were the fetter for the eye, this living of the holy life for the complete destruction of suffering would not be discerned.
But because, friends, the eye is not the fetter for forms, nor are forms the fetter for the eye;

rather, the desire and lust that arise there in dependence upon both of them—that is the fetter there. Therefore, the living of the holy life for the complete destruction of suffering is discerned... [and so on]."
"Friends, if the tongue were the fetter for flavors, or if flavors were the fetter for the tongue, this living of the holy life for the complete destruction of suffering would not be discerned.

But because, friends, the tongue is not the fetter for flavors, nor are flavors the fetter for the tongue—rather, the desire and lust that arise there dependent upon both of these is the fetter therein; therefore, the living of the holy life [is discerned]."
"It is discerned for the complete destruction of suffering...

Friend, if the mind were the fetter of mental phenomena, or if mental phenomena were the fetter of the mind, this living of the holy life would not be discerned for the complete destruction of suffering.
But because, friend, the mind is not the fetter of mental phenomena, nor are mental phenomena the fetter of the mind..."
And whatever desire and lust arise there dependent upon both of these—that is the fetter there; therefore, the living of the holy life is discerned for the complete destruction of suffering.
By this method, friend, it should be understood how the eye is not the fetter of forms, nor are forms the fetter of the eye;
rather, whatever desire and lust arise there dependent upon both of these—that is the fetter there... [and so on].
The tongue is not the fetter of tastes, nor are tastes the fetter of the tongue;
the mind is not the fetter of mental phenomena, nor are mental phenomena the fetter of the mind.
Whatever desire and lust arise there dependent upon both of these—that is the fetter therein.
"Friends, the Blessed One possesses the eye;
the Blessed One sees forms with the eye.
Yet, in the Blessed One, there is no desire or lust."
The Blessed One is well-liberated in mind.
Friend, the ear exists for the Blessed One;
the Blessed One hears sound with the ear.
The Blessed One has no sensual lust.
The Blessed One is well-liberated in mind.
Yet, friend, the Blessed One possesses a nose.
The Blessed One smells an odor with the nose.
In the Blessed One there is no sensual lust;
the Blessed One is well-liberated in mind.
"Friends, the Blessed One possesses a tongue.
The Blessed One tastes flavors with his tongue.
Yet, in the Blessed One, there is no desire or lust."
The Blessed One is well-liberated in mind.
Friend, the body of the Blessed One still exists;
the Blessed One touches tangible objects with his body.
The Blessed One has no sensual lust.
The Blessed One is well-liberated in mind.
Yet, friend, the Blessed One possesses a mind.
The Blessed One cognizes mental phenomena with the mind.
In the Blessed One, there is no desire or lust.
The Blessed One is well-liberated in mind.
"By this method, friends, it should be understood how the eye is not the fetter of forms, nor are forms the fetter of the eye;
rather, the desire and lust that arise there dependent upon both of them—that is the fetter there. It is not the ear... [and so on for the other sense bases].

The nose is not the fetter for odors, nor are odors the fetter for the nose; rather, the desire and lust that arise there in dependence upon both of them—that is the fetter therein. The tongue is not the fetter for tastes, nor are tastes the fetter for the tongue; rather, the desire and lust that arise there in dependence upon both of them—that is the fetter therein.
The body is not a fetter for mental phenomena, nor are mental phenomena a fetter for the mind;
rather, the desire and lust that arise there dependent upon both of these— that is the fetter therein.”

Having exchanged greetings and pleasantries, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Venerable Kāmabhū said this to the Venerable Ānanda:
“Friend Ānanda, is the eye the fetter for forms, or are forms the fetter for the eye?
… [and so on] … is the tongue the fetter for tastes, or are tastes the fetter for the tongue? … [and so on] …
“Is it that the mind is the fetter of mental phenomena, and mental phenomena are the fetter of the mind?
“No, friend Kāmabhū, the eye is not the fetter of forms, nor are forms the fetter of the eye.
Rather, the desire and lust that arise there dependent upon both of them—that is the fetter there... [and so on for the other sense bases].”
The tongue is not the fetter of tastes, nor are tastes the fetter of the tongue...
[and so on] ...the mind is not the fetter of mental phenomena, nor are mental phenomena the fetter of the mind.
Whatever desire and lust arise there in dependence upon both of these—that is the fetter there.
"Suppose, friend, there were a black ox and a white ox tied together by a single rope or yoke.
Would anyone who spoke thus:
'The black ox is the fetter for the white ox; the white ox is the fetter for the black ox,' be speaking rightly?"
“No, friend. “Indeed, friend, the black ox is not the fetter for the white ox, nor is the white ox the fetter for the black ox.
Rather, that by which they are bound together—whether by a single rope or a yoke—that is the fetter there.”
In the same way, friends, the eye is not the fetter of forms, nor are forms the fetter of the eye; ...pe...
the tongue ...pe...
the mind ...pe...
"And whatever desire and lust arise there in dependence upon both of those—that is the fetter there.
The sixth.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 35.234. (SN 35.234, SN 35.193, PTS SN IV 166)
18. The Chapter on the Ocean:
The Discourse to Udāyī.
On one occasion, the Venerable Ānanda and the Venerable Udāyī were dwelling at Kosambī in Ghosita’s Park.
Then, in the evening, the Venerable Udāyī emerged from seclusion and approached the Venerable Ānanda. Having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Venerable Ānanda.
After exchanging polite and courteous conversation, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Venerable Udāyī said this to the Venerable Ānanda:
"Friend Ānanda, just as this body has been declared, revealed, and explained by the Blessed One in many ways:"

“Is it possible, friend Udāyī, to declare, teach, describe, establish, reveal, analyze, and clarify this consciousness in the same way as one might say: ‘Thus this body is non-self’—namely, ‘Thus this consciousness is non-self’?
“Just as this body, friend, has been declared, revealed, and explained by the Blessed One in many ways;”

“Just as it can be declared, taught, described, established, revealed, analyzed, and made plain that ‘thus this body is non-self,’ so too can it be declared, taught, described, established, revealed, analyzed, and made plain that ‘thus this consciousness is non-self.
“Friend, eye-consciousness arises dependent on the eye and forms,” [he said].
“Yes, friend,” [the other replied].
“Friend, if the cause and the condition for the arising of eye-consciousness were to cease entirely, in every way, and without remainder—would eye-consciousness still be discerned?
“No, friend. “It is by this method, friend, that it has been declared, revealed, and made plain by the Blessed One: ‘Thus, this consciousness is non-self. …pe…
“Friend, does tongue-consciousness arise dependent on the tongue and flavors?”—
“Yes, friend.”— “If, friend,
that cause and that condition for the arising of tongue-consciousness were to cease entirely, in every way and without remainder, would tongue-consciousness still be discerned?”
“No, friend.
“By this method also, friend, has it been declared, disclosed, and revealed by the Blessed One: ‘Thus this consciousness is non-self.
… [as before] … “And, friend, does mind-consciousness arise dependent on the mind and mental phenomena?”
“Yes, friend.
“Friend, if that cause and that condition for the arising of mind-consciousness were to cease entirely, in every way, completely, and without remainder, would mind-consciousness still be discerned?
“No, friend.”
“By this method also, friend, has it been declared, disclosed, and made clear by the Blessed One: ‘Thus this consciousness is non-self.
Suppose, friend, a man needing heartwood, seeking heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood, were to take a sharp axe and enter a forest.
There he would see a large plantain trunk, straight, fresh, and not gnarled.
One would cut it down at the root; having cut it down at the root, one would cut it off at the top; having cut it off at the top, one would peel away the leaf-sheaths.
Therein, one would not find even softwood, let alone heartwood.
Even so, friend, a bhikkhu does not regard himself or anything belonging to himself in the six bases of contact.
Thus, not viewing things in this way, one does not cling to anything in the world.
Not clinging, one is not agitated. Being unagitated, one personally attains final Nibbāna.
One understands: “Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.”
Seventh.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 35.235 (SN 35.235, SN 35.194, PTS SN iv 168) 18.
The Chapter on the Ocean (Samuddavagga)
The Discourse on the Simile of the Burning House:
“Monks, I will teach you the Dhamma discourse called ‘The Simile of the Burning.
Listen to it.”
And what, monks, is the discourse on the burning, the discourse on the Dhamma?

It would be better, monks, for the faculty of the eye to be completely rubbed away by a red-hot iron rod, burning, blazing, and glowing, than for one to grasp at the signs or secondary characteristics in forms cognizable by the eye.

For consciousness, monks, if it were to persist while persisting, would persist because it is attached to the gratification in signs; or it would persist because it is attached to the gratification in secondary characteristics.
Or if one were to die at that time, it is possible that one would go to one of two destinations:
either hell or the animal realm.
It is seeing this danger, monks, that I speak thus.

“Monks, it would be better for the ear faculty to be completely rubbed away by a sharp iron spike that is burning, blazing, and glowing, than to grasp at the signs or the details of sounds cognizable by the ear.

If consciousness, while persisting, were to persist attached to the gratification in signs or attached to the gratification in details, and if one were to die at that time, it is possible that one would go to one of two destinations: [either hell or the animal realm].”
Or the realm of hell, or the animal womb.
It is having seen this danger, monks, that I say this:

"Better, monks, it would be for one's sense of smell to be thoroughly rubbed away by a sharp nail-cutter that is burning, blazing, and glowing, than to grasp at the signs and secondary characteristics in odors cognizable by the nose."
“Bhikkhus, consciousness persisting while persisting might persist either attached to the gratification in signs or attached to the gratification in details.
If at that time one were to die, it is possible that one would go to one of two destinations:
either hell or the animal realm.”
"Having seen this danger, monks, I say this:

It would be better, monks, for the faculty of the tongue to be completely rubbed away by a sharp razor that is burning, blazing, and glowing, than to grasp at the signs or the secondary characteristics in tastes cognizable by the tongue.

For consciousness, monks, might persist while remaining attached to the gratification in the sign, or it might persist while remaining attached to the gratification in the secondary characteristics; and one might even pass away at that time."
"It is possible that he will go to one of two destinations:
either hell or the animal realm.
It is seeing this danger, monks, that I speak thus."

“Monks, it would be better for the body-faculty to be completely rubbed away by a sharp spear that is burning, blazing, and glowing, than to grasp at the signs or secondary characteristics in tactile objects cognizable by the body.

For if consciousness were to persist while clinging to satisfaction in the sign or clinging to satisfaction in the secondary characteristics, and if one were to die at that time, it is possible that one would go to one of two destinations: [the realm of hell or the animal realm].”
"Either hell or the animal realm.
It is having seen this danger, monks, that I say:
'Better, monks, is sleep.'"
But, bhikkhus, I say that sleep is barren for those who live; I say it is fruitless for those who live;
I say it is delusion for those who live—yet one should not entertain such thoughts as those by which, having fallen under their sway, one would cause a schism in the Saṅgha.
"Monks, having seen this fruitless danger in life, I speak thus.
In this regard, monks, the instructed noble disciple reflects:
'Let alone the eye-faculty being completely rubbed away by a red-hot iron pin, burning, blazing, and glowing.'"
"Come now, I shall attend to this very thing:
'The eye is impermanent, forms are impermanent, eye-consciousness is impermanent, eye-contact is impermanent;
and whatever feeling arises conditioned by eye-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too is impermanent.'"
Let alone the ear-faculty being completely destroyed by a sharp iron spike that is burning, blazing, and glowing.
Come now, I shall attend to this very thing:
"Thus, the ear is impermanent, sounds are impermanent, ear-consciousness is impermanent, ear-contact is impermanent, and whatever..."
Feeling—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that arises conditioned by ear-contact is also impermanent.
Let alone the nose-faculty being rubbed away by a sharp nail-cutter that is burning, blazing, and glowing;
come now, I shall attend only to this.

Thus the nose is impermanent, odors are impermanent, nose-consciousness is impermanent, nose-contact is impermanent, and whatever feeling arises conditioned by nose-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too is impermanent.
Let alone the tongue-faculty being completely rubbed away by a sharp razor that is burning, blazing, and glowing;
come now, I shall attend only to this: [the impermanence of the mind].

Thus the tongue is impermanent, tastes are impermanent, tongue-consciousness is impermanent, tongue-contact is impermanent, and whatever arises conditioned by tongue-contact …pe… that too is impermanent.
Let alone the tactile faculty being struck by a sharp spear that is burning, blazing, and glowing;
let me instead attend to this very thing: [the impermanence of the body].

"Thus the body is impermanent, tactile objects are impermanent, body-consciousness is impermanent, body-contact is impermanent, and whatever feeling arises conditioned by body-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neutral—that too is impermanent.
Let the ear be for now;
come, I shall attend to this very thing."
"Thus, the mind is impermanent; mental phenomena are impermanent; mind-consciousness is impermanent; mind-contact is impermanent;
and whatever feeling arises conditioned by mind-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too is impermanent.

Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the well-taught noble disciple becomes disenchanted with the eye, disenchanted with forms, disenchanted with eye-consciousness, and disenchanted with eye-contact... [and so on]...
Whatever feeling arises conditioned by mind-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—one becomes disenchanted with that as well.
Through disenchantment, one becomes dispassionate; through dispassion, one is liberated. In liberation, the knowledge arises: "It is liberated. One understands:
"Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being."
“This, monks, is the discourse on the burning, a discourse on the Dhamma.
The eighth.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 35.236 (SN 35.236, SN 35.195, PTS SN IV 171).
18. The Chapter on the Ocean.
The First Discourse on the Simile of Hands and Feet:
“Bhikkhus, when there are hands, the taking up and laying down of things is discerned;”
When there are feet, going forward and returning are discerned;
when there are limbs, bending and stretching are discerned;
when there is a belly, hunger and thirst are discerned.
In the same way, monks, when there is the eye, conditioned by eye-contact, there arises within one pleasure and pain...
[and so on] ...when there is the ear... the nose... the tongue... the body... when there is the mind, conditioned by mind-contact, there arises within one pleasure and pain... [and so on].
Monks, when hands do not exist, taking up and putting down are not discerned;
when feet do not exist, advancing and retreating are not discerned;
when joints do not exist, contracting and extending are not discerned.
"When there is no womb, hunger and thirst are not found.
Even so, monks, when the eye does not exist, conditioned by eye-contact, internal pleasure and pain do not arise...
[and so on] ...when the tongue does not exist, conditioned by tongue-contact, [internal pleasure and pain] do not arise..."
"When the mind does not exist, with the cessation of mind-contact as condition, internal pleasure and pain do not arise.
Thus ends the ninth [discourse]. Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.237 (SN 35.237, SN 35.196, PTS SN IV 171).
18. The Chapter on the Ocean (Samuddavagga) The Second Discourse on the Simile of the Hands and Feet:
“Monks, when there are hands, there is the taking up and putting down [of objects].”
When there are feet, there is advancing and retreating;
when there are limbs, there is bending and stretching;
when there is a belly, there is hunger and thirst.

In the same way, monks, when there is the eye, conditioned by eye-contact, there arises within one pleasure and pain... [and so on] ...when there is the ear... [and so on] ...when there is the nose...

[and so on] ...when there is the tongue... [and so on] ...when there is the body... [and so on] ...when there is the mind, conditioned by mind-contact, there arises within one pleasure and pain... [and so on].
Monks, when there are no hands, there is no taking up or laying down;
when there are no feet, there is no advancing or retreating;
when there are no limbs, there is no bending or stretching.
"When there is no womb, there is no hunger or thirst.
In the same way, monks, when there is no eye, conditioned by eye-contact, neither internal pleasure nor pain arises...
[and so on] ...when there is no tongue, conditioned by tongue-contact, neither internal pleasure nor pain arises."
"When the mind does not exist, conditioned by mental contact, internal pleasure and pain do not arise.
The tenth.
The third chapter on the Ocean.
Its summary verse:
Two oceans, the fisherman,
the milk-tree, and Koṭṭhika.
Kāmabhū and Udāyī,
with Āditta as the eighth;
and the two similes of the hand and the foot.
Thus the chapter is called by that name.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 35.238 (SN 35.238, SN 35.197, PTS SN IV 172). 19. The Chapter on the Venomous Snake (*Āsīvisavagga*).
The Discourse on the Simile of the Vipers:
“Bhikkhus, suppose there were four vipers of fierce power and deadly venom.
Then a man might come along, desiring life, not desiring death, desiring happiness, and averse to suffering.”
They would say this to him:

"Good man, these four venomous serpents of yours have fierce heat and terrible poison; they must be made to emerge from their holes at the proper time, bathed at the proper time, fed at the proper time, and put to bed at the proper time.
And whenever, good man, you [attend to] these four venomous serpents of fierce heat and terrible poison..."
"Either this one or that one will fall away; therefore, O man, you shall meet with death or with suffering amounting to death.
Do, O man, what must be done by you!"
Then, monks, that man, being afraid of those four venomous snakes of fierce power and terrible poison, would flee hither or thither.
Then they would say to him:
"Good man, here are five assassins and enemies following closely behind you, thinking: 'Wherever we see him, right there we shall deprive him of life.'"
“Whatever you must do, good man, do that!
Then, monks, that man, terrified of those four venomous snakes of fierce power and deadly poison, and terrified of the five assassins and enemies, would flee in one direction or another.
They would say to him:
‘Good man, this is your sixth assassin wandering within, following closely behind you with sword raised, thinking: “Wherever I see him, right there I shall strike off his head!
Good man, do whatever must be done.
Then, monks, that man was terrified of those four venomous snakes of fierce power and deadly poison.
Fearing the five executioners who were his enemies, and fearing the sixth executioner who followed him with a raised sword,
he would flee hither and thither.
He might then see an empty village.
Whatever house he might enter, he would enter it as empty, as hollow, as void.
Whatever vessel he might touch, he would touch it as empty, as hollow, as void.
They would say this to him:
"Now, good man, bandits who plunder villages are entering this empty village.
Do whatever you must do, good man!
Then, monks, that man, terrified of those four venomous snakes with their fierce power and terrible poison, [acted accordingly].
Fearing five murderous enemies, fearing a sixth murderer who stalks him with a raised sword,
and fearing bandits who plunder villages, he would flee hither and thither. He would see a vast expanse of water,
where the near shore was dangerous and fearful, while the far shore was safe and free from fear.
And for him there would be no boat to ferry across, nor a bridge to cross over, for going from the hither shore to the further shore.
Then, monks, that man would think thus:

‘This great expanse of water has a dangerous and perilous hither shore, while the further shore is safe and free from danger; yet there is neither a boat to ferry across nor a bridge to cross over for going from the hither shore to the further shore.’
‘What if I were to gather grass, sticks, branches, and foliage, bind them together into a raft, and relying on that raft, by exerting myself with my hands and feet, cross safely to the other shore?

Then, monks, that man would gather grass, sticks, branches, and foliage, bind them together into a raft, and relying on that raft, by exerting himself with his hands and feet, he would cross safely to the other shore; having crossed over...
The brahmin has gone to the further shore and stands on dry land.
Monks, this simile has been employed by me for the purpose of making the meaning known.
And here is the meaning:
“Monks, ‘four venomous serpents of fierce power and terrible poison’ is a designation for these four great elements:
the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the air element.
‘Five assassins and enemies,’ monks, is a designation for these five aggregates of clinging, namely:”

The aggregate of form subject to clinging, the aggregate of feeling subject to clinging, the aggregate of perception subject to clinging, the aggregate of volitional formations subject to clinging, and the aggregate of consciousness subject to clinging.
"The sixth assassin moving within with sword raised," monks, is a designation for delight and lust.
"The empty village," monks, is a designation for the six internal sense bases.
If, monks, a wise, competent, and intelligent person examines it from the perspective of the eye, it appears as empty, it appears as hollow, it appears as void...
[and so on] ...if, monks, he examines it from the perspective of the tongue...
[and so on] ...if, monks, a wise, competent, and intelligent person examines it from the perspective of the mind, it appears as empty, it appears as hollow, it appears as void.
“Bhikkhus, ‘robbers who plunder the village’ is a designation for these six external sense bases.
The eye, bhikkhus, is struck by agreeable and disagreeable forms;
the ear, bhikkhus, … [and so on] …”
The nose, monks, ...
the tongue, monks, is struck by agreeable and disagreeable tastes;
the body, monks, ... [is struck by agreeable and disagreeable tactile objects].
“Bhikkhus, the mind is struck by agreeable and disagreeable phenomena.
‘The great ocean,’ bhikkhus, is a designation for these four floods:
the flood of sensuality, the flood of existence, the flood of views, and the flood of ignorance.”
“Bhikkhus, ‘this shore’ is a designation for identity (*sakkāya*), which is fraught with danger and fear.
‘The further shore’ is a designation for *nibbāna*, which is secure and free from fear.
‘The raft,’ bhikkhus, is a designation for the Noble Eightfold Path; that is to say:”
“Right view... [and so on] ... right concentration.
‘He exerts with hands and feet,’ monks, is a designation for the arousal of energy.
‘The brahmin who has crossed over, gone beyond, and stands on firm ground,’ monks, is a designation for the arahant.”
First.
Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.239 (SN 35.239, SN 35.198, PTS SN iv 175) 19.
Āsīvisavagga (The Snake Chapter)
The Discourse on the Simile of the Chariot:
“Bhikkhus, possessing three qualities, a bhikkhu dwells abundant in happiness and joy in this very life, and the foundation for the destruction of the taints has been initiated for him.
What are the three? [Text continues]”
He is one who guards the doors of the sense faculties, is moderate in eating, and is devoted to wakefulness.
And how, monks, is a monk one who guards the doors of the sense faculties?
Here, monks, having seen a form with the eye, a monk does not grasp at its signs nor grasp at its secondary characteristics.
Since, if one were to dwell with this faculty of the eye unguarded, covetousness and dejection—evil, unwholesome states—might flow in upon him, he practices for its restraint;
he guards the faculty of the eye; he attains restraint over the faculty of the eye.
Having heard a sound with the ear...
Having smelled an odor with the nose… having tasted a flavor with the tongue… having touched a tangible object with the body…
Having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, he does not grasp at its signs or its secondary characteristics.
Since, if he were to dwell with the faculty of mind unrestrained, covetousness, dejection, and other evil unwholesome states might flow in upon him, he practices for its restraint;
he guards the faculty of mind; he achieves restraint over the faculty of mind.
“Bhikkhus, suppose there were a chariot harnessed to thoroughbreds standing on level ground at a crossroads,
with a goad ready at hand. A skilled trainer, a master of taming horses, having mounted it,
would take the reins in his left hand and the goad in his right hand, and drive it wherever he wishes, in whatever direction he desires, and bring it back again.
In the same way, monks, a monk trains for the guarding of these six sense faculties; he trains for their restraint, training for their taming, training for their pacification.
It is in this way, monks, that a monk is one whose doors of the senses are guarded.
And how, monks, is a monk moderate in eating?
In this case, monks, a monk reflects wisely and takes food:

"Neither for sport, nor for intoxication, nor for physical beauty, nor for adornment, but only for the maintenance and preservation of this body, for the allaying of hunger, and for supporting the holy life;
thus I shall put an end to old feelings [of hunger] and..."
‘I shall not give rise to new feeling, and there will be for me sustenance, blamelessness, and a comfortable abiding.
Just as, monks, a man would apply ointment to a wound only for the sake of its healing, or just as one would oil an axle only for the sake of carrying a load;
even so, monks, a monk reflects wisely and partakes of food:
‘Neither for sport, nor for intoxication, nor for adornment, nor for embellishment, but only for the maintenance and sustenance of this body,

for the allaying of hunger, for the promotion of the holy life, so that I may put an end to old feelings and not give rise to new feelings, and thus there shall be for me health, blamelessness, and a comfortable dwelling.’
In this way, monks, a monk is moderate in eating.
And how, monks, is a monk devoted to wakefulness?
Here, monks, during the day a monk purifies his mind of obstructive states while walking back and forth and sitting.
During the first watch of the night, he purifies his mind of obstructive states by means of walking and sitting.

During the middle watch of the night, he lies down on his right side in the lion’s posture, with one foot resting upon the other, mindful and clearly comprehending, having fixed his mind on the perception of rising.
During the last watch of the night, having risen, he purifies his mind of obstructive states by means of walking and sitting.
"In this way, monks, a monk is devoted to wakefulness.
Endowed with these three qualities, monks, a monk dwells abundant in happiness and joy in this very life, and the foundation for the destruction of the taints has been established for him.
This is the second [discourse].

Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.240 (SN 35.240, SN 35.199, PTS SN iv 177) 19. Āsīvisa-vagga The Simile of the Turtle “Bhikkhus, suppose there were a tortoise living in the great ocean. At the end of each hundred years it would once raise its head from the water. And suppose there were a yoke with a single hole, driven by the wind across the great ocean. Now what do you think, bhikkhus, would that tortoise, at the end of each hundred years raising its head from the water, eventually meet with that yoke with a single hole? “It is possible, venerable sir, that this tortoise, at the end of each hundred years raising its head from the water, might eventually meet with that yoke with a single hole. “But what do you think, bhikkhus, would that tortoise, at the end of each hundred years raising its head from the water, eventually meet with that yoke with a single hole even after a hundred thousand years, or two, three, four, five, or six hundred thousand years? “Even after a hundred thousand years, or two, three, four, five, or six hundred thousand years, it is still possible, venerable sir, that this tortoise, at the end of each hundred years raising its head from the water, might eventually meet with that yoke with a single hole. “So too, bhikkhus, it is possible that one who has not developed and cultivated the mind might eventually obtain a human state after many hundreds of thousands of eons. But when one has obtained a human state, it is possible that one will be born in a noble family or a brahmin family with great wealth and property. When one has been born in such a family, it is possible that one will hear the True Dhamma. When one has heard the True Dhamma, it is possible that faith will arise in one toward the Tathāgata.
