When faith has arisen, it is possible that one will go forth from the household life into homelessness. When one has gone forth, it is possible that one will develop and cultivate the mind so that one attains final knowledge in this very life. Therefore, bhikkhus, you should train yourselves thus: ‘We will develop and cultivate the mind so that we attain final knowledge in this very life. It is in such a way that you should train yourselves.”
“Once upon a time, monks, in the evening, a tortoise was seeking food along the bank of a river.
A jackal, too, monks, in the evening, was seeking food along the bank of that same river.
Then, monks, the tortoise saw the jackal from afar as he was seeking food.”
Having seen him, he drew his five limbs, including the trunk, into his own shell and lay there, indifferent and silent.
Then, monks, the jackal saw from afar the tortoise and turtle intent on feeding.
Having seen him, he approached the tortoise and turtle; having approached, he stood waiting before the tortoise and turtle.

‘When this tortoise, the turtle, extends any one of his five limbs—the four feet and the head—then we shall seize him right there, tear him apart, and eat him. But when, monks, the tortoise, the turtle, does not extend any one of his five limbs—the four feet and the head—then the jackal, finding no opportunity, departs from the tortoise in disappointment.

In the same way, monks, Māra the Evil One is constantly and continuously waiting for you: [thinking], ‘When these bhikkhus develop the mind of loving-kindness even for a single day, or for half a day, or for a meal-time, or for half a meal-time, or for as long as it takes to snap the fingers, then I will seize them right there, tear them apart, and eat them. But since, monks, these bhikkhus do not develop the mind of loving-kindness even for a single day, or for half a day, or for a meal-time, or for half a meal-time, or for as long as it takes to snap the fingers, Māra the Evil One, finding no opportunity, departs from them in disappointment.”
‘Perhaps I might find an opening through their eye...
[and so on] ...perhaps I might find an opening through their tongue...
[and so on] ...perhaps I might find an opening through their mind.’
Therefore, monks, dwell with the doors of the sense faculties guarded.
Having seen a form with the eye, do not grasp at its signs, nor grasp at its secondary details.
For when one dwells with this faculty of the eye unguarded, covetousness and dejection—evil, unwholesome states—might arise.

If, when you have gone to the forest, to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut, unwholesome, covetous, and unrighteous states of mind were to arise within you, you should practice for their restraint; guard the faculty of the eye, and attain restraint over the faculty of the eye.
Having heard a sound with the ear...
having smelled an odor with the nose...
Having tasted a flavor with the tongue...
having touched a tangible object with the body...
having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, do not grasp at its signs, and do not grasp at its secondary characteristics.
“Bhikkhus, since covetousness and dejection—evil, unwholesome states—might flow in upon one who dwells with this faculty of mind unrestrained, you should practice for its restraint;
guard the faculty of mind; attain restraint over the faculty of mind.
When you dwell with the doors of the faculties guarded, then Māra the Evil One, finding no opportunity, will depart from you in disappointment.”
Like a jackal from a tortoise:
as a tortoise draws its limbs within its own shell,
so should a bhikkhu withdraw his mental thoughts.
“Independent, not harming others,
fully extinguished, one should not revile anyone. Thus ends the third [verse].

Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.241 (SN 35.241, SN 35.200, PTS SN iv 179) 19. Āsīvisavagga First Discourse on the Simile of the Log “Bhikkhus, suppose a man were to throw a log of wood into a pit of fire that was burning with a great flame. If the log were to fall upon the embers, it would burn completely. What do you think, bhikkhus? Would that man be able to say: ‘I have thrown this log into the fire, and it has not burned’? “No, venerable sir. “Or suppose he were to say: ‘I have thrown this log into the fire, and it has burned away entirely. Would he be speaking truthfully? “Yes, venerable sir. “In the same way, bhikkhus, if a bhikkhu is asked: ‘What is the origin of form? What is its cessation? and he answers: ‘The origin of form is craving; its cessation is the remainderless fading away and cessation of that very craving,’ he would be answering correctly. “If he is asked: ‘What is the origin of feeling... perception... volitional formations... consciousness? What is their cessation? and he answers: ‘The origin of consciousness is craving; its cessation is the remainderless fading away and cessation of that very craving,’ he would be answering correctly. “Just as that man who threw the log into the fire could not truthfully say that it had not burned, so too, if a bhikkhu is asked about the origin and cessation of these five aggregates, and he answers accordingly, he is answering correctly. “Therefore, bhikkhus, you should train yourselves thus: ‘We shall understand as they really are the origin and the passing away of form; we shall understand as they really are the origin and the passing away of feeling... perception... volitional formations... consciousness. Thus, bhikkhus, should you train yourselves.”
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Kosambī on the bank of the river Gaṅgā.
There he saw a large log being carried away by the current of the river Gaṅgā.
Having seen it, he addressed the bhikkhus:
“Bhikkhus, do you see that great log being carried away by the current of the river Ganges?
“Yes, venerable sir.
“If, bhikkhus, that log does not go to the near shore, nor does it go to the far shore;”
It will not sink in mid-ocean, nor will it run aground on the shallows;
it will not be seized by human beings, nor seized by non-human beings, nor seized by whirlpools; nor will it become rotten within.
For in this way, monks, that log will slope toward the ocean, incline toward the ocean, and tend toward the ocean.
For what reason?
Monks, the current of the river Ganges flows toward the ocean, inclines toward the ocean, and tends toward the ocean.
Even so, monks, if you do not approach the hither shore, nor approach the further shore;

"You will not sink in the middle, nor will you founder on the shore; you will not be seized by a human predator, nor seized by a non-human predator, nor seized by a whirlpool; you will not become internally putrid.
In this way, monks, you will be inclined toward Nibbāna, sloping toward Nibbāna, leaning toward Nibbāna.
For what reason? Because..."
“Bhikkhus, right view slants toward Nibbāna, inclines toward Nibbāna, and tends toward Nibbāna.
When this was said, a certain bhikkhu asked the Blessed One:

“Venerable sir, what is the near shore? What is the far shore? What is the whirlpool in midstream? What is the high ground on dry land? What is the seizure by humans? What is the seizure by non-humans? What is the seizure by a whirlpool? What is the state of internal putrefaction?”
“‘This shore,’ bhikkhu, is a designation for these six internal sense bases.
‘The further shore,’ bhikkhu, is a designation for these six external sense bases.
‘The whirlpool in between,’ bhikkhu, is a designation for delight and lust.”
“‘A rise on dry land,’ bhikkhu, is a designation for the conceit ‘I am.
And what, bhikkhu, is the grasping after men?

Here, bhikkhu, one dwells in close association with householders, sharing their joys and sorrows; one is happy in their happiness and suffers in their suffering, and when there are duties or tasks that have arisen, one personally engages in them.”
This, bhikkhu, is called grasping for the human state.
And what, bhikkhu, is grasping for the non-human state?

Here, bhikkhu, a certain person leads the holy life aspiring to a particular class of devas, thinking: “By this virtue, or observance, or austerity, or holy life, I shall become a deva or some other kind of deva.”
This, bhikkhu, is called being seized by a non-human being.
“Being ensnared,” bhikkhu, is a designation for the five strands of sensual pleasure.
And what, bhikkhu, is internal corruption?

“Here, bhikkhu, a certain person is immoral, of evil nature, impure and suspicious in his conduct, secretive in his actions, not a recluse though claiming to be one, not living the holy life though claiming to do so, inwardly rotten, leaking, and corrupt.
This, bhikkhu, is called ‘inward rottenness.
Now at that time, Nanda the cowherd was standing not far from the Blessed One.
Then Nanda the cowherd said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, I shall not go to the near shore, nor shall I go to the far shore;
I shall not sink in midstream, nor shall I be stranded on dry land; neither shall I be seized by human predators, nor by non-human predators.”
“I shall not take hold [of them] by the horns; I shall not take hold by twisting them; I shall not become internally putrid.
Venerable Sir, may I receive the going-forth in the presence of the Blessed One; may I receive the full ordination.
“In that case, Nanda, you must hand over the cows to their owners.”
“They will go away, Bhante, the cows longing for their calves.

“Nanda, you must hand over the cows to your owners,” [the Blessed One said]. Then the cowherd Nanda, having handed over the cows to his owners, approached the Blessed One; having approached, he spoke thus to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, the cows have been returned to their owners.
May I receive the going-forth in the presence of the Blessed One; may I receive full ordination.
Then Nanda the cowherd received the going-forth in the presence of the Blessed One; he received full ordination.
Not long after his full ordination, the Venerable Nanda, dwelling alone and withdrawn...
[as before] ...the Venerable Nanda became one of the Arahants. Thus ends the fourth [discourse].

Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.242 (SN 35.242, SN 35.201, PTS SN iv 181) 19. Āsīvisavagga The Second Simile of the Log “Bhikkhus, suppose a man were to throw a log of wood into a great forest. It would be struck by a thunderbolt and split into two pieces. A man would come along seeking heartwood, desiring heartwood, searching for heartwood. He would think: ‘This log of wood has been struck by a thunderbolt and split into two pieces. Perhaps there might be some heartwood here. He would cut it into lengths, split the lengths into slabs, and split the slabs into splinters. Having split them into splinters, he would blow on them to remove the dust, and then examine them carefully. As he examined them carefully, he would not find even soft heartwood, let alone hard heartwood. “So too, bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu examines form as impermanent, he does not find any self in form; when he examines feeling... perception... volitional formations... consciousness as impermanent, he does not find any self in consciousness. “When, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu does not find any self in form, nor any self in feeling, nor any self in perception, nor any self in volitional formations, nor any self in consciousness, he is called a bhikkhu who dwells with mind well-released, a bhikkhu who has reached the ultimate end of the spiritual life, a bhikkhu who has done what was to be done, a bhikkhu who has laid down the burden, a bhikkhu who has lived the holy life, a bhikkhu whose goal is accomplished, a bhikkhu who is completely liberated through final knowledge. “This, bhikkhus, is the highest noble truth among the noble truths, namely: ‘This is the cessation of suffering. And this is the highest noble practice among the noble practices, namely: ‘This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.’”
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Kimilā on the bank of the river Gaṅgā.
There the Blessed One saw a large log being carried away by the current of the river Gaṅgā.
Having seen it, he addressed the bhikkhus:
“Do you see, monks, that great log of wood being carried away by the current of the river Ganges?
“Yes, venerable sir.
… [as before] … When this was said, the Venerable Kimila addressed the Blessed One as follows:
“Venerable sir, what is the near shore?
… [as before] … And what, Kimila, is being rotten within?
Here, Kimila, a bhikkhu has fallen into some defiled offense for which no means of rehabilitation is prescribed.”
“This, Kimila, is called internal corruption.
The fifth.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 35.243 (SN 35.243, SN 35.202, PTS SN IV 182).
19. The Snake Chapter.
Discourse on the Way of the Lustful.
At one time the Blessed One was dwelling among the Sakyans at Kapilavatthu in the Nigrodha Park.
Now at that time, a new assembly hall had recently been built by the Sakyans of Kapilavatthu, which had not yet been occupied by any ascetic, brahmin, or human being.
Then the Sakyans of Kapilavatthu approached the Blessed One;
having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, they sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the Sakyans of Kapilavatthu said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, here the Sakyans of Kapilavatthu have recently had a new assembly hall built, which has not yet been inhabited by any ascetic, brahmin, or human being.
Venerable sir, may the Blessed One be the first to use it;
once the Blessed One has used it first, afterwards the Sakyans of Kapilavatthu will use it.”
"That will be for the long-term welfare and happiness of the Sakyans of Kapilavatthu.
The Blessed One consented by remaining silent.
Then the Sakyans of Kapilavatthu, understanding the Blessed One’s consent, rose from their seats and [approached] the Blessed One.
Having paid homage and circumambulated him, they approached the new assembly hall.
Having arrived, they spread a complete carpet over the assembly hall, prepared seats, set out a water jar, and lit an oil lamp.
Then they approached the Blessed One and said this to him:
“Venerable sir, the assembly hall has been completely strewn with carpets, seats have been prepared, a water-jar has been set out, and an oil lamp has been raised.
Now, venerable sir, let the Blessed One do as he deems fit.
Then the Blessed One dressed, took his bowl and robe, and went together with the Saṅgha of bhikkhus to the new assembly hall.
He approached [the assembly hall]; having approached and washed his feet, he entered the assembly hall and sat down leaning against the central pillar, facing eastward.
The community of monks also, having washed their feet, entered the assembly hall and sat down leaning against the western wall, facing eastward with the Blessed One at their head.
The Sakyans of Kapilavatthu, having washed their feet, entered the assembly hall and sat down against the eastern wall facing west, with the Blessed One before them.
Then the Blessed One, having instructed, urged, inspired, and gladdened the Sakyans of Kapilavatthu for much of the night with a discourse on the Dhamma, dismissed them, saying:
"The night has passed, Gotamas."
"Now is the time for you to do as you think fit.

"So be it, Bhante," the Sakyans of Kapilavatthu replied to the Blessed One. Having risen from their seats, they paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him keeping him to their right, and departed.
Then, not long after the Sakyans of Kapilavatthu had left, the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna:
“Moggallāna, the Saṅgha of bhikkhus is free from sloth and torpor.
Let a Dhamma talk occur to you, Moggallāna, for the bhikkhus.
My back is aching.”
“I shall lie down upon him.
“Very well, Bhante,” the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna replied to the Blessed One.

Then the Blessed One, having spread out his outer robe folded fourfold, lay down on his right side in the lion’s posture, placing one foot upon the other, mindful and clearly comprehending, having fixed his mind on the perception of rising.
There, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna addressed the bhikkhus:
"Friends, bhikkhus.
"Friend," those bhikkhus replied to the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna.
The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna said this:
"Friends, I will teach you the discourse on the lustful and the discourse on the non-lustful.
Listen to it and attend closely; I shall speak."
“Yes, friend,” those bhikkhus replied to the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna.
The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna said this:
“In what way, friends, is one ‘tainted’?”

"Here, friends, having seen a form with the eye, a bhikkhu is intent upon a pleasing form and reacts with aversion toward a displeasing form. He dwells with unestablished mindfulness of the body and with a limited mind;
he does not understand, as it really is, that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom wherein those arisen evil unwholesome states cease without remainder...
[and so on] ...having tasted a flavor with the tongue..."
Having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, one becomes attached to phenomena that are pleasing and feels aversion toward phenomena that are unpleasing;

one dwells without mindfulness established in the body and with a limited mind, and does not understand as it really is that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom wherein those arisen evil, unwholesome phenomena cease without remainder.
This, friends, is called a bhikkhu who is "outflowing" regarding forms cognizable by the eye... [and so on].
Lusting after tastes cognizable by the tongue … pe … lusting after mental phenomena cognizable by the mind.
When a bhikkhu dwells in such a way, friends, if Māra approaches him even from the eye, Māra gains an opening; Māra gains a foothold … pe …
If Māra approaches him through the tongue, Māra gains an opening; Māra gains an object. ... [and so on] ...
If Māra approaches him through the mind, Māra gains an opening; Māra gains an object.
It is just as if, friends, there were a reed-thicket or a grass-thicket, dry, withered, and standing for only a year.
If a man were to approach him from the eastern direction with a burning grass torch, the fire would surely find an opening, the fire would find a foothold;
and if a man were to approach him from the western direction with a burning grass torch...
[and so on] ...if a man were to approach him from the northern direction... [and so on].
If it were from the southern direction... [and so on] ...if it were from below... [and so on] ...or if it were from above...
If a man were to approach it from anywhere with a burning grass torch, the fire would certainly find an opening; the fire would certainly find an opportunity.
Even so, friends, if Māra approaches a bhikkhu who dwells in such a way through the eye, Māra will certainly find an opening; Māra will certainly find an opportunity...
[and so on] ...if Māra approaches him through the tongue... [and so on].
If Māra approaches him even from the mind, Māra indeed finds an opening; Māra finds an objective basis.
For a bhikkhu dwelling in such a way, friends, forms overcome him, and he does not overcome forms;
sounds overcome the bhikkhu, and he does not overcome sounds.
Odors have overcome the bhikkhu, the bhikkhu has not overcome odors;
tastes have overcome the bhikkhu, the bhikkhu has not overcome tastes;
tangibles have overcome the bhikkhu, the bhikkhu has not overcome tangibles.
Phenomena overwhelm the monk; the monk does not overwhelm phenomena.

This, friends, is called a monk who is overwhelmed by forms, overwhelmed by sounds, overwhelmed by odors, overwhelmed by tastes, overwhelmed by tangibles, and overwhelmed by phenomena—one who is overwhelmed, not one who overcomes, whom evil unwholesome states have overwhelmed.
"Phenomena that are subject to defilement, leading to renewed existence, accompanied by distress, resulting in suffering, and pertaining to future birth, aging, and death.
In this way, friend, one is 'inundated.
And how, friend, is one 'not inundated'?"
"Here, friends, having seen a form with the eye, a bhikkhu is not intent upon a pleasing form and does not feel aversion toward a displeasing form.

He dwells with mindfulness established in the body and with a mind immeasurable, and he understands as it really is that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom wherein those arisen evil unwholesome states cease without remainder...
[and so on] ...having tasted a flavor with the tongue..."
Having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, he is not intent upon agreeable phenomena nor does he feel aversion toward disagreeable phenomena;

he dwells with mindfulness established in the body and with a mind immeasurable, and he understands as it really is that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom wherein those arisen evil unwholesome states cease without remainder.
This, friends, is called a bhikkhu who is untainted regarding forms cognizable by the eye... [and so on].
He is untainted regarding mental phenomena cognizable by the mind.
Friends, when a bhikkhu dwells thus, even if Māra approaches him through the eye, Māra finds no opening and finds no foothold...
even if Māra approaches him through the tongue... [and so on].
Even if Māra approaches him from the mind, Māra finds no opening and finds no foothold.

Just as, friends, if there were a gabled house or a hall with thick clay walls and a smooth plaster coating, and a man were to approach it from the eastern direction with a burning grass torch, the fire would find no opening and find no foothold... [and so on for the other directions].
If one were to direct it toward the west...
if one were to direct it toward the north...
if one were to direct it toward the south...
Even if a man were to approach it from below with a blazing grass torch, or even from above, or from any direction whatsoever, the fire would find no opening and would find no foothold.
In the same way, friends, if Māra approaches a bhikkhu who dwells thus, even through the eye, Māra finds no opening and finds no foothold...
[and so on] ...even if Māra approaches him through the mind, Māra finds no opening and finds no foothold.
A bhikkhu who dwells thus, friends, masters forms; forms do not master the bhikkhu.
The bhikkhu overcomes sounds; sounds do not overcome the bhikkhu.
The bhikkhu overcomes odors; odors do not overcome the bhikkhu.
The bhikkhu overcomes tastes; tastes do not overcome the bhikkhu.
The bhikkhu overcame tangible objects; tangible objects did not overcome the bhikkhu.
The bhikkhu overcame mental phenomena; mental phenomena did not overcome the bhikkhu.
This, friends, is called a bhikkhu who has overcome forms, who has overcome sounds, who has overcome odors, who has overcome tastes, and who has overcome tangible objects.
One who has mastery over phenomena, a conqueror, unconquered— such a one overcomes those evil, unwholesome states that lead to defilement,
to renewed existence, to agitation, that result in suffering, and lead to birth, aging, and death in the future.
It is in this way, friend, that one is "unflooded."
Then the Blessed One rose and addressed the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna:
“Excellent, excellent, Moggallāna!
It is well indeed that you have spoken to the bhikkhus on the discourse concerning the lustful and the discourse concerning the non-lustful.”
Thus spoke the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna.
The Teacher approved.
Those bhikkhus, being uplifted, rejoiced in the words of the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna.
The Sixth.
Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.244 (SN 35.244, SN 35.203, PTS SN iv 188) 19.
Āsīvisavagga (The Snake Chapter)
The Discourse on Phenomena Subject to Suffering “Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu understands, as they really are, the origin and the passing away of all phenomena subject to suffering,

then sensual pleasures are seen by him in such a way that, while he sees them, whatever desire for sensual pleasures, affection for sensual pleasures, infatuation with sensual pleasures, and feverish passion for sensual pleasures there may be do not underlie his mind.”
Moreover, his way of conduct and his mode of dwelling are such that, while he conducts himself and dwells in this way, covetousness, dejection, and evil unwholesome states do not persist within him.

And how, monks, does one understand, as they really are, the origin and the passing away of all things subject to suffering? "Such is form, such its origin, such its passing away; such is feeling... such is perception... such are volitional formations...
such is consciousness, such its origin, such its passing away."
Thus is feeling...
thus is perception...
thus are volitional formations...
‘Such is consciousness, such is the origin of consciousness, such is the passing away of consciousness.
It is in this way, monks, that a monk understands, as they really are, the origin and the passing away of all things that are subject to suffering.

And how, monks, are sensual pleasures seen by a monk? It is when, as he sees sensual pleasures, whatever desire for sensual pleasures, affection for sensual pleasures, infatuation with sensual pleasures, and feverish passion for sensual pleasures there may be, do not underlie his mind.
“Monks, suppose there were a charcoal pit deeper than a man’s height, filled with glowing coals, smokeless and emberless.
Then a man might come along, desiring life, not desiring death, seeking pleasure and recoiling from pain.
Two strong men, seizing him by both arms, might drag him toward that charcoal pit. He would twist his body this way and that.”
For what reason?
Because that man knows, monks: "I am about to fall into this pit of coals; on account of that, I will meet death or suffering amounting to death.

In the same way, monks, sensual pleasures are seen by a bhikkhu as being like a pit of coals, such that as he views sensual pleasures, whatever desire for sensual pleasures, affection for sensual pleasures, infatuation with sensual pleasures, or fever for sensual pleasures there may be, does not underlie his mind.
"And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu’s course and dwelling understood, such that while he courses and dwells thus, covetousness and dejection—evil, unwholesome states—do not flow over him?
Suppose, bhikkhus, a man were to enter a thicket full of thorns.
There would be a thorn before him, a thorn behind him, a thorn to his north, a thorn to his south, and a thorn below him."
"Even above there is a thorn. One should advance mindfully and retreat mindfully, thinking: 'Lest the thorn [pierce] me.
In the same way, monks, whatever in the world is of a pleasant nature and of a delightful nature—this, in the discipline of the Noble One, is called a thorn.
Having understood this, restraint and non-restraint are to be known.
And how, monks, does lack of restraint come about?

Here, monks, having seen a form with the eye, a monk becomes obsessed by a form that is pleasing, he becomes repelled by a form that is unpleasing, and he dwells with mindfulness of the body unestablished and with a limited mind;
he does not understand, as it really is, that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom wherein those arisen evil, unwholesome states cease without remainder... [as before] ...
Having tasted a flavor with the tongue …pe… having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind,
one becomes attached to agreeable phenomena and feels aversion toward disagreeable phenomena; one dwells with unestablished mindfulness of the body and with a limited mind,
and does not understand as it really is that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom wherein those arisen evil, unwholesome states cease without remainder.
In this way, monks, there is non-restraint.
And how, monks, is there restraint?

Here, monks, a bhikkhu, having seen a form with the eye, is not infatuated with a pleasing form, nor does he feel aversion toward an unpleasing form; he dwells with mindfulness established regarding the body and with a mind of immeasurable range.
And he understands, as it really is, that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom wherein those arisen evil unwholesome states cease without remainder...
Having tasted a flavor with the tongue...

Having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, he is not intent upon agreeable phenomena and does not feel aversion toward disagreeable phenomena; he dwells with mindfulness established in the body and with a mind of boundless measure.
And he understands, as it really is, that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom wherein those arisen evil unwholesome states cease without remainder.
In this way, monks, there is restraint.
But if, monks, while that bhikkhu is practicing and dwelling in this way, at some time through a lapse of mindfulness...
Evil, unwholesome, sensual thoughts that lead to fetters arise; slow, monks, is the arising of mindfulness.
Yet he quickly abandons them, dispels them, brings them to an end, and causes them to vanish.
Just as if, monks, a man were to drop two or three drops of water into an iron cauldron heated all day.
It would fall. Monks, the falling of drops of water is slow, yet they quickly reach exhaustion and disappearance.
Even so, monks, if for that bhikkhu who conducts himself thus and dwells thus, at some time or other...
"Evil, unwholesome thoughts of sensual desire, which are fetters, arise through a lapse of mindfulness. But, bhikkhus, the arising of mindfulness is swift.
Then one quickly abandons them, dispels them, brings them to an end, and makes them non-existent.
It is in this way, bhikkhus, that a bhikkhu’s course and abiding are well understood, such that while he courses and abides, covetousness and dejection—evil, unwholesome states—do not flow into him."
If, monks, while a bhikkhu is living and dwelling in such a way, kings or royal ministers, friends, colleagues, relatives, or kinsmen should invite him with wealth, saying:
"Come, good man! Why do these saffron robes burn you?
Why do you wander about shaven-headed with a bowl?"
"Come, having turned back to the inferior life, enjoy wealth and perform meritorious deeds.
Monks, it is impossible that a monk who conducts himself thus and dwells thus would renounce the training and turn back to the inferior life; such a thing cannot happen.
Monks, it is just as if the river Ganges were inclined toward the east, sloping toward the east, and flowing toward the east, and then a great multitude of people...
Suppose someone were to come along carrying a spade and a basket, saying: "We shall make this river Ganges slope westward, incline westward, and flow westward.
What do you think, monks?
“Would that great multitude of people then cause the river Ganges to flow westward, to incline westward, and to trend westward?
“Certainly not, venerable sir.
“And for what reason?”
“Venerable sir, the river Ganges slants, slopes, and inclines toward the east;
it is not easy to make it slant, slope, and incline toward the west.
Moreover, that great multitude of people would only partake of exhaustion and frustration.”
“In the same way, monks, if kings or royal ministers, friends, colleagues, relatives, or kinsmen should invite a bhikkhu who is practicing and dwelling in this manner with wealth, saying:
‘Come, good man! Why do these saffron robes burn you?
Why do you wander about shaven-headed with a begging bowl?’”
"Come, having turned back to the inferior life, enjoy wealth and perform meritorious deeds.
Monks, it is impossible that a monk who conducts himself thus and dwells thus would, having renounced the training, turn back to the inferior life. Why is that?
“Bhikkhus, as for that mind which for a long time has slanted toward seclusion, inclined toward seclusion, and tended toward seclusion—it is impossible that it would turn back toward the inferior.
The seventh.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 35.245 (SN 35.245, SN 35.204, PTS SN IV 191).
19. The Chapter on the Viper: The Discourse on the Simile of the Kiṃsuka Tree.
Then a certain bhikkhu approached another bhikkhu; having approached him, he said this to that bhikkhu:
“To what extent, friend, is a bhikkhu’s vision well-purified?
“When, friend, a bhikkhu understands as they really are the arising and the passing away of the six bases of contact, to that extent, friend, a bhikkhu’s vision is well-purified.
Then that bhikkhu, dissatisfied with that bhikkhu’s answer to his question, approached another bhikkhu and said to him:
“To what extent, friend, is a bhikkhu’s vision well-purified?
“When, friend, a bhikkhu understands as they really are the origin and the passing away of the five aggregates of clinging, to that extent, friend, a bhikkhu’s vision is well-purified.
Then that bhikkhu, dissatisfied with that bhikkhu’s answer to his question, approached another bhikkhu and said to him:
“To what extent, friend, is a bhikkhu’s vision well-purified?
“When, friend, a bhikkhu understands as they really are the origin and the passing away of the four great elements, to that extent, friend, a bhikkhu’s vision is well-purified.
Then that bhikkhu, dissatisfied with that bhikkhu’s answer to his question, approached another bhikkhu and said to him:
“To what extent, friend, is a bhikkhu’s vision well-purified?
“When, friend, a bhikkhu understands as it really is that whatever is subject to arising is all subject to cessation—to this extent, friend, a bhikkhu’s vision is well-purified.
Then that bhikkhu, dissatisfied with that bhikkhu’s answer to his question, approached the Blessed One.
He approached him and, having approached, said this to the Blessed One:
"Here, Bhante, I approached a certain bhikkhu and, having approached, said this to that bhikkhu:
'To what extent, friend, is a bhikkhu’s vision well-purified?’"
When this was said, venerable sir, that bhikkhu said to me:
“When, friend, a bhikkhu understands as they really are the arising and the passing away of the six bases of contact, to that extent, friend, a bhikkhu’s vision is well-purified.
Then, venerable sir, dissatisfied with that bhikkhu’s answer to my question, I approached another bhikkhu and, having approached him, said this to that bhikkhu:
“In what way, friend, is a bhikkhu’s vision well-purified?
When this was said, bhante, that bhikkhu said this to me:
“When, friend, a bhikkhu [regarding] the five aggregates of clinging …” [and so forth].
“He understands, as it really is, the arising and the passing away of the four great elements...
he understands, as it really is, that whatever is subject to arising is all subject to cessation. “Friend, it is to this extent that a bhikkhu’s vision is well-purified.
Then, venerable sir, dissatisfied with that bhikkhu’s answer to my question, I approached the Blessed One. (...)
“To what extent, venerable sir, is a bhikkhu’s vision well-purified?
“Suppose, bhikkhu, there was a man who had never seen a *kiṁsuka* tree before.
He would approach a certain man who was familiar with the *kiṁsuka* tree. Having approached him, he would say to that man:”
‘What kind of tree, good man, is the *kiṁsuka*?
He would say this:
‘The *kiṁsuka*, good man, is black—just like a charred stump.’
Moreover, monk, at that time the *kiṃsuka* tree would be exactly as that man had seen it.
Then, monk, that man, dissatisfied with that man’s answer to his question, would approach another man who was an observer of the *kiṃsuka* tree; having approached him, he would say to that man:
“Sir, what is a *kiṃsuka* tree like?”
Then one might say:
“Good man, the *kiṃsuka* tree is red, just like a piece of flesh.
For at that time, monk, the *kiṃsuka* tree would appear to that person exactly as it was seen by him.

Then that monk, being dissatisfied with that man’s explanation of the question, might approach another man who was an eyewitness to the *kiṃsuka* tree; having approached him, he would say to that man:
"Sir, what is a *kiṃsuka* like? He would reply:
“‘O man, the *kiṃsuka* tree has indeed produced its bark, yet it is like a *sirīsa* tree because its shoots have not yet emerged.
Now at that time, O bhikkhu, the *kiṃsuka* tree was exactly as that man perceived it to be.

Then that man, dissatisfied with the other man’s answer to his question, would approach another man who was an expert in observing *kiṃsuka* trees; having approached him, he would speak to that man thus:”
‘What kind of tree is a *kiṃsuka*, good man?
He would say this:
‘A *kiṃsuka*, good man, has thick foliage and leaves and provides abundant shade, just like a banyan tree.’”
"And at that time, bhikkhu, the *kiṃsuka* tree was just like the vision of that man.
In the same way, bhikkhu, to whatever extent the vision of those true persons is well-purified for those who are intent upon them, to that same extent has it been declared by those true persons.
Just as if, bhikkhu, there were a king’s frontier city with strong foundations, strong ramparts and gate-towers, and six gates."
There, his gatekeeper would be wise, competent, and intelligent—one who keeps out strangers and admits those he knows.
Suppose a pair of swift messengers were to come from the eastern direction and say to that gatekeeper:
“Sir, where is the lord of this city?”
Then one might say:
“Venerable sir, here he is, sitting in the middle of the crossroads.
Then that pair of swift messengers, having delivered the message to the master of the city exactly as it was, would set out upon the path by which they had come.
A swift pair of messengers coming from the western direction... [and] a swift pair of messengers coming from the northern direction...
[and] a swift pair of messengers coming from the southern direction would say this to that doorkeeper:
‘Sir, where is the owner of this city?
He would say:
‘Venerable sir, he is sitting there at the center of the crossroads.’”
Then that pair of swift messengers, having delivered the message exactly as it was to the owner of the city, would set out on the path by which they had come.
This simile, monk, has been made by me for the purpose of making the meaning known.
And this is the meaning here:

“‘City,’ bhikkhu, is a designation for this body composed of the four great elements, born of mother and father, nourished by boiled rice and gruel, subject to impermanence, to being rubbed and massaged, and to breaking up and disintegration.
‘Six gates,’ bhikkhu, is a designation for the six internal sense bases.
‘Gatekeeper,’ bhikkhu, is a designation for mindfulness.”
“‘A swift pair of messengers,’ bhikkhu, is a designation for serenity and insight.
‘The lord of the city,’ bhikkhu, is a designation for consciousness.
‘The crossroads in the center,’ bhikkhu, is a designation for the four great elements.”
The earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the air element.
“‘Speech as it really is,’ bhikkhu, is a designation for Nibbāna.
‘The path as it has come to be,’ bhikkhu, is a designation for the Noble Eightfold Path; that is to say:”
“...of right view ... up to ... right concentration.
The eighth.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 35.246 (SN 35.246, SN 35.205, PTS SN IV 195).
19. The Chapter on the Venomous Snake:

The Simile of the Lute “Bhikkhus, if in any bhikkhu or bhikkhunī, desire, lust, hatred, delusion, or even mental resentment should arise toward forms cognizable by the eye, they should restrain the mind from that.”
"This path is fearful and terrifying; it is thorny, overgrown, a bypath, a wrong road, and difficult to traverse.
This path is frequented by the ignoble, not frequented by the noble.
You ought not to follow it."
Then one should restrain the mind from forms cognizable by the eye...
[and so on] ...Monks, whatever desire, lust, hatred, delusion, or mental resentment might arise in a monk or a nun toward tastes cognizable by the tongue...
[and so on] ...or toward mental phenomena cognizable by the mind—one should restrain the mind from that.
"This path is fearful and terrifying; it is thorny, overgrown, a wrong road, a bypath, and difficult to traverse.
This path is frequented by wicked persons; it is not frequented by the virtuous.
You are not worthy of this."
Then one should restrain the mind from mental phenomena cognizable by the mind.
Bhikkhus, it is just as if there were a field of grain that had ripened,
and the guardian of the grain were negligent, while a grain-eating ox, having descended into that field, would eat its fill and become intoxicated with negligence.

"In the same way, monks, the uninstructed worldling, acting without restraint toward the six bases of contact, falls into intoxication and negligence to his heart's content regarding the five cords of sensual pleasure.
Just as, monks, if a field were full of grain and the guardian of the field were negligent while a bull that eats grain were to descend upon that grain,
the guardian of the field would seize him firmly by the nose."
Having grasped it firmly by the nose, one would hold it securely by the upper jaw;
having held it securely by the upper jaw, one would strike it well with a staff;
and having struck it well with the staff, one would let it go.
A second time, monks, and even a third time,
monks, the grain-eating ox might descend into that grain.
Then the grain-guard would seize it firmly by the nose.
Having grasped it firmly by the nose, he would hold it securely by the upper jaw;
having held it securely by the upper jaw, he would strike it well with a stick;
having struck it well with a stick, he would let it go.
"For in this way, monks, that grain-eating ox, whether it has gone to the village or to the forest, if it spends much time standing or sitting, would not return to that grain again,
as it recollects that previous touch of the stick. In the same way, monks,
when a bhikkhu’s mind is well-restrained and thoroughly restrained in regard to the six bases of contact, it settles down right within himself, becomes quieted, one-pointed, and concentrated."
“Just as if, monks, a king or a king’s high minister had never before heard the sound of a lute,
and he were to hear the sound of a lute;
he would say this:”
‘O friends, whose sound is this—so intoxicating, so charming, so exhilarating, so stupefying, so binding?
They would say to him:
‘Venerable sir, this is called a lute; it is its sound that is so intoxicating, so charming, so exhilarating, so stupefying, so binding.’”
He might say this:
"Sirs, go and bring that lute for me.
And they would bring that lute to him.
They would say to him:
“Venerable sir, this is that very lute from which this sound comes—so intoxicating, so charming, so exhilarating, so captivating, and so binding.
He would reply:
‘Enough for me, sir, with that lute; bring me that very sound.
They would say to him:
‘Venerable sir, this thing called a lute consists of many components and requires a great assembly of parts.’
"It speaks when undertaken with many constituent parts, namely:
depending on the sounding board, the leather, the neck, the supports, the strings, the plectrum, and the appropriate effort of a person; it is in this way, venerable sir, that this lute [speaks]."
"It is called 'possessing many components' or 'possessing a great mass of components' because it is produced by many components," he said.
He might split that lute into ten or a hundred pieces; having split it into ten or a hundred pieces, he would reduce it to individual fragments.
Having broken it into pieces, one might burn it with fire; having burned it with fire, one might reduce it to ashes.
Having reduced it to ashes, one might scatter it in a great wind or carry it away in a swift-flowing river.
Then someone might say:
‘This thing called a lute, sirs, is truly worthless; it is just some such thing as a lute, yet people here are excessively intoxicated and infatuated with it.
In the same way, monks, a bhikkhu investigates form as far as the extent of form’s range;
he investigates feeling as far as the extent of feeling’s range; he investigates perception as far as the extent of perception’s range; he investigates volitional formations...
To the extent that there is a range for formations, consciousness investigates it; to the extent that there is a range for consciousness, he investigates it.
As he investigates form, to the extent that there is a range for form... as he investigates feeling...
perception... [and so on].
For one who investigates volitional formations … consciousness, as far as the range of consciousness extends—
even that which he has [regarding it] as "I" or "mine" or "I am," that too does not exist for him.”
The Ninth.
Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.247 (SN 35.247, SN 35.206, PTS SN iv 198) 19.
Āsīvisavagga (The Snake Chapter)
The Discourse on the Simile of the Man with Sore Limbs: “Bhikkhus, suppose a man with sore limbs and festering wounds were to enter a thicket of reeds.
Thorns and brambles would prick his feet, and the reed leaves would scratch his limbs.”
"In this way, monks, that man would experience even greater suffering and mental distress on that account.
In the same way, monks, here some bhikkhu, whether gone to the village or gone to the forest, receives criticism:
'This venerable one acts in such a way and behaves in such a way; he is an impure thorn in the side of the village.'"
Having understood that it is a thorn, both restraint and non-restraint should be understood.
And how, monks, does non-restraint come about?

Here, monks, having seen a form with the eye, a monk is obsessed by a pleasing form and feels aversion toward an unpleasing form; he dwells without established mindfulness of the body and with a limited mind.
And he does not understand, as it really is, that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom wherein those arisen evil unwholesome states cease without remainder.
Having heard a sound with the ear...
having smelled an odor with the nose...
Having tasted a flavor with the tongue...
having touched a tangible object with the body...

having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, one becomes attached to agreeable phenomena and feels aversion toward disagreeable phenomena; one dwells without established mindfulness of the body and with a limited mind.
And he does not understand, as it really is, that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom wherein those arisen evil, unwholesome states cease without remainder.
It is just as if, monks, a man were to take six creatures with different domains and different ranges and bind them together with a strong rope;
he would take a snake and bind it with a strong rope.
One would seize a crocodile and bind it with a strong rope;
one would seize a bird and bind it with a strong rope;
one would seize a dog and bind it with a strong rope.
One would take a dog and bind it with a strong rope;
one would take a monkey and bind it with a strong rope.
Having bound them with a strong rope and tied a knot in the middle, one would let them go.
Then, monks, those six creatures, each with its own domain and its own range, would each draw toward its own respective domain and range:
the snake would draw toward it, thinking, "I shall enter the anthill"; the crocodile would draw toward it, thinking, "I shall enter the water";
the bird would draw toward it, thinking, "I shall fly into the sky"; the dog would draw toward it, thinking, "I shall enter the village"; and the jackal...
One might pull [the monkey], thinking, "I will enter the charnel ground," while the monkey pulls, thinking, "I will enter the forest.
When those six creatures, monks, become exhausted and fatigued, then whichever among those creatures is the strongest, the others will follow it, conform to it, and come under its control.

In the same way, monks, for whatever monk body-contemplation has not been developed and frequently practiced, his eye is pulled toward pleasing forms, and unpleasing forms become repulsive... [and so on].
The mind is drawn toward agreeable phenomena, while disagreeable phenomena become repulsive.
In this way, monks, there is non-restraint.
And how, monks, is there restraint?
"Here, monks, having seen a form with the eye, a monk is not intent upon a pleasing form, nor does he feel aversion toward a displeasing form;

he dwells with mindfulness established in the body and with a mind immeasurable, and he understands, as it really is, that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom wherein those arisen evil unwholesome states cease without remainder...
[and so on] ...having tasted a flavor with the tongue..."
Having cognized a phenomenon with the mind, one does not become attached to phenomena that are pleasant, nor does one feel aversion toward phenomena that are unpleasant;

one dwells with mindfulness established in the body and with a mind immeasurable, and one understands as it really is that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom wherein those arisen evil, unwholesome phenomena cease without remainder.
Just as if, monks, a man were to catch six creatures, each with a different range and a different habitat, and bind them together with a strong rope.
One might seize a snake and bind it with a strong rope;
one might seize a crocodile and bind it with a strong rope;
one might seize a bird... [and so on].
Having seized a dog...
having seized a jackal...
having seized a monkey, one would bind it with a strong rope.
"Having bound it with a strong rope, one would tie it to a stout post or stake. Then, monks, those six creatures,
each having its own domain and its own range, would pull toward their respective domains and ranges— the snake would pull, thinking,
'I shall enter the anthill,' and the crocodile would pull, thinking, 'I shall enter the water.'"
A bird might struggle, thinking, “I will fly into the sky”; a dog might struggle, thinking, “I will enter the village”;
a jackal might struggle, thinking, “I will enter the charnel ground”; a monkey might struggle, thinking, “I will enter the forest.
But when those six creatures are exhausted and weary, bhikkhus, they would simply stand, sit, or lie down right there by that same post or pillar.
In the same way, monks, for whatever monk body-contemplation has been developed and cultivated, his eye does not crave for agreeable forms, nor do disagreeable forms become repulsive to him...
[and so on] ...his tongue does not crave for agreeable tastes... [and so on].
The mind does not long for agreeable mental phenomena, nor do disagreeable mental phenomena become repulsive.
In this way, monks, there is restraint.
"A firm post or pillar," monks, is a designation for mindfulness directed to the body.
"Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus:
'Mindfulness directed to the body shall be developed by us, cultivated, made a vehicle, made a foundation, established, consolidated, and properly undertaken.
It is in this way, monks, that you should train yourselves."
The Tenth.
Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.248 (SN 35.248, SN 35.207, PTS SN iv 201) 19.
Āsīvisavagga (The Snake Chapter)
The Discourse on the Sheaf of Barley:
“Bhikkhus, suppose there were a sheaf of barley placed at a crossroads,
and then six men were to come along carrying sickles.”
They might strike that sheaf of barley with six types of hammers.
In this way, monks, that sheaf of barley would be well-beaten when struck with those six types of hammers.
Then a seventh person might come along, carrying a hammer in his hand.
Thus, monks, one would strike that sheaf of barley with a seventh blow of the flail;
for in this way, monks, that sheaf of barley would be better threshed when struck with a seventh blow of the flail.
Even so, monks, the uninstructed worldling is struck in the eye by agreeable and disagreeable forms... [and so on].
One is struck by the tongue through agreeable and disagreeable tastes...
[and so on] ...one is struck by the mind through agreeable and disagreeable mental phenomena.

If, monks, that uninstructed worldling intends for future renewed existence, then that foolish man, monks, becomes even more thoroughly struck down, just like that sheaf of barley being struck by the seventh flail.
“Once upon a time, monks, a battle between the devas and the asuras had been arrayed.
Then, monks, Vepacitti, the lord of the asuras, addressed the asuras:
‘If, dear sirs, when the battle between the devas and the asuras has been arrayed, the asuras should conquer and the devas should be defeated, then—’”
“Bind Sakka, the lord of the gods, with bonds fastened at the neck—the fifth—and bring him before me to Asurapura.
Then, monks, Sakka, the lord of the gods, addressed the Tāvatiṃsa devas:
“If, sirs, when the battle between the devas and the asuras has been joined, the devas should be victorious and the asuras defeated...”
“Bind Vepacitti, lord of the asuras, with bonds fastened around his neck and bring him into my presence at the Sudhamma assembly hall of the devas.
Now, monks, in that battle the devas were victorious and the asuras were defeated.

Then, monks, the Tāvatiṃsa gods bound Vepacitti the lord of the asuras with five bonds, including one around his neck, and brought him into the presence of Sakka, the lord of the devas, to the Sudhamma assembly hall of the devas.
There, monks, Vepacitti the lord of the asuras remained bound by those five bonds, including the one around his neck.
And when it occurred to Vepacitti the lord of the asuras:
"The gods are righteous, O King, while the asuras are unrighteous; I shall go from here to the city of the gods.
Then he perceives himself as freed from the bonds, with the neck as the fifth, and, endowed and possessed of the fivefold divine strands of sensual pleasure, he enjoys them.
And when, monks, it occurs to Vepacitti, the lord of the asuras:
‘The asuras are indeed righteous, while the devas are unrighteous; therefore, I shall go from here to the city of the asuras.
Then he perceives himself bound by fetters with the neck as the fifth, and he is deprived of the fivefold divine strands of sensual pleasure.
So subtle, monks, is the bond of Vepacitti.”
But subtler than that is the bond of Māra.
For, monks, one who conceives is bound by Māra; one who does not conceive is freed from the Evil One.
“I am,” monks, is a conceiving; “This I am” is a conceiving; “I shall be” is a conceiving.
‘I shall not exist’—this is a conceit; ‘I shall be possessed of form’—this is a conceit; ‘I shall be formless’—this is a conceit;
‘I shall be percipient’—this is a conceit; ‘I shall be non-percipient’—this is a conceit;
‘I shall be neither percipient nor non-percipient’—this is a conceit.
“Bhikkhus, conceiving is a disease, conceiving is a tumor, conceiving is a dart.
Therefore, bhikkhus, you should train yourselves thus: ‘We shall dwell with a mind free from conceiving.’”
“‘I am,’ monks, this is a fluctuation; ‘this I am,’ this is a fluctuation; ‘I shall be,’ this is a fluctuation;
‘I shall not be,’ this is a fluctuation; ‘I shall be possessed of form,’ this is a fluctuation; ‘I shall be formless,’ this is a fluctuation; ‘I shall be percipient,’ this is a fluctuation;
‘I shall be non-percipient,’ this is a fluctuation; ‘I shall be neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient’—”
‘They will come to be’—this is a fluctuation.
Monks, fluctuation is a disease, fluctuation is a tumor, fluctuation is a dart.
Therefore, monks, one should dwell with the thought: ‘We shall dwell with a mind that does not fluctuate.’
Thus, monks, you should train yourselves:
"‘I am’—this, monks, is a trembling; ‘This I am’—this is a trembling;
‘I shall be’ … ‘I shall not be’ … ‘I shall be possessed of form’ … ‘I shall be formless’ … ‘I shall be percipient’."
‘I shall be non-percipient’… ‘I shall be neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient’—this is a quivering.
Monks, this quivering is a disease, this quivering is a tumor, this quivering is an arrow.
Therefore, monks, one should dwell with a mind that does not quiver, thinking: “We shall dwell with a mind that does not quiver.”
"Thus, monks, you should train yourselves:
'I am'—this is a proliferation; 'This I am'—this is a proliferation; 'I shall be'... 'I shall not be'...
'I shall be possessed of form'... 'I shall be formless'... 'I shall be percipient'..."
‘I shall be non-percipient’ … ‘I shall be neither percipient nor non-percipient’—this is a proliferation (*papañca*).
Monks, proliferation is a disease, proliferation is a tumor, proliferation is a dart.
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: “We shall dwell with a mind free from proliferation.”
"Thus, monks, you should train yourselves:
'I am'—this is a state of conceit; 'This I am'—this is a state of conceit; 'I shall be'—this is a state of conceit;
'I shall not be'—this is a state of conceit; 'I shall be possessed of form'—this is a state of conceit."
‘I shall be formless’—this is a state of conceit; ‘I shall be percipient’—this is a state of conceit; ‘I shall be non-percipient’—this is a state of conceit;
‘I shall be neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient’—this is a state of conceit.
Monks, what is involved with conceit is a disease, what is involved with conceit is a tumor, what is involved with conceit is a dart.
"Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: 'We shall dwell with a mind that has humbled pride.
The eleventh.
The fourth chapter is the Āsīvisa-vagga (The Snake Chapter).
Its summary verse is:
Āsīviso, ratho, kummo.
Two logs of wood, one leaking; two *kiṃsuka* trees subject to suffering;
a lute, and a sheaf of barley with six living beings.
The fourth fiftieth section in the Chapter on the Six Sense Bases is completed.
Its summary verse is:
"The Destruction of Delight" and the "Method of Sixty."
And the ocean with the serpent;
these forty-five [sections] have been explained among the Nipātas.
The Connected Discourses on the Six Sense Bases are complete.
